ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Te Puke Otara Community Centre
1. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Recreation and Sport: Has he read the
Auckland Star of 16 November 1977, which reports the management committee chairman of
the Te Puke Otara Community Centre, Mr Garfield Johnson, as having said, "The
Government's decision to stop paying two cleaners at the Te Puke Otara Community Centre
could be the 'straw that breaks the camel's back' ", and furthermore stating that the centre
will have to close unless it can get some money from the Government, and, if so, what action
is the Government taking to ensure that this vital social and community asset is not closed?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Recreation and Sport): Mr Johnson has very recently
told me that the centre's main need is for help towards the salary of its manager. He is paid
from the discretionary staffing allowances made available to two local colleges. I am advised
that the Department of Education is looking into the continuation of such an arrangement.
Cleaners have been employed under the special work scheme on a short-term basis pending
their finding regular employment. This arrangement has already been extended to the end of
January. I have been advised that the centre is free to discuss some further extension of this
period with the Manukau office of the Department of Labour should this be needed.
Mr Isbey: Does this mean that if the management committee of the Te Puke Otara
Community Centre discusses the position with the Department of Labour a scheme will be
evolved so that cleaners can continue in employment next year?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: The whole basis of the special work scheme is that the jobs are of
a temporary nature. If an approach is made to the Department of Labour a sympathetic
hearing will be given to the application.
Mr Isbey: What about an assurance?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Surely the member realises that as Minister of Internal Affairs I
cannot give an assurance concerning another department. The information I have is that a
very sympathetic hearing will be given to the application.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Armed Forces Joint Exercises
2. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Defence: Can he indicate
those joint exercises in which the armed forces will be associated with units of Australian and
American defence forces in the next 6 months?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): Four joint exercises are planned for
the next 6 months, two in Australia, one in Hawaii, and one being hosted by New Zealand.

Rural Bank Loans to Fishermen
3. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), asked the
Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation: How many fishermen
have received corporation assistance, and what is the average amount of these loans?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Acting Minister in
Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation. Details of loans made to fishermen,
including companies, for the purpose of vessel purchase, re-engineering of vessels, refinance
of vessels, for fishing gear and equipment, improvements to vessels, flake ice plants and cool
stores, and for the initial development costs of rock oyster and mussel farms are as follows:
for the year ended 31 March 1977, 36 loans totalling $3.3 million, with an average loan of
$91,666; and for the period 1 April 1977 to 8 November 1977, 55 loans totalling $4.68
million, with an average loan of $85,000.
Mr Courtney: How many loans were for fishing vessels?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The loans were for catching fish, not for fishing vessels. Loans are
often made by the Rural Bank for fish processing facilities. The suspensory loans are outside
the totals I have given.

Arapawa Island Goats
5. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: Has he any information
to suggest that the goats on Arapawa Island are genetically similar to the "rare old English
breed" of goat which is now extinct in Britain?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I do not know whether they are all extinct,
actually. It has been claimed that the feral goats inhabiting Arapawa Island are the
descendants of an old English breed of goat brought to New Zealand by Captain James
Cook, but there is no firm evidence to confirm this assertion. From information supplied by
the Rare Breeds Survival Trust of England, it is known that if the original Arapawa goats
were liberated by Captain Cook they probably would have been a native British breed.
These goats have now been largely supplanted by modern milking breeds, although a few
still remain in the British Isles. It is possible that the Arapawa goats are descended from the
native British goat, but the history of these animals is not so precisely known, and therefore
any claim of uniqueness can neither be rejected nor upheld.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that the mirth of Opposition members is related
to the closeness of the question to their own circumstances?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I cannot allow that sort of comment. The honourable

member will withdraw it.
Dr Shearer: I withdraw.
Mr Wetere: What research is being done by the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research to allay the claims the Minister alluded to, that the goats on Arapawa Island are of
the breed he mentioned?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Research is taking place. The control plan for the goats has been
deferred by 1 year. In the intervening period approximately 150 goats have been transferred
from Arapawa Island to Banks Peninsula. In the meantime, decisions will have to be made
by the Forest Service in consultation with the Maritime Park Board on the question of to
what degree the remaining goat numbers must be reduced, or whether they should be
eliminated.

Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot answer that question precisely, but I know that members
opposite would be concerned that there are some endangered species around.

Prime Minister's Staff-American Trip
6. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Prime Minister: In view of his reply to
my question of 15 November relating to his trip to North America, in which he stated that
the estimated expense of sending Mr Galvin to Washington was $1,655, and of Mr Plimmer
$2,900, and as the first-class fare including travel tax to Washington is $2,697.20, and to Los
Angeles is $2,268.20, are hotel or other expenses not included or has some error been made,
and, if so, what error?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): No error has been made. The
honourable member's question of 15 November asked for an estimated cost of staff
accompanying the Prime Minister to North America. This was given. However, after
accompanying the Prime Minister on the Washington leg of his visit, Mr Galvin took the
opportunity to visit Canada as Chairman of the New Zealand Intelligence Council. Thus, the
expenses incurred by Mr Galvin in Canada, and his return air fare, are not included in the
cost estimate for the Prime Minister's visit.
Mr Prebble: Does the Acting Prime Minister know the extra expenses that Mr Galvin
must have incurred, unless he walked home?
Hon. T. F. Gill: A point of order, Mr Speaker. The supplementary question suggests
that the Acting Prime Minister gave an incorrect answer. The procedures of the House
require a back-bencher, however immature and inexperienced, to accept an answer by a
Minister as being factual, and not to be questioned.
Mr Prebble: Mr Speaker, I wish to put to you very strongly that a back-bencher has as
much right to have a question answered as any Minister, no matter how self-important he
may think he is. [Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! We will have a discussion on the point of order raised,
and I remind honourable members that I will hear it without the assistance of those who wish
to interrupt the member I have called. Perhaps I could remind honourable members that
there are doors round here that we might invite them to go through temporarily if they are
unable to restrain themselves while we are discussing this point of order.
Mr Prebble: While I am prepared to admit it is debatable whether Mr Galvin's air fare
back from Washington can be included, I wish to assure the Acting Prime Minister that when
I asked my question I expected the air fare both ways to be included, and I should like to
know Mr Galvin's total expenses for the American trip.
Mr Birch: The point of order raised by my colleague is simply that the honourable
member asking the supplementary question was implying that the answer that had been
given by the Acting Prime Minister was in error. The honourable member should know that

Massey University-TV Recording Studios
7. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Education: Why does
Massey University need two fully equipped TV recording studios plus one fully equipped
mobile TV recording studio, and what are the individual costs of each of the three TV
recording studios?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Massey University has informed me that
it does not have two fully equipped TV recording studios, and one mobile studio as such. It
does have a range of selected TV recording equipment, which is deployed over 10 locations
on the campus to meet a wide variety of teaching and research needs. One location has been
specifically designed as a studio. The remainder are general purpose spaces that have had
limited TV facilities installed. Some equipment is also installed in a caravan, which is taken
out to schools for the video recording of school work. The total cost of the equipment in use
was $115,000.
Mr Lithgow: Is it usual for universities to have this sort of TV recording equipment and
facilities?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, it is. To give the honourable member an idea, the
agricultural and horticultural faculty has a studio, the education faculty has a laboratory, the
psychology department has a studio, and the veterinary and social science faculties have
similar equipment. This sort of facility is being used increasingly in secondary schools. A
very good example is Rongotai College, where a television camera is used to enable pupils to
see deformities and other physical characteristics that might be revealed while they are
taking remedial exercises. The equipment has a very useful and widespread purpose.
Mr Marshall: Does the Minister intend to scrutinise more closely expenditure for such
equipment in universities?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The University Grants Committee very carefully scrutinises,
evaluates, and audits, the setting up of such equipment in a university department or faculty
before a grant is finally made. One has to realise that these research tools are not cheap.
Mr Lithgow: Is it fair to say that in future there will be further expenditure on TV
equipment in universities?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Yes, I think that in future all tertiary and secondary schools will
have some form of electronic equipment, probably television or its equivalent.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

School Leavers-Subsidised Apprenticeships
8. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he received a
letter from the Hokianga - Bay of Islands development committee on a subsidised appren-
ticeship scheme for school leavers, and, in view of the increasing difficulties school leavers
are having in finding suitable work, will he ensure that the proposal receives prompt and
favourable consideration?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I have received a letter from the Hokianga-
Bay of Islands development committee suggesting that the Government subsidise appren-
tices' wages to encourage eligible employers to take on more apprentices. As the level of
work available in each industry, rather than the wages payable to apprentices, is the main
determinant of the number of new apprenticeship contracts, there is no certainty that the
suggested subsidy would result in an increase in the number of apprenticeships available for
school leavers. Furthermore, because of the holiday season and the normal recruitment
period, it will not be possible until well into February to ascertain the exact number of young
people who actually leave school and do not obtain jobs. Should the situation at that time
require the implementation of further measures to provide employment for school leavers I
will ensure that the suggestion is given consideration.
Mr Isbey: Will the Minister confirm that it is preferable to pay the school leavers and
employers who want to have them as apprentices a subsidy, rather than have the school
leavers on the dole?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: That could well be the case at a later date, and if the member
cares to consult me-as the member for Northern Maori did on a question he asked last
week-I will indicate why it is not advisable to give a more detailed answer in the House
tonight.
Mr H. N. Austin: Will the Minister confirm that he has had extensive discussions with
the member for Hobson on this subject, and that those full and frank discussions took place
before he gave his decision?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Yes, the member for Hobson had seen me to express concern,
particularly for the outlying areas. I appreciate the difficulties in that part of his electorate
that forms Hokianga.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Was the member for Hobson satisfied with the Minister's decision
not to take any action at this time?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, but he accepted the reasoning behind it.
Mr Elliott: Can the Minister confirm that, although that scheme did not go ahead, more
than 150 young people in Northland have been placed in employment through the private
subsidy employment scheme, and that many of those young people were in the area of the
member for Hobson?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is well beyond the scope of the original question or any
of the answers.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Oil Exploration, Great South Basin
9. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), asked the
Minister of Energy Resources: Can he indicate what quantities and volumes or combinations
of quantities and volumes of oil, condensate, or gas would constitute an economic productive
field if discovered more than 100 miles off shore in the region of the Great South Basin?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): It is not possible to give a precise
answer to this question as no oilfield or gasfield has been developed in the depth of water in
which Kawau, for example, is being drilled. Present indications are that for an oilfield to be
economic it would need to be of a similar size to the larger North Sea fields, which have daily
flow rates of more than 300 000 barrels. The structures at present being drilled have this
potential. At this stage, in terms of current technology, it is not considered that a gasfield or
a gas-condensate field would be economic to develop.
Mr W. R. Austin: While it is correct, as the Minister states, that a gasfield or a gas-
condensate field would not be an economic development at this stage, would it not have a
potential in combination with the very large coal deposits on the Southland plains?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: No, there are technological problems in developing any potential gas
that is in the Great South Basin. I gather that there would be even greater technological
problems in developing coal in the Great South Basin, because we must remember it is at
least 2200 ft under water, and below that under a considerable depth of the structure of the

earth. However, I do not doubt that in the fullness of time technology will overcome the
problems, even if well into the future. I remind members that the Russians are at present

Mr W. R. Austin: I am sorry, but I think the Minister may have misunderstood the
question. I was talking about bringing the gas ashore to combine with oil for a possible liquid
fuel industry.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The question still implies that it is technically and financially or
economically possible to bring the gas ashore, and that is the question that has not yet been
answered at the present stage of technology. In fact, I should like to advise members that in a
discussion with one of the Hunt oil company executives in my office not very long ago he
described the problems in the Great South Basin as being at the rough end of technology,
and that is the present situation.

Regional Development-Plant Depreciation Rates
11. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland
Revenue Department: Has he seen the report in the two Dunedin newspapers of 12
November in which the Labour candidate for Dunedin North is reported as advocating
special depreciation rates for plant and machinery as part of regional development policy,
and can he confirm that these are in being as a result of the 1976 National Government
Budget?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department):
Yes, I have read the reports, and find them rather surprising. In 1976 the Government
enacted legislation providing for a number of investment allowances specifically designed to
encourage regional investment. These were: the regional development allowance of up to 20
percent; the export production allowance of up to 20 percent; the industry development
allowance of up to 40 percent; and the farming and fishing allowance of 40 percent. These
investment allowances, which are of course in addition to the first-year depreciation
allowance of 25 percent, have the effect that the overall write-off for taxation purposes over
the life of the plant and machinery may amount to more than its cost price. I should have
thought it would be difficult to beat that as an example of incentives for regional develop-
ment.
Richard Walls: Can the Minister confirm that as a result of the Budget action a typical
investment of say $50,000 in a first-year manufacturing company in Dunedin or any other
high-priority regional development area would have a tax saving of $4,500 over a similar
company established in Auckland or Wellington?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I hope I understood that question correctly, but I should
think that is basically correct. On my understanding, the incentives are designed to ensure
that there is a major incentive for the man in Dunedin. I would need to look at the figures in
more detail to be certain, but I think that that would be correct.
Mr MacDonell: As all those incentives for regional development are available, can the
Minister say why they are not working?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am absolutely certain that, in terms of the economic
situation, they are working as well as they can. I could give the honourable member
examples, if he does not know of any himself.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: A supplementary question, Mr Speaker.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I think we will press on. Question 12.

Maori Pre-Apprenticeship Courses
12. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the
Minister of Education: What provisions are there to ensure that tutors for the Maori pre-
apprenticeship courses are able to understand and communicate easily with their students,
both Maori and Polynesian?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): In selecting tutors for the courses every
endeavour is made to ensure that background and personal qualities indicate not only
teaching ability but also an empathy which will bring about the best response from students.
Tutors and course supervisors in the field have always taken a special interest in the trainees,
and there are notable instances of tutor involvement in and recognition of extramural
activities such as hangis and tramping trips. Trade training officers from the Department of
Maori Affairs pay frequent visits to the institute to discuss progress and, where necessary, to
advise tutors. The Vocational Training Council Polynesian advisory officers and a Samoan
officer from the Industrial Training Service work closely with the institutes.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Native Plants Protection Act
13. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Lands: Are there any plans to
review the Native Plants Protection Act 1934?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): There are numerous statutes such as the
Reserves and Domains Act, the National Parks Act, the Land Act, the Trespass Act, the
Police Offences Act, and the Forests Act which, in addition to the Native Plants Protection
Act 1934, give a measure of protection to native flora. A degree of protection is also
suggested in the draft provisions of the Town and Country Planning Bill. The Nature
Conservation Council is preparing a submission to me on the question of a review of the 1934
legislation and, if the present legislation requires revision, particularly in so far as
endangered plants are concerned, this will be undertaken.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Students-Vacation Employment
15. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Labour: How many applica-
tions have been received from students seeking to take advantage of the vacation employ-
ment scheme?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As no detailed classification is made of
those enrolling for work with the Department of Labour's employment service I am unable
to tell the member how many students have applied for work as a result of the introduction
of the student community service programme. I can, however, advise students who have not
been able to obtain vacation employment, and wish to participate in this scheme, to enrol at
their nearest employment service office.
Mr Lange: Have the district offices of the Department of Labour now received the data
necessary to enrol such applicants?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot answer for every office, but certainly the main offices
have the required information. I know that the vast majority of offices have the material
relating to the farm employment scheme because I have seen results flowing in from that. I
should be very disappointed if the offices did not have the data for the community service
scheme.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the Minister take steps to ensure that the Auckland office, which
has not yet received details of the Government's proposal, does receive the data as soon as
possible so that those interested can take full advantage of the scheme?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The difficulty about the question arises from the different
schemes, and here I must refer to the supplementary question asked by the member for
Mangere. The farm scheme is relatively simple, because you are dealing with a single
employer asking for one or two employees. With the community scheme the main difficulty
is to have the scheme approved in total, and in such community schemes the Minister of
Internal Affairs plays a key role. The Auckland office has the basic details and will be
recording any inquiries from youths, particularly university students.
Mr Wellington: Since the scheme involves local authorities to a great extent, can the
Minister confirm that the information relating to the schemes has already been dispatched to
them?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I should like a definition of "them" before I answer that
question. Most of the local communities that could qualify should be aware of the position
either through press releases or through information sent out from the department. One or
two may not be aware. I know of two that did not realise they could have qualified if they
had lodged an application.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Education-School Library Service
16. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui), on behalf of Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), asked the
Minister of Education: What steps is the school library service taking to provide for the
increasing book needs of younger pupils under the recently introduced ERIC scheme?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Book loans to infant classes are
provided by the School Library Service according to the book stock and staff resources of
each district office. No significant increase in demand has resulted from the recently
introduced ERIC scheme, and no formal request for extra provision has been made to the
School Library Service by the Department of Education.
Mr Marshall: If as the result of further experience with the ERIC scheme an increase in
demand becomes evident, will the Minister indicate what his response might be?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I think there may be a slight misunderstanding about what this
scheme is. The expression ERIC stands for early reading inservice courses training. It is an
audio visual inservice course for early reading which has been developed and evaluated by a
team set up in the Department of Education in Auckland. The course is being made
available to other districts. It is essentially a voluntary course and is designed to prevent
failure in learning to read, particularly for those in their early years of school. It is essentially
a course to assist teachers and to enable children to read better and to get through any
reading difficulties they may have. It is not likely that as a result of the course there will be an
upsurge in interest or a requirement for further books. If there is an increase in demand we
will certainly meet it.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Transport Distance Charge-Bus Services
17. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Transport: How will privately
and publicly owned commuter bus transport services be affected by the introduction of the
heavy transport distance tax as from next April?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The heavy motor vehicle distance
charge will apply to both privately and publicly owned commuter bus transport services as
from 1 April next year. Under the new scheme, operators will not be required to pay mileage
tax for diesel vehicles and all petrol tax will be refunded. However, the Government
recognises there may be a need for some form of special assistance to urban public passenger
transport operators, and officials are presently preparing a report for the Government's
consideration.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: When will the report be made public?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I cannot give the exact date. It has already been indicated
that next year a council will take over this responsibility. In the meantime, the Government
will carry the responsibility. At the moment I am unable to answer the question.

Christchurch Aged People's Welfare Council
18. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: In view of the
report in the Christchurch Star of 9 November of his statement at the International Senior
Citizens Congress that, "more Government aid for the elderly was being considered", what
action is he prepared to take to help the Christchurch Aged People's Welfare Council
overcome its present financial difficulties?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The report in the Christchurch Star
referred to the statement in my speech that the Government accepted that the proper role of
residential accommodation provided by both the private sector and charitable bodies in this
country should be to cater for the more dependent elderly person. I said that to encourage
this approach the Government had in mind the possibility of some subsidy assistance relating
to the level of staffing required in a residential home caring for the dependent elderly. This
proposal is being examined by the Cabinet committee on social affairs. I have had
discussions recently with the National Old People's Welfare Council about the financial
position of the organisation. I appreciate the most useful role the council plays in promoting
and advancing the welfare of old people in New Zealand, and I am investigating fully its
request for assistance.
Miss Dewe: Could the Minister say whether he has received any representations from
the Christchurch Aged People's Welfare Council regarding its financial position, and, if so,
has he made any grants?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I have no record of any representations being made, either
directly by the Christchurch Aged People's Welfare Council or by the national body on
behalf of the council. However, a report in the Evening Post of 11 August stated that a grant
of $15,000 had been made to the Christchurch Aged People's Welfare Council from Lottery
Board profits.

claims section is spent handling accident compensation claims. The above proportion of time
employed in processing accident compensation claims does not include the executive time of
the manager or the time of staff such as the mail clerk and the telephone operator, whose
duties embrace the whole work of the branch.

Colquhoun Park Kindergarten, Milson
3. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What chance is there of
Government financial support being made available to the kindergarten now established at
the Colquhoun Park pavilion at Milson?


## p. 4686 (#122) ###########################################

4686
23 November
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Until the Colquhoun Park
kindergarten can be provided with its own building under the Government subsidy scheme
for free kindergartens, it has been established as a private kindergarten registered and
licensed by the Department of Social Welfare under the Child Care Centre Regulations
1960. This action has been taken by the Manawatu Free Kindergarten Association to provide
an interim service until it is possible to erect a second recognised free kindergarten to serve
the Milson district. Established policy, as agreed with the New Zealand Free Kindergarten
Union, provides for Government financial support to be limited to free kindergartens
established in purpose-designed buildings or, in a very few cases, in premises where the
kindergarten has sole use of the buildings and the kindergarten association has control of the
building by means of a lease for at least 10 years. The Colquhoun Park pavilion at Milson has
been rented by the Manawatu Free Kindergarten Association on a yearly tenancy basis. As
this type of rental does not meet the present criteria for recognition as an established
kindergarten, no Government financial support can be made available. A site for pre-school
purposes is to be provided on the future primary school site in Milson. When the site
purchase is finalised and the kindergarten association has met the criteria on the number of
children and finance available to meet its share of the cost, Government subsidy or loan
assistance normally available in respect of a free kindergarten building and equipment costs
will be available to the proposed Milson No. 2 kindergarten. My department is considering
ways in which assistance might be provided through the Education vote to kindergarten
associations which are providing services such as that now offered through the Colquhoun
Park kindergarten.
(4/11/77)
Rastus Burn Skifield
4. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Lands: (1) What factors did
the Land Settlement Board take into consideration before approving the Mount Cook and
Southern Lakes Tourist Company's proposal to build a skifield in the Rastus Burn; (2) for
what reasons did the board feel it was necessary to disregard the Department of Lands and
Survey's Remarkable and Hector Mountains management study findings and recommenda-
tions; and (3) why was it reported that stringent safeguards during the construction of the
road and skifield would be released on 5 October when this announcement has not yet been
made?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: (1) The Land Settlement Board, in
arriving at its decision to agree in principle to the establishment of a skifield in the Rastus
Burn by the Mount Cook and Southern Lakes Tourist Co., took into account all information
and evidence available to it, including: (a) the management study produced by the Depart-
ment of Lands and Survey; (b) an environmental impact report prepared by the Mount Cook
and Southern Lakes Tourist Co. and audited by the Commission for the Environment; (c) a
further report prepared by the Mount Cook and Southern Lakes Tourist Co.; and (d)
submissions received from the general public. A subcommittee of the board also inspected
the area on the ground, and in addition to the above reports the following points were also
taken into account by the board: (a) the overall need for further alpine tourist and skifield
facilities on Crown land within the southern lakes region; (b) the intrinsic suitability of the
Rastus Burn basin for development as a skifield; (c) other potential recreational uses and
water and soil conservation requirements in the area; and (d) any potentially viable skifield
or access alternatives, e.g., development in the Doolans Creek and/or access over Coal Pit
saddle from Gibbston. (2) The Land Settlement Board did not disregard the recommenda-
tions of the management study prepared by the Department of Lands and Survey. This
report was only one of several reports that were considered by the board in reaching its
decision. (3) While it is correct that it was stated that the conditions of allocation would be
fixed at the October meeting of the board, this has not proved possible because the input by
other interested parties was not available. Until such time as these are available the board is
not in a position to fix the terms and conditions of the allocation to the company.
(4/11/77)
Overseas Students
5. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Education: (1) Is Government
policy towards private overseas students to be reviewed for next year; (2) how many students


## p. 4687 (#123) ###########################################

23 November
4687
Questions and Replies
will be accepted next year, and from which countries; and (3) how many students have been
approved to offset the cut of 46 percent in the number of first-year private overseas students,
and which countries are they from?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: (1) Government policy towards
private overseas students is under continuous review but no special exercise is contemplated
for next year. Early in 1976 the Government decided on a limitation of the intake of first-
year Malaysian students covering the next 2 years, and this policy has another year to run.
(2) The quotas for the number of private overseas students (except Malaysians) to be
admitted is determined annually by the universities. Not all these quotas have been notified
as yet, so that it is not possible to supply a total at this stage. These quotas are by faculty in
each university and not by country or origin. Qualified students fill the places in the
particular faculties according to academic merit. Numbers by country of origin cannot
therefore be known in advance. (3) As indicated in my answer to the previous questions, the
only quota by country of origin is for Malaysians. It was this group that was cut by 46
percent, not the total number. It is expected that the numbers from the other countries for
which there are no quotas will gradually rise, but in addition the Government is offering
places for students from Middle East countries. It is hoped that there will be 12 each from
Iran and Iraq next year, with increasing numbers later.

State Tenants-Rent Arrears
15. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: What is the latest
percentage of State tenants in arrears of rent, and how does this compare with December
1976 when the then Minister promised that a firmer line would be taken with defaulters?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: At 7 October 1977, 6.29 percent
of corporation tenants were in arrears of rent compared with 7.14 percent at 3 December
1976. This is a reduction of the number of tenants in arrears from 4030 at 3 December 1976
to 3610 at 7 October 1977. In areas where the effort has been more concentrated the results
have been even more satisfactory. For example, in Otara the percentage has dropped from
14.27 to 11.69 in the same period, the total amount in arrears has been reduced from $56,317
to $38,402, and the number of those who are more than $250 overdue has declined from 60
to 26.

(16/11/77)
ORAL QUESTIONS
Transferred as Written Questions under S.O. 82
Teachers' Appointment Rights
29. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the
widespread concern about falling rolls in secondary schools and the effect of this on
displaced teachers, what measures is he taking to ensure that the priority of appointment
rights held by displaced teachers is safeguarded?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Regulation 81 (1) of the Education
(Assessment, Classification, and Appointment) Regulations 1976 provides that an applicant
for appointment to a full-time permanent teaching position in a State secondary school is
entitled to be appointed to that position if he produces evidence in his application that he has
lost or is about to lose his position by reason of a fall in the attendance of the school or
through the reorganisation of the school. The only exceptions to this priority right of
appointment are where some other applicant is appointed on the same ground or where the
controlling authority has satisfied the Minister that the applicant with the priority right is not
suitable for appointment. This priority right of appointment is, therefore, provided by
regulation and is enforceable through the courts.
(4/11/77)
New Zealand Atlas
30. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Lands: What plans have been
made to use the collective expertise of the staff assembled within his department for the
preparation of the New Zealand Atlas?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The New Zealand Atlas was published by
the Government Printer on 22 March 1976. It is intended that the publication remain in print
for up to 10 years. Adequate stocks are held by the Government Printer. No staff of my
department is currently engaged on the New Zealand Atlas, although varying staff numbers,
up to a maximum of eight, were engaged on the project between November 1971 and August
1975. Quite separately, there is a proposal from the National Committee for Geography to
the Royal Society of New Zealand for a National Atlas. This is based on a comprehensive
joint report by the New Zealand Geographical Society and the New Zealand Cartographic
Society. This proposal, submitted to the Minister of Science of the last Government and
referred by him to the then Minister of Lands for consideration by the New Zealand Atlas
Committee, envisages a continuing production of a much more comprehensive publication
than the New Zealand Atlas. Although the proposal is under investigation in the Depart-
ment of Lands and Survey, the study does not have a high priority because of the need in the
present economic situation and with a reducing staff ceiling to concentrate available staff on
mapping projects of more immediate national importance.

superannuation, plus $10 Post Office Savings Bank interest, which the Minister described as
"a private income"?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: As the honourable member

approach their member of Parliament seeking special consideration. This person will, of
course, like all other national superannuitants, receive in August 1978 a substantial increase
in his income when national superannuation is to be based on 80 percent of the average
ordinary-time wage instead of the present 70 percent.

Forestry Encouragement Scheme-Planting of Special-purpose Species
40. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Forests: What encouragement is
given forestry encouragement grantees to diversify their planting into species that will
provide special-purpose timbers?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied on behalf of the Minister of Forests:
The forestry encouragement grants scheme is available to all landholders who wish to
undertake afforestation with any commercial species. Every project is considered on its
merits, and the only limitations imposed are the suitability of site and location for utilising
the material grown. Courses and field days are held for those interested in special-purpose
species, and the New Zealand Farm Forestry Association is actively supporting trials into
alternative shelter and production species. Landowners are becoming more aware of special-
use species, and recent applications approved show a growing preference for alternative
species where quality growing sites are available. A survey is being undertaken to ascertain
the most suitable special-purpose species for specific districts, and the results will be made
known to intending grantees to encourage diversification in the future.

Pacific Island workers and Industrial Relations Act
41. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Immigration: Has his department taken
any steps to inform workers from the Pacific, either before or after arrival, of their
obligations as employees under the Industrial Relations Act and the awards and agreements
made under it?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: Under the memoranda of understand-
ing concerning the official work permit scheme, which was agreed between the New Zealand
Government and the Governments of Fiji, Tonga, and Western Samoa, it is the responsibil-
ity of the Island Governments to select workers and to provide them with pre-departure
instruction on working and living conditions in New Zealand, and on union membership,
and to improve where necessary their ability to commmunicate in English on arrival.
Suitable information on such matters is available to the Island Governments through the
New Zealand high commissions in Suva, Nuku'alofa, and Apia. Where employers seek
authority to bring workers to New Zealand under the official work permit scheme they are
advised that they have a responsibility to inform workers of their rights and obligations.
After arrival in New Zealand, workers from the Pacific have access to the same sources of
information on these matters as all New Zealand workers.

Farming Investment and Export-earning Capacity
46. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What estimated effect
will the recent economic measures announced in the mini-Budget have on farm investment
levels and thus the export-earning capacity of the farming industry?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture) replied on behalf of the Minister
of Agriculture: In view of the many variables involved, and the ongoing nature of some of
the agriculture measures announced in the recent economic statement, it is not possible to
quantify accurately their impact on the export-earning capacity of the farm sector. However,
as the assistance has been directed towards furthering farm development and investment on
the one hand, $20 million, and encouraging the additional processing of New Zealand's
primary exports on the other, $10 million per annum, it is considered that the total sum made
available to agriculture is likely to lift the export-earning capacity of the sector by at least $30
million within a 3-year period. Beyond this pay-back period, of course, there will be a
continuing flow of export income which represents profit on the nation's investment.

which the honourable member refers were reported the Acting Prime Minister said that the
action of the South African Government in banning newspapers and black organisations and
detaining key leaders in the black consciousness movement was totally repugnant to the New
Zealand Government. He went on to say that they did little to endear it to New Zealand or
the rest of the world, and referred to my statement on the general debate at the thirty-second
session of the United Nations General Assembly. Media reports I have seen indicate that
that statement did not pass unnoticed in South Africa, and I have no doubt that the same is
true of the Acting Prime Minister's comments.
(4/11/77)
Economy-International Factors
54. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Finance: What major factors in the
international economy persuaded him to consider the various measures contained in the
mini-Budget?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Finance: "As I said in my statement to the House on 28 October 1977 the present state of the
world economy does not offer us much hope for a rapid growth in the sales of our exports.
The major economies are growing more slowly than last year. Some economies, such as
West Germany, have experienced no growth at all in the mid-1977 period. While some
Governments have introduced or are going to introduce reflationary measures, these do not
appear to be substantial enough to offer us any hope of a significant upturn in international
trade. It was in this context that the economic package was determined."
(4/11/77)

Coromandel Peninsula-Foreshore Reserves and Farm Parks
62. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Lands: What area of land has been
set aside as foreshore reserves on the Coromandel Peninsula, and what is the total area of
farm land now purchased and established as farm parks?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The process of setting aside coastal
reserves on the Coromandel Peninsula has been going on from the earliest days of settlement
in New Zealand, but no cumulative record of reserve areas has been maintained. The coastal
survey of 1968 confirmed that much of the outstandingly scenic coastline and many of the
beaches were being considered for housing subdivisions, and that if some of these areas were
to be reserved for posterity early action was required. Since the special fund for the purchase
of reserves was established in 1972, 3840 hectares have been reserved on the Coromandel
coastline, including 3696 hectares in farm parks.

any suitably qualified women who might be willing to accept appointment as magistrates.
The appointment of judges is a matter for the Attorney-General. The member will
appreciate, however, that the field is limited, because there are relatively few women in
private legal practice.

RNZAF-Retention of Dakota
67. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Defence: What consideration
can be given to the retention of one RNZAF Dakota to be held at an RNZAF air base for
historical purposes?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence) replied: When it was decided to
withdraw the six Dakotas from RNZAF service consideration was given to retaining one for
historical purposes, particularly as an RNZAF Historical Centre has recently been estab-
lished. However, while appreciating the Dakota's long and faithful service to the RNZAF
and therefore its part in military aviation in New Zealand, its most significant role in this
country was in the field of civil aviation. This has been appropriately recognised by the
inclusion of a Dakota in the aircraft display at the Museum of Transport and Technology,
Auckland. With this in mind, and in the knowledge that the ex RNZAF Dakotas have a not
inconsiderable commercial value, it was decided to dispose of them through the Government
Stores Board.

what action the Minister of Labour had taken during the recent costly union dispute at the

Government is to refrain from interfering in domestic union disputes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Yes, I can confirm that the disruption

indeed the position could have deteriorated quite significantly. However, the Government is

Agriculture: On 8 November 1977-2 days ago-the value of the pound sterling against the
New Zealand dollar was about 1 percent greater than on 28 October 1977 when its recent
movements against the United States dollar commenced. If this 1 percent appreciation were
maintained it could result in about a 1.3c a kilogram increase in the PM lamb schedule at

markets.

121. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Are his

Industrial Unions-Unqualified Preference Ballots
122. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the fact that the
Industrial Relations Act requires unqualified preference ballots to be conducted by awards
rather than unions and that few unions with more than one award have rolls by award, so
that in most cases it will be necessary for the Department of Labour to compile new rolls for
each award, how long does he estimate it will take to ballot the entire New Zealand labour
force?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Although it is true that a great number
of unions are covered by more than one award or industrial agreement the Industrial
Relations Act requires that the unions shall supply the registrar with a list containing the
names and postal addresses of those people entitled to vote. It is not, therefore, true to say
that it will be necessary for the department to compile new rolls. The department must be
satisfied that the list provided by the union is as complete as possible. If it is not satisfied
other means, such as newspaper advertisements, will be used. It is not possible to say
precisely how long it will take to conduct all of the ballots, but, as has been previously stated
in the Government's policy, it will take a number of years.

movement accrues to freezing workers as a result of the freezing works conciliation, which is

agreement. The question of any further general wage adjustment flowing from the freezing
workers' negotiations remains open, but I can inform the House that the industry and
Federated Farmers have had what seems to be satisfactory talks about longer-term effects on
killing charges.

Penal Institutions and Rehabilitative Programmes for Women
154. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Justice: What prisons, deten-
tion centres, borstals, and rehabilitative programmes for women are there in New Zealand?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): At present there is one women's prison in
Christchurch, Arohata Women's Borstal Institution near Wellington, and one female
periodic detention centre in Queen Mary Avenue, Auckland. There is also a small remand
unit attached to Mt. Eden Prison for females remanded from the Auckland courts or serving
very short sentences. Negotiations are in progress for the purchase of a property in Auckland
to provide a further prison for women serving longer sentences. A pre-release hostel in
Auckland will be available for women and girls from Arohata borstal and Christchurch
women's prison from January of next year.
Rehabilitation efforts for women have largely been concentrated on educational measures
and the implementation and expansion of release to work and community involvement
programmes. Full-time teachers are employed at Christchurch women's prison and Arohata
borstal. Other part-time specialist assistance is available in the psychiatric and psychological
fields. The establishment in 1975 of the Auckland non-residential periodic detention centre
for women provides the courts with an alternative to imprisonment, enabling some female
offenders to remain within the community instead of being separated from their families
and/or employment. In areas where periodic detention is not available, probation with
community work often provides a suitable alternative to incarceration.

experience of Cabinet procedure will know, substantial delays are incurred in bringing to
charge expenditure on ministerial overseas travel. Indeed, it is anticipated that the 1978-79
estimates will include expenses of Labour Ministers for their 1975 travel. As a result, and
because it is impossible to include an allowance for specific travel items not yet charged due

available through the Department of Education towards the cost of batteries, new ear
moulds, repairs, and maintenance of aids for children enrolled in special schools and classes
for the deaf."

Violence and Lawlessness-Police Strength
171. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Police: As the latest
police survey revealed a need for 483 additional uniformed officers and civilian staff, and
since the Government has granted approval for only 280, will he, in view of the mounting
violence and lawlessness, now seek approval for a further 203, plus transport and other
needs, so that the police can operate with maximum effectiveness?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): My department is directing its attention
towards the recruitment of the additional 280 staff recently approved by the Government,
and it is anticipated that the increased staff establishment will be attained towards the end of
the current financial year. Due to problems associated with the recruitment and training of
this number of staff it would not be possible to increase the establishment further before 31
March 1978. For example, in January 1978 the largest recruit wing for some years, totalling
150 constables, will enter the Police College. This is the maximum number that can be
comfortably handled at any one time, bearing in mind the accommodation, administration,
and logistic requirements of such an exercise.

Marsden Point Refinery-Refining Fee
173. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is it
intended that the refining fee charged at the Marsden Point refinery will be increased when
the refinery is expanded, and, if so, what effect will this have on petrol prices?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): It is intended that the
refining fee charged at the Marsden Point refinery will be increased when the refinery is
expanded, but the fee increase is expected to be more than offset by the reduced costs of
petroleum products when the expansion comes on stream. Therefore, in the longer term,
petrol prices should be lower with the expanded refinery than without it.
(16/11/77)
Land-use Policy
174. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Lands: What progress is being
made towards the development of a comprehensive land-use policy for New Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The development of comprehensive land-use
policies for New Zealand depends on the availabilty of adequate information. Progress is
being made with the assembly of information through a series of regional or sub-regional
land-use studies, such as the King Country and South Westland studies, from which regional
and New Zealand policy can be developed. In addition, the Land Use Advisory Council has
made good progress with the investigation of a New Zealand land formation system, which
would ensure the ready availability of information to policy makers and assist in the
examination in depth of the options open.

URGENT QUESTION
Freezing Works Tradesmen-Effect of Wage Increases
184. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Labour, as an urgent question,
was the report in last night's Evening Post correct on a massive increase for freezing works
tradesmen, and, if so, what effect will it have on killing charges, and if this is significant does
he propose any action today before our primary industry costs get out of hand and jeopardise
our whole economy?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The Government understands that
negotiations are continuing on an offer made by the freezing companies association for an
increase of 50c an hour on tradesmen's rates. The Government views with grave concern the
possible effect of substantial wage increases that may occur in the industry, leading to
increased killing charges. If the proposal covers productivity payments it cannot be reflected
in killing charges. But I understand the employers are desirous of paying this within basic
rates. The principal parties have had lengthy discussions with the Government on these
issues and the Government has expressed its opinion on the possible effects on the economy
and in particular on the farming industry. The Government is therefore most anxious that
any increases in killing charges are kept to a minimum.

Maori Purposes Bill
THURSDAY, 24 NOVEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
MAORI PURPOSES BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Maori Affairs): I move, That the Maori
Purposes Bill be introduced. This is the annual washing-up Bill, which contains amendments
proposed to a number of statutes affecting Maori people and Maori land. The Bill will go to
the Maori Affairs Committee to allow members of the committee and other people
interested to express their views on or to question the provisions. The provisions are
designed to be non-controversial.
The Bill contains 10 clauses, divided into two parts. Part I contains amendments to the
Maori Affairs Act 1953; all are of a machinery nature, and will clarify and simplify the
existing procedures. Clause 4 will simplify the transfer of incorporation shares to
beneficiaries in an estate. Clause 5 is designed to enable the Maori Land Court to give wider
powers of investment to some Maori incorporations—a provision that has been requested.
Clause 6 will enable an incorporation comprising former Maori reserve land to use
unclaimed funds held for shareholders.
Part II has four miscellaneous amendments to other enactments. Clause 7 will bring
Maori housing policy into line with that of the Housing Corporation by reducing the period
before Polynesians from the South Pacific Islands become eligible for housing assistance
from 5 years to 3 years. Clause 8 is in line with the Budget announcement, and increases by
50 percent the annual grants to the Arawa, Taranaki, Tainui, and Tuwharetoa Maori trust
boards. Clause 9 redefines the waters comprising Lake Rotoaira. It is a housekeeping
measure, taking into account the changed shoreline since the construction of the huge
Tongariro hydro scheme. It will bring the definition into line with the actual shoreline.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): The Opposition has no objection to the Bill's being
introduced, because it will be referred to a committee. Opposition members welcome the
opportunity to scrutinise one or two important matters, particularly the extension of criteria
for the powers of investment to be given to Maori incorporations. My colleagues will have a
few words to say about that. One provision reduces the eligibility period for Maori housing
assistance for South Pacific Islanders from 5 years to 3 years. That will increase the number
of persons seeking housing assistance. In view of the amount that has been appropriated for
this purpose, does the Government intend to increase the amount available for housing
loans? If the amount is not increased, it makes no sense to alter the eligibility, because an
increased number of persons will want to obtain financial assistance under clause 7. I
welcome the change for trust boards; it will go a long way toward offsetting inflation and
other charges. That clause will be scrutinised during the committee hearing.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Minister will be aware that clause 5 applies to the
Taharoa C incorporation in my electorate. For 2 years the incorporation has tried to have the
principal Act amended, and has gone so far as to have a private empowering Bill introduced
into the House. The Bill met a very quick fate. The clause in this Bill does not give the
incorporation the power that it seeks. The new section 46A provides for the dispersal of
revenue, and the application of revenue from an incorporation. Section 46 reads: "The
application of revenues of incorporations. The revenues derived from its operations by any
incorporation may be applied . . .”—and then it lists the various methods in which the
revenue may be applied. The amendment gives the court the power, but the court cannot be
given that power under that section. The amendments sent to the Minister and the
department would have changed the objects of the incorporation under sections 27 and 28 of
the Maori Affairs Act 1953. The court can be given that power only by amending sections 27
and 28 of the principal Act.

refer a Bill to a select committee. Parliament does that, usually on the motion of a Minister.
It is a small point, but I think it is important. Members should realise that this is a
prerogative of Parliament, and not one of the Executive or the Minister.
The procedure in a select committee is of no concern to the House. When a Bill has
been referred to a select committee, it is up to the committee itself to decide what
submissions it will hear, or what procedures it will adopt, provided, of course, it acts within
the Standing Orders. The House is not interested in what happens to a petition, a Bill, or any
other matter until it has been reported back to the House from the select committee. In fact
it is not possible for the House to deal with matters referred to a select committee until that
committee has reported back.
The question for members at the moment is whether they will vote for or against the
introduction of the Bill. They can give reasons for that. At this stage they have also the
opportunity to ask themselves whether they will agree to the Bill's being referred to a select
committee, or whether they oppose that, and they can give reasons for that, but they cannot
give a long dissertation on the agenda of a select committee. That is not relevant to the
question of whether the Bill should be referred to a select committee. It is for the committee,
after it has received the Bill, to decide what time it will devote to hearing submissions, or to
deliberations. That is not our concern; it is the concern of the select committee if the Bill
goes to it.

QUESTIONS-ADMISSIBILITY
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I
take this early opportunity to draw to your attention question 1 on the Order Paper for
tomorrow, Friday, and question 4 calling for a written reply due on 30 November.
Tomorrow's question deals with the number of journalists or media representatives attend-
ing a press conference, and question 4 for 30 November deals with column inches of reports
in a number of newspapers.
I submit that both these questions are out of order in terms of Standing Order 45;
particularly question 4 set down for written answer seeking the news coverage in column
inches of the Prime Minister's visit to various United States cities. Standing Order 75
stipulates that questions may be put to a Minister relating to public affairs with which he is
officially connected, to proceedings in the House, or to any matter of administration for
which he is responsible. There may be doubt as to who is responsible for the number of
people attending a press conference, but there is no doubt that the Prime Minister is not
responsible for the number of column inches about his visit in various newspapers.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): The questions are relevant to the discharge of ministerial
functions in respect of publicity for the New Zealand Government. Either the Minister in
Charge of Publicity or the Prime Minister might be able to tell the House what impact was
made in the United States.

Kahikatea Production, State Forests
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: What was the total
production of kahikatea logged from State forests in 1976, and what is the primary use to
which this timber is put?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Statistics on sawn timber production are
collected in March years. Kahikatea sawn timber produced from State forest logs during the
year ended 31 March 1977 totalled 10 609 cubic metres. It is not possible to express the major
end uses of kahikatea on a percentage basis because of lack of quantitative data. However
the timber is now being used for joinery, boat building, weatherboards and mouldings,
scaffold planks, woodware-bowls, spoons, breadboards, etc.-turnery items, toys, furni-
ture, stepladders, benches, sink tops, clothes pegs, and veneer production.
Dr Shearer: Is our native timber being put to any worthwhile use?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I presume the member is relating his question to kahikatea
and not other timber.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I assume the member is referring to kahikatea. I would think that
using the timber for bowls, spoons, turnery items, and other high grade goods is a proper
use.

Electricity Expenditure
5. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Electricity: How much of the
$67,783,000 provided in the main and the supplementary estimates for the vote Electric
Supply (fuel for power stations) is to be expended on (a) imported fuel, and (b) the energy
resources levy?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity): Of the $67,783,000 provided in the main and
supplementary estimates for vote Electric Supply (fuel for fuel power stations) it is estimated
that $23,127,000 will be expended on oil fuel and $19,529,000 on the energy resources levy
on gas and coal. However, not all the oil fuel is imported—a substantial proportion is of local
content, being made up from Kapuni gas condensate residue, which is blended with overseas
oil. The oil industry cannot give a precise percentage of local content for the 1977-78 year as
this varies according to the refinery programme and the particular off-take for the period.
Some bulk deliveries to NZED would have a local content of 50 percent, while others would
have more or less.
Hon. F. M. Colman: How does this year's expenditure on imported energy and the
energy resources levy compare with that for the previous year, and does the Government
have a firm proposal to reduce the heavy reliance on imported fuel for power stations?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I do not have those figures. The honourable member will be aware
that the energy resources levy is a comparatively recent development, so the reference to last
year would have little meaning. I assure the honourable member that the Government is
endeavouring to hold the imported oil needs of the Electricity Department to a reasonable
minimum. The member knows that emphasis is being placed on the hydro and geothermal
side of the Electricity Department's plans for the foreseeable future.

Food and Drug Act Prohibitions
8. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: Is there any provision in
the Food and Drug Act 1969 to prohibit the manufacture and sale of sweets in tablet form
bearing a close resemblance to prescription and dangerous drugs, and, if not, what can be
done to prevent such activities?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Health. There is no provision in the Food and Drug Act 1969 to prohibit the
manufacture and sale of sweets in tablet form similar to drugs. The Department of Health
has studied this problem, and certain tableted drugs are being required to be packaged in a
form that will minimise some of the dangers. The department has also adopted an education
programme that highlights the necessity of keeping all drugs out of the reach of children.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that new consumer protection legislation that
should ensure that there is a clear differential in packaging and appearance between food
substances like sweets, and poisonous or harmful substances like pharmaceuticals and other
household articles, is envisaged?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am keen to discuss consumer protection legislation
with interested parties and with members of the House, but there is no positive proposal
before the Government at present. However, the Department of Health is taking positive
steps to deal with the problem within its own area of authority and competence.
Mr Lange: Will the steps taken by the Department of Health be to prohibit the
manufacture and sale of prescriptions and poisons in sweet form bearing a close resemblance
to sweets and attractive readily available confectionary?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: On the contrary; the policy being adopted adminis-
tratively now is to require certain drugs to be strip packaged. The medicines concerned are
aspirin, paracetamol, iron preparations, barbiturates, certain tranquilisers, and certain anti-
depressants. The question of strip packaging has been discussed fully with the interested
parties, and strip packaging is considered to be more safe than safety caps and containers.
That is required now of the manufacturers of these drugs.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: As this very important issue has been raised, will the Government
ask the Department of Health and those representing the interests of the consumer to
formulate a plan to stop commercial exploitation of this type forthwith?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It is very difficult to stop the manufacture of sweets,
but, as Minister of Trade and Industry, I can say that I am prepared to talk to the Minister of
Health about further measures. However, it is very difficult to stop the production of
raspberry drops that happen to look like a pharmaceutical preparation. I believe the
Department of Health is on the right lines, but I am prepared to have discussions with the
Minister of Health.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Wage Calculations
11. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Labour: Is it correct that the 7
percent cost of living allowance (with a maximum of $365 per year) awarded to public
servants in June 1976 was not included in the calculation of the average ordinary-time weekly
wage in April 1977, and, if so, what would the figure have been if the allowance had been
incorporated?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. The cost of living allowance operative from 25 June 1976 of 7 percent of taxable
earnings up to a maximum of $365 per year was included in the calculation of the average
ordinary-time weekly earnings of April 1977 for the Government sector. It was also included
in all other sectors—that is, private, local authority, and Government corporations.
Mr Marshall: How much effect did it have on the average?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It might be better if the member were to put another
question to the Minister, with notice.

Student Community Service Programmes
13. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga), on behalf of Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill),
asked the Minister of Recreation and Sport: In view of the fact that students have now
completed examinations and left tertiary institutes, what student community service pro-
grammes have been introduced, where are they to be located, and what efforts are being
made to acquaint students of the existence of these and other programmes?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Recreation and Sport. A scheme has been established to help community organisations to
mount projects creating additional job opportunities for tertiary students. Details of the
scheme have been very widely circulated, including to student, youth, and educational
organisations. This publicity is being supplemented by news media coverage and newspaper
advertising. Discussions have also been held with student organisations and the National
Youth Council. By yesterday, 75 applications had been received under the scheme. Thirty-
four of these have been approved: in Auckland, Rotorua, Wellington, Nelson, Greytown,
Taradale, Porirua, New Lynn, Whakatane, Papakura, Napier, Cambridge, Dunedin, and
Otautau.

Budget?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department):
The saving will vary according to the level of individual earnings. For example, a taxpayer
with weekly gross earnings of $200 would gain $3.51 a week, or $182.42 on an annual basis,
while weekly gross earnings of $350 would result in a gain of $7.31, or $380.02 a year.

Prime Minister's American Trip
17. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Prime Minister: As the total cost of
sending him and his staff to North America is given as $70,153.60, and the travel and other
expenses of the staff given on 16 November were only $26,818.40, is $43,335.20 the cost of
the Prime Minister's and Mrs Muldoon's travel?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): The figure of $70,153.60 given in an
answer to a question on 15 November represented the total estimated cost for the Prime
Minister's visit to North America. While the figure of $43,335.20 referred to by the
honourable member does include provision for the expenses of the Prime Minister himself
and Mrs Muldoon, it also includes the estimated cost of a formal dinner for the Vice-
President of the United States, travel within the United States other than by air, embassy
expenses resulting from the visit, gifts, and provision for miscellaneous contingencies that
inevitably arise and cannot be foreseen when budgeting for such a visit.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Consumer Price Index, Vegetables
18. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he read the item
entitled "C.P.I. should drop vegetable listing" in the October 1977 issue of New Zealand
Commercial Grower, and, if so, can he indicate: (a) whether the case in favour of dropping
fresh vegetables from the consumer price index has merit and (b) whether the matter is likely
to be considered by any review committee?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): I have seen the article referred to by
the honourable member. Because of the importance of fresh vegetables in New Zealand
household expenditure, their inclusion along with fresh fruit in the consumer price index is
considered essential. Fresh vegetables and fresh fruit account for 24 percent of the base
expenditure on all goods and services covered. A full review of the composition and
structure of the consumer price index will be undertaken by an index revision advisory
committee during 1978.
Dr Shearer: In that full review is there any contemplation of removing alcohol and
cigarettes from the list?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: That would be a matter for the advisory committee. I
certainly have no indication of that.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) moved to insert the following new
clause:
73. Enforcement of fines-(1) If any fine adjudged or ordered to be paid by any
service organisation in respect of any offence against this Act is not paid in full within 1
month after the date when it was imposed or within such further time as may be allowed
or fixed for the payment thereof, all persons who were members of that service
organisation at the time when the offence in respect of which the fine was imposed was
committed shall be jointly and severally liable to pay the fine as if it has been adjudged
to be payable by them personally (except that no person shall be liable under this
subsection for a larger sum than $50 on account of any such fine).
(2) For the purpose of subsection (1) of this section, a certificate under the hand of
the Registrar of a Magistrate's Court stating the amount of any fine remaining unpaid by
any service organisation and the names of any persons who are jointly and severally
liable to pay that amount by virtue of subsection (1) of this section may be filed in the
office of a Magistrate's Court and every such certificate shall, unless a Magistrate
otherwise directs, be conclusive evidence of the liability of the persons so named as
being jointly and severally liable.
