HIGHER SALARIES COMMISSION BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill makes statutory provision for the Higher Salaries Commission, which at
present is set up under Part II of the Wage Adjustment Regulations. In the Government's
view, the work of the commission is important in achieving a degree of consistency in higher
salaries in public and quasi-public bodies, having regard to the responsibilities and expertise
each of the positions under its jurisdiction carries. The commission, which was established by
the last Administration, has jurisdiction over a number of important areas. Of the 747
positions over which the commission exercises determination, 13 are for members of
Parliament, 73 are in statutory corporations and research associations, 8 are university vice-
chancellors or University Grants Committee positions, 623 are in the local authorities area,
and 30 are various statutory officers such as the members of the State Services Commission.
The commission's work load falls into two distinct areas: the general review of all
positions under its jurisdiction at between 1- and 3-yearly intervals, and the continuing
interim reviews of specific positions which can be modified between general reviews at the
request of the employing authority or the employee affected. The Bill sets down the
procedures to be followed by the commission for each type of review, and allows for
recognition of various affected parties by the commission.
The Bill is to come into force on a date to be appointed by the Governor-General, by


## p. 4770 (#206) ###########################################

4770
24 November
Higher Salaries Commission Bill
Order in Council. Clause 2 defines the commission and the Minister, who is to be the
Minister of Labour. Clause 4 establishes the Higher Salaries Commission as the same one set
up by Part II of the Wage Adjustment Regulations. Clause 5 provides for three members of
the commission to be appointed by Order in Council, and provides for a chairman and a
deputy chairman. Clause 6 appoints members for 3 years, and provides for reappointment on
a rotational basis.
Clause 12(1) sets out the jurisdiction of the commission and its functions. Its functions
under paragraph (a) are to consider and to determine: (i) members of the House of
Representatives' salaries and allowances; (ii) the salary of the highest paid executive of each
of the corporations or bodies set out in Parts I and II of the first schedule, and the salaries of
such other officers of those corporations or bodies as the commission specifies from time to
time; (iii) the salaries of the university vice-chancellors, and other persons employed by the
universities or the University Grants Committee as the commission from time to time
specifies; (iv) the salaries of local body positions referred to in the second schedule; (v) the
salaries of senior positions in the State services, as defined in clause 20(2) of the State
Services Conditions of Employment Bill, which is now before the House; (vi) the salaries of
the statutory officers set out in the third schedule; (vii) the salaries of medical practitioners
and persons studying to be medical practitioners, employed by the hospital boards; and (viii)
the salaries of university teachers.
Under clause 12(1)(b) the commission was to consider and make recommendations
through the Prime Minister on parliamentary superannuation. I should like to report to the
House that, as a result of the talks held yesterday between the officials and members of the
Labour Committee, that that provision will be changed. A Supplementary Order Paper is
being drafted and will be made available shortly. It was unanimously agreed that this should
be done by way of determination and not by way of recommendation, and fortunately we
found a legal way of doing that. Clause 12(1)(c) empowers the commission to consider and
make recommendations on the salaries, allowances, and superannuation of the judiciary,
and paragraph (d) to carry out functions conferred on the commission by this Bill or any
other enactment. Subclause 12(2) allows the commission to fix scales of salaries, and
prescribe rules regarding application.
Clause 13 is fairly important, bearing in mind the size of the schedules. It allows
additions or deletions to the first, second, and third schedules by Order in Council.
Comments of local authorities may have some bearing on the probable deletion in a
relatively short time of many of the bodies currently listed. Clause 14 re-enacts the existing
provision dealing with the implementation of decisions of the commission.
Clause 15 is new, and establishes the ground rules regarding the release of the
commission's determinations. Subclause (1) requires the commission to ensure that they are
made known to the persons who have a direct interest in them. Subclause (3) requires the
commission to publish particulars of its general reviews, subject to subclause (4), which
provides that certain particulars of a general review need not be published if the commission
considers that to be in the public interest. This is to cover the situation where publication
would not be desirable for competitive reasons-for example, in the case of Air New
Zealand. Subclause (5) requires the commission to release its determinations to the
Government Statistician if he requires them.
Clause 16 is new, and sets out the way in which determinations on parliamentary pay
and allowances are to be published. The committee also agreed yesterday, not on a change
to this Bill, but on the modus operandi—that will be the terminology I shall use-whereby we
shall try to ensure that promulgation of parliamentary salaries, pay, and allowances is
achieved in a way similar to that under the original regulations when the parliamentary law
counsel played a role in the determination. That will be done administratively.
Clause 18 establishes that general reviews are to be carried out at between 1 and 3 years,
the next to be as at 1 April 1978. Limits are set on the amount of backdating possible, and
the 12-month rule is set out in the same clause. Clause 19 deals with interim adjustments to
determinations issued at each general review. Certain bodies may apply for interim adjust-
ments as set out in the Bill. Subclause (2) provides that general or interim increases in the
State services may be applied to salaries under the commission's jurisdiction, and the
commission must consult with the public sector tribunal or the chairman of the State services
co-ordinating committee on the manner of the application.
Clause 21 allows certain representatives to make recommendations to the commission
on salaries of directly affected parties to which the commission must have due regard. Clause
24 sets out the powers of the commission. Subclause (3) is new, and gives the commission


## p. 4771 (#207) ###########################################

24 November
4771
Higher Salaries Commission Bill
such powers as are reasonably necessary to carry out its functions. I propose to provide, by a
Supplementary Order Paper, power for the commission to delegate certain of its jurisdiction
in a very limited way.
Clause 29 enables determinations of the commission to override contracts of service.
Clause 30 requires employers to consult with the commission in certain circumstances,
specifically where relativities between salaries set in other jurisdictions or by negotiation and
salaries determined by the commission are likely to be disturbed. Clauses 31 to 34 contain
consequential amendments, repeals, and savings provisions. I propose to introduce the
Supplementary Order Paper, as outlined, to make some additions to and deletions from the
schedule specifying the commission's jurisdiction so as to bring it up to date in the light of
submissions made since the Bill was first introduced.
As I indicated when introducing the Bill, it is the last of the Government's legislative
package giving effect to its wages and industrial relations policy. We have had wide
consultation, and various organisations have considered the Bill. That consideration will, I
hope, enable the House to have a better understanding of the intent of the legislation.

WANGANUI COMPUTER CENTRE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When the Wanganui Computer Centre Act was being passed last year I said that
the Government recognised the benefits that the computer could bring to society, while
recognising that some people felt that the computer could be a threat to the privacy of the
individual. When any Government department or other organisation collects confidential
information on individuals it has an obligation to ensure that the information remains
confidential. The Wanganui Computer Centre Act provides the safeguards for such confi-
dentiality. The proposed amendments in the Bill are aimed at giving fuller effect to
preserving confidentiality of records at the computer centre, and ensuring that the provisions
of the Act can be operated effectively. The amendments have arisen out of suggestions made
by the Privacy Commissioner and the policy committee, who see the changes to the
legislation as being highly desirable for the proper functioning of the computer system.
The amendment Bill permits the authorised users of the computer system to feed


## p. 4774 (#210) ###########################################

4774
24 November
Wanganui Computer Centre Amendment Bill
fictitious information into the computer system. This can be done for training employees or
for testing the computer system. In these instances any fictitious information must be clearly
identified as such, and must at all times be kept distinct from the real information stored in
the computer system. Fictitious information may also be fed into the computer system for
the purpose of detecting any misuse or potential misuse of the computer system. This can be
done only with the approval of the Commissioner of Police, who in turn is required to report
the matter forthwith to the Privacy Commissioner. The use of fictitious information rather
than live information in these three circumstances is clearly in keeping with the tenor of the
present Act, and reflects the responsible attitude being taken towards preserving the
confidentiality of the live information stored in the computer system and under the control of
the policy committee.
The Privacy Commissioner is given wide functions under the Wanganui Computer
Centre Act, not only to investigate complaints from individuals, but also to inquire of his
own motion into any other matters relating to the operation of the Act. He is not, however,
given any express powers under the present legislation to obtain evidence from persons he
feels may be able to assist with his inquiries. The amendment Bill will remedy this by giving
the Privacy Commissioner powers similar to those possessed by the ombudsmen to obtain
evidence during their investigations. The main departure from the ombudsmen's powers is
that the Privacy Commissioner is not able to obtain evidence if the Attorney-General
certifies that the production of such evidence may be prejudicial to the investigation or
detection of offences. This reflects the nature of the information involved in the computer
system. At the same time, however, I should comment that the nature of the information on
the computer system is such that it has not been necessary to include all the restrictive
qualifications that attach to the powers of the ombudsmen.
One other qualification is to be made by Supplementary Order Paper to the power given
to the Privacy Commissioner to obtain evidence. The Privacy Commissioner will not be able
to require any person to produce evidence that may disclose matters relating to any process
or determination of the policy committee. We had a somewhat unique situation in which the
Privacy Commissioner was trying to get the policy committee to give evidence. A new
offence has been created for failing to comply with any lawful requirement of the Privacy
Commissioner, or obstructing or misleading him in the exercise of his powers under the Act.
A further change has been made in relation to the Privacy Commissioner. He is now
able, with the prior approval of the Governor-General in Council, to delegate part of his
powers under the Act to any of his staff. The powers that may be delegated are the power to
receive requests and acquire information under section 14 of the Act, and the power to
receive and investigate complaints under sections 15 and 16. The power to delegate does not
extend to reporting on those complaints—and that is very important.
Several new offences are created by the Bill. I have already referred to one area where
new offences have been created. The offences of attempting to gain access and interfering
with the computer system have now been extended to incorporate the substantive act as well.
The other new offences relate to the misuse of information obtained from the computer
system. The offences cover the wilful disclosure of such information in an unauthorised
manner by a person having lawful access to the computer system. It will be an offence to fail
to comply with any directions given by an officer of an authorised department for the return
or disposal of any record or information obtained from the computer system. A prosecution
under these provisions can be brought only with the consent of the Attorney-General.
The amendments have been prepared to enable the continuing protection of the rights
of the individual without at the same time hindering the legitimate functions of the user
departments. The need for these amendments was raised by both the Privacy Commissioner
and the policy committee. The Government feels that these amendments will improve the
operation of the legislation.

with this Bill I shall be quite brief, but I do have a couple of comments to make. I was
somewhat intrigued, when overseas recently, to read in a New Zealand newspaper of the

STAMP AND CHEQUE DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The main purpose of the Bill is to give further effect to this year's Budget


## p. 4776 (#212) ###########################################

4776
24 November
Stamp and Cheque Duties Amendment Bill
announcements about the purchase and sale of home and farm properties. The Bill also
provides the machinery to enable the development of a simplified method of payment of
stamp duty on shares sold through the stock exchanges.
Clause 1 is the short title, and provides for an application date for transactions entered
into on or after 22 July 1977. Clause 2 inserts three new sections in the principal Act to
provide an exemption from conveyance duty on the purchase of a first home, the purchase of
a first farm, the sale of a large family home to growing families, and the purchase of suitable
smaller accommodation. The first home exemption will apply to a person who purchases his
or her first home, or buys a first section with the intention of building a home. While the
exemption applies to the conventional dwellinghouse, a town house, home unit, or owner-
ship flat represented by the ownership of shares will also qualify.
As with all revenue exemptions, certain tests must be met. In broad terms, the
requirements are: the dwellinghouse or section is to be bought for the occupation of the
purchaser as his or her home. For example, the purchaser, including the spouse, must not
have previously owned an interest in a dwellinghouse or a residential section. The previous
ownership of business premises that were also used as a residence would create difficulties.
For example, a grocery business with accommodation attached, and a farm property with a
homestead, would be a debarring factor. Similarly, the previous ownership of shares in an
own-your-own flat would exclude the buyer from the exemption.
Mr Prebble: What's so good about that?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am just setting out the details. The area of land is not to be
more than 4500 square metres, but the Commissioner of Inland Revenue is given authority
to grant exemptions where larger areas are required for reasonable occupation. A
Supplementary Order Paper will be introduced during the Committee stage to amend the
definition of "interest". This broadens the meaning to meet some of the points made on the
introduction of the Bill. The amended definition will make it clearer that the first-home
relief could still be given even though the purchaser may have previously held a small
interest in land if there was no personal right of use or occupation-for example, a fractional
interest acquired through a deceased estate, in Maori land, or as a mortgagee.
Dealing with the first-farm exemption, the incentive for possible farm ownership has
been encouraged by such incentives as farm ownership savings schemes, improved loan
facilities, and now exemption from stamp duty. As with first homes, there are certain
conditions to ensure that people who own or have owned a substantial interest in a farm
property do not qualify. The exemption will apply to the transfer of farm land and to the
purchase of shares in a farming company, which gives the purchasing shareholder a
controlling interest in that company. The main requirements are: the purchaser, or his
spouse, cannot have previously owned a substantial interest in farm land, or in a farming
company; the property being purchased is capable of supporting a full-time economic
farming operation; the purchaser must undertake in writing at the time of purchase to
actively farm the property, either alone or in partnership, as his main occupation within 2
years of purchase or a reasonable time after that; and the purchaser or purchasers must have
acquired a controlling interest in the farm land or in the farm company.
Certain expressions are used in the Bill, such as "substantial interest", "actively farm",
and "farm land". "Substantial interest", where it relates to the ownership of an existing or
previous farm, means an interest in farm land having having a value of more than $50,000.
This is considered to be a realistic figure on which to operate. The definition of "actively
farm" is a safeguard so that the benefit of the exemption is not available to hobbyists,
speculators, or any non-genuine farmers. The definition of “farm land" is simply land that is
capable of being farmed as an economic unit. It would cover every type of farming, from
afforestation to berry and poultry farming. "Controlling interest" means that a purchase by a
company is deemed for the purposes of this Bill to be a purchase by the shareholders, so that
the same criteria for the exemption can be applied as if they had purchased as individuals.
The third relief provided in clause 2 relates to the sale of large family homes by older
couples or individuals to growing families, and is another part of the Government's policy to
encourage the better use of existing homes. The exemption applies to the larger family home
purchased for a growing family, provided the purchaser or the spouse does not currently own
a home or an interest in a home. When the older person who is selling subsequently buys a
suitable smaller home, the stamp duty exemption will also apply to the purchase of that
smaller home. In effect, both parties to the original transaction can now get relief under the
Bill.
The terms "growing family", "large family home", and "older person" are defined in

Stamp and Cheque Duties Amendment Bill
the Bill and are to a degree self-explanatory. A "growing family" means a family unit which
has at least one person more than the persons selling the large family home. Although the
exemption is directed at the conventional family of husband, wife, and children, it could
apply equally to other family situations, such as an aged parent living with a married couple.
The Supplementary Order Paper to be introduced will make a slight amendment to the
definition of "growing family", to make it clear that it relates to persons who habitually live
together as a family. A "large family home" is defined as a dwellinghouse of not less than
three bedrooms, and “suitable smaller accommodation" is restricted to a maximum of two
bedrooms. Questions will no doubt arise as to what constitutes a two-bedroom or a three-
bedroom home, and here of necessity it will be left to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue,
after consultation with the Housing Corporation, to decide if a property comes within the
definitions. That is one of the reasons for the powers given to the commissioner in subclause
5.
The amendment in clause 3 of the Bill is a machinery provision to ensure that objection
rights apply to the exercise of the commissioner's discretion in regard to the first-home and
first-farm exemptions. The proposed new section 51A referred to in clause 4 is a provision
that could prove of real administrative assistance to the Department of Inland Revenue, but
principally it will help sharebrokers and registrars of companies. It gives legislative authority
to the commissioner to enter into an agreement with the Stock Exchange Association of New
Zealand for the composition of stamp duty payable on shares and securities sold through a
sharebroker, which are officially listed on the stock exchange. This is to provide a simplified
method of payment to be negotiated with the stock exchanges. Under existing provisions,
each transfer of shares-and there are almost 300 000 transfers each year-has to be
presented to the department for assessment and payment of stamp duty. The agreement
between the commissioner and the Stock Exchange Association will, of course, have certain
safeguards and will not, for instance, relate to shares in private companies or shares that are
sold for less than full value.
Clause 5 refers to the schedule to the Bill, and brings fines and penalties for offences
more in line with present-day values. This is being done progressively in all the Inland
Revenue Acts.
Clause 6 inserts a proposed new section 92A, which is a machinery provision that arises
from the proposed method of dealing with stock exchange transactions. The Bill contains
important forward measures in relation to the sale and purchase of homes and farms.

SUBMARINE CABLES AND PIPELINES PROTECTION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. Members will recall that when I introduced the Bill I explained the need to
strengthen the provisions of the principal Act. The Act provides the mechanism for the
protection of submarine cables and pipelines, some of which—for example, the Cook Strait
power cable—are vital to New Zealand's economy. For this reason it is essential to provide a
real deterrent to activities that might damage these cables and pipelines.
Clause 3 inserts two new sections-6A and 6B. The new section 6A requires the owner of
a submarine cable or pipeline to notify the Minister of Transport when use of a cable or
pipeline ceases and is unlikely to be resumed. The new section 6B provides the machinery for
the removal of disused cables and pipelines that constitute a hazard to fishing or anchoring in
the vicinity. There is an increasing tendency to use the seabed for pipelines and cables, and it
is essential that the Minister be informed whenever these are no longer required, so that
restrictions on fishing operations and anchoring can be kept to an absolute minimum.
Clause 4 amends section 7 of the principal Act to enable the Minister of Transport, by
notice in the Gazette, to allow specific ships to anchor in protected or restricted areas. Faults
in submarine cables can occur without warning, and often require rapid repair. The present
method of enabling repair ships to anchor in protected or restricted areas by means of an
Order in Council has proved too slow to deal with what we call emergency situations. Clause
5 inserts the new sections 7A, 7B, and 7c. The new section 7A makes it an offence to conduct
fishing operations or to anchor in a protected or restricted area, and sets a maximum fine for
this offence. In doing so, it tightens the present provisions considerably and puts a greater
onus on the owner and the master of a vessel fishing or anchoring in a protected or restricted
area.
The penalty is increased from $1,000 to $5,000, although the present penalty of
imprisonment is removed. Experience has shown that an economic penalty is a much more
effective deterrent than imprisonment, which is rarely imposed, anyway. The present level
of fine, which was set 11 years ago, has become no more than a licence fee, so it has been
raised substantially. The new section 7B enables ships to be ordered out of a protected or
restricted area by a superintendent of mercantile marine if he has reasonable grounds for


## p. 4781 (#217) ###########################################

24 November Submarine Cables and Pipelines Protection Amendment Bill
4781
believing that fishing operations are being conducted or that a ship is anchored within a
protected or prohibited area. Non-compliance with such an order is punishable by a fine not
exceeding $1,000.
The new section 7c enables a superintendent to seize any fishing equipment that he
finds in the water within a protected or restricted area. Such equipment as crayfish pots can
damage power and telephone cables, and it is essential that they be removed if found in the
vicinity of such a cable. The section also makes provision for the disposal of seized
equipment, subject to notice of the seizure being given at the nearest police station.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The primary objectives of the amending Bill are to
prevent damage to submarine cables and pipelines where possible, and to ensure that when
damage occurs the courts have jurisdiction to impose the appropriate penalties. Damage to
cables or pipelines on the seabed is most likely to be caused by boats either anchored or
trawling over the cables. The new section 7A increases the penalties for fishing operations
that contravene the provisions of the principal Act. The new section 7A(2) inserted by clause
5 reads: "Every person who fails to comply with or acts in contravention of any Órder in
Council under section 7 of this Act commits an offence against this Act and is liable on
summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $5,000.”

1000 percent. The Minister spoke about the considerable increase. During the introduction
debate I also mentioned the principal Act's provision for imprisonment, which has been
removed. After examining the provisions in the Bill and the principal Act, I see no grounds
for objecting to the increased fine.
I understand that the Maui development, the organisation most affected by the Bill, has
been consulted and is not concerned about the provisions in clause 3 relating to the
requirement that owners notify the Minister when use of a submarine cable or pipeline
ceases or when a cable or pipeline is removed. In instances in which cables or pipelines may
be a navigational hazard, the clause is a distinct improvement on the principal Act. Since the
organisations most likely to be affected are satisfied with the provisions of the Bill and the
objectives of the 1966 Act are retained, the Opposition does not oppose the measure.

COMPANIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill makes three amendments to the Companies Act 1955. The first
amendment clarifies the purpose for which the Registrar of Companies may inspect a
company's books and papers. The second amendment confirms the registrar's power of
inspection after an appeal has been lodged against an inspection. The third amendment
provides machinery to allow a company to raise a loan overseas by the issue of a prospectus
without having to comply strictly with the prospectus provisions of the Companies Act 1955.
Clause 2 makes it clear that the purpose of an inspection includes the detection of
offences against the Act, and the consideration of whether the registrar should exercise any
of his rights under the Act. This will place beyond doubt the authority of the registrar to
inspect a company's records to see whether, for example, it is trading fraudulently, and to
consider whether he should petition the Supreme Court for an order that the company be
wound up.
Clause 3 makes it clear that an appeal against a registrar's inspection does not in the first
place prevent the registrar from continuing an inspection, and, in the second place does not
excuse a company from producing its records for inspection in the meantime, irrespective of
the outcome of an appeal. This clause also provides for the destruction or expunging of
records of information derived in the course of an improper inspection, and provides that
such information is not admissible in any proceedings. The intention of this clause is to
confirm that an appeal does not frustrate an inspection, and to ensure that the effect of a
successful appeal is not diminished.


## p. 4782 (#218) ###########################################

4782
24 November
Companies Amendment Bill
Clause 4 provides that in respect of a particular overseas loan the Minister may, on the
recommendation of the registrar, exempt a company from all or any of the prospectus
provisions of the New Zealand Act. The intention of this clause is to provide the machinery
to allow a company to meet the law and accepted practices of the place where the loan is to
be raised, to the extent that such law and practice differs from New Zealand law.

SALE OF LIQUOR AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill makes what I believe are minor and non-controversial amendments to
the Sale of Liquor Act. Some of the provisions contained in the Bill are inserted at the
request of interested parties, while others are drafting amendments arising out of last year's
Sale of Liquor Amendment Act. I have circulated an explanatory note on the Bill to all
members of Parliament, setting out in some detail the purpose of the amendments contained
in it. I hope, therefore, that it will not be necessary for me to dwell in detail on the drafting
amendments contained in the Bill.
Clause 2 meets the request of the Wholesale Wine and Spirit Merchants Federation that
the requirement to sell beer in certain quantities to unlicensed persons be amended to take
account of modern packaging methods. In addition, the minimum amount of liquor that may
be sold by a wholesaler is being reduced from 9 litres to 8 litres to give legal effect to what has
erroneously but traditionally been regarded as satisfying the minimum purchase require-
ment. This is the sale of 2 dozen 340-millilitre bottles, which contain just over 8 litres, not 9
litres.
An extension of the hours available under a booth licence is contained in clause 3 at the
request of the trotting clubs. Its effect is to permit an extension of the present booth licence
closing hour from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, along the lines of the
extended hours available on those days to hotels and taverns. The actual hours available
under the booth licence will still be determined in each case by the chairman of the local
licensing committee.
Clause 4 repeals the obsolete requirements that a winemaker must specify the quantity
of wine he intends to produce when applying for or renewing his licence. It has the
agreement of the Wine Institute. In addition, it is made a condition of the renewal of a fruit
winemaker's licence that the applicant has paid his Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council levy.
There is already a similar provision for grape winemakers.
The effect of clause 5 is to restore the machinery provisions for applications for and
objections to the removal of a wine reseller's licence that were in use before last year's Sale
of Liquor Amendment Act. As I indicated in the explanatory note I have circulated, these
provisions were inadvertently repealed last year. The position relating to applications for
removal of these licences in the interim awaits the decision of the Supreme Court at the
moment, and this clause will not affect that decision. Clause 6 limits the application of a
manager's certificate to particular types of liquor outlets only.
At present, a manager's certificate entitles the holder to manage any licensed premises
in which managers may or must be appointed. The general principle underlying this clause is
agreed to by both the Hotel Association of New Zealand and the New Zealand Licensing
Trusts Association. Clause 7 meets the request of the Hotel Association for an increase in
the aggregate period for which an acting manager may be appointed while a manager is on
leave, and the increase is from 1 month to 6 weeks. Those acting as managers while the usual
manager is on leave are not required to obtain a manager's certificate for that period. The
amendment merely takes account of the increases in annual leave that have been granted to
managers in line with our ormal industrial legislation.
Clause 8 implements the request of the New Zealand Liquor Industry Council for a
modification of the provisions relating to suspension of licences. At present, a licensing
committee is required to suspend a licence if it is satisfied that the licensee has failed to
comply with a health or fire requirement to such an extent that the health or safety of those
using the premises is likely to be endangered. The effect of the clause is to permit the
licensing committee to close the affected part of the premises for a specified time rather than


## p. 4783 (#219) ###########################################

24 November
4783
Sale of Liquor Amendment Bill
suspend the licence completely in cases where the danger has arisen as a result of
circumstances beyond the control of the licensee.
Clause 9 creates a permit to allow the supply of liquor, but not its sale, at social
gatherings promoted by the permit holder on premises in respect of which there is a general
ancillary licence. As I indicated in the note I circulated to all members, difficulties will arise
with general ancillary licence premises that are used by organisations other than the licence
holder. Before general ancillary licences were created, these organisations could hold social
gatherings on their unlicensed premises under section 219 of the principal Act.
If one organisation obtains a general ancillary licence the premises will no longer be
unlicensed, and other organisations using the premises will not be able to hold social
gatherings at which liquor is supplied without those attending such gatherings committing an
offence. The new permit provided for in clause 9 is designed to remedy this. The new permit
will also allow the use of the premises by members of an organisation holding a general
ancillary licence for functions such as receptions or anniversary celebrations. In addition, it
will enable outsiders to hire the premises after hours and use them for social gatherings. I can
see no objection to this, as a number of licence holders will have premises that are very
suitable for use by outside people or organisations. That is probably particularly true in rural
areas.
On the introduction of the Bill, the member for Auckland Central was concerned that
this permit could enable general ancillary licence holders to enter the catering business. A
similar view has been expressed by the Licensing Trusts Association. Given that the permit
will be available for a specified day only and will not allow the sale of liquor, I doubt whether
this could occur. Nevertheless, there may be some temptation for general ancillary licence
holders to contemplate such an activity if they themselves are able to obtain the permit.
To ensure that this will not occur, I intend to move an amendment in the Committee
stage to preclude a permit of this type being issued to the holder of a general ancillary licence
or anyone on its behalf. In addition, I have instructed my department to include in the
regulations currently being prepared to give effect to the provisions of the Bill a requirement
that a Police report be obtained before a permit is issued. This will be along the lines of the
present requirements for extended hours permits. Paragraph (b) of the proposed new section
218B (3) will, therefore, become redundant, and I intend to move its deletion in the
Committee stage of the Bill.
I intend also to move a further amendment to clause 9 to make it a condition of the
permit that the licence holder may not supply liquor to the permit holder or those attending
the gathering held under the permit. I believe these three proposals will tighten up the clause
considerably, and ensure that the permit is not used for purposes for which it was not
designed.
Contrary to some reports in the news media upon the introduction of the Bill, clause 10
does not provide for later closing hours for licensed cabarets. Last year's amending Act
extended the closing time for cabarets from 11.30 p.m. to 3.00 a.m. the next morning. As I
explained in the note I circulated to all members, clause 10 is purely a drafting amendment to
bring the penal provisions of the principal Act into line with the extended hours for cabarets
enacted last year. Clause 11 implements a request from the Licensing Control Commission
that its consent be obtained by the holders of wholesale licences and club charters before
alterations are made to their premises. This is a requirement at present for a number of other
licences authorised under the principal Act.
Clauses 12 and 13 are purely drafting amendments arising out of last year's Sale of
Liquor Amendment Act. I have outlined the need for and the effect of these amendments in
the explanatory note I have circulated to members.
I do not believe any further comment is warranted at this stage. As I have said, the Bill
makes minor amendments to the principal Act, and I believe that careful and full considera-
tion of each clause will show that the amendments contained in the Bill are not controversial.
A number of other amendments to the principal Act have been sought over the last year by
interested parties. However, as the primary purpose of the Bill is to correct the omissions
arising out of last year's amending Act, I have deliberately refrained from including the more
contentious amendments sought by interested parties to ensure that the Bill is acceptable to
most of the community and is enacted this year.

LICENSING TRUSTS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The enactment of a Licensing Trusts Amendment Bill this year is necessary to
correct two minor matters arising out of last year's liquor legislation: first, to put district and
suburban licensing trusts on the same footing as the private trade in later closing; and,
secondly, to clarify the administration of licences, charters, and permits that may be issued
to private organisations within a district or suburban trust area.
In addition, I have included in the Bill, at the request of the Invercargill Licensing
Trust, provisions authorising district licensing trusts to operate catering outlets. These are to
be found in clause 3. Under the proposed new section 28c referred to in clause 3, a district
licensing trust will be able to operate catering premises in its district in exactly the same
manner as a private caterer may under a caterer's licence. A district trust will be able to sell
liquor for consumption on its catering premises to people attending a social gathering at
which food is consumed. The trust will also be entitled to sell liquor from its premises for
consumption on someone else's premises at which it is catering, whether those premises are
inside the trust's district or not. A district trust will also be entitled to obtain a permit to
allow it to sell liquor for consumption on someone else's premises at which it is catering,
whether those premises are inside the trust's district or not.
A caterer's licence under the Sale of Liquor Act may be issued to private operators
within a district licensing trust area, and private caterers outside such an area may cater at
functions held inside such an area. Private caterers and district trusts operating catering
premises will be competing on an even footing in this respect. Since the introduction of the
Bill I have been advised that a consequential amendment to section 32(4) of the principal
Act is required to give full effect to the provisions in clause 3. This is because that subsection
prohibits the sale of liquor by a district licensing trust for consumption on the premises unless
accommodation is provided. The exceptions to this prohibition are taverns, restaurants,
cabarets, and booth premises, and catering premises need to be added to the list. I intend to
introduce a Supplementary Order Paper in the Committee stage to make the addition.
I have circulated to all members an explanatory note on the Bill, in which I have
outlined the position of suburban and local licensing trusts on catering outlets. I do not
propose to go into that in detail now. However, I feel I should say that the concern expressed
on the introduction of the Bill about the possibility of discriminatory treatment of the three
types of licensing trusts in the operation of catering premises is misplaced. The differences
that arise are due solely to the different nature of the three types of trust, and apply at
present to other outlets, such as restaurants and cabarets.
Clause 4 is a machinery provision that applies some of the new provisions of the Sale of
Liquor Act to both district and suburban licensing trusts, in conjunction with clause 7. The
provisions will mean that, generally speaking, the permitted hours of sale are not obligatory.
They also relate to the closure of hotel and tavern bars in the event of emergencies, or if
fighting or serious disorder breaks out. Clause 5 is necessary to correct an anomaly arising
out of last year's liquor legislation, and applies to both district and suburban licensing trusts.
It puts those trusts on an equal footing with the trade by providing that the extended hours
available for hotels and taverns are to be in addition to the permitted 11-hour maximum


## p. 4785 (#221) ###########################################

24 November
4785
Licensing Trusts Amendment Bill
opening time in any one day.
Clause 6 is designed to clarify doubts that have arisen about district licensing trusts by
making it clear that all licences and permits that may be granted in their area may be
administered by the licensing committee of the licensing district adjoining the trust area.
This is done by repealing section 35 of the principal Act and replacing it with an updated
description of all licences, permits, and charters that may be issued in a district licensing trust
area. A new subclause is added to make it clear that the administration of those licences and
permits is to be carried out by the neighbouring licensing committee. Suburban trusts are
provided for in section 73(1) of the principal Act, but I believe it to be desirable to add the
same provision contained in subsection (2) of the new section 35 to section 73 of the principal
Act. This will ensure that the doubts that have arisen over the administration of licences in
district licensing trust areas will not arise over private licences in suburban licensing trust
areas. I intend to introduce the appropriate amendment during the Committee stage of the
Bill. Clause 7 relates to suburban licensing trusts only, and is purely a machinery measure.
The purpose of the amendments is set out in my explanatory note that has been
circulated to all members, and I do not believe I need to go into that any further. Parts II and
III of the Bill apply the provisions of clauses 3, 4, and 6 to the Masterton and Invercargill
licensing trusts. The section of the principal Act being amended by clause 5 already applies
to those two trusts and no further amendment to their statutes is therefore required.

GAMING AND LOTTERIES BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This is an important measure that consolidates and amends the law on gambling
in New Zealand. The only major form of gambling not dealt with in the Bill is legal betting
on horses and greyhounds, which is governed by the Racing Act 1971. As I explained when
the Bill was introduced, the present law-the Gaming Act of 1908-dates back to 1881, and
the principles on which it is based reflect the public attitudes of the time and the problems
being faced in the late nineteenth century. Although amendments have been made since
1908, the changes have merely been grafted on to the old legislation, the original purpose of
which was to limit opportunities for gambling. The mixture has not been a happy one. It is
time that the legislation more clearly reflected present-day attitudes. That is what the Bill
before us is designed to do.
At the outset, I thank the chairman and members of the Statutes Revision Committee
for the careful consideration they gave to the Bill. As members will have noted, the
committee has proposed a number of amendments which, with minor exceptions arising
from a misunderstanding that I shall refer to later, I am satisfied improve the Bill and should
be adopted. I am grateful to the select committee for the improvements, some of which
clarify the Government's intentions in this complex legislation.
It is my intention to introduce, by way of a Supplementary Order Paper, an amendment
to Part VII of the Bill to make it clear that the Lottery Board of Control has the power to
allocate funds to the recently announced proposed Film Commission. At the same time, the
opportunity has been taken to correct the misunderstanding over the changes to Part IX
agreed to by the Statutes Revision Committee.
I am sure that members will agree that gambling laws should reflect the wishes of the
large majority of people and be drafted in such a manner that they are easily understood. On
both counts the present law is decidedly deficient. Although there are some who consider
that all gambling is morally wrong-and I am sure they hold those views most
sincerely-most of us love a little flutter, whether it is a small investment at the races, trying
for a prize in a Golden Kiwi jackpot, or spending an evening at housie. There are also some
individuals and organisations who regard any legislative restrictions on gambling as unneces-
sary. It is significant that the Statutes Revision Committee did not receive submissions
supporting the two extreme points of view. Indeed, there were surprisingly few
submissions-only eight in all. That suggests that the provisions of the Bill are generally
acceptable-clarifying the present situation as they do, removing those of the present
restrictions that are no longer essential but retaining safeguards to ensure that the public
interest is protected, and incorporating machinery for the authorisation of additional forms
of gambling in the future should there be a widespread demand for them.
The Bill applies to the four types of gambling-games of chance, bookmaking and
betting, prize competitions, and lotteries—and only when some stake, either money or


## p. 4786 (#222) ###########################################

4786
24 November
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
money's worth, is involved. If no such consideration is present, the legislation does not
apply. The new draft legislation is not concerned with where a game of chance is played, but
rather how it is played, and for what purpose. On this we have been fortunate to be able to
learn from experience in the United Kingdom, where loopholes in the 1960 Betting and
Gaming Act resulted in some 1000 gaming clubs coming into existence within a few years,
many of a commercial nature. The Bill makes it clear that commercial gambling remains
illegal in New Zealand.
The Minister of Internal Affairs is given discretion to license games of chance, prize
competitions, and lotteries conducted by societies for authorised purposes-both terms
being defined in clause 2. An authorised purpose is any charitable, philanthropic, cultural,
or party political purpose, or any other purpose that is beneficial to the community or any
section of it. The definition of a "society" in the Bill excludes any organisation of a
commercial nature. A major change made to clause 2 by the committee is the definition of
the term "authorised employee". This definition, together with the inclusion of the term in
the relevant clauses, will enable societies to use employees engaged for other work in
organising, for part of their time, gambling activities authorised under the Bill.
Part I deals with games of chance. The present Gaming Act merely states that all games
of chance are illegal, but makes no attempt to define what a game of chance is. Under the
provisions in the Bill all games of chance are legal unless they fall within the definition of
illegal games of chance set out in clause 3. Some members may be of the opinion that the
definition is unduly complex, but in drafting gaming legislation extreme caution must be
exercised to avoid the very loopholes that resulted in the undesirable experience of the
United Kingdom. I have no doubt that there are people who will take the opportunity to
profit from gambling by others, given only half a chance to do so. As a result of giving
explicit definition and meaning to an illegal game of chance, the concept of a common
gaming house and the complicated provisions of the present Act need no longer be retained,
but the prohibitions against organising or participating in illegal games of chance are
continued.
Under clause 8 the Minister is given power to grant licences to societies for conducting
games of chance that would otherwise be illegal, provided he is satisfied the money to be
raised is to be used for approved purposes. Any such licences will be operated under
regulations that will lay down conditions to ensure that the public interest is safeguarded.
The existing practice of societies conducting games of chance of a restrictive nature at fairs
and galas is authorised, subject to specified conditions being met. Amusement machines
with the prize being another opportunity to play the game or get your money back are also
authorised. However, care has been taken to prevent the emergence of machines commonly
known as "fruit machines" or "one-armed bandits". These machines are explicitly illegal
under the Bill, and I am sure all members, recognising the undesirable consequences
inherent in the operation of such machines, will welcome their continued prohibition.
Under Part II, the bookmaking provisions of the present Gaming Act are retained
largely unchanged. One change has been made, however, by deleting the mandatory prison
sentence upon a second or subsequent conviction for bookmaking-at the same time
substantially increasing the maximum fines for such offences.
Part III deals with prize competitions, which are a new concept in gaming legislation in
this country. At present there is a grey area concerning competitions that are not a lottery or
a game of chance, and the new provisions should remove that grey area. Clause 2 contains
the definition of a prize competition, and members will note this is one of the provisions that
the Statutes Revision Committee has improved. Competitions such as "How far will the car
travel on X litres of petrol?" and "Spot the ball" fall into this category. Such competitions
may be conducted by a society for authorised purposes, either under licence if the total value
of prizes exceeds $500 or subject to specified conditions in other cases, and as "house"
competitions in places of work, residence, or social gathering where the total value of prizes
does not exceed $50, and subject to the stipulated conditions being met.
Prize competitions and sales promotion schemes were the subject of most submissions
received by the select committee, and this part of the Bill received particularly careful
attention. In some submissions concern was expressed that sales promotion schemes would
generally be exempt from the provisions of the Bill. Members will note that the Statutes
Revision Committee has inserted a new clause making this very clear. I am fully in
agreement with the committee's view that this Bill, designed to control gambling, is not the
proper means of exercising restraint on commercial practices to promote trade. The courts
have held over many years that, for such sales promotion schemes to fall outside the


## p. 4787 (#223) ###########################################

24 November
4787
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
provisions of the Gaming Act, they must require an element of skill to avoid being classed as
a game of chance, not require any consideration for entry, and have the winners determined
other than by chance. This is the situation under the Bill.
The Trading Coupons Act 1931, which restricts the issue of trading coupons, is
unaffected by the Bill, and if it is considered desirable or necessary to introduce restraints on
sales promotion schemes I suggest that it should properly be done in commerce legislation.
Part IV of the Bill deals with lotteries-the term "raffle" as used in the present Act has
been dropped, although I have no doubt it will continue to form part of our vocabulary.
Members will note that the current licensing requirements for lotteries have been consider-
ably relaxed and that no licences for lotteries or prize competitions will be required unless
the aggregate value of prizes exceeds $500. As in the case of prize competitions, lotteries
may be conducted by societies for authorised purposes, either under a licence if the prizes
exceed $500 or subject to the stipulated conditions in other cases. "House" lotteries are also
permitted if the conditions are met and the prizes do not exceed $50 in the aggregate.
For smaller lotteries, at least, licensing seems to be regarded these days as an
unreasonable requirement, and I suspect it is ignored at least as frequently as it is observed.
We all know of office raffles and sweeps operated without a permit. Melbourne Cup sweeps,
for instance, are probably run in most places of work and are accepted as harmless diversions
without thought that they may be illegal. They clearly do no harm. To perpetuate a situation
in which the law is broken daily with the open consent of the community at large would be
irresponsible. The Bill recognises this, and in place of licensing proposes a number of
requirements that will have to be met by those conducting unlicensed lotteries and prize
competitions. In both cases, the conditions are kept to what is considered to be the minimum
to ensure that the public is reasonably protected and has the opportunity of ensuring that the
lotteries and prize competitions participated in are run fairly.
Part V is a major innovation-providing for the licensing of gaming promoters. Many
organisations find it extremely difficult to raise funds through the traditional voluntary
methods simply because they have insufficient manpower to devote to such time-consuming
activities—the Crippled Children's Society, paraplegics, and the blind, are three examples
that come readily to mind. The Bill has recognised this by providing for the licensing by the
courts of promoters who may be engaged to assist societies wishing to conduct larger prize
competitions and lotteries. The provisions in the Bill, while permitting the licensing of
promoters, also allow strict controls to be exercised over their operations to protect not only
the society engaging the promoter but also the public at large. It is proposed that further
conditions will be provided in the Gaming and Lotteries Regulations, which are currently
being drafted, and which will be necessary to give effect to the various licensing proposals
contained in the Bill.
As I have already mentioned in reference to clause 2, the Bill provides for persons
employed by non-commercial societies to conduct authorised gambling activities on behalf of
those societies. Such employees, termed "authorised employees" in the Bill, must be
principally employed for purposes other than conducting games of chance, prize competi-
tions, or lotteries on behalf of the society, and no additional remuneration by way of
commission is to be paid to them for conducting such activities. I am sure that these two
provisions will be welcomed by the very many community organisations for which fund
raising is essential to their very existence, and which at present have to rely entirely on the
voluntary efforts of their members to sell raffle tickets, run housie, etc. I am satisfied that the
provisions do not provide an opportunity for the promotion of organised gambling for
private profit by undesirable elements in our communities.
Part VI contains provision for the Minister of Internal Affairs to raise the various
monetary limits in the Bill by notice in the Gazette. Provision is also made for the Minister to
permit overseas prize competitions and lotteries to be conducted in New Zealand. To ensure
that the profits of gambling conducted in this country are devoted to purposes beneficial to
the community, no lottery or prize competition promoted overseas may be conducted within
New Zealand without such permission. I have no present intention of interfering with the
standard lotteries operated by Tattersalls, but I shall certainly look very carefully at any
other request from an overseas promoter that would compete with our national lotteries,
which are run for the benefit of community purposes in this country.
Members on both sides of the House will have witnessed the considerable growth of our
national lotteries since the inception of the Lottery Board of Control in 1962. In the
intervening 15 years, many millions of dollars have been distributed by the board to the
various distribution committees the welfare of the aged, welfare services, medical


## p. 4788 (#224) ###########################################

4788
24 November
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
research, scientific research, and other organisations such as the Queen Elizabeth the
Second Arts Council, the mountain and water safety committees, and the Historic Places
Trust. It would be true to say that the community as a whole has benefited significantly from
the proceeds of our lotteries. The organising and conducting of these lotteries over many
years without the merest whisper of malpractice is testimony to the honesty and integrity of
all those persons engaged in their operation. Consequently, the current provisions in the
Gaming Act are continued with little amendment in Part VII of the Bill.
The Bill proposes to change the name of the Lottery Board of Control to the New
Zealand Lottery Board, and our national lotteries will in future be known as New Zealand
lotteries to avoid confusion between national lotteries and other lotteries currently known as
raffles. In future, national lotteries and prize competitions, which it is proposed the Minister
shall be authorised to promote, may be conducted for special purposes as well as general
community purposes. The Statutes Revision Committee has included provision for the
Minister to determine the entitlement to minor prizes not exceeding $20 in value to be
determined otherwise than by means of a draw. This provision would enable the introduc-
tion of such innovations as "instant prizes", a method used very commonly and successfully
overseas, which has proved to be very popular with the general public.
Minor amendments are included to give the board greater freedom in investing its
funds, and a 5-year period is provided in which prizes may be claimed. Currently there is no
such restriction, but experience has shown that if a claim is not lodged within 5 years it is
unlikely that it ever will be. The proposal will be of considerable assistance to the
Department of Internal Affairs and the organiser of the New Zealand lotteries in finally
disposing of unclaimed prizes dating back to the old art unions, with their attendant
documentation, which causes serious storage problems and to which valid claims are
extremely unlikely to arise. The Bill also protects the name "Golden Kiwi", by which all
national lotteries are now known.
In Part VIII the provisions relating to criminal proceedings have been updated, and the
provision in section 79 of the present Act for the court to order that up to one moiety of a
fine be paid to the informer or person prosecuting has not been repeated. Part IX introduces
a code of gaming law based on traditional attitudes that gaming debts should not be
enforceable at law, which I feel is still the view of most New Zealanders.
Through a misunderstanding, some proposals considered by the Statutes Revision
Committee have been included as amendments proposed by the committee. The only change
in this part that should have been included is the new section 125A concerning the recovery
of stakes. The Supplementary Order Paper corrects the matter. As a result of the various
proposals contained in the Bill, particularly the freeing up of the need to obtain licences for
prize competitions and lotteries and the licensing of promoters, a need was seen to provide
for the appointment of inspectors of gaming. This is included in Part X.
I am satisfied that the Bill fulfils the two needs that caused the Government to include
this measure in its legislative programme-it updates what is in many respects an outdated
and archaic measure and now reflects the present attitude of most New Zealanders to
gambling. It also sets out the restrictions in a way that can be easily understood.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The Minister quite properly described this Bill as
important. I believe that it is. I believe, also, that the Minister was quite right in presenting it
as he did tonight, because it will affect every member of the House and many constituents.
The Bill changes the basic principle of legislating against gambling. The law we have
inherited is very strict, but has been enforced in a very lax way. As the Minister said, more
than half the smaller lotteries are illegal. Members on this side of the House support the Bill,
because we believe that the law should be clearly understood and should be realistic; but we
have an important proviso that we want to make very clear to the Minister, and we would
like an assurance from him tonight that his attitude is the same. We believe that, the law
having been liberalised to a reasonable degree, it should now be enforced.
Following liberalisation of the law in Great Britain in 1960, professional organisations
moved in and, under cover of being charitable bodies, managed to set up over 1000 major
gambling institutions and casinos and the like. Britain has had to suffer for that move,
because they cannot now be eradicated. We on this side of the House do not believe that
such institutions are a social advantage. The Department of Internal Affairs and the police
have looked on gambling with a somewhat benign and sometimes blind eye, and some clear
examples of illegal gambling have been ignored. That attitude will now change, and it should
be made clear that the law will be strictly enforced.
We should also have an assurance-in the Committee stage at least-that the Minister

2. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Education: Does he envisage the

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Yes, I envisage the continuation of the

Mr Elliott: Does the Government intend to move more rapidly towards greater internal

Hon. L. W. GANDAR: No. Some subjects are internally assessed for obvious reasons,

continue with a balance of internal assessment and external examination.

Accident Compensation for Sportsmen Overseas
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Labour: Has any considera-

tion been given to including sportsmen and women officially representing their sport

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Consideration has been given in the past to

Wanganui Computer Centre
9. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert), on behalf of Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY Hender-
son), asked the Minister of Justice: Can he confirm that local authorities are now expected to
supply to the Wanganui Computer Centre extensive details of those prosecuted for minor
offences, including the failure to register dogs and the infringement of building bylaws, both
before and after conviction, and will he advise the extent of the details required and if any
assistance will be provided for the paper work involved?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The local authorities initiating prosecu-
tions have been asked to supply personal information about defendants in the same form as
has been given for many years by the Police and the Ministry of Transport. The information,
which includes the sex, date of birth, and place of birth of the defendant, is used to assist in
the identification of the defendant in the Wanganui Computer Centre system and to
maintain the integrity of the record in that system. The honourable member will be aware of
the concern to ensure that the information stored in the Wanganui Computer Centre system
is accurate so that it may be used for future law enforcement purposes. There has been no
insistence that this information be provided to registrars, and if local authorities are unable
to provide it this does not in any way prevent them bringing the prosecution. However, the
availability of this information will assist courts should they have to take enforcement action
to collect any fine that might be imposed, and as most of that fine is paid to the local
authority there is ultimate benefit to the authority if it is able to supply the data.
Hon. W. W. Freer: What possible purpose is served by imposing this restriction or
demand upon local bodies for such minor offences?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is entirely over to the local authorities whether proceed-
ings are initiated.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does this indicate that there will be variation of the application of
this scheme through the country, with some local bodies co-operating and others not?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: As with other prosecutions, it is for the initiating authority to
make up its mind about it, not the Department of Justice.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Will the local authorities that co-operate have the names of persons
placed in the computer files, but in areas where authorities do not co-operate the people who
could be offenders will not have their names placed in the computer files?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I do not catch the implication in the member's question. Let
me repeat the answer. "The local authorities initiating prosecutions have been asked to
supply personal information about defendants . . ." They have been asked, but it is entirely
over to them whether they do it or do not do it. As I said in the original answer, the
availability of the information will assist courts should they have to take enforcement action
to collect any fine that might be imposed, and as most of that fine is paid to the local
authority there is ultimate benefit to the authority if it is able to supply the data. It is a matter
entirely for a local authority to supply the data, and it is to the authority's benefit eventually
to do so.

doing so. It was favoured by the Maoris in the Bay of Plenty and East Coast areas. It is not
the Captain Cooker, which is a much leaner and rather razor-backed specimen.
Mr Wetere: Are any figures available of the number in New Zealand at present?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: The number is not known, but it is understood that some
specimens are held in captivity in the Waikato area. I believe there are two at the Hilldale
Game Farm near Hamilton.

Maori Infant Mortality Rates

statement in Time magazine of 22 November in which it is stated that Maori children "have
one of the highest infant-mortality rates in the world, and, according to Maori psychologist
Donna Awatere, one in every four dies before his first birthday", and, if so, can he say
whether this is correct?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Yes, I have seen the statement in Time
magazine. The statement is both incorrect and irresponsible. In 1975, the latest available
figures, the Maori infant mortality rate was 20.5 per thousand live births, not 250 as the
statement claims. From World Health Organisation statistics, a comparison of 61 countries
studied reveals that 21 countries, or 34 percent, have a lower infant mortality rate than
Maoris, and 40 countries, or 66 percent, have a higher mortality rate.
