BUSH WORKERS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Bush Workers Amendment
Bill be introduced. The Bill amends the Bush Workers Act 1945, which makes provision for
the safety and protection of bush workers. One of the industrial rights of all workers is the
right to a safe working environment. The Government has taken, and will continue to take,
active legislative steps to improve industrial safety in this and other industries. Earlier this
year we took the step of including the farming industry amongst those that are regulated by
safety legislation. We regard the safety and health of the workers as being the paramount
consideration in any industrial environment.
Bush work is of its very nature a dangerous activity, involving as it does tree-felling and
logging operations, and the Government is concerned at the high number of fatal and serious
accidents occurring in this work. Fatal accidents alone have averaged 12 for each of the past
5 years. In comparison with other industries that rate and the injury severity rate are
extremely high. We are convinced that one of the main factors, if not the main factor,


## p. 4801 (#237) ###########################################

25 November
4801
Bush Workers Amendment Bill
contributing to those high rates is the wide-spread lack of training and supervision of bush
workers. Accordingly, in this relatively small amending Bill we have given prominence to
provisions requiring adequate instruction and supervision of workers. One of the major
innovations will be the requirement that employers appoint a safety supervisor where they
cannot themselves supervise any bush undertaking. This is parallel to the situation currently
in force under the Construction Act.
Protection against harmful noise is also dealt with. On the recommendation of the Noise
Advisory Committee, similar noise provisions are being inserted in all revised industrial
legislation. Other provisions of the Bill extend slightly the powers of inspectors, and, in line
with the Industrial Relations Act, require the keeping of wage records for 6 instead of 2
years. I shall be recommending to the House that the Bill be referred to the Labour
Committee for recess study. It is a short but important Bill which it is expected will go
further towards making the bush a safer place in which to work.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): The Labour Party welcomes any Bill that will assist in
protecting the lives and limbs of working people. As the Minister stated, bush workers have
an urgent need for such legislation. Their work involves them in an industry with one of the
highest, if not the highest, incidence of accidents and death in any industry in New Zealand.
I am very pleased that the Minister has brought the Bill before us. From a quick perusal, it
seems to cover the main requirements. As it is to be referred to a select committee it may be
possible to find ways and means of improving it, but I repeat that the Labour Opposition
welcomes its introduction.
Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast): I endorse the remarks made by the member for
Grey Lynn. Because of the type of work in which they are involved, bush workers, more
than any others, require protection. The Bill could also be extended to include those who
handle the timber after it leaves the bush and goes into the factories. It is only in recent years
that demands for safety devices have been placed on the bush workers, who in the main work
with sharp saws, axes, falling trees, breaking wires, and other hazards. The noise factor is
not as bad in the bush as it is in the sawmill. The present-day methods of transporting timber
and getting it on to the roads does present a noise problem. I am pleased that the Bill is to be
referred to a select committee. Indeed, I believe Opposition members are as pleased as
Government members that the measure is about to be introduced and that it will be enacted.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Bush Workers Amendment
Bill be referred to the Labour Committee, and that the proceedings of the committee during the
hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news media.
Motion agreed to.
ROAD USER CHARGES BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Road User
Charges Bill be introduced. The Bill I propose to introduce into the House today follows in
the wake of one of the most significant policy initiatives made in the transport area in the last
decade. The measures contained in the Bill, along with those dealing with the relaxation of
the limits on road competition with rail passed by Parliament last September, form a package
developed by the Government after very exhaustive deliberations over the last 2 years. The
culmination of those investigations was announced in this year's Budget: on the one hand
there was to be an easing of the limits on road/rail competition, and on the other the basis of
heavy motor-vehicle taxation was to be fundamentally revised. The first of the measures was
put into effect on 1 October this year. This Bill gives effect to the second step in the policy.
As the Government pointed out in July, the measures announced in the Budget on the
new road taxation system for heavy vehicles and the forward roading programme demons-
trate the Government's awareness, as stated in its election manifesto, of the need to put
roading finance on an assured basis and to put roading taxation on a more economic basis.
The revision of the system of heavy motor vehicle taxation is an extremely complex and
involved issue-and I believe all honourable members know that to be true. I intend,
therefore, in introducing this legislation, first to go back to the basics and to explain the
Government's intentions in so radically revising the taxation system. Having explained the
policy intention, I shall now explain how the policy is to be implemented through the Bill
now before the House and the Bill I seek the approval of the House to introduce.
Basically, the intention is to restructure road taxation as an instrument of transport
policy rather than allowing the present system of unrelated revenue-collection measures to


## p. 4802 (#238) ###########################################

4802
25 November
Road User Charges Bill
continue. The major objective in doing so is to ensure that each type of vehicle is taxed
according to the costs it imposes on the roading system. In simple terms, this means that the
Government intends that in future the user-pays principle will become more clearly evident
in the financing of road construction and road maintenance.
As I pointed out at the time of the Budget, there are three reasons for restructuring the
heavy vehicle taxation system. First, it will assist in establishing more economic price
relativities between road and rail transport. The charging of more accurate roading costs will
provide a financial incentive to all road operators to economise on the use of the roads in one
way or another, and the revenue from road taxation can be adjusted to match roading
expenditure attributable to the very heavy vehicles. The Government announced in the
Budget that the revision of heavy motor-vehicle taxation would be introduced from 1 April
1978.
I now turn to the Bill itself. Its aim is to establish the new taxation system. The key
element is contained in a distance charge calculated according to the weight of the vehicle
and the distance that vehicle travels. The charge will be made in the form of the compulsory
purchase of a special licence for each vehicle. The Bill describes the types of licence that
vehicle operators will have to purchase according to the size and use of the vehicle.
Procedures are established whereby the cost of the licences can be calculated according to
the amount of wear and tear each individual vehicle causes to our roading system. Measures
are also included to provide for the collection of charges and the actual enforcement of the
system. There will be two basic categories of licence-a distance licence and a time licence.
Except for certain exemptions from the system, vehicles will be required to have one of these
licences. Which licence will be required will depend on the type of vehicle and the purpose
for which that vehicle is actually used.
At this stage, I shall make only a brief comment on the computation of charges. The
charge for the distance licence will be calculated with the assistance of an accurate reading of
the distance the vehicle travels. The accurate reading will be obtained from the required
fitting of a measuring device—a hubodometer-to a non-retractable wheel on the left-hand
side of the vehicle. I shall go into much greater detail on this during the second reading stage,
and will fully describe the details of this licensing system and the actual calculation of the
charges.
For the benefit of members, however, I must point out that this is a completely separate
system from either the annual licence that every motor vehicle is required to have or the
distance limit which governs what we call road-rail competition. Licences will be purchased
at post offices and will be paid for in advance. Operators of vehicles affected by the
provisions of this Bill will be responsible for displaying the appropriate sticker on the
windscreen of their vehicles with all necessary details supplied and correct, and for the
installation of the hubodometers. The Bill contains provisions for certain penalties to be
imposed on both the driver of the vehicle and the owner responsible, if these requirements
are not met. I sense that, in view of the debate we had earlier on railways, the Opposition
will agree with me that this provision was necessary to enable the railways system to operate
as we would wish.
I should like to comment briefly on the effect the measures contained in this Bill will
have on the industry as a whole and on the operating costs of the individual owner. The
Government has given an undertaking that the total taxation burden on the road transport
industry will not increase as a result of revising the basis of the taxation system. This
undertaking will be honoured. However, the amount of tax the operator will have to pay is
likely to be affected. Because inequalities inherent in the present piecemeal system will be
rectified, a result of the new measures will be that operating costs to some vehicle owners
will rise while for others they will fall.
As I have said before in this House, evidence shows that those in the private car field
and the operator with small trucks have been paying more than their share towards the
damage to our roads, whereas the heavy operator has been paying less than his share. At the
same time, I am mindful that those who use heavy vehicles in certain parts of New
Zealand—parts of Southland, the King Country, and Northland in particular-will be
affected, but there is room in the Bill to adjust anomalies which could exist.
As I said at the beginning, this new system is designed to place a more realistic burden
for the cost of providing the nation's roads on those who cause the greatest damage and the
most wear. In the course of many discussions between Government officials-I do not know
just how many discussions, but they have certainly spread over 18 months--and representa-
tives of the transport industry, concern has been expressed over a liquidity problem which

4803

could arise in the industry around the time the first payments for licences are due—that is,

In response to this expression of concern, the Government has temporarily relaxed the
present taxation burden on the road transport industry-and this has seldom been
mentioned in the last few weeks-by reducing by 50 percent the heavy traffic fees due for
payment by 1 December 1977 for the quarter ended 28 February 1978. Also, the appropriate
regulations will be amended shortly to remove the requirement to pay heavy traffic fees from
the end of February next year, a full month before the distance charge provisions of this Bill
come into force. It is estimated that in taking this action the Government will be able to help
improve the cash-flow position of the industry to the extent of between, say, $5 million and
$6 million; in other words, to put it more simply, they will have $5 million or $6 million in
their pockets before they come to the starting line, which is April Fool's Day next year.
An additional factor that will smooth the introduction of the new system is the phasing-
in process. The charges will not be made at the full amount until 1 April 1980. For the benefit
of those who have stated something different, both publicly and in the newspapers, I
emphasise that the full charges will not be payable until 1 April 1980, by which date sales
tax-and how many times have we talked about road tax while sales tax has not been
mentioned?—on these vehicles will have been reduced progressively from the present 40
percent to 10 percent in line with another of the Government's 1977 Budget announcements.
As I have said before, total tax payments by the industry for each year will not be
greater than the amount that would have been payable had the present taxation on the road
industry system been continued. The Government is doing all it can to introduce the new
system of heavy motor vehicle taxation in an orderly and sensible manner. The long-term
effect will be a much greater degree of rationality in the way funds are obtained to provide
and maintain New Zealand's roading system. I do not need to stress the absolutely vital
nature of our transport system and our roading network to the New Zealand economy.
A move in the direction we are taking this morning in introducing this Bill has been in

should somebody be unduly hurt. After all, the Minister of Finance is not bound by any
Budget which he brings into Parliament if he finds someone is being unduly hurt and
Parliament believes that person should be relieved of a burden. That could be the case here.

that the railways will lose all the traffic under the 150-kilometre limit.
The Bill tries to assess a reasonably fair charge, across the board, for heavy road usage.
Many people know that as we changed to bulk milk tankers, the effect of heavy road
transport on second-class, or class 2, country roads became apparent. The Opposition
objects to the suggestion that the industry is being asked to pay an excessive figure ahead of
usage. One does not have to go too far back in time to realise that the industry changed
dramatically in the past 10 or 12 years from petrol power to diesel power, although a
significant amount of petrol is still used in the cartage industry.
The tax has always been paid 3 months in advance, and in most cases it is probably
nearer to 5 months. If one bought petrol on 1 January, filled the bulk tank, used that through
January and half way through February, and refilled the tank, at the end of the March
quarter a claim was lodged for a refund of petrol tax. Speaking from personal experience, by
the time that was processed it was about 5 or 6 weeks before you got your cheque. Now
operators are being asked to pay ahead on an estimate for a month or 3 months, and if they
go beyond that they will buy a supplementary licence. The member for Timaru mentioned
hubodometers. The key to this is that there is one for each vehicle, and if it goes on the left-
hand side-
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: On a non-retractable wheel.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Yes, and I hope it is a non-spinning wheel. Many operators have
hubodometers on vehicles now-and it does not matter whether the vehicle goes backwards
or forwards, the unit keeps on registering; one cannot subtract by reversing. A finer point is
that if the unit is on the left-hand front wheel the operator can choose to drive round a
paddock in an anti-clockwise direction, and register a lower milage because of the
hubodometer being on the left.
Hon. C. C. A. McLachlan: I hadn't thought of that one.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: One has to think of these things when one is getting as hard up as
some farmers are. Speakers so far have overlooked a significant factor in this legislation: a
marked advantage to the light commercial vehicle—the four- five- and probably six-ton
type. An added advantage is that the Bill provides for a legitimate claim for off-road
running, which has always been a bone of contention. I remember that several years ago,
when I was in charge of the Transport Department, we used to worry about coloured petrol;

We admit that the Bill is not perfect. Inevitably, anomalies come out as one works one's

exactly the same revenue as it receives at present, although the revenue will be reallocated,

The member for Heretaunga talked about the lazy axle, the dummy axle, the self-
balancing one. If an odometer is on the front wheel, one will not have slippage if one is in the
field, and add some more in the paddocks or anywhere greasy. The key is in the schedule to
the Bill-it is the charge paid for the vehicle whether loaded or unloaded, whether the
dummy axle is on the road or not on the road. It is based on a calculated assessment of total
loading probability. Obviously, a beer tanker, even if it is calculated at about 55 percent or
60 percent, will get only one-way loading, unless it carts water back to make the beer.
Specialised vehicles would suffer detrimentally.
An opposite view taken by the agricultural industry is that the Bill will encourage better
utilisation of vehicles by two-way loading; a bonus is given if a two-way load at an economic
rate is found. At the same time, I suggest respectfully to the member for Heretaunga, it will
not destroy the railway system; we cannot allow that. The Bill, although complex and
difficult, had to be brought into the House. Having made a decision about the 150-kilometre
limit-and heaven knows we have been mucking around with transport policy and what we
should do about it for at least 4 years to my knowledge-this is at least a genuine attempt to
try to meet the needs of the industry today, and to apportion the revenue fairly to the
National Roads Board.
I was called Pete the Ripper by the member for Heretaunga a moment ago. I take no
exception to that, because I have yet to hear a complaint from anyone in a district in which I
have closed a railway line. I was told that all the roads would break up. However, every
week I drive up and down the Roxburgh State Highway 8, and the road is in better condition
now than it has ever been. Improvements are taking place, and the roads board will maintain
the areas on which there is increased heavy traffic. It is a fundamental, and, indeed, a moral
requirement of the Bill that the user will pay, and the roads board has to maintain the road if
heavy traffic uses it. Equally, the railways will continue carrying bulk and specialised traffic,
for which they are suited, even below the 150-kilometre limit. I welcome the Bill.

Hon. W. L. YOUNG: (Minister of Works and Development): I support the Bill, and I

part of the package was the extension of the road operators' limits to 150 kilometres, giving

possible in the past. At the same time, it was recognised that the operators of heavy trucks
were not paying their fair share for wear and tear on roads and the stresses on bridges. The
Bill sets out to correct that and to provide relief to the users of lighter vehicles.
The member for Heretaunga referred to the forward planning of the National Roads
Board. It is true that the board carries out forward planning over a 3-year period, but while
planning it has never had an assurance that the funds required to implement its plans would
be available. The Bill means that not only will the National Roads Board be able to plan for
a 3-year programme, but it will also be able to plan with an assurance from the Government
that the funds for its planned programme will be available. Opposition members will know
that because of the lack of sufficient funds, many of the projects commenced by the National
Roads Board take up to 3 years to complete. The uncertainty that has plagued the board in
the past will now be removed.

chairman of the board. The question has been raised of where district roads councils fit into
the pattern. They will follow the role they have adopted in the past and make recommenda-
tions to the board, and the board will consider those recommendations when setting its
priority.
I consider that the most important provision in the Bill is clause 36, on programming. It
places responsibility on the board to have its works programme completed before 31
December each year. Taking into account the recommendations of the district roads
councils, the board will be able to provide details of a balanced programme earlier than it has
been able to in the past, so that everybody will be able to see where he is going. Working
with this earlier advice, the district roads councils and other bodies will be able to undertake
the details and the arrangement of final programmes much earlier than they can at present.
With that type of background, I believe that Opposition members who consider the Bill
in detail will realise that it is a forward step and that it provides for the utilisation of our
roads in a responsible manner. Those who are placing the strain on the roads will pay for the
stress they cause, and those who do not place any strain on the roads will be relieved of their
present burden. On that basis, and because the Bill is part of a package deal providing for a
more efficient transport system, I welcome its introduction.

MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Municipal
Corporations Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a small Bill of two operative clauses. The
principal of these is clause 2, which implements a Budget announcement and recognises the
importance of thermal insulation in the Government's insulation policy. Clause 3 makes a
minor consequential amendment, which I shall explain shortly.
Clause 2 makes it mandatory for every council to make bylaws by 1 April 1978 requiring
new residential buildings to be provided with thermal insulation to reduce heat losses. The
bylaws will have their effect through each council's building permit procedure. Bylaws made
by local authorities for this purpose will require the approval of the Minister of Energy
Resources, and provision is made in clause 2 for his action in case of default by councils. The
Minister has indicated to me that his approval will be given to bylaws requiring levels at least
comparable to those produced by the Standards Association committee. The standard of
insulation required is not specified in the legislation itself. Standards must be flexible to take
account of developments in building materials and methods, and in insulation techniques. It
is expected that most, if not all, municipalities will apply through their bylaws the standard
recently developed by committee of the Standards Association of New Zealand, which
worked with Government departments, local authorities, and the building industry.
The home insulation loan assistance scheme, which began in 1975, has to date assisted in
the insulation of over 50 000 homes. However, only a very small percentage of these have
been new homes. About an equal number of homes have been insulated outside the scheme,
but here again the new homes have been in the minority. As a consequence, only 20 percent
or so of new homes currently have an acceptable standard of insulation installed in walls.
This is of concern, because in practice walls can be insulated only at the time a house is built.
However, the matter will be rectified for the future by the enactment of this legislation. To
help meet the cost of complying with this standard the loan scheme has been extended,
following the Budget, to provide an interest-free, 4-year loan of up to $400. The cost of the
insulation will be recovered by home owners through reduced energy bills.
The Government's proposals were discussed in principle with the Municipal Associa-
tion, and I am pleased to record the association's endorsement of the objects of the Bill.
Indeed, at its 1975 conference the association passed a remit asking the Government to
implement legislation to institute some form of mandatory insulation of buildings. I am
informed that the association's technical advisers are confident in the capacity of local
authorities to undertake this additional responsibility.
Clause 3 makes a consequential amendment arising from the Land Valuation Proceed-
ings Amendment Act 1977, the effect of which is simply to place the jurisdiction in land
valuation matters, previously exercised by the Administrative Division of the Supreme
Court, with the land valuation tribunals established by that Act.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): As the Minister stated, this Bill gives effect to a Budget
provision and is a logical development in the home insulation scheme introduced by the
previous Labour Government as a valuable conservation measure. To be truly effective, not
only ceilings need to be insulated. As the Minister quite rightly pointed out, the logical time
for insulation is when the dwelling is being constructed. It is almost impossible to insulate
fully an existing dwelling of the normal type. I am surprised to learn that so few new
dwellings have been insulated since the energy crisis. The benefits of total home insulation
will flow both to the home owner and to the nation, which largely provides the sources of
energy.

Municipal Corporations Amendment Bill
The Minister pointed out that the Budget made provision for an interest-free loan of

insulating an ordinary average-sized new dwelling. Is there likely to be a gap between that
$400 loan and the actual cost? I see the Minister is shaking his head. I mention this because

Even though the $400 home insulation loan is interest free, it still has to be repaid over 4
years. However, most home builders will recognise the long-term benefit through savings in
energy costs.
I turn now to the phasing-in period. The Budget pointed out that it will not be easy to
define bylaws or requirements for all types of buildings that will be covered by this
legislation. In quite rightly pointing out the difficulties associated with the scheme, the
Budget said: "Arrangements will be made to phase in over a number of years those forms of
construction which cannot immediately comply with the desired insulation standard. The
Government is prepared to sponsor a joint programme of research with producers of
products which cannot at present comply with this standard."
The Minister said he had had discussions about this with the Municipal Association.
What difficulties does he envisage? This measure is due to come into effect on 1 April, and
councils will be required in the interim to make the necessary bylaws and send them to the
Minister for approval. They will have difficulty in knowing what type of buildings and
insulating material will be covered by the Bill, and that could pose some real problems,
because councils must ensure that their bylaws cover all types of buildings. Does the Minister
intend his department or the Ministry of Energy Resources to formulate guidelines or model
bylaws as a pattern for councils? Some of the smaller councils will have great difficulty in
determining the type of insulation required for buildings.
The Budget mentioned a research programme. That should assist in the orderly
development of acceptable materials for an insulation programme. How is the research
developing? How will the results of that research be used? Generally, the Opposition
welcomes the Bill, because it will be of benefit to home builders, and in the long term the
insulation of homes will pay for itself through the conservation of energy.
Dr WALL (Porirua): The Minister has spoken about standard specifications, and the
Bill provides for bylaws to be altered in accordance with variations in standards. One of the
difficulties about putting such a requirement into legislation is that changes alter the effect of
that legislation. Which standards are referred to in subsection (3) of the proposed new
section 387c in clause 2? Are those standards sufficiently flexible and comprehensive to deal
with the two main variables-the climate, and the availability of different building materials?
The insulation needed in Kerikeri is vastly different from the insulation needed at Mt. Cook.
Obviously a building that has sarking, brick, and paper has very much greater thermal
insulation than a building made solely of dwangs and paper, with a concrete wall. A roof that
is fully sarked with paper, felt, and concrete tiles is a very different proposition from a roof
made of corrugated iron over paper and wire. It would be quite unjust, merely for the sake
of complying with regulations, to require people who have gone to considerable expense in
constructing an intrinsically sound roof to expend the same amount on insulation as someone
who had built to minimal standards. Will the new standards be sufficiently flexible to allow
for differences in construction, and the development of new insulating methods? Innovations
in building materials could result in thermal insulation, and unless there is provision for
variations in the quality or type of materials the standards could rapidly become out of date.
Also, the building industry would quickly come into ill repute.
Will an intelligent appraisal of requirements be made; or, if local bodies have to make
the decisions, will they be given guidance by way of technical assistance, particularly with
variable requirements and building materials as they relate to climate? Has the Minister had
an assurance from local bodies that sufficient thought has been given to the bylaws to enable
councils in the Bay of Islands and Wallace County to pick a model bylaw off a shelf, knowing
that it will be absolutely tailored to meet their conditions, or will local bodies be required to
rush something through over the Christmas period when consultants are not readily
available, to have it ready before 1 April?

AGRICULTURE (EMERGENCY REGULATIONS CONFIRMATION) BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Agriculture
(Emergency Regulations Confirmation) Bill be introduced. This is an annual washing-up Bill,
which is introduced at about this time every year to validate and confirm regulations made
under the Agriculture (Emergency Powers) Act 1934. As with other Bills of a similar nature,
it is required so that regulations made under the Act do not expire at the close of the present
session of Parliament. This year the House is repealing validating Acts passed over the last
20 years. The Bill merely tidies up the Act.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
PRIMARY PRODUCTS MARKETING REGULATIONS CONFIRMATION BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Primary
Products Marketing Regulations Confirmation Bill be introduced. This Bill is similar to the
previous Bill, and will validate and confirm regulations made this year under the Primary
Products Marketing Act 1953. Sections 3 and 4 of the Primary Products Marketing Act
provide that all regulations made under the Act shall be laid before Parliament and shall
expire on the last day of the session in which they were made, except so far as they are
expressly validated or confirmed by Act of Parliament passed during that session. The Bill
does that.

taken place. Therefore, the unsatisfactory nature of the leases has protected the wildlife
refuge by chance.

only to Marlborough but to the whole of New Zealand because of its part in countrywide
ecological change, should have better protection than that afforded by the almost chance
leasing arrangement. A provision was included that the leasing arrangements should be
under the control of the Minister. However, I still view the matter with some concern,
because the intention is to provide a lease sufficiently wide for those leasing the area to make
it economic, and to clear out the noxious weeds that are becoming a problem to the rest of
the farming community, but are no problem to wildlife. If a sufficiently long lease is granted
to make it economic to carry out that sort of development it might be found, when some
more satisfactory arrangement is made about the care and supervision of the wildlife refuge,
that it is tied up with a lease that inhibits the transference of ownership or full control by the
responsible Government department.

main concern is the preservation of our ecological environment. We have provided that a
lease must be approved by the Minister, but I suggest that the Minister at some stage should
assure the House that no leases will be granted for such a long period or with such rights of
renewal as to inhibit in any way the proper organisation and control of the lagoons as a
national asset. It is at this stage that we can stop difficulties arising. The House would not be
well served unless it got a firm assurance from the Minister, on behalf of his department, that
there would be no inhibition of the transfer of those lagoons to a department that is capable
of preserving them properly in the national interest.

ROAD SAFETY COMMITTEE
Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): I am directed to present the report of the Road Safety
Committee for the year 1977. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. There are a couple
of matters that seem to be of importance, and worthy of comment. The committee has
functioned, as always, as a bipartisan one; as a result it has been able to view in a relatively


## p. 4819 (#255) ###########################################

25 November
4819
Road Safety Committee
dispassionate way many of the present problems associated with road safety. As chairman, it
is fitting that I should place on record the co-operation the committee has had from members
opposite, particularly the co-operation and assistance of the member for Timaru who, as is
well known in the House, is very experienced in these matters.
A matter of major concern that is brought out in the committee's report is the increase
in road fatalities this year. Fatalities have risen before, and the pattern fluctuates. So far this
year the fatal accident road toll stands at 600, which is 65 more than the figure at the
corresponding time last year. It is possible that the 1977 road toll will exceed that of 1974,
when the total figure was 676. Before that, in 1971, it peaked at 677. It is little consolation
that there have been years when the figures were even higher-I refer to what is called the
pre-seat-belt era in 1972 and 1973-when there were 713 and 843 deaths respectively.
However, despite fluctuations, the evidence from the trend that developed early this year is
that urgent action is required to meet a problem that is of growing concern to responsible
people.
It must be a major concern when 600 deaths have resulted from road accidents, despite
measures introduced over the years. The report explores the problem, and poses questions
about possible solutions. Proposals for increased penalties are mentioned, but the committee
has found that they are already pretty high, and that maxima are by no means generally
enforced.
With a road toll like this there is always great concern about the contribution made by
alcohol, and this year the committee considered numerous submissions based on the role it
plays.
The committee's view is that, whatever else can be done to improve matters, there
should be two major thrusts. The first major improvement will be to enable traffic officers to
spend more effective time on the roads. At present they seem to be too occupied with
administrative and other duties that remove them from their enforcement role. To achieve
this, it will be necessary not merely to relieve officers of those extraneous administrative
duties that they now discharge but also to simplify many prosecution and court procedures,
and others centring on blood alcohol testing. These and other matters are traversed in the
report.
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): Several major features are contained in the report
of the Road Safety Committee, and I urge that it be widely read and considered. The
committee considered in depth many recommendations, and spent long hours investigating.
Committee members are deeply indebted to all departmental officers who worked so long
and diligently with them on some worth-while evidence and recommendations. As the
chairman said, it has always been accepted that the Road Safety Committee is bipartisan; it
does the best it can with the submissions placed before it.
Pedestrian crossings came under consideration and the report states: "It was felt that
under the new regulations confusion could arise in the minds of pedestrians, especially the
elderly, as a result of the necessary judgment involved being left to the motorists." It was felt
that a return should be made to the old regulations in the meantime in order to avoid the
confusion that is occurring. We hope that the Minister of Transport will act upon that
recommendation without wasting too much time. It is also recognised that some amend-
ments to the law about pedestrian crossings are needed, and three recommendations have
been made accordingly.
The other issue that I found of tremendous interest was that of the drinking driver. The
Road Safety Committee has played a major part in publicising this problem, and the average
man in the street is starting to realise that drinking and driving should no longer be tolerated
as a purely social illness-it can be regarded as criminal. When we see the carnage and the
resulting distress and misery caused by the thoughtlessness of people who cannot handle
alcohol, I think we have to pay long and hard attention to finding remedies. That is why the
committee devoted considerable space to alcohol in this year's report.
I suggested an evidential breath testing system using a mechanical appliance to measure
a driver's blood alcohol content so that the medical profession would not be involved as
much as it is now. The committee thinks this would assist considerably in policing the law. A
device has yet to be found, and approved by the committee, but some worth-while
equipment is on the market. Members were able to look at some, to gauge its accuracy. It
could help in policing the law, and relieve the medical staff in hospitals of much of the
present tedium of testing blood samples. The idea is that the traffic officer should have the
equipment, which will be tested by scientists and technicians from time to time to ensure
accurate operation.

The man in the street has to be educated into realising that drinking and driving is no

IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Mr LUXTON (Piako): I am directed by the Labour Committee to present the report of
the committee on the Immigration Amendment Bill. The committee recommends that the
Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. I want to
explain the effects of some of the amendments made by the select committee after hearing
evidence. Amendments were made to clause 2, which deals with work permits, because
occasionally a person who enters New Zealand on a visitor's permit wishes, once in New
Zealand, to obtain a work permit from the Department of Labour. It will frequently be in
the interests of New Zealand, as well as of the person concerned, to grant that work permit,
as such a person can be expected to make inquiries about available work before he applies
for the permit-if it is not an offence to seek employment without first obtaining a work
permit. With this amendment, it will be an offence to obtain employment, or engage in
activities for gain or reward, without the consent of the Minister. That will be endorsed on
the permit. Clause 4, under which it is an offence to employ persons not holding work
permits, has been amended.
Most of the evidence presented to the committee was on this clause. The amendments
now make it an offence for an employer to employ or to continue to employ, a person if he
knows—rather than has reason to know-that the person is not entitled to work. Secondly, it
is made clear also that it is an offence to continue to employ and not just to engage, if the
employer knows the person is not entitled to work. As the clause was worded previously, an
employer would not have committed an offence in continuing to employ a person if the
relevant information had been obtained only after he had engaged that person. Thirdly, the
amendment provides that it is the employer who may be prosecuted for the offence and not
one of his servants, such as the foreman or supervisor who might be responsible for engaging
staff. Fourthly, the amendment makes it clear that this clause applies only to persons
engaged after the Act comes into force. For example, an employer would not commit an
offence if he knowingly continued to employ someone who was in New Zealand without the
requisite authority, if that person had been working for him before this section of the Act
came into force.
Clause 5 deals with the deportation of prohibited immigrants. One amendment results
from a drafting oversight in the original Bill. Without the change, it would not have been
possible to enforce the deportation from New Zealand of a person who had been ordered to
be deported as the result of conviction on a criminal offence. It was thought that the Minister
of Immigration would be in a better position than the Minister of Finance to assess whether it
would be more fitting for the deportee to pay the whole or part of the expenses connected


## p. 4821 (#257) ###########################################

25 November
4821
Immigration Amendment Bill
with his or her deportation from New Zealand.
Clause 6 deals with appeals to the Minister against deportation, and again there was a
drafting oversight in the original Bill. Clause 6 is concerned only with appeals against
deportation for immigration offences, whereas clause 22(5) is concerned with the deporta-
tion of persons convicted of criminal offences. It is not feasible for people in both categories
to be covered by the same appeal provisions.

Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): The Opposition believes that the Bill should be sent back to
the select committee. It is an important Bill, because it introduces two entirely new concepts
in immigration, and those two new concepts need thorough examination before we proceed.
Clause 4 appears to intrude on the civil rights of employers. It should go back to the
committee, because everybody who made submissions complained about the lack of time
they had had to prepare those submissions. The National Council of Women pointed out
that the time allowed for presenting submissions expired 2 days before copies of the Bill were
available from the Government Printer. The council said it was impossible to do a good job
on the Bill because of the shortage of time.
Another group said that when controversial legislation concerning civil liberties was
introduced, and when only a fortnight was allowed for the preparation of submissions-the
reference was to a previous Bill-the situation was impossible. It was stated that the more
time allowed for people to prepare their submissions, the more helpful their comments and
suggestions would be.
Neither the Minister of Immigration nor the Minister of Labour attended the select
committee hearings. I appreciate that probably they both had urgent public business
elsewhere, but on such an important Bill it would have been preferable to have one of the
Ministers at the committee hearings. We saw one or two new faces from the Government
back benches at the hearings. They were not regular attenders of Labour Committee
hearings, and did not appear to appreciate the work carried out by the committee on which
they were sitting. One Government member even asked questions on the wrong submis-
sions; it seemed that he was attending the wrong select committee. That was a poor
demonstration in a responsible select committee considering important legislation. In
addition, the committee had to consider the Bill in a very limited time, and, as a result, heard
the submissions rapidly and rather vaguely.
We consider it imperative that the Bill be referred back to the select committee for more
careful examination; it could be polished up considerably. Some people wanted to make
submissions on clause 4, but found they could not do so because of the lack of time.
Clause 4 provides for penalties to be imposed on an employer who knows that someone
in his employ has contravened the immigration regulations. That is a most important
departure from any other provision in civil rights legislation. In no other field of law except
industrial law is an employer liable for his employee's conduct. He can employ a bigamist, an
illegal bookmaker, or someone who has committed an offence under the Customs Act,
without being subject to any penalty. Indeed, the employer has no right to take any action
against such a person, or to sack an employee who has committed an offence under the
criminal code. However, under this Bill, the employer will become a law enforcement
officer. If he knows that a person in his employ is an illegal immigrant, and he takes no
action to sack him, he becomes subject to a fine. In other words, the employer will become a
vigilante. We object to that provision. The work place is established for a specific productive
process, and has nothing to do with the enforcement of the criminal or civil code of law. The
main purpose of an employer in industry is to employ men to operate his plant and carry out
the productive process. Why should the National Government impose upon an employer an
obligation in one sector of the criminal and civil law, despite his own increase of activity, and
say that he must carry out that obligation under threat of penalty?
It is important that the Bill be referred back to the select committee so that clause 4 can
be evaluated properly. The employers are concerned about it. Indeed, they obtained a legal
opinion, and their lawyer wrote to the select committee saying that in his opinion the
wording was bad.
The National Government is rushing the measure through the House-that is our main


## p. 4822 (#258) ###########################################

4822
25 November
Immigration Amendment Bill
objection. It should be referred back to the select committee so that it can be made into a
much better Bill. To me, it seems to say: "I, as the Minister of Immigration in charge of the
immigration division, have failed completely to administer my portfolio efficiently, and now
I want employers throughout the country to do the job that the immigration division should
be doing.'
The Bill is an admission by the Minister of Immigration that he has failed in his job, and
he is trying to coerce or force employers to act as vigilantes in this sector of the law. The
employer is not subject to any penalty for employing a criminal, but if he employs an illegal
immigrant he will be subject to legal penalty. That is why the Bill should be referred back to
the select committee, so that it can be examined thoroughly and a much better measure can
be reported back to the House.

select committee. That sort of misinterpretation of what happened in the committee was
typical of the whole speech of the member for Grey Lynn.
I am pleased that the New Zealand Employers Federation, which made submissions,
nas stated categorically that it is now satisfied there is no conflict between this Bill and the
Race Relations Act. I quizzed the federation's representative at some length on this because
of the irresponsible statement made by a member of the federation at the time the Bill had its
first reading. I asked the federation's representative whether his organisation had made it
clear to the news media that the original statement had been inaccurate. He said it had not
done so, and I asked him if he would undertake to make a statement to the news media. His
reply was that, if the media did not choose to publish the contents of the federation's
submissions, he would make a special statement to the media to clear up the inaccuracies of
the original statement. I raise this, because I have seen no such retraction in the press, and
no attempt by the media to publish the contents of the submissions from the Employers
Federation which cleared up that matter.
Two important steps are covered in the Bill, the first being that the Minister is
empowered to exercise a discretion in favour of those who have been found guilty of an
immigration offence and therefore are at risk of being deported by the court. This provides
an additional and more flexible process, whereby someone who has found himself in conflict
with our immigration laws may make an appeal to the Minister, even though the court has
found him guilty. Some people making submissions argued that that discretion should be in
the hands of the court, and that the adversary system of court argument would better bring
out the facts in some immigration matters. But it was clear from the evidence that we were
discussing people who are not New Zealanders by birth, people with language problems and
cross-cultural conflicts. Sometimes it would not be advantageous to them to go through the
adversary court system, with lawyers and legal arguments they cannot understand if they do
not speak English. Rules about hearsay evidence would apply in court, and so on. All these
difficulties are removed if the appeal is to the Minister, who has complete flexibility, who can
look at a case with all its nuances and overtones, and without any of the restrictions or
limitations imposed at court hearings. That part of this Bill is a major improvement.

Immigration Amendment Bill
Clause 4, which places a new onus on employers, was the subject of many submissions. I
was surpised at the consistency with which many of those who made submissions completely
misunderstood the Government intention. The member for Auckland Central still does not

legally entitled to after the passing of the legislation.

surprised at the number of people who misunderstood the Bill's intentions, and it has to be

various parts of the Bill to make quite clear what was always intended. Because submissions
to the committee were often made on the basis of misunderstandings, the matters contained
in them are used incorrectly if they are used as an argument that the Bill should not proceed.

their visas. I hope that all employers in Auckland will take note of their federation's attitude,
particularly some of those with whom I am in daily contact, who are continuing to encourage

Commonwealth-Establishment of Common Fund
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What
positive steps have been taken by the Government to follow up the Prime Minister's support
at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' conference in June for the establishment of a
common fund?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Following the
Commonwealth Prime Ministers' conference in London last June, New Zealand participated
in discussions on the common fund with developed countries, including those held under
OECD auspices in Paris. This was with a view to reaching a common position in preparation
for the resumed negotiating conference on a common fund. New Zealand is participating in
these negotiations, which commenced on 7 November and will conclude on 2 December.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Has there been any change in any of the interested departments in
the priority accorded consideration of the common fund since June?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The honourable gentleman said "interested depart-
ments". Does he mean the departments of the New Zealand Government?
Hon. W. W. Freer: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Department of Trade and
Industry.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: No. There has been no difference that I know of.
The Cabinet economic committee has had a series of reports over the months since the
UNCTAD conference in Nairobi. These come forward regularly. So far as I know, there has
been no difference of opinion between the two departments. The position of the New
Zealand Government is that we have been prepared to go along with a group B proposal,
providing group B can get agreement. Once we see the shape of the proposal we can make

our decision.

Immigration-Permanent Residence Refusal
3. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Immigration: Why has he refused to
grant Mr Gopal Krishna, a maths and science teacher at Waitara High School, permanent
residence in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Mr Gopal Krishna has not been granted
permanent residence in New Zealand because it is not our policy to recruit skilled staff from
developing countries more in need of that skill than we in New Zealand are. Mr Krishna had
an application for permanent entry declined at the beginning of 1976. He then applied for
authority to visit New Zealand for the purpose of obtaining future employment, which
application was also declined. He applied for authority to make a 1-month non-working visit
to New Zealand for the purpose of touring the country in the course of returning to India
from Fiji. Following his arrival in New Zealand Mr Krishna approached a number of
secondary schools throughout the country, in contravention of the conditions of his entry
authority and in full knowledge that his application to work or remain in New Zealand would
not be approved.
Mr T. J. Young: Is recruiting going on around the world at present for maths and
science teachers to come to New Zealand while we are sending this one away?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I can deny that recruiting is going on around the world. New
Zealand is a signatory to the 1976 World Employment Agreement, which requires that we
refrain from recruiting skilled staff from developing countries which have greater need of
that skill than we have. We adhere to that agreement, and the recruiting that is going on is
restricted to countries that are fully developed and have a surplus of skills in that particular
area.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that in the last week a science teacher in
Hamilton, who is from overseas, has been granted residency in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I cannot positively confirm that—a number of such applications are
approved each day-but the teaching of maths and science at secondary school level is
certainly a skilled occupation, and providing the person is under the age of 45, meets the
other requirements, and comes from a developed country, he will almost certainly be given
permanent residence.

6. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: What is the best estimate

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): The effect of the Federation of
Labour's ban upon New Zealand exports to Chile cannot be quantified, as many potential
exporters have sought other markets because of the ban, and Chilean importers have
undoubtedly turned to other suppliers.
Mr Brill: Can the Minister give figures covering exporters with a history of sales to
Chile, excluding further potential exporters who might have come in if the trade ban had not
been applied?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Until the year ended June 1975 New Zealand's major export
to Chile was skim-milk powder. Exports dropped from a peak of $10.9 million f.o.b. in the
year ended June 1974 to nil in the year ended June 1976. However, the Dairy Board has
pointed out that when the Allende Government was overthrown the new Government
discontinued purchases of skim-milk powder, and therefore the loss of that trade cannot be
attributed to the FOL ban, but my understanding is that the new Government is now
reinstating a similar scheme. However, it is simply not possible, by going back into old
trading history, to be sure that that pattern would have continued.
Mr Malcolm: Has the ban been applied only by the FOL or has it received support from

Party?

two factories in the Hutt Valley. Workers are suspended as a result of routine testing and
before any risk to their health occurs. The number of suspensions is an indication of the care
with which the supervision of lead process workers is undertaken in those factories where
exposure to lead fumes and dust is known to be present. This concentration of workers at
risk is because one of the two factories involved produces 65 percent of all the lead batteries
and 100 percent of all the heavy industrial batteries used in New Zealand. Also, the number
of firms engaged in lead processing, the number of persons under supervision, and the
number of examinations are greater in the Hutt health district than in any other health
district.

Auckland Supreme Court-Delays
19. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Justice: In view of the
fact that the Royal Commission on the Courts has been given an extension of 6 months in
which to complete its report, does he intend to take interim measures to relieve the delays
now taking place in the Auckland Supreme Court, as reported in the New Zealand Herald of
18 November?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The article referred to gives quite a
distorted perspective of the workload in Auckland. The Government has taken action twice
in the last 12 months to increase the number of Supreme Court judges independently of any
recommendation which may flow from the Royal Commission on the Courts. In December
1976 the number of judges was increased from 19 to 21, and last month the Judicature
Amendment Act increased this number to 22 judges. The Government does not intend to
make any further increases in the number of judges until the recommendations of the Royal
Commission on the Courts are received and considered. The last three judges appointed to
the Supreme Court bench are all stationed in Auckland.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is it not a fact that the Government has been reluctant to take
any long-term measures pending the report of the royal commission, and, having regard to
the congestion not only in Auckland but as publicly reported in Christchurch, Dunedin, and
elsewhere, does the Government feel it should defer any action for at least a further 6
months, which must necessarily elapse before the report is available?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The Government has not deferred action. It has taken
action, as I indicated in my answer. The workload in Auckland is proportionately very
similar to the workload in Wellington and Christchurch. The newspaper article quoted in the
member's original question does give a distorted perspective, in that 65 percent of the
actions set down for hearing in the Supreme Court in Auckland do not proceed to trial,
whereas in Wellington the figure is only 35 percent, as I indicated to the Auckland district
law society's "Northern News".
Mr McLay: Can the Minister also confirm that only 332 actions, not 600 as claimed in
the article, are at present waiting hearing in the Auckland Supreme Court, and on the basis
of the percentage figure he gave approximately only 117 of those can be expected to come to
an actual hearing before a judge?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That is certainly the assessment given to me by the depart-
ment when I called for a report on the New Zealand Herald article. The overall comment on
the article is that, looking at the work situation overall other than for civil cases, the volume
of business waiting hearing is no worse now than it was at the beginning of the year. In
respect of criminal trials the position is much better. At the beginning of the sitting year
there were 72 criminal trials awaiting hearing, and on 11 November only 46 such trials were
awaiting hearing. That suggests that the action we have taken is reducing the work load.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Does the Minister dispute the assessment made by a respected
member of the Auckland bar that the time lag between the setting down and trial in civil
cases is usually at least 12 months?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The advice I received when I ordered this check on the New
Zealand Herald article is that from a survey carried out to obtain information for submis-
sions to the Royal Commission on the Courts it was found that more than 80 percent of civil
cases which required hearings obtained one within 6 months of the request for a fixture. It
stated that there had, however, been a substantial increase in the volume of civil business
since that information was gathered and that the situation may have deteriorated somewhat.

UNEMPLOYMENT-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received the following
letter dated 29 November from the member for Roskill:
"Dear Mr Speaker, Pursuant to Standing Order 89, I give notice that I propose to move
on Tuesday 29 November that the House be now adjourned for the purpose of discussing a
definite matter of urgent public importance. This is the failure of the government to provide
adequate relief measures to cope with the rapidly escalating levels of unemployed. In spite of
the fact that on 28 October 1977 in a Statement issued by the Right Hon. R. D. Muldoon
various measures were announced to provide employment, the Minister of Labour revealed
on 25 November 1977 that the number of people registered as unemployed or on special
work rose in the period between 28 October and 18 November by an unprecedented 2088.
"In the above-mentioned Statement the Prime Minister announced a Special Training
Programme, a Maori Trade Training Scheme and an Auckland Trade Training Scheme
(none of which will have any effect until 1978), a Farm Employment Scheme (which has only
just been advertised and is thus still inoperative), three programmes which will deal with
tertiary students' vacation employment (which, as announced by the Department of Internal
Affairs on Morning Report 29 November 1977 have a total budget of only $300,000), and an
accelerated Maintenance Scheme (which will employ only 250 persons).
"In view of the fact that the recent alarming employment statistics reveal that the
announced measures are either insufficient or too late to provide the 23 000-28 000 young
people that even the Minister of Labour acknowledges to be facing employment problems,
Her Majesty's loyal Opposition requests that this House do now adjourn to discuss this
urgent matter of public importance. In view of the fact that this request is not framed in
general terms and relates to a particular case of recent occurrence which requires the
immediate attention of the House and government and which involves the administrative
responsibility of government, I hope you will give this matter your favourable consideration.
Yours faithfully, A. J. Faulkner.'
Standing Order 90 states: "The statement of the matter proposed to be discussed on a


## p. 4837 (#273) ###########################################

29 November
4837
Unemployment-Notice Under Standing Order 89
motion for the adjournment of the House . . . shall not be framed in general terms but shall
deal with a particular case of recent occurrence which requires the immediate attention of
the House and the Government and which involves the administrative or ministerial
responsibility of the Government." I have examined this letter carefully. I find that the
matter to which it relates is stated in the following terms: "This is the failure of the
government to provide adequate relief measures to cope with the rapidly escalating levels of
unemployed."
A similar proposal was brought before the House on 27 September, when the Leader of
the Opposition sought to move the adjournment for the purpose of discussing the increase in
the numbers of those out of work and on Government relief work. At that time I gave the
proposed motion careful consideration in the light of a ruling earlier this year by Mr Speaker
Jack. I came to the conclusion then that an application to adjourn to discuss a continuing
problem, such as increasing unemployment, is not within the provisions of Standing Order
90. It seems to me that that ruling is directly relevant to the present case. The application has
been lodged within the time required by the Standing Order and it conforms to the
requirement that ministerial responsibility is involved, but in the light of earlier rulings I
must hold that it does not relate to a particular case of recent occurrence and is, therefore,
not contemplated by Standing Order 90.

NOXIOUS ANIMALS BILL
Mr Talbot (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Committee
to present the report of the committee on the Noxious Animals Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. The committee was impressed by the generally high standard of the 39
submissions received on the Bill, of which 20 were oral submissions. Of course, as members
know, the purpose of the Bill is to make better provision for the control of introduced wild
animals, to regulate helicopter hunting-or, more correctly, noxious animal recovery
operations on all Crown-owned land, including national parks, and to recognise, provide
for, and supervise recreational hunting to achieve concerted action and more effective
noxious or wild animal control.
Ten submissions stressed the inappropriateness of the word "noxious" in the title of the
Bill, and the effect it may have on the export of wild or farm venison or goat meat. While
there is some force in this argument, the committee considered a more compelling reason for
change is the present public attitude towards the so-called noxious animals held on deer
farms and in private and public zoos throughout the country. It is therefore recommended
that the title of the Bill be changed to Wild Animals Control Bill, and that noxious animals
be called wild animals under this legislation.
Another change that the committee supported is the inclusion of a clause setting out the
general purposes of the Bill. Clause 4 states in some detail that control is the general
objective, but in national parks, or other scientific, unique, or special areas, eradication may
be the local objective when it is necessary and practicable. Another change to the Act
proposes that the Minister of Forests may delegate any or all of his powers to a board such as
a national park board, or any officer employed by a land-holding department of State-for
instance, an officer of the Department of Lands and Survey or a national park ranger. Their
powers would, of course, be restricted to the land over which they held some jurisdiction.

killed or had in a person's possession in any part of New Zealand, unless that person has
authority to be on the land where he carries out the act of hunting, or killing, or capturing he
acts unlawfully. Federated Farmers of New Zealand and the Deer Farmers Association gave
strong support to the proposition. Concern was expressed by the Deerstalkers Association,
however, that the provisions could affect recreational hunters who were inadvertently
trespassing. Clause 9 clarifies the point that a wild animal belongs to the person who has
taken it only when it is taken lawfully; otherwise all wild animals shall remain the property of
the Crown. Strengthening Crown ownership is important, as it negates any argument over
ownership if a wild animal is taken when a person has been trespassing. Previously, when a
trespasser was caught with deer carcasses both parties could claim ownership, and proceed-
ings were sometimes resorted to and judgment given in favour of the trespasser.
There were many submissions on the proposed new powers of forestry officers. The
committee had the advice of the New Zealand Law Society, and made several changes to the
offending clause and related clauses. Written comments by the Federated Mountain Clubs
were acknowledged and acted upon. However, the strongest support for such powers came
from the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association, which even wanted the powers of seizure
to extend to aircraft. Throughout the clause it is now stated that in the exercise of his duty,
and on the production of his warrant of appointment if so required, every forest officer may,
if he has good reason to believe that an offence is about to be, has been, or is being
committed, do certain things.
These strong powers are needed to regulate the helicopter-using hunting industry and to
ensure that wild animals are not held unlawfully or liberated on land outside their feral
range. Not every Forest Service officer will hold these powers. Possibly less than 100 senior
officers will be issued with warrants of appointment, and all such officers will be personally
selected by the Director-General of Forests on the recommendation of his conservators.
The clause covering entry to land for the purposes of the Act-clause 16-has been
amended to allow for prior notice to be given to the occupier, and for the occupier to have
the right of appeal to the Minister. The Minister is now required to satisfy himself that any
entry requirement he authorises does not conflict with any Act or bylaw, or cause indirect
hardship to the land owner or occupier. Otherwise, the clause is little changed from section
10 of the old Act. The Bill also introduces a special provision relating to courts, which was
worked out in consultation with officers of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries and
Federated Farmers.
Part II contains five clauses. It is interesting to note that recommendation B.2 of the
Labour caucus committee stated that an independent licensing authority should be estab-
lished for the licensing of commercial game meat hunters. The procedures laid down in this
Bill whereby entry to Crown-owned land is controlled by one permit-issuing authority will
regulate the recovery of wild animals by helicopter hunters on such land, which is where
most of the hunting takes place. No cause could be found for setting up an independent
licensing authority with elaborate appeal procedures, and a system of licensing all hunters
who, however illegally, sold carcasses of wild animals. Such a scheme would have been
virtually impossible to enforce and extremely costly to operate.
There were many submissions on the five classes of Part II, most of which suggested
changes that were accepted by the committee. A major change to the draft Bill had to be
made once the committee was advised that the Air Services Licensing Bill would not be
introduced this session. The only acceptable workable compromise was for the Noxious
Animals Bill to provide for the interim licensing of aircraft operators, a proposal that had
been made in submissions from game recovery firms and the aviation industry. A new clause
provides for licensing and appeal procedures.
Other new material included in the Bill allows for the setting up of purely recreational
hunting areas to be managed under wild animal control licences by sportsmen and hunters.
These clauses were welcomed by the Deerstalkers Association and the Big Game Hunters
Association.
The most controversial clause was clause 37, which placed the responsibility for proving
his innocence on the alleged offender. The committee has amended it so that it now provides
that if any person found on land where wild animals are usually present has a firearm or
other means of hunting, this may be evidence from which the court may infer that he was
hunting. In its amended form it should not prove to be controversial, and it now parallels
section 61 of the Wildlife Act 1953. The penalty for liberating wild animals will be quite
stiff-$1,000 in fact—and the penalty for offending while engaged in wild animal recovery


## p. 4839 (#275) ###########################################

29 November
4839
Noxious Animals Bill
will range from $1,000 to $5,000. Also at the suggestion of Federated Farmers, the
committee considered and adopted the proposal for increased maximum penalties for second
and subsequent offences.
The committee spent considerable time on the Bill, and in the time I have available to
me it is impossible to report on all the amendments made. The committee was mindful of the
public interest, and of the obvious sincerity and concern of most of those who made
submissions. There is no doubt that it is a much better Bill as a result of the hearings and the
changes that have been made.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition does not want to discuss the report at
length. The Bill is bipartisan, and has been around for some time. In 1974 the Labour
Government set up a select committee to study noxious animals. Because of the efforts of
that committee the Bill is better than was expected. The chairman said that many parts of the
legislation are of of concern; but of particular concern to Opposition members are Forest
Service officers' powers, with which we will deal in the second reading.
The Bill goes some way towards clearing up the licensing of helicopters, which
concerned the Minister earlier this year. Although the amendment is an interim measure, it
will go a long way towards alleviating the problems and the pressure put on the board, the
Minister, and those associated with the industry. The Fiordland National Park Board has
faced problems, and expressed concern to the committee about a loss of power; the
redefining of that power in the legislation may be wider than expected. The change of name
to the Wild Animals Control Bill is of some significance and puts the matter in its right
perspective, as there could be complications with exports of these animals in the years
ahead.

Without reflecting on the chairman of the committee, I want to say that there were
many unsatisfactory features about the hearings. About seven or eight submissions were
made to the committee, and every person complained that insufficient time had been given
for adequate consideration of the Bill. It appears that the closing date was 2 days after the
Bill became available to one of the groups making a submission. Let us trace the history. The
Bill was brought into the House on 2 November, but was not available to the public through
the Government Printing Office until about 9 or 10 November. Submissions had to be
received by the committee within 4 or 5 days.
The Federation of Labour complained about the short time for the preparation of
submissions, and complained also that, as an organisation concerned with employees'
interests, it had at no time been consulted about the Bill. Employees and employers are
vitally concerned with the measure. The New Zealand Manufacturers Federation gave
similar testimony. The National Council of Women said that submissions had to be with the

Printer. The same complaint was made by the public questions committees of the Presbyte-

Resettlement also complained about the insufficient time available to make submissions.
Every person making submissions indicated that if he or she had had more time to consider
the matter, deeper reflection would probably have been given to some of the issues involved.
Members have been asked to amend one of the clauses. I think the Opposition would
agree to the amendment to clause 6, which results from a reversal of a provision put forward
in clause 5 of the 1976 Immigration Amendment Bill. On page 3 of the January 1977 issue of
the Auckland District Law Society's bulletin, the society said of the 1976 amendment: "The
Immigration Amendment Bill was received from the Government Printer by Bob Eades,
new legislation subcommittee convenor, 9 days after its introduction into Parliament, and a
day or so later the Bill was passed into law." The article then described the inequities in
clause 5, which are being remedied in clause 6 of the present Bill, and stated that the haste
with which legislation is dispatched through Parliament towards the end of parliamentary
sessions is disturbing. It further stated: "Because we have no second Chamber in New
Zealand, Parliament needs to be especially careful that what it passes is law that is
reasonable and comprehensible, and does not infringe without good cause the freedom of
the citizens." Those words have to be taken to heart as we look at the procedure we are
faced with on this measure.
Another disturbing fact was the absence of a Minister from the committee hearings. For
reasons best known to himself, the Minister in charge of the Bill was not present during the
hearings, nor was he represented by any other Minister. As there was some contention about
the Bill, the committee could have been helped considerably by the presence of at least one
Minister conversant with the legislation. I dissociate myself from the statement made by the
member for Eden that most witnesses did not understand the Bill. All witnesses clearly
understood the Bill, the amendments to which have arisen either from questions put by
Opposition members of the committee, or from submissions received from the public. We
are getting the message loud and clear that the people are getting thoroughly fed up with
having to make submissions on legislation that concerns them, and at the treatment they are
at present receiving. Parliament looks to the people to help with the enactment of
legislation, but the way the Government treats them tends to discourage them from playing a
vital part.
For those reasons I am dissatisfied with the course of the Bill and have moved that it
should be sent back to the committee for further consideration. When the Bill was
introduced we found that it was retrospective. One clause cures some of the retrospection by
providing that no offence is created before the passing of the Bill. But the Bill also provides
that if an employer knowingly employs an overstayer he commits an offence under the Bill;
and even if the overstayer later leaves the employment the offence is not overcome. Once
committed the offence can be prosecuted after the matter is remedied. In other words, the
retrospection in the legislation attacks the freedom of the individual, and we are opposed to
it.
