provided appeal rights for criminal deportees; that mistake was picked up in the select
committee. The Government thinks it can make instant decisions in sensitive areas.
The amendment moved by the member for Hutt should be agreed to so that the
Minister will have at his disposal on the select committee the collective wisdom of
experienced people. We shall then have legislation that will work in a humanitarian way,
which will be much better than leaving the decisions to be made in a rough and ready way by
employers under economic pressure. Those decisions should properly be made on behalf of
the Minister by Government officials.
Mr LUXTON (Piako): I want to speak against the amendment and to answer the
accusations of the member for Petone and the member for Roskill. The Bill was introduced
at the beginning of November, and we asked that, if possible, submissions be received by 9
or 10 November. The interested parties co-operated, and the committee was able to begin
hearing submissions on 16 November, thanks to the Federation of Labour and the
Employers Federation. We spent the whole morning on this six-clause Bill, discussing the
aspects that affected the two organisations I have mentioned. Nothing was rushed, although
the two organisations did say they would have liked more time to prepare their submissions.
Further submissions were heard on 22 and 23 November—including the afternoon of 23
November, enabling the committee to deliberate and bring down its report expeditiously.
The committee heard all interested parties, except one private citizen from the Waikato
who wanted to make a personal submission. It received one or two written submissions, and
I have no doubt that everybody had adequate time to prepare a case. The Minister of Health
was involved with the Commonwealth Health Ministers' conference, but I consulted him
frequently when he was here outside conference hours, and he was kept fully informed.
Some suggestions put forward in the submissions have been included in the Bill. I do not
support the amendment before the House, but support the motion.

New Zealand Planning Bill
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): It is advisable to report to you briefly on the third
reading the substance of the debate in the Committee. Opposition members registered their
concern at the way the recommendations of Sir Frank Holmes had been treated by the
Government. The task force originally recommended the setting up of an independent
planning council.
On page 384 of its report, the task force made the following recommendation, "The role
which we envisage for the Planning Council and its committees would make it inappropriate
to include members of Parliament and other obviously political appointees in the member-
ship." That recommendation has not been followed, and from the Bill as reported back it is
quite clear that political appointees will be put on to the planning council. We objected to
that, particularly to clause 6(b), which provides for the appointment of the Minister. We find
that the National Government Minister has appointed himself to the Planning Council, a
move that is directly contrary to the advice given by the task force. We believe that that will
nationalise the Planning Council, and it means that any advice that it gives will be lessened. I
moved as an amendment that the Minister be dropped from the Planning Council in an
endeavour to give the council a non-partisan construction, but unfortunately the Minister
refused to accept that advice. Thus he put himself on to the council.
The member for Wanganui put forward the argument that if the Planning Council was
to look at the National Government's superannuation scheme, who would believe that the
scheme would be dealt with impartially, particularly when the Minister was committed to
having it implemented. Because he is on the council he will have an influence. He will not be
a link between the Planning Council and the Cabinet. He will be a director, from the
Cabinet, on the Planning Council. We are thus being asked to finance the National Party's
next election policy, and I object to that.
The Government had a great opportunity to set up an independent planning council,
but it has ignored it. Thus it is with a sense of disappointment that I report what happened to
the Bill in the Committee stage. As a result of what happened the planning council will now
be seriously handicapped. The recommendations of the task force have been mangled by the
Government. We do not believe that this council will be any more successful than previous
attempts by the National Government, each of which has resulted in disaster. It is worth
remembering that a sure sign of a National Government in trouble is when it sets up a
planning council, because we then realise that its manifesto plans are coming apart.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): I expected the member for
Auckland Central to argue as he did. He repeated the points he made in the Committee,
without success and without due justification. He was wrong when he said that it had been
proposed that there should be no Minister on the Planning Council. The task force report
suggested that there should be no Minister. The Planning Council was created by the
Government after the task force had presented its report. The Government had an
opportunity to consider the recommendations in that report, and decided, I believe,
correctly, that the planning council would be a more effective instrument if it had a link with
the Cabinet; but clearly it will not be controlled by the Cabinet. I am but one member of the
Planning Council; there are 13 others.

by the member for Auckland Central-gave an assurance that some future Labour Govern-

Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): It is necessary to report that the Committee stage
of the Potato Industry Bill, as it is now known-it was originally the Potato Growing
Industry Bill was sneaked through the House during the early hours of last Friday morning.
The Government knew that the Bill contained controversial provisions to which the
Opposition took strong exception. It voted against clause 4, and will object to the third
reading of the Bill. Opposition members will outline their objections to clause 4, as well as
their objection to the Committee stage being taken at the end of a long list of measures after
urgency had been taken.
The Opposition objects to the composition of the proposed potato board for the reasons
outlined during the second reading debate by my colleague the member for Western Maori;
and those reasons were also outlined during the Committee stage. Under clause 4, six grower
representatives will be nominated, three by the New Zealand Potato Growers Federation,
with one person representing each of three wards, and three ward representatives to be
nominated by the New Zealand Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation.
Most of the evidence before the select committee favoured six wards, three in the North
Island and three in the South Island, with a representative from each ward to be elected by
potato growers. The Minister and the members opposite argued that the major grower
organisations-the Potato Growers Federation and the Vegetable and Produce Growers
Federation-supported the Bill, but they overlooked the fact that the major growing ward of
the Potato Growers Federation opposed the three-ward concept and supported the central
ward of the federation.
Mr Birch: The federation supported it.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: It is unfair to the traditional main crop growers in the South
Island and the lower part of the North Island to have three growers nominated by the
Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation. The structure proposed in the Bill would
favour the northern part of the North Island. Opposition members know of no reason why
the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation should be represented, and neither do most


## p. 4848 (#284) ###########################################

29 November
Potato Industry Bill
of the people who came before the select committee. Eight submissions were opposed to the
Bill, and only five were in favour. Some of the submissions favoured other alternatives, such
as four wards-two in the North Island and two in the South Island.
An amendment to the Bill provides that a person growing up to half a hectare of
potatoes will be required to register the crop. That means that representatives of the

larly in South Canterbury. There was, and probably still is, some argument about main-crop
and early-crop potatoes, but the whole purpose of the Bill should be to bring about a
satisfactory conclusion, with no discrimination between early-crop and main-crop potato
growers. The amendment supported by the Opposition would have done that.
The member for South Canterbury has been told the views of his constituents. Mr
Taylor, who I understand is a member of the Potato Board, said: "The voice of the district is
forgotten once it hits the Beehive." One of the growers seated at the rear of the meeting was
heard to say that next year there would be a general election. That comment was not aimed
at the Opposition, but at the member for South Canterbury. Very cleverly, he did not tell the
House what his own constituents think. Strongly worded letters were sent to him, and to all
of us. In fact, they were sent before the Bill came into the House, early in September. We
tried to entice the member for South Canterbury into telling the House during the
Committee stage exactly where he stood on the Bill, but he would not, yet he has the
audacity to tell the Opposition it should support the Bill. If the Government had taken the
initiative and got the whole industry involved, we could have reached agreement and a
satisfactory conclusion.
The member talked about organisations that supported a six-ward system. There were
seven, most of them from his own electorate. I had hoped he would take the initiative
tonight, and walk across the floor of the House, as one of his constituents suggested, to vote
with the Opposition for a six-ward system; but no way. The member for South Canterbury
sold out his constituents in the second reading, in the Committee stage, and again tonight.
Equitable representation is the only way to solve the problems. Most of the submissions
to the committee stated that if there was equitable representation agreement would be
reached. The department's report clearly showed that a six-ward system would bring that
about. Federated farmers said that that would achieve the objective, and the Potato Board
agreed. It was also supported by the Southland Potato Growers Association, the Temuka
Potato Growers Association, the mid Canterbury Potato Growers Association, and the
central ward, but not one of them was supported by the member for South Canterbury. The
House should support the concept of bringing the industry together. It was rather sad to hear
the member for South Canterbury blasting off, and saying that the Opposition was divisive.
Mr Talbot: Which you are.
Mr WETERE: We are not. I assure the House that we are definitely not divided on this
issue; we are unanimous in trying to meet the wishes of the majority of those who made
representations to the committee. Indeed, we made that clear during the Committee stage,
and I repeat it again tonight. We hope that when the Minister rises to reply he will have a
little twinkle in his eye, and say that he is having second thoughts. It is vital to the success of
the potato industry that the board comprise members representative of the entire industry. I
hope that Government members of the select committee will give further consideration to
our suggestion, because I sincerely believe that unless the board is given full support we will
not obtain harmony within the potato industry.

Hon. F. M. COLMAN: I thank the House for giving me the privilege of taking the call to
speak on the third reading of this very important Bill. A stable industry is in the best interests
of both the potato growers and the consumers. That point was made abundantly clear in the
select committee, and it has been emphasised during the various stages of the Bill in its
passage through the House. However, the Government, for its own reasons, appears
determined to pass a compromise Bill that will not give satisfaction to anyone associated with
the industry. I venture to predict that the legislation will again have to be amended before
very long for one or more of the reasons Opposition members outlined during the
Committee stage, and again in the third reading.
The Bill is designed to perform some very important functions. One of its major
objectives is to promote and assist in the orderly development of the potato growing
industry, and another is to ensure that, as far as is practicable, an adequate supply of
potatoes is available for consumption. A third objective is to set stable and fair prices for
both the grower and the consumer. Those are very worthy objectives, and if we thought they
were being fulfilled we could say, as a Parliament, that we were ensuring justice for the
industry. However, I am afraid that the very opposite is the case.
The Committee stage of the Bill was taken in the small hours of the morning, and it
could be said to be legislation by exhaustion. The country wants a stable and viable industry.
That would be in the best interests of the growers, the distributors, the retailers, and
certainly the consumers of potatoes. The whole history of the potato industry is one of wild
fluctuation and instability. The Bill was designed to alleviate those fluctuations and bring
about a better deal for all. The past season has seen a glut of potatoes and very poor returns
to the growers. Probably every member of the House has seen the roadside stalls of potato
growers, who have been trying to unload their surplus potatoes at virtually give-away
prices-prices that must be disastrous to the industry.
Over the past 8 years successive Governments have tried to bring together the
conflicting interests in the potato industry, and in the Committee stage we emphasised some
of the evidence given by those conflicting interests to the select committee. For the reasons
we gave then we believe that the Government should have another look at the Bill, if indeed
its objective is to give effect to its principles.
The weight of evidence given to the select committee, as was mentioned in the
Committee stage, was overwhelmingly against the Bill in its present form. In fact, I believe
the select committee did a good job in trying to make a bad Bill a better one. It made no
fewer than five pages of amendments, but that does not mean to say that all the Opposition's
objections to the Bill have been overcome. We would like to see it further amended to make
it a completely satisfactory measure. Certainly we believe that should be done after the time,
effort, and debate members have put into it. However, as we said during the Committee
stage, the Bill is just a compromise between the sectional interests in the industry—the


## p. 4854 (#290) ###########################################

4854
29 November
Potato Industry Bill
growers, who are confined solely to growing potatoes, and, on the other hand, the New
Zealand Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation. It seems to me that Government
members are bending over backwards to try to accommodate the federation, and for that
reason they have not agreed to the formula suggested or the amendments suggested to the
committee by those most closely associated with the potato growing industry. We mentioned
that point in both the second reading and the Committee stage of the Bill.
The Bill increases the membership of the board from seven members to nine. One
member of the board is to be the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries. Three
members are to be nominated by the New Zealand Potato Growers Federation, three are to
be nominated by the New Zealand Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation, one is to be
nominated by the New Zealand Agricultural Merchants Federation, and one is to be
nominated by the New Zealand Fruit and Produce Merchants and Auctioneers Federation.
We pointed out in the select committee and during the Committee stage that it is spelt
out in the Bill that the function of the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries, who is
one of the Minister's nominees, is to have regard to consumer interests. We believe that is
not enough. In the select committee the consumer interests asked for a direct voice on the
newly constituted Potato Board. In the Committee stage we moved, as an amendment, that
the board be increased by one member to represent the consumers. We believe that the
consumers-the housewives-are those who really make the industry. If consumers are
satisfied and are getting the product they want, if they have a voice on the marketing, retail
price, and quality of the product, we will have a better board, and the growers will reflect
that interest.
In Committee the Opposition moved an amendment that consumers have direct
representation instead of the arrangement in the Bill whereby the Director-General of
Agriculture is their spokesman. We believe that he or his nominee will have more pressing
matters to deal with in the industry and, as a consequence, consumer interests will be
secondary. Growers appearing before the select committee said that consumers should be
more directly represented on the board, and that the price consumers had been asked to pay
in the past had been unreasonable for both growers and consumers. Some retail mark-ups
had been grossly exorbitant. One grower told the committee that some retail mark-ups had
been as high as 300 percent to 800 percent above the amount the grower received.

being perpetuated in the Bill. The Opposition wanted to eliminate this aspect. The Potato

the board rather than to the unification of the industry.

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I do not intend to take long in

interested in the Bill, but believe they have an opportunity to attack the chairman of the

efficient way, chaired the committee, did not bow to arguments extraneous to the Bill,
listened to the submissions, and deliberated fairly. All Opposition members who have
spoken have used the Bill as a mechanism not to promote the potato industry but, to attack
the member for South Canterbury. They believe there is political capital to be made out of
such tactics because there is some dissatisfaction in his electorate. They are wrong, of course,

Canterbury. The arguments put forward by the Opposition were affected by blight. The
longer they talked, the weaker and more wilted their arguments became. First we heard the
member for Timaru saying that the Labour Opposition did not support the Bill. Then the
member for Petone said he supported the Bill, but it could have been better. Why cannot the
Opposition make up its mind?
I shall analyse the Bill briefly to see what members opposite object to. Do they object to
a clear producer majority on the board? That is what the member for Timaru opposes. That
provision is not in the existing legislation, and we have now introduced it. The principal Act
did not provide for consumer representation on the Potato Board, but such provision has
been included in this Bill to allow consumers to have a voice through the Ministry of
Agriculture and Fisheries—a similar representation to that on the New Zealand Apple and
Pear Marketing Board, to mention just one other producer board. Is the Opposition
opposed to registration of all growers so that we can know the actual crop and take the steps
necessary to prevent any outbreak of disease? We all know the problems in the industry
because of potato cyst nematode.
Are members opposite opposed to regulating the imports and exports of potatoes to
ensure an adequate and constant supply of high-quality potatoes? The Bill is designed to do
that, but members opposite say they are opposed to the Bill. The legislation is designed to
bring about the growth of the potato industry, to bring about its stability, and to work for the
benefit of those in it. For the first time we included in the Bill, under the functions of the
board, a requirement that the board provide adequate information to consumers on quality
standards and the like. Are members opposite opposed to that? Do they not believe that
consumers are entitled to that information? I see the member for Nelson nods.
I now deal with clause 4, which members opposite have used to gallop around the
paddock for some time as though they had found something new. We all know that there has
been a division in the potato industry between the growers of main-crop potatoes and the
growers of what are termed early potatoes. We have tried to bring both parties together, and
have therefore decided that a national body representing both sectors of the industry should
have equal rights to nominate equal numbers of members to a reconstituted board. Surely
nothing could be fairer than that. The suggestion has been made that we were selling out to
one section, but three from each side is not selling out.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Yes; it is not fair.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: It is straight fair representation from both sections, yet the
member for Timaru says it is not fair. Members opposite interpret equal shares as being four
and three, with the four being for them. The member for Timaru decided to go one stage
further. He thought he would strengthen his argument by making disparaging comments
about the chairman and vice-chairman of the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation.
He said one was a pea grower and the other a tomato grower. Does that degrade them? It
does not lower them in my eyes. Many main-crop potato growers are substantial sheep
farmers or grain growers. Is their standing reduced if they are also potato growers? The
honourable member is trying to say that if you grow peas you know nothing about potatoes,
but if you grow sheep you know everything about potatoes. That argument is fallacious and

Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2)
INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. As I mentioned when introducing the Bill, there are 40 clauses, including
the short title and application section, 17 clauses covering the balance of the 1977 Budget
proposals, 10 clauses adding to or amending existing provisions, and 11 clauses that are
simply machinery or clarifying provisions.
A Supplementary Order Paper has been prepared to give effect to the income tax
measures announced by the Minister of Finance in his financial statement of 28 October
1977; it also makes some other minor amendments to the Bill as introduced. The Bill is
deemed to be part of the Income Tax Act 1976 and, unless otherwise provided, will apply to
tax on income derived during the year ending 31 March 1978 and future years.
As I did on the introduction, I propose to deal first with the clauses relating to the 1977
Budget proposals. The House will recall that the Government has a full review of the various
existing export incentives under way, to ensure they meet the needs of the times. Mean-
while, the existing provisions will continue to apply, together with further provisions set out
in the Budget, the Minister of Finance's recent statement, and this Bill. Clause 7 introduces
the new fishing vessel ownership scheme, which provides a rebate of 45c in the dollar on
eligible deposits in a special savings account up to a maximum of $4,000 in any year, and
$50,000 in any account. The provisions are identical with the existing farm ownership savings
scheme and will be a real stimulant to our fishing industry. The clause should be read in
conjunction with the Budget announcement that the Rural Banking and Finance Corpora-
tion will grant loans equal to 40 percent of the cost of a locally built fishing vessel, plus other
generous loan facilities.
Clause 24 provides that the tax treatment on the remission of similar suspensory loans
will apply equally to the fishing industry suspensory loans. They will be assessable income,
with the option of spreading the amount involved over the year remitted, and up to the two
succeeding years. Clauses 27 and 33 are consequent upon the provisions of clause 7. If
withdrawals are made from fishing vessel savings accounts for purposes other than the
acquisition of fishing vessels, the same tax liability arises as for similar withdrawals for farm
and home ownership savings accounts.
Clause 14 includes deer among the classes of livestock for which a nil value may be
adopted for increased numbers carried in excess of the basic herd. This clause also corrects a
drafting error in the Income Tax Act 1976. The definition of "livestock” applies only for the
purposes of the nil value system, and not the ordinary standard values system. Clause 16
applies to the meat export industry. It allows an optional first-year depreciation allowance of
20 percent of cost in the year of expenditure, instead of 30 percent of cost in the year of first
use in relation to new buildings erected, or alterations or extensions to existing buildings, if
this is to conform with export hygiene requirements. This optional deduction complements
the Budget proposals for special meat industry improvement grants of 10 percent, or 7
percent of the cost of new plant and machinery acquired to meet hygiene requirements.
Clause 19 provides that plant and machinery subject to these special meat hygiene grants
cannot also qualify for the investment allowance.
Clause 17 permits a supplementary depreciation allowance of 3 percent depreciation
value and 6 percent depreciation value respectively on new or secondhand plant and
machinery used in two-shift or three-shift operations. The allowance, which first applies for
the year commencing 1 April 1978, is in addition to ordinary depreciation. It will apply in the
second, third, fourth, and fifth years of the asset's use. Existing plant that is within the fifth
year of use during the year commencing 1 April 1978 will qualify if it is used in two-shift or
three-shift operations. I am sure these additional export provisions, coupled with existing
incentives, will be seen as constructive and worth while by our export traders.
Clause 22 deals with forestry. Farmers operating under the former and more restrictive
loans scheme that applied to woodlots begun before 1970 are to be encouraged to convert to
the grants scheme. This clause details the tax implications involved. Any portion of the
former loans and accumulated interest remitted will not be assessable income, but the
qualifying expenditure represented by those loans will not be deductible against subsequent
profits when the timber matures.
Clause 6 allows a tax rebate of up to $25 for rates paid by owner-occupiers on their
principal residence. If a husband or wife owns or jointly own and occupy a residence, the
rebate will be allowed to whichever is the principal income earner. In other cases of joint

ownership, including tenancies in common, the rebate will be apportioned equitably
between the parties. Supplementary Order Paper 68 sets out a simpler meaning of the word
"residence", and makes it clear that rates on own-your-own flats qualify for the rebate.
Clauses 8, 10, and 11 relate to Budget proposals concerning the interest on certain types of
mortgage, and premiums payable on redemption of inflation-adjustment bonds. Clause 8
provides a tax rebate of 20c in the dollar, with a maximum of $500, on interest derived from
mortgages by elderly couples or sole occupants who vacate a family home to live in smaller
accommodation. The mortgage must be guaranteed by the Housing Corporation under its
housing mortgage guarantee scheme, and approved by the Housing Corporation for the
purposes of the rebate. In effect, the vendor must leave at least 50 percent of the
Government valuation on mortgage for 7 years at an interest rate not exceeding 10 percent
per annum. Clause 10 extends from $100 to $300 the tax exemption on interest derived by
individuals on other housing mortgages guaranteed by the Housing Corporation.
Clause 11 exempts from income tax any premium received on redemption of inflation-
adjusted bonds issued pursuant to the relevant Act recently passed in the House. It also
exempts 50 percent of the interest derived by a farm vendor from either an approved farm
vendor mortgage guaranteed by the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, or a farm
vendor finance bond issued on behalf of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation by the
Reserve Bank. The mortgage or bond must be guaranteed, or issued under the Rural
Banking and Finance Corporation's farm mortgage guarantee scheme.
Clause 9 implements a further Budget proposal, and effectively increases the maximum
qualifying amount of charitable donations and private school tuition fees from $200 to $350,
and changes the tax benefit from a special exemption before tax to a rebate from the tax
itself of 50c in each dollar of qualifying donations and school fees. It also includes World
Vision and the Save the Children Fund as approved organisations to which donations for
overseas use can qualify. For depreciation purposes, clause 15 increases the cost price of
business motorcars, acquired on or after 1 April 1977, from $6,000 to $7,000.
Clause 20 gives effect to another important Budget item relating to energy conservation.
The clause permits the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to allow a deduction in the year of
expenditure of the full cost price of certain capital expenditure incurred on or after 22 July
1977 for energy conservation in industry. If the total claim for any year amounts to or
exceeds $20,000, the claim is to be supported by an engineer's certificate. When any asset is
sold within 5 years of acquisition, the claim may be reviewed. Clause 25 provides for the
pioneer regional development suspensory loans to be treated in the same way as regional
development suspensory loans for tax purposes.
I shall now cover the clauses relating to non-budgetary items. Clause 5 extends the
existing retrospective pay rebate to arrears of superannuation, including national superannu-
ation, and certain payments of accident compensation. Clause 18 authorises a deduction of
the full cost of acquiring and fitting approved safety devices in taxi cabs. The deduction is
allowable in the year in which the device is fitted, or, if the taxi is purchased with a new
approved safety device attached, in the year in which the car is purchased. Only one
deduction may be allowed in respect of the same safety device.
Clause 21 permits the commissioner to review tax assessments to disallow a previous
deduction for farming or fishing development expenditure incurred in buying an otherwise
depreciable asset when that asset is sold within 5 years of acquisition. This is merely a
refinement of an existing provision, and prevents undue advantages being gained from tax
exemptions. Clause 23 provides for an optional customs duty relief, on the approval of the
Minister of Customs, instead of an income tax deduction for increased export sales by certain
overseas controlled companies, which are unable to obtain any benefit from income tax
concessions because of their domestic taxation laws.
Clause 26 amends in two ways the provisions relating to companies within a wholly
owned group of companies. First, it deems to be assessable income profits derived by any
company in the group that would have been assessable if the activities of the group as a
whole were undertaken by one company. This clause is to prevent undue advantage being
gained through some profits being regarded as capital gains when received by a single
company when in reality they are revenue profits in the context of the overall business
activities of a group of commonly owned companies. The second amendment covers losses
incurred by one company in a group being offset against income derived by other companies
in the same group. It provides for the loss company to nominate the company, or companies,
against whose incomes the loss is to be offset.
Clause 28 increases the monetary fines that may be imposed for offences under the

principal Act to bring them more into line with current values. Clause 29 removes any doubt

The remaining clauses of the Bill, as I indicated before, are clarifying or machinery
provisions. Clause 4 validates tax assessed and to be assessed for any year for which the
annual taxing Act has been repealed. The specific application date for last year's amend-
ments to section 4 was inadvertently omitted when the tax Act was consolidated last year.
Clause 3 remedies that. The second Supplementary Order Paper gives effect to the Act's
intentions on two other points relating to that section. Clause 12 clarifies two items relating
to the employee share option or purchase scheme. First, it deems the actions of a trustee to
be the actions of the person for whom the trustee acts. Secondly, clause 12 makes it clear that
when there is a right or option to purchase shares the shares are deemed to have been
acquired when that right or option is exercised. Clause 13 amends section 69 of the principal
Act relating to adjustments for incorrect accounting practices, to cover cases involving part
of the business profits as well as all of the business profits. Clause 34 substitutes a new third
schedule to the Act detailing the terminating date for the various tax incentives. Clauses 35
and 36 correct minor drafting deficiencies.
Clauses 37 and 38 delete from the Income Tax Act two terms which no longer
apply "universal superannuation" and "non-assessable income". Clause 39 gives effect to
the various provisions transferred from the Human Rights Bill. Clause 40 repeals three
provisions, which have long been redundant, relating to non-resident traders.
The first Supplementary Order Paper will include five clauses to give effect to the tax
concessions announced by the Minister of Finance in his statement on 28 October. It will also
give effect to two other small amendments to the Bill. Clause 6, as stated earlier, simplifies
the definition of the term "residence" for the purpose of the rates rebate and ensures that
shareholders in own-your-own flats qualify for the rebate. As announced by the Minister of
Finance, clause 18A covers a 40 percent investment allowance applying to new plant and
machinery acquired or leased for use in an approved high-priority activity. The allowance
will continue until 31 March 1982. The second schedule is consequentially amended. Again,
as announced, clause 23A provides for an extension of the existing incentive deductions for
professional services performed overseas to be applied to royalties and know-how payments,
arising substantially from work or research performed in New Zealand. To qualify, the
overseas exchange earnings must be remitted back to New Zealand.
Clause 23B gives further effect to the recent statement of the Minister of Finance by
providing an incentive deduction for any foreign currency earnings derived from qualifying
projects carried out overseas. The deduction of 10 percent of the net foreign currency
earnings applies to whatever proportion of those earnings is remitted back to New Zealand.
If any contract extends over 2 or more income years, the commissioner has the power to
permit interim deductions during the term of the project. The incentive expires on 31 March
1980, and the second schedule is amended accordingly.
Clause 29 remedies an omission in the original Bill and provides for the amendments to
apply to tax falling due and payable on or after the passing of this amendment Bill. Clause 41
provides for the 5 percent rebate of individual income tax that applies from 1 February 1978
to be allowed in the annual assessments for the year ended 31 March 1978. Clause 42 amends
the PAYE tables as from pay periods ending on or after 1 February 1978, to take into
account the 5 percent rebate. The tables will continue to operate after 31 March 1978 until
amended by legislation. A new second schedule to the main Act is included in the
Supplementary Order Paper.
The second Supplementary Order Paper clarifies two additional points relating to the
meaning of the term "dividends" in section 4 of the principal Act. First, it makes it clear that
the exclusion of non-deductible donations from the meaning of "dividends" in subsection (2)
relates only to charitable, cultural, and philanthropic donations by proprietary companies
and does not extend to donations or gifts to any shareholder or an associated person of any
shareholder. Such donations or gifts are deemed to be a dividend in the hands of that
shareholder. Secondly, it more clearly expresses the real intention of last year's amendment

is not likely to undertake the investment that the Bill provides for. It is also true that, unless
we provide tax incentives for workers to increase productivity in the same way as we are
providing tax incentives in the Bill for the manufacturer who increases his export earning, we
will not increase our export earnings.
The difficulty and the injustice of the Bill are best measured in clause 41, under which a
person on a gross weekly wage of $125 receives a tax cut of $1.74, and increases his wage by
1.8 percent; whereas a person on a gross weekly wage of $192.31, or $10,000 a year, receives
a tax cut of $3.32, an increase in wages of 2½ percent. This indicates the priority of the
Government: these tax measures give to those who are already in a better position with a
higher income, and tend to take from those on lower incomes. Those on lower incomes have,
because of inflation, been pushed up into higher income tax brackets, and will continue to be
pushed up and pay a higher and higher percentage of their wages as tax as they move up
through the income tax brackets.

way than lending the money to finance the stocks in the warehouse. It will get the economy
moving. Certainly there will be some pressure on overseas exchange, but we will have that
anyway.

SAFETY OF CHILDREN'S NIGHT CLOTHES BILL
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I move That this
Bill be now read a second time. Peculiar things happen in the House, but I cannot think that
this Bill will engender the same type of debate as we have just had. There should not be a
great deal of cut and thrust in it. I will be as brief as I can.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: The Acting Prime Minister said he would not run the House
into the early hours of the morning.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: This is a very important Bill. I have been trying to
get it up on the Order Paper. It is here now and I intend going on with it. The problem has
been before various committees for a considerable period. The Bill substantially represents
the findings of the Flammable Fabrics Committee set up by the Labour Government in 1975,
and chaired, I believe, by the member for Dunedin Central. In addition, I set up a one-man
committee-Mr Clendon-earlier this year to examine appropriate regulations for the
legislation. I want to refer to that as I go through the Bill.
Clause 1 states that the Act comes into force on 1 January 1979. I recognise that many
would have preferred an earlier date, but the special committee to which I have
referred Mr Clendon-and the Commerce and Mining Committee, considered that,
because of the effect of changes on importers, retailers. and manufacturers, the lead time
requested was the minimum that could be allowed.
Clause 2 deals with definitions. I draw particular attention to two of these. The
definition of the word "sale" has quite deliberately been widened so as to cover all sales,
even the occasional sale made by people who are not normally engaged in selling goods. The
intention is to prevent the sale of garments which do not comply with the Act. It would
clearly be wrong to impose restrictions on shops, and yet to allow sales in other places. It is


## p. 4875 (#311) ###########################################

29 November
4875
Safety of Children's Night Clothes Bill
recognised that this law cannot prevent individual people from making non-complying
garments for their own use. It is hoped, however, that publicity concerning garments for sale
will also influence those who make garments themselves. The definition of the word
"garment" refers to those garments under New Zealand Standard Specification 8705 which
are suitable for children aged 12 months to 14 years inclusive.
Clause 3 classifies garments into two kinds: Class 1 garments are made wholly from
fabrics conforming to New Zealand Standard Specification 8704.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: What makes them holey?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: They can be holey, but they have to be flame-
resistant garments, fabrics of a low fire risk-whether holey or not-with trimmings and
attachments which conform to Part I of NZS 8705. Class 2 garments are those which,
although the fabric may not conform to NZS 8704, are of such design that they conform to
NZS 8705. These designs are form-fitting styles designed to reduce the risk of accidental
burning.
Clause 4 provides that at the time of sale every representation, statement, or other
indication made by the seller in relation to the fire risk of the garment being sold must
include the words "low fire risk" in relation to a class 1 garment. Where a class 2 garment is
being sold, no such description or statement shall include the words "low fire risk" or words
implying that the garment has a low fire risk. The purpose of this clause is to prevent a
consumer from being misinformed as to the fire risk of a particular garment.
Clause 5 specifies the particular instructions and warnings to be included on the label.
Class 2 garments are to be labelled "designed to reduce fire risk, keep away from fire". A
class 1 and class 2 garment containing any fabric that melts will be marked "Warning, do not
wear under any fabric that burns". The advisory committee recommended that such
labelling should be compulsory to avoid the possibility of any buyer being unaware of these
specific dangers. It is considered necessary to avoid any doubt whatsoever in regard to
particular risks of fire hazard. In addition, warnings are needed to point out where materials
used in garments have been treated to make them fire-resistant, but those resistant qualities
could be reduced by laundering: "Do not use soap, wash in synthetic detergent", "Do not
boil", together with necessary specific warnings against particular cleaning materials or
methods where such use could lessen the effectiveness of fire-resistant treatment given to a
fabric.
Clause 6 lays down requirements for the method of marking garments. The aim of these
requirements is to ensure the clearness of the markings and ease of reading by the mother in
the home or other person involved in washing children's night clothes. In addition, where
garments which require labelling are packaged and the prescribed marking is not readily
visible to a prospective buyer, the package itself shall be prominently marked in order that
necessary instructions and warnings can be seen at the point of sale by anyone wishing to buy
a garment that has been packaged.
Clause 7 empowers the Minister of Trade and Industry to authorise, by notice in the
Gazette, any person to issue certificates of compliance stating that a garment is a class 1 or
class 2 garment, or, where a fabric is concerned, stating that it complies with New Zealand
Standard 8705 in that it is a fabric of low fire risk where he is satisfied, after carrying out
necessary testing, that the garment or fabric so complies.
Clause 8 empowers the Examiner of Commercial Practices to investigate any possible
breaches of the Act. Specifically, he may authorise any person to require the production of
books or documents from any person for the purpose of obtaining information on a matter
under investigation. Alternatively, in investigating a possible offence against the Act he may
require a seller of goods to make specified garments or fabrics available for testing. I believe
it is proper that the Examiner of Commercial Practices should have those powers.
Clause 9 lists the offences under the Act. Clause 10 imposes penalties for an offence
against the Act on summary conviction, and the details are set out in that clause. In clause 11
it is recognised that some time must be allowed for shops to sell existing stocks, and for that
reason the measure will not be fully effective until 1 January 1980. After that date no
garments that do not comply with the Act may be sold. Such garments may not be made or
imported after 1 January 1979, and the period of 1 year is allowed for the clearance of
manufacturers' and retailers' stocks of garments that do not conform.
I believe that the Bill represents an important step in consumer-protection legislation. I
appreciate the co-operation and understanding of the trade associations. In many respects it
will not be at all easy for manufacturers. We have done the best we could to heed their
representations, but we certainly have not been able to go as far as they wished in respect of

The Labour Government circulated a questionnaire in which mothers were asked what

ready-made or made them at home. That questionnaire showed that parents buy two-thirds

is cotton. The third point was that most children-certainly more than 80 percent-wear

that the least expensive fabric used for children's nightwear is the most dangerous, and,
being the least expensive, it will be the most preferred in today's economic climate.
Because of the economic circumstances, more New Zealand children will be wearing the
most dangerous fabric for their nightwear. We know that all fabric will burn but that cotton
and rayon catch fire easily and burn quickly. That is the most popular choice because of
price. Most synthetic fabrics ignite more slowly and melt as they burn. If mixed with cotton
or rayon or worn with other cotton or rayon garments they can burn fiercely and melt and
stick, causing deep burns. That is in the medium-expense bracket and the next preferred.
Wool is one fabric that is both difficult to ignite and slow to burn, but it is also the most
expensive. Most New Zealand families are deprived of it, because it is more expensive and
they cannot afford to buy it.
The point I am making is that families on a high income can afford to buy the most
expensive woollen garments, but the increasing number of families at the disadvantaged end
of the scale are forced to buy the most dangerous fabric because it is the least expensive.
Another point is that manufacturers have found that much less time is expended in the
manufacture of loose-fitting night clothes, so, being the least expensive style, more are
made. They are cheaper, and more housewives will therefore buy them-more particularly
today. In fact, the loose-fitting clothes burn more readily, because the air and flames rush up
as in a chimney. As to fabrics, the more loosely woven are more flammable, and they are the
least expensive. That fact is clearly of more concern to women and housewives and mothers
than it seems to be to Government members, despite the time of morning. This is a matter of
Government stewardship.
I return to my point-if more families, because of the Government's economic
mismanagement, are forced because of much lower incomes to buy the cheapest garments,
which are the most dangerous and catch fire and burn more readily and more fiercely and
cause more harm, then the Government has an obligation to introduce whatever protective
measures it has in mind as quickly as possible. There is absolutely no need to wait until 1

Marine Pollution Amendment Bill (No. 2)
WEDNESDAY, 30 NOVEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
MARINE POLLUTION AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Marine Pollution
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. As the Bill consists of only 13 clauses, my
introductory remarks will be fairly brief. The purpose of the Bill is to provide the means to
deal with marine oil pollution. At present the full cost of providing equipment and materials
to deal with oil spills is borne by harbour boards for limited spills occurring within harbour
limits, and by the Government, through the Ministry of Transport, for spills occurring
elsewhere. In all cases the cost of cleaning up spills is the liability of the offending party, if
that party can be identified.
The Bill provides for levying ships on the basis that potential polluters should pay for
the provision of a national stockpile of equipment and materials as well as for the costs of
cleaning up spills from unidentified sources. The levy will apply to all ships over 100 gross
tons entering New Zealand ports, whether they are foreign-going, home-trade, or fishing
vessels. The only exemptions will be for ships to which the Marine Pollution Act does not
apply-naval vessels, ships entering New Zealand ports for emergency reasons only, and
ships owned by harbour boards-which already have to provide equipment to cope with oil
spills within harbour limits.
The machinery for collecting the levy is to be based on an existing tax for shipping, and
will be relatively easy to administer. The levy is based primarily on gross tonnage, and will be
collected annually except for overseas ships, which will have the option of paying either
annually or on each voyage. Clause 29B specifies the principles upon which the scheme will
be based, and sets out the maximum rate of the levy. The maximum levy for all ships other
than those carrying a cargo of persistent oil will be 60c a gross ton. For an overseas ship
paying on the basis of individual voyages, the maximum levy will be 2c for each gross ton at
the first port of entry on a voyage, and 1c a gross ton for each subsequent port of entry.
However, for a ship carrying a cargo of more than 2000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk, the
maximum levy will be five times the normal rate. This is to allow for the greater potential of
tankers to cause large and costly oil spills.
Although the Bill specifies the maximum rate for the levy, it is intended to charge only
half the maximum rate when the levy is introduced in April 1978. The proposed scheme has
been widely circulated and discussed with interested parties. Wherever possible the draft
legislation has been amended to allow for objections made in submissions to my ministry. In
addition to these consultations the legislation provides for the establishment of an oil
pollution advisory committee. I will shortly be calling on the shipping and oil industries, and
the Harbours Association, to nominate representatives for the advisory committee.
In conclusion, I want to stress the importance I attach to the Bill. Overseas experience
has shown the hazards of oil pollution to the marine environment generally. I believe there
must be effective and practical means of dealing with oil pollution, and the Bill aims to meet
this objective by making financial provision.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I am not surprised that this Bill has been brought

Government in 1974, and the second amendment this year. The first amendment was not

at this Bill it seems that it could also fall into the non-controversial category. However, I
have one or two questions to ask. I notice that clause 3, the major clause, inserts a new Part
IIIA in the principal Act to provide for levies as outlined by the Minister. The explanatory
note states that the fund will be available to reimburse harbour boards that have dealt with
Marine pollution but despite reasonable endeavours, have not been able to recover the costs
from the persons liable. This matter was raised during discussion on the earlier
amendment—and I just refer to this in passing—and shippers, as agents, and owners were
dealt with, and the provisions tightened up.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Electrical Supply Authorities-Charges
1. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Electricity: If the reported
expected profit of $700,000 of the Wellington City Corporation Municipal Electricity
Department for the current financial year is typical of the profits being recorded by other
supply authorities, does the Government propose any relief in charges to consumers?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity): Supply authorities such as the Wellington
Municipal Electricity Department which achieve higher surpluses than expected are
expected to carry out a greater proportion of their capital work from revenue and also to
take into account uncommitted surpluses when fixing their tariffs for next year.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Are surpluses such as that recorded by the Wellington Municipal
Electricity Department typical of the surpluses being recorded by other supply authorities,
and, if so, is the policy of using that money for capital works approved by the Government?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I cannot tell the honourable member whether it is typical. As the
honourable member knows, there is a great diversity and variety of supply authorities. I
doubt that this is typical of many of them. Because the mid-winter weather was milder than
average the supply authorities peak demand, and consequently peak charges, are expected
to be lower than forecast for this financial year. The honourable member might be interested
to know that for the year ended 31 March 1977 the Wellington Municipal Electricity
Department surplus was $510,992 from an income of $14,772,973. Here is an example of
how capital works can be operated from the surplus given by last year's return for the same
supply authority. The appropriation of surplus for capital works was $688,912, apparently
including a surplus carried over from the previous year. That shows that the Municipal
Electricity Department makes every endeavour to use any surplus to offset the cost of capital
development.

Flooding, Western Hutt Road Subway
9. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Works and Development: What action
does his department intend taking to ensure that in the event of further flooding, such as was
experienced in December 1976 and on 22 November this year, the culvert adjacent to the
subway crossing the Western Hutt Road by Belmont School is of a sufficient size to cope
with the water flow?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Works and Development. The flooding at Speedy stream on the Western Hutt Road
resulted from the culvert inlet being blocked by the mass of debris carried down the stream.
A proposal is being devised to overcome the problem of debris collecting in the culvert inlet.
The pipes through the culvert are adequate to cope with the water flow.
Mr T. J. Young: When the culvert fails the subway can fill with water within 2 minutes.
Will urgent attention be given to this matter, because 200 children use the subway each day?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I know that the Minister of Works and Development is working very
actively on this matter. One of the problems is that the debris includes large trees from an
earthwork development further up the watershed. The trees tend to float down the stream
sideways and lie across the entrance to the culvert. I understand that one proposal likely to
be adopted is the extension of the centreline of the culvert to turn the debris end on so that it
can pass through the culvert without blocking it.

NATIONAL PARKS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-

## p. 4892 (#328) ###########################################

4892
30 November
National Parks Amendment Bill
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. The committee received only three submissions on the Bill, which
deals mainly with the reconstituted Egmont National Park Board and the powers of the park
board rangers. The submissions made by the New Zealand Deerstalkers Association were
wide, and dealt with many facets of the National Parks Act 1952. The submission of the
Federated Mountain Clubs of New Zealand supported in general terms the amendments
made in the Bill.
Perhaps the most significant submission received was that of the Taranaki Maori Trust
Board. A large deputation from the Maori people in Taranaki, including representatives of
eight tribes, attended the committee hearing, and put forward views about the park board
land in Taranaki. Members of the deputation said that the importance of the park land in
Taranaki related to the mana and self image of the Maoris in Taranaki. They said also that,
while on the surface the Bill is simple one dealing with changes in administration, they
hoped they could convey its deep emotional and historical significance to the Maori people.
At a time when there is a need for a renewed effort by both pakeha and Maori to foster
understanding, they hoped that the committee appreciated the deep feelings of the Maori
people about the matter.
The committee accepted a recommendation in the submission by the Taranaki Maori
Trust Board that the reconstituted park board include a member of the Taranaki Maori

Board.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): I endorse the remarks made by the member for South

should be made by the Taranaki people. This matter was the subject of a petition in 1972,
and was considered and referred to the Government in 1975. The Taranaki Maori Trust
Board told the committee exactly what the mountain in Taranaki meant to the tribes there,
and to Maori people throughout New Zealand. Mount Egmont has always been called
Taranaki by the Maoris. History records that most of the land administered by the Egmont
National Park Board was wrongfully confiscated from the Maori owners under the terms of
the New Zealand Settlement Act 1863, and the feelings of the Taranaki people go back to
that time.
The Bill goes some way towards recognising the mana of the mountain. As mentioned
by the chairman, the sacredness of the mountain is embodied in the mana. That is a point
that might have been missed. I have no doubt that the Taranaki people will again try to
convince the House and the country that this is what they are asking for. Since the days of
confiscation, or since 1932 when the Taranaki Maori Trust Board was formed under the
provisions of the Trust Boards Act, the Taranaki people have presented submissions to
Parliament on this matter. I believe they will welcome the amendment to the Bill now being
reported back. I have no doubt that the Minister, who lives at the foot of the mountain, will
do likewise, even though during the hearing he said he was unaware of the mountain's
sacredness, and what it meant to the people of Taranaki and to all New Zealand Maoris.
Special reference was made to Te Rere-o-Kapuni, commonly known as Dawson Falls,
as probably being the most sacred part of the mountain. Because of that, the Taranaki
people will continue to approach their members of Parliament and the House about
changing the name of the Egmont National Park Board to the Taranaki National Park
Board. The department considered there was insufficient strength in the submission for that
step to be taken at present. However, there was a lot of sympathy from committee members,
and the matter might be considered again.
The appointment of a member of the Taranaki Maori Trust Board to the national park
board will help to alleviate some of the misunderstandings that have occurred over the years,
and to bridge the gap between our two peoples. I welcome the report, and look forward to
further discussion during the second reading.

Racing Amendment Bill
RACING AMENDMENT BILL
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to present the
report of the committee on the Racing Amendment Bill. The committee recommends that
the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
Several amendments made by the committee dealt mainly with representation of the
greyhound racing nominee on the racing authority. An amendment was also made to enable
the New Zealand Standardbred Breeders Association to appoint a nominee in conjunction
with the Trotting Owners, Trainers, and Breeders Association, and the Trotting Horsemen
and Trainers Association. It was decided that when a nominee could not be agreed upon, as
has sometimes been the case in the past, the Minister should have the right to require an
election by the parties involved. The relevant amendment has been made to clause 3.
The only other amendment I shall mention deals with the right of clubs to appeal direct
to the authority against decisions made by either the Racing Conference or the Trotting
Conference. The committee was concerned at the resentment aroused by the fact that both
conferences, especially the Racing Conference, were making undemocratic decisions with-
out any clubs having the right of appeal against such decisions. The committee was
sympathetic, but learned that the Racing Conference intends to invite four independent
individuals to form a committee to look at the whole matter of Racing Conference
representation. The two representatives from the conference gave the committee an
assurance that the four-man committee would be formulated forthwith, and would make
recommendations to the Racing Conference at the next annual meeting in July 1978.
Because of this assurance the committee decided it was unwise to give individual clubs, or
members for that matter, the right to bypass the conference and appeal direct to the
authority.
On behalf of the committee I thank the officials involved; they were most helpful. I also
want to thank the Opposition members of the committee who worked very closely with the
Government members on this issue.
Motion agreed to.
WOOL INDUSTRY BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill brings together the work of many years directed at reshaping the
many aspects of the wool industry. I should like to be able to say that there has been
unanimity in the wool industry, but unfortunately those who have been associated with it
know that that is not so. However, it is unanimously accepted that the activities of the Wool
Board and the Wool Marketing Corporation should be brought together as one organisation,
with the new New Zealand Wool Board overseeing its operations. The new board will
replace the Wool Board, set up under the 1944 Wool Industry Act, and the Wool Marketing
Corporation, set up under the 1972 legislation. It is fair to say that both organisations-the
Wool Board for a much longer period-have served the woolgrowers well for many years.
The advantages of a single organisation and board are widely recognised. The composi-
tion of the new board is of importance to the industry, and was discussed by the Government
and the industry before it was agreed to. The new 10-man board will have a majority of 6
producer members with 2 others nominated by the Minister of Agriculture because of their
commercial expertise and experience, one nominated by the Wool Board because of his
commercial experience, and the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries. I believe, as
did the members of the select committee, that this provides a very acceptable balance
between the needs of the producers to have their point of view represented strongly, and the
need to have a considerable commercial input in the board's activities. As I said earlier, the
present composition of the board will be balanced, and will work well for the benefit of the
industry. The single board, compared with the previous two boards, should provide a greater
degree of efficiency and avoid duplication in some areas. That point was made by the Wool
Board in its submissions to the committee.
Many of the amendments made in the committee were dealt with by the chairman when
he recently reported back to the House. The amalgamation of the board and the corpora-
tion, and the principles embodied in the provisions of the Bill, were in general proposed by
the New Zealand Wool Board; they then went to the electoral committee of the New
Zealand Meat Producers Board and the New Zealand Wool Board, and to the meat and
wool section of Federated Farmers. Those organisations supported the amalgamation of the
two statutory bodies. The merger is widely supported, and no evidence opposing the


## p. 4894 (#330) ###########################################

4894
30 November
Wool Industry Bill
amalgamation was received by the committee.
The provisions of the Bill, if one studies them carefully, are essentially those of the
Wool Marketing Corporation Act 1972 and key elements of the Wool Income Stabilisation
Regulations 1976, with some amendments to meet the changing circumstances and to take
into account the functions and powers of the present Wool Board. Basically, it could be said
that the Bill brings the provisions of two Acts and one set of regulations into a new Act. To
go back slightly further, many of the provisions of the Bill were first studied by a select
committee and considered by Parliament in 1972, when the Wool Marketing Corporation
Bill was discussed. Most of the proposed amendments are to clarify certain matters that
otherwise would be difficult to interpret, and there are a few minor amendments to correct
printing errors and the like. The remaining amendments are designed to clarify further some
of the points made to the committee.
Most of the amendments were referred to by the chairman of the committee when he
reported back. In clause 3 we inserted provisions requiring the board to give 3 months'
notice of its intention to hold a referendum on the question of bringing Part V of the Act into
force. Part V permits the annual pooling and marketing of wool by the Wool Board, and we
have provided in the Bill that before that part comes into force there should be a referendum
of growers, and 3 months' notice before such a referendum takes place. The referendum
would have to be passed by 60 percent of the voters before the annual pooling and marketing
by the board could take place. This subject generated considerable heat and argument in
1972, but the Bill now provides that it can only operate when there is a referendum, and a
majority of growers support the proposal.
There was some argument as to how directors could be replaced if an extraordinary
vacancy occurred. We resolved that quite simply by saying that if there is less than 1 year to
run the other producer members may nominate a director, but, if the period is longer, the
normal electoral process will be adhered to. That is a logical and reasonable approach.
One of the questions we were asked to consider was whether all wool should be brought
into the orbit of the New Zealand Wool Board, particularly for stabilisation and support
proposals, or whether we should exempt dag wool. We believed it was desirable-because of
the difficulties of supervising the sale of dag wool, and the provision of levies and
supplementation as required from time to time-that dag wool should be exempted from the
provisions of minimum-price protection and the levies to fund price support. We received
strong submissions from the co-operatives, who were concerned that their methods of
purchasing wool might exclude them from the support procedures in the Bill. That was not
the intention, and we have made some amendments to the methods by which this wool
should be sold in a period when supplementation is paid, to ensure that normal and fair
supplementation goes to wool sold to co-operatives, as it would to wool sold in any other
way.
Part IV makes amendments to the wording, and deals with the provisions of the Wool
Stabilisation Regulations 1976 relating to the individual grower income retention scheme. It
was suggested that Part IV should not be included in the legislation. It was suggested to the
committee, and it has been suggested in other forums, that the provisions relating to
individual growers' accounts for the retention of moneys taken off when wool goes through
the trigger price should be in other legislation. The Government and the committee listened
to those arguments, but we still believe that, as stabilisation provisions are an important and
integral part of the whole question of the production and marketing of wool, Part IV should
remain in the Bill as printed. It has come back to the House in that manner, and I believe it is
the correct and proper manner.
Clause 46 in Part IV deals with the refund of retention account moneys if a grower dies.
There was some argument as to how the money should be refunded. The amendment has
made it clear that the money will go to the grower, or to his estate in the case of the death of
he producer, and if there is a lien or security over his wool. However, this does not extend
to money in his stabilisation account. In other words, the money is put in by the grower, and
it remains his or his estate's-it cannot be given by way of lien or security to someone else.
That is the position now, and I believe it should remain.
It was suggested not only that Part IV should be deleted, but that Part V, dealing with
the annual pooling and marketing by the board, should also be deleted. We rejected that
argument, because we believe there is sufficient protection in the provision that a referen-
dum be held before Part V comes into operation. I have some difficulty in following some of
the comments made by members opposite when the Bill was reported back, because the


## p. 4895 (#331) ###########################################

30 November
4895
Wool Industry Bill
House will recall that the referendum provisions were put into the original legislation in 1972
by the former National Government, and were deleted in 1973 by the Labour Government. I
find the Opposition's attitude on this question somewhat ambivalent.
I believe that members opposite would like to support the Bill, but they seem to have
some slight hang-up as to whether the referendum clause should be there or not, or whether
Part V should be there. Those provisions complement each other. The producers are totally
protected from any action that the majority does not support, and that, after all, is the
intention. The reason for Part V is, of course, to give the growers a clear indication of what
they would be voting for in a referendum, and I believe it should stay in the Bill.
There was no argument on some of the earlier parts of the Bill. A moment ago I touched
briefly on Part IV, the stabilisation package. As a Government we believe that stabilisation
is an important part of the wool industry, and that it should be incorporated in the legislation
before us. We do not accept the argument that it should be withdrawn from this legislation
and put into other legislation in exactly the same form. We see no logical or desirable reason
for that.
That covers most of the important matters in the Bill, which is of extreme importance to
one of our major export industries. It provides for a new platform on which we can expect
the industry to grow and prosper. The growers are doing what we have asked many sectors of
New Zealand industry to do—that is, streamline their operations to face up to changing
circumstances, and put their house and their management in order so as to face up to the
challenge of marketing in a world that is much more competitive than it was.
I believe that, with the new board proposed in this legislation-a board firmly
controlled by growers but with a large infusion of commercial experience and expertise--the
industry can look forward with confidence to the fact that in the new Wool Board it has an
organisation that will be able to promote the industry and bring maximum benefits to the
individuals involved in it, and also the maximum benefit to New Zealand.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Wool Industry Bill is of major importance to the
country's economic well-being. It legislates for an industry responsible for about 25 percent
of New Zealand's export returns. For that reason, I am glad the second reading debate was
not held at about 1.30 this mroning, and that it has been given some significance by being
placed first on today's Order Paper. I say that sincerely, because I am well aware of the
importance of the legislation, and the impact it will have on our future. About 40 major
submissions were presented on the Bill, most of which supported the amendments.
The Bill contains three main parts. The first provides for the amalgamation of the Wool
Board and the New Zealand Wool Marketing Corporation. The other important sections are
Parts IV and V, which I shall turn to later. I believe the proposed amalgamation was
inevitable. As the Minister said, the idea has been circulating throughout Parliament for
some time. Both parties, when they have been in Government, have considered the
proposal, and it was considered by the Wool Board as early as 1970. However, the Wool
Marketing Corporation was established in 1972. The Minister of Agriculture in the Labour
Adminsitration considered the idea, and held consultations with the Wool Board and with
various other people involved in the industry. Those consultations have continued to the
present day.
I feel it would be of benefit to the House if I read from the Wool Board's submissions:
"In March 1977 after I had brought members of the Electoral Committee up to date upon
the negotiations which were being carried out with Government, the committee resolved
unanimously 'That this Electoral Committee strongly supports the Wool Board in the steps
that it is taking in amalgamating the two industry organisations and urges it to proceed with
all possible haste'." The Opposition had been concerned that, at this late stage of the
session, the Bill might be rushed through the House. We wondered whether there had been
sufficient consultation with the growers, and those representing other sectors of the industry.
We were glad to learn from the Wool Board's submissions that lengthy consultations have
taken place. Submissions were also made by the Sheep and Cattlemen's Association, and the
House may recall the rather boastful attitude of that association when the Wool Marketing
Corporation Bill was being considered by the House in 1972. However, I believe that since
then that association too has mellowed.
I now turn to Part V. The meat and wool section of Federated Farmers recommended
that provision should be made in this section for the intention to conduct a referendum to be
advertised by the Minister at least 3 months in advance. The electoral committee of the Wool
Board and the Sheep and Cattlemen's Association said that 6 months' notice should be given

The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries said that it had no strong views on the

proposed amalgamation and that meeting accepted the steps that the board was taking." The
board then pointed out the advantages of the proposed amalgamation, and perhaps I could
run through them quickly. There would be greater efficiency in operation, avoidance of
duplication, undivided responsibility, easier and more effective liaison with the International
Wool Secretariat, greater co-ordination with Australia and South Africa, improved relations

fact, the converse applies when savings can be obtained, and there is indeed a far greater
possibility that the two-body system would be more conducive to producing empires." The
board clearly pointed out the advantages that would accrue not only to the board itself but to
the country and to the whole industry.
With that in mind I return to the question of board representation. We made strong
representations to the effect that there must be strong commercial representation on the
board. The Bill provides for superior grower representation, and does not have the same
regard for other sections of the industry. The brokers and wool buyers, together with other
sectors of the industry, are restricted to two representatives, but it is hoped that those
nominated and elected to the board by the growers will be the best people possible. If that
eventuates, the new board will no doubt ensure that the industry is a viable proposition, and
one of which the country can be justly proud. Not only the growers, but all sections of the
industry, and particularly persons with marketing expertise, must be included on the board.
That is an important consideration when selecting board representatives. The Bill will
receive the Opposition's support.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries): I thank the

considered it desirable to have a single board covering the amalgamated Wool Marketing
Corporation and Wool Board. We believe that the select committee's proposals meet the
needs of the industry, and the needs of New Zealand.
