Geothermal Energy Amendment Bill
GEOTHERMAL ENERGY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill contains three clauses that amend the Geothermal Energy Act 1953.
Clause 2, by repealing section 5 of the Geothermal Energy Act 1953, removes the authority
for a landowner to investigate for geothermal energy on his property without first obtaining a
licence to do so. The use of geothermal energy already requires a licence if the bore
concerned is more than 61 metres in depth.
This will ensure that the Ministry of Works and Development will know in good time of
any proposal to sink a geothermal bore, and will enable suitable provisions to be included in
the licence to protect both any persons in the vicinity of the bore and the geothermal
resource. In practice, this provision has rarely been used. A licence is already required
before any geothermal energy from the bore can be used. Very few people have been, or are
likely to be, willing to risk the expense of sinking a bore without first ensuring that they will
be permitted to use the energy they hope to derive from it. The repeal of section 5 of the
present Act will cause no hardship to anyone.
Clause 3 relates to the setting of a rental for the use of geothermal energy. The present
Act prices geothermal energy at 2.5c per gigajoule. This is equivalent to a price of 60c for a
tonne of coal, and it is less than 0.01c per kilowatt hour. Although this may have been
appropriate when energy prices were generally low, it is certainly not appropriate now. The
Government's energy pricing policy, which was announced in October 1976, stated in part
that, where private development of geothermal and hydro energy resources is agreed to, a
rental should be negotiated on a case-by-case basis that would reflect the worth of the
resource, having regard to the alternative energy cost. Suitable provision for escalation and
review would need to be made in each case. Clause 3(1)(a) puts this policy into effect.
The rental will provide an adequate promotional margin to encourage the use of
geothermal energy in preference to a potential user's next cheapest source of energy. The
present rental is payable only on the amount of energy used in excess of 10 terejoules.
Several consumers use more than 10 terajoules of energy per annum, including the Rotorua
Public Hospital. Individual negotiations on a case-by-case basis would not be appropriate for
these users, as the cost of undertaking such negotiations would be excessive in relation to the
benefits derived by the user. It is much better to raise the limit so that it is clear of these
commercial and small industrial users. The lower limit of 40 terajoules for case-by-case
negotiation is equivalent to 1700 tonnes of Waikato coal, or 11 000 000 kilowatt hours of
electricity. At this level individual negotiations become well worth while. Negotiating
individual agreements in this way will make it possible to take fully into account the
circumstances of each user. This will include the cost of alternative energy sources, the cost
of adapting the user's plant to use geothermal energy, and any other relevant increased costs
or cost savings incurred.
In clause 3(1)(b) provision is made for the establishment by regulations of a tariff for
users of geothermal energy with an annual consumption below 40 terajoules. Commercial
and industrial users of geothermal energy, apart from the smallest, obtain a substantial
benefit from using geothermal energy instead of other fuels. This is not the case for most
domestic users, who incur high costs in the development of geothermal energy compared to
the amount of energy used. The Government has no intention of introducing any such
regulation under clause 3(1)(b) for the time being, but it is prudent when altering the
geothermal energy pricing structure to make provision for such a tariff.
Clause 4 gives the Minister of Works and Development the power to develop and
manage any bore or group of bores for the purposes of selling geothermal energy to
industrial or other users. By utilising the capability of the Ministry of Works and Develop-
ment in this way, users and potential users will be relieved of the considerable capital
commitment and financial risks involved in developing geothermal energy. It is hoped this
measure will enable and encourage a much wider use of this renewable energy source, and
hence relieve pressure on our fossil fuel resources and reduce the need to import fuel. The
sale of geothermal energy to industry under this clause could be worth as much as $4 million
next year. I would expect it to grow rapidly in following years.
This Bill needs to be viewed within the context not only of the energy pricing policy, but
also of the Government's acceleration of its geothermal investigation programme so that 14
to 16 exploration wells can be drilled in a year, instead of 4 to 6 wells as previously. This is
sufficient to enable investigation to proceed on more than one field at a time. The first


## p. 4898 (#334) ###########################################

4898
30 November
Geothermal Energy Amendment Bill
priority is to complete investigations at the Broadlands field in preparation for the construc-
tion of the proposed power station. This should also make it possible to provide an enlarged
steam supply to the Broadlands Lucerne Company's drying plant. Further work will be
undertaken at Kawerau to prove that field's ability to supply the full steam requirements of
the Tasman company, and, I hope, also that company's electricity needs. Drilling has
already commenced at Ngawha, in Northland, where there are good prospects of finding a
steam field like the one at The Geysers in California. Future investigations will be extended
to other locations, with high priority being given to fields that could be used by industry. I
am satisfied that this Bill will encourage the wider use of geothermal energy in industry by
making it easier to obtain a supply, while encouraging the wise use of geothermal energy by
allowing it to be priced at its true value against other forms of energy.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): As the Minister said, the Bill has only four clauses. As
it has not been to a select committee, no submissions on it have been received, but it extends
the Government's policy of applying levies and charges to indigenous energy. In effect, it is a
further method of gathering taxation and putting it into the Government's coffers. The
proceeds will go directly into the Consolidated Revenue Account, and will not be used for
the benefit, at least directly, of geothermal energy.
The Opposition would have welcomed a Bill of this nature had it been more positive,
and given some urgency to the development of geothermal energy. There is no doubt in the
minds of many people that geothermal energy has a large role to play in the future energy
scene. Possibly one of the greatest needs faced by New Zealand today is to make itself less
reliant on imported energy. About $550 million a year, or $1 in every $6 of import payments,
is spent on importing energy, so surely we should give priority to developing our indigenous
resources.
The Minister said this is part of the Government's energy pricing policy. Perhaps the
Government is more interested in gathering revenue than in promoting energy. This is
parallel to the early provisions, whereby the Government placed levies on natural gas and
coal, and in a full year received more than $40 million in income from the levies. Electricity
consumers are paying about $18.5 million in levies because of that policy, which the
Government claimed was to maintain relativity with imported energy. In other words, the
price of indigenous energy resources was tied to the price of oil on the world markets, and a
relative competitiveness was maintained.
Any levy or increase in charges must be a deterrent to the development of our own
resources. The further you close the gap between the world price of oil and what it actually
costs in this country for indigenous fuels, the less competitive you must make them for users,
particularly industry, which may be considering the options available. The higher one puts
the cost of the local indigenous resources, the further one closes the gap between that
resource and imported oil, and the less attractive it is. The Minister has said that there is
likely to be an annual income of $4 million from the rentals and levies proposed in the Bill.
That will add to the $40 million being collected at present from natural gas and coal users.
All those charges will be passed on to the end user, the consumer, who has no choice but to
meet them. The Minister is to consider certain cases above certain levels, on a case-by-case
basis.
I am pleased that the charges will not apply to small users of geothermal energy,
particularly in the geothermal regions of Taupo and Rotorua where there are many who use
the resource for heating pools, and for central heating. They can be thankful that the
Government has not penalised them. The Tasman company is one that will be caught by the
energy levy, which is regrettable in the present difficult financial state of that company. One
would have thought that further geothermal energy would have benefited the company.
However, it will be caught by the levy, which will be an extra charge on its production.
Clause 4 gives the Minister power to develop and manage any bore or group of bores on
any land for the purpose of selling geothermal energy to industrial or other users. As the
Minister has said, this could be necessary because of the cost of developing such schemes,
and because of the inability of some industrial users to develop their own. Geothermal
energy in this country has a long way to go to be fully developed. It has been estimated by Mr
Bolton, the chief geothermal engineer of the Ministry of Works and Development, that
geothermal energy resources could provide 20 to 30 percent of the country's electricity
demand in 20 years' time if we had the same rate of increase in demand as applied before
1975. That is equivalent to two Huntly power stations, or two nuclear power stations-a
significant potential.

development programme. I am pleased that the member for Petone did not oppose the Bill,
and I am sure that in the fullness of time he will realise that the Bill is a useful measure,
not just legislative machinery with which to impose another levy.
Bill read a second time.

Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill makes a number of important changes to the Social Security Act, and I
should first like to refer members to clause 3, which relates to the national superannuation
entitlement of a married person with an unqualified spouse-for example, a married person
over the qualifying age of 60, but whose spouse is under that age. Regardless of their
financial circumstances, such people have a choice of applying for the single rate of national
superannuation, or the married couple rate subject to an income test. As the law stands at
present, if they choose to receive the married couple rate subject to an income test, they
receive less cash in hand than a married couple, both of whom qualify for national
superannuation.
People in this position have, quite naturally, been unable to understand why they
receive less than other married couples. The reason for the anomaly is the differing tax
liability of the two categories of superannuitants. A married person with a non-qualified
spouse is taxed at the married rate on the full national superannuation payable, whereas if
both parties are qualified, each is entitled to half the gross married couple rate of national
superannuation, and each half is taxed at the single rate. The result is that under present
national superannuation and taxation rates, the married couple with an unqualified spouse
receives $2.49 a week less than the married couple with both eligible for national superannu-
ation.
Clause 3 removes this anomaly by amending section 16 of the Social Security Act, with
effect from the beginning of the next tax year, to allow the Social Security Commission to
pay half the amount of national superannuation payable under the section to a married
person with an unqualified spouse direct to the non-qualified spouse, and for that payment
to be regarded as the unqualified spouse's income for tax purposes. The effect of this
amendment will be to reduce the couple's tax liability and place them in the same cash-in-
hand position as a married couple when both spouses qualify for national superannuation.
About 13 000 married couples are affected by the amendment, and at the present rate of
national superannuation these people will receive an additional amount of about $2.50 a
week from 1 April 1978. The basic rate of national superannuation will be adjusted in
February, in line with increases in the wage rate as measured by the Department of Labour's
October survey. The gross rate of national superannuation will be increased to 80 percent of
the average ordinary-time weekly wage in August 1978.
Clause 5 implements a recommendation of the recent domestic purposes benefit review
committee, which commented: "If a girl of, say, 16 years has a child, she can receive a
benefit. If she retains the care of the child for 15 years, or until the child becomes self-
supporting, she would become entitled, under the 'woman alone' provisions of the benefit,
to remain on the basic domestic purposes benefit plus a possible additional benefit. It would
therefore be possible for her to remain on that benefit, if she chose, until she became entitled
to national superannuation-in other words, she need never work."
In the review committee's view, the automatic entitlement of a domestic purposes
beneficiary to continuation of the benefit after her youngest or only child ceases to be
dependent should be abolished, on the grounds that beneficiaries without dependants can be
expected to join the work force unless they are of an age when it would be unreasonable to
expect them to take up employment. The Government agrees with this view, and from 1
April 1978 the right of a woman alone without dependent children to a domestic purposes
benefit, unless she becomes a woman alone after reaching the age of 50, will be withdrawn
under clause 5. If her youngest or only child ceases to be dependent before she reaches that
age, it is considered that she can reasonably be expected to support herself by working. If for
some reason she cannot get a job, she will, of course, subject to normal conditions, be
entitled to a sickness or unemployment benefit, both of which are payable at the same rate as
the domestic purposes benefit. I stress that the existing rights of women alone to the
domestic purposes benefit are preserved in subclause (2) of clause 5. This means that the
new provisions will apply only to a beneficiary whose youngest or only child ceases to be
dependent after 1 April 1978.
The Bill makes two other minor amendments to the domestic purposes benefit provi-
sions. Clause 4 makes it clear that a basic qualification for the benefit to solo parents is that
the applicant has obtained a maintenance order against the father of her children, or has
entered into a satisfactory maintenance agreement. There is, of course, nothing new in this
requirement; it is at present contained in subsection (4) of section 27B of the Act. But the
8°


## p. 4902 (#338) ###########################################

4902
30 November
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
present provision does not, as the Government considers it should, stipulate that the
provision is a basic qualification for the benefit. I make it clear, however, that the clause
makes no change to existing practice. If, as is now the case, there is a good reason why an
applicant for a domestic purposes benefit cannot obtain a maintenance order against the
father of her children, there is provision for the requirement to be waived.
The other minor amendment to the domestic purposes benefit provisions is contained in
clause 6. Under subsection (4) of section 27F of the Act, when a domestic purposes benefit is
granted to a solo parent the Social Security Commission is required to notify the registrar
of the court that made or registered the maintenance order against the father of the
beneficiary's children. The purpose of this is to ensure that future maintenance payments
made under the order are paid into the Consolidated Revenue Account to defray expendi-
ture on the domestic purposes benefit. In some cases the father of the beneficiary's children
pays maintenance direct to the beneficiary. It is considered appropriate, therefore, that the
father too should be formally notified of the granting of a benefit, and the requirement that
future maintenance payments are to be paid into the Consolidated Revenue Account.
Clause 6 makes that provision.
Clause 8 makes some changes to provisions under which family benefits can be paid 52
weeks in advance on the birth of the first child of the marriage, or when a child commences
intermediate or secondary schooling. At present, applications for the advance payments
must be lodged within 3 months of the first child's birth, or the commencement of
intermediate or secondary schooling. Clause 8(1) extends the period in which application can
be made from 3 months to 6 months. This will give parents more time to lodge their
application.
The purpose of the advance payment for the first child of the marriage is to help the
parents meet the non-recurring expenses that arise when their first child is born, such as the
cost of a pram, a cot, and so on. Parents who adopt their first child are faced with these
expenses in the same way as other parents, but, as section 36 is currently worded, they can be
excluded from the advance payment. Clause 8(2) rectifies this by making it clear that parents
who adopt their first child can qualify for the advance payment at the time the child is first
placed with them. Sub-clause (2) also makes it clear that if a married couple have a step-child
or children they can still qualify for the advance payment on the birth of the first child of
their marriage. The current wording of section 36 is not clear on this point.
Under section 54A of the Act, a married person can be paid a sickness benefit without
regard to the income of his or her spouse for a period of 13 weeks, provided that both the
applicant and the applicant's spouse have "been in full-time employment for a period of not
less than 12 months immediately preceding the date on which the applicant became
incapacitated for work". This requirement was intended to restrict the benefit to married
couples who have relied on two incomes over a prolonged period, and who have adjusted
their commitments accordingly.
Difficulties have arisen with married couples when both parties have worked over a
prolonged period, but during the 12 months preceding application for a sickness benefit
under section 54A either the husband or the wife has had a brief period off work because of
sickness or some other good reason. The brief period off work can, as section 54A is
currently worded, preclude a grant of benefit. It is considered that if the period of 52 weeks'
full-time employment of both parties of a married couple was interrupted by a brief period of
unemployment because of sickness or other good reason, entitlement to a sickness benefit
under section 54A should not be affected. Clause 10 legislates for that by giving the Social
Security Commission discretion to disregard such periods.
Clause 11 makes a minor amendment to the additional benefit scheme under which
social security beneficiaries with limited income and cash assets can receive up to $16 a week
for a married couple, and up to $12 for single beneficiaries, over and above their benefit.
The definition of "cash assets" for additional benefit purposes has caused some difficulty,
particularly if an applicant has an interest in land that is not required for his personal use.
Clearly, the value of that interest should be taken into account in determining his entitle-
ment to additional benefit, particularly when it is remembered that additional benefit is
intended to be a supplement to the basic benefit for those with limited resources of their
own. Clause 11 provides for cases such as this by amending section 61G of the Act to give the
Social Security Commission discretion to take into account in assessing additional benefit
entitlement any unrealised assets not required for the applicant's personal use. Assets
required for personal use, such as home properties, cars, caravans, and so on, will continue


## p. 4903 (#339) ###########################################

30 November
4903
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
to be disregarded for additional benefit purposes.
Clause 15 may also be of interest to members. The Social Security Act at present
precludes payment of a social security benefit if the beneficiary is in a penal institution. In
some cases a prisoner may, during the period of his prison sentence, be transferred from a
penal institution to a hospital for treatment. To all intents and purposes these people are still
in prison, despite the fact that they are primarily in hospital. Clause 15 recognises this by
precluding payment of a benefit in respect of any period during which a beneficiary, serving
a term of imprisonment, is in a psychiatric or general hospital.
I also want to mention briefly clause 17, which inserts a new section 84A in the Social
Security Act to make it clear that the granting of a social security benefit does not in any way
restrict a beneficiary's right to maintenance under the Domestic Proceedings Act or any
other Act. This is consistent with the long-standing principle that the primary responsibility
for supporting separated and divorced wives and their children and ex-nuptial children rests
with the father of the children rather than the taxpayer.

DUNEDIN ANGLICAN SOCIAL SERVICES (CHILD WELFARE) BILL
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The


## p. 4908 (#344) ###########################################

4908
1 December
Dunedin Anglican Social Services (Child Welfare) Bill
Bill arises from the changing emphasis on the care of children who, for a variety of reasons,
have been deprived of a stable family background. The Dunedin diocese has run some three
homes for children, the first having been established in 1883. For the most part, their
continued existence has been assured by the gifts and legacies set out in the schedule to the
Bill. However, in recent years it has become apparent that the institutional form of care for
children is less appropriate than it was earlier in the century. In fact, the demand for
institutional care has lessened appreciably. Accordingly, the diocese disposed of one and
then the remaining two of its homes. These decisions were reinforced by the state of the
buildings and the cost of replacing them, a project which was by no means economic.
Since 1971, therefore, the diocese has sought to meet its obligations in three ways: first,
by encouraging through counselling services the retention of the family unit, thus enabling
children to be brought up in their own family homes; secondly, by placing children in foster
homes where they can retain and enjoy the benefits of being brought up in a family
environment, albeit not theirs originally; thirdly, if neither of the foregoing options is
practicable, arranging for placement in one of the residential institutions still being operated
by other organisations in the district. A fourth method being investigated by the diocese is
the possible acquisition of a family home unit to accommodate foster parents who, in the
absence of financial assistance, would not otherwise have adequate facilities.
Inasmuch as the funds set out in the schedule were to be applied to and for the
maintenance of the diocesan institution, the Bill will enable such funds, and those arising
from legacies yet to come, to be used for the benefit of the non-institutional social work of
the diocese. I should add that the Bill will allow the diocese to use the funds in joint
ventures; for example, an Anglican-Methodist family care centre already operating in
Dunedin. The centre's work could be expanded considerably were some of the scheduled
funds made available to it. Basically, the Bill is intended to provide the Dunedin diocese
with greater flexibility in the way in which it applies legacies intended originally to benefit
deprived children accommodated in an institution.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Members on this side of the House
fully support the Bill. We appreciate the position in which the Dunedin Anglican social
services organisation finds itself and its policy of placing emphasis on caring for children of
broken homes within the community rather than in large institutions. The crux of the Bill is
to relieve the Dunedin Anglican social services body of the terms of the trust deed which,
because of changing times and more enlightened methods used in caring for unfortunate
children, places it in some difficulty. We are all aware of the high quality of service the
Dunedin Anglican social services organisation gives to the community and, in particular in
this case, to deprived children. I have much pleasure in supporting the honourable member
for St. Kilda on the second reading of his Bill.
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda): May I say, simply and sincerely, how very much I
appreciate the comments of the Minister of Social Welfare. I am sure the sponsors will be
delighted to know that the Bill will be supported, not just by my colleagues and myself, but
also by the Government-in fact, Parliament.
Bill read a second time.

Wanganui Computer Centre
1. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Justice: In view of the fact that local
authorities are expected to supply the Wanganui Computer Centre with extensive details of
those prosecuted for minor offences such as failure to register dogs and infringements of
building bylaws, does this operate conversely, with local authorities being able to obtain this
type of information about their citizens from the centre?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The right of access to the centre to
retrieve information stored on the system is set out in the Wanganui Computer Centre Act
1976. Subject to the right of any person to apply to the Privacy Commissioner for a copy of
all or part of the information recorded about him on the system, the only agencies authorised
to store, process, and retrieve information are the Police Department, the Ministry of
Transport, and the Department of Justice.
Mr McLay: Can the Minister confirm that the member for Grey Lynn could have
obtained the same information by reading the Wanganui Computer Centre Act, which was

Coal-Test Drilling, Mataura Valley
2. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) asked the Minister of Mines: What stage has been
reached in test drilling for coal in the Mataura Valley basin?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): The first phase of the Mines Department's
exploratory drilling of the eastern Southland lignite deposits consists of a broad drilling
programme covering the area from Gore to Invercargill and including the Mataura Valley.
About 120 holes have so far been drilled. Later on, the most promising parts of the field will
be drilled more closely in an endeavour to identify areas which could be mined.
Mr W. R. Austin: Can the Minister confirm that the result of this indicative exploration
shows that this is one of only two major coalfields in New Zealand?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: We are in the process of embarking upon a 12- to 15-year proving
programme of our coal deposits. This proving programme will cost about $40 million in
today's money terms. I can confirm that this is potentially quite a considerable field, but the
degree to which the field will have readily accessible and commercially viable seams has yet
to be finally established. More detailed drilling of this area will shortly be commenced to
quantify the extent of the lignite reserves. It is too early at this stage to put a figure on this. I
should point out that a characteristic of the field which has been revealed by drilling to date
is that the coal tends to be in a number of seams, one below the other, interspersed by
overburden, and some of them are quite thin. This could present problems in future mining.
Several areas of promise have already shown up. One of those is in the Mataura Valley.
Mr W. R. Austin: Did I understand the Minister correctly when he said that $40 million
would be spent over the next few years on this type of exploration? What proportion will be
spent for that purpose in Southland?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Yes, $40 million is the figure. It will take between 12 and 15 years to
spend it. The 1977-78 financial budget for the drilling programme in Southland is $720,000.
A similar budget proposed for next year should see the programme extended into other parts
of Southland and into the Otago lignite field.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

New Zealand-"Bureaucrat's Paradise"
3. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Prime Minister: In view of the claim of
the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation reported in the New Zealand Herald of 25
November 1977 that "New Zealand was a bureaucrat's paradise-over-ruled, over-
governed, over-serviced", and calling for an overhaul, would he advise what steps, if any,
the Government proposes to take to remedy this situation?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): It would first be necessary to ascertain if
the allegation is correct. There was in fact more Government intervention in private business
during the time of the Labour Government than there is today.
Hon. M. Rata: As the National Government passed 322 regulations in 1976-a record
for the past 33 years-in addition to all the Bills passed, does that not give substance to the
claim by the federation?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, the reason being that a large number were correcting
the mismanagement of the Labour Government. I remember very well back in 1972 when
the then leader of the Labour Party said that far too many regulations were being passed by
the then National Government. When he became Prime Minister he proceeded to beat the
previous record year after year.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Because of metrication.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Oh, I see. The position in 1976 was that it was necessary to
bring in a considerable number of regulations to reverse the Acts and regulations passed by
the previous Government. I can think, for example, of national superannuation. Do
members opposite remember that? In accordance with our election policy we had to repeal
the very unpopular regulations. We did so quite early, and then we had to bring in further
regulations relating to the new national superannuation, the good one.
Mr Falloon: Would the Prime Minister agree that one of the measures of Government
involvement in the community is the number of people employed in the public sector, and
that the Government has made every effort to reduce the number of people employed in the
public sector, as opposed to the Labour Party, which increased the number by 10 percent in 3
years?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The honourable gentleman is absolutely correct, as always.
Mr Lange: Would the number of people who have been taken into the public sector
recently include vast numbers of people on special relief schemes?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: As was the case during the time of the former Labour
Government, when the honourable gentleman was practising law in Auckland, the answer
is, that is correct.
Hon. M. Rata: Can I take it from the Prime Minister's reply that he does not intend to
remedy the situation referred to by the federation?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not accept the allegation made, because the National
Government has been carrying out a policy of less Government involvement. I could speak
for some time and give details. I would have thought the member would be well aware of the
details, because he has voted against many of them.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: In view of the Prime Minister's earlier reply complaining about the
number of regulations the National Government has had to reverse, can we all look forward
to fewer regulations being published next year?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That depends on a number of things, some of which are
concerned with the economy. A regulation was passed a week or two ago to deal with the
intransigence of the member's friends in the Labour movement. The Government may have
to publish a few more, but if the member would talk to his friends it may not have to publish
so many.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Prime Minister say how many times this year he has had to
use regulations to deal with industrial disputes?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I would have thought the member would know that
without having to ask me.

ECONOMY-NOTICE UNDER STANDING ORDER 89
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received the following
letter from the honourable member for Roskill, addressed to me as Acting Speaker: "The
statements made by the Prime Minister yesterday on his return to New Zealand, after an
absence of over three weeks, prompts me to notify you again of my intention to move the
adjournment of the House under Standing Order 89.
"This is for the purpose of discussing his admission that all matters referred to in my
letter to you of the 29th November came as no surprise to the Government and that they,
and others, some of which have become manifest since the date of that letter, according to
the Prime Minister, are still to occur, and all of which intensify the deepening depression
'were expected' by the Government.
"This is in complete contradiction of statements and prophecies made by Government
spokesmen at the time of the financial statement of 28 October and call in question the
capacity of the Government to deal with mounting unemployment and the general down
turn of the economy with all its social and other consequences, or even its inability to
understand it.
"These factors, which might have been accepted at their face value on October 28, have
now, and only now, been admitted, and revealed to be without foundation.
"There has, therefore, arisen a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely,
whether the Government has or has not plans to replace the programme of the 28 October
with something more effective, now that its harmful consequences have been admitted as
inevitable.
"This is of recent occurrence and it is hard to imagine anything which more deeply
involves the administrative and Ministerial responsibilities of the Government, or more
urgently requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government."
Standing Orders 89 and 90 enable the House to debate some particular event of recent
occurrence that demands the immediate attention of the House and of the Government. The
requirement for a particular case or event rules out debates on general continuing matters;
for example, cost of living or unemployment. Also, the event must be of recent occurrence.
It is not the announcement of an event that the House debates under the Standing Orders,
but the event itself. The event must be of recent occurrence, not just the announcement.
Finally, there must be a requirement that the House needs to give the event its immediate
attention, and it cannot wait even until tomorrow before dealing with the subject. It has to
be dealt with today, urgently.
As I have pointed out in my earlier rulings, and as Sir Roy Jack's earlier ruling makes
clear, Standing Order 90 is only for the purpose of debating some definite particular matter,
not general subjects that might be raised, for instance, in a Budget debate or on the third
reading of an Appropriation Bill. The member has given notice in his letter that he wishes to
raise matters of a far more general nature than he is able to do in terms of the Standing
Orders. For these reasons, I do not think that the matters raised in the letter are ones
contemplated by the Standing Order. I therefore regret that I must rule that this request
does not come within the Standing Orders.
Perhaps I should add a few remarks of a more general nature on the Standing Orders
providing for this type of adjournment debate. I do not think that these Standing Orders
provide a means for members to initiate general debates on the economy or on other matters
by arguing that, because of an alleged adverse situation in respect of some matter, the House
ought to give it its attention. By "alleged" I mean that an honourable member has alleged. I
am not doubting the veracity of his allegation. These types of debates take place frequently


## p. 4918 (#354) ###########################################

4918
1 December
Economy-Notice Under Standing Order 89
throughout the session, on the Address in Reply, the Budget, the estimates, the supplemen-
tary estimates, the imprest supply Bills, and in any time made available by the Government
for adjournment of debates.
Standing Order 89 provides for debates on definite events that suddenly occur, so that
the House has built into its rules an element of flexibility that enables it to depart from its
normal programme and give its attention to an urgent matter. As such, it should not be put
into effect lightly so as to devalue its significance. The stringent conditions written into
Standing Order 90 are designed to ensure that. Whilst I can appreciate that honourable
members will not necessarily be happy with my ruling, I believe it is in accordance with the
Standing Orders. Until such time as the Standing Orders are changed, they are there for me
to uphold for the benefit of Parliament, and, therefore, for the benefit of all members.
MOTUEKA BOROUGH RECLAMATION BILL
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The provisions in the Bill enable the Motueka Borough Council to build
oxidation ponds for the treatment of raw sewage, which is now disposed of in a comminuted
form directly into the sea. The reasons for the introduction of the Bill are best outlined in the
environmental report produced by the Cawthron Institute for the Motueka Borough
Council, in which it was stated that the system will: “(1) Protect coastal beaches and waters
from pollution and nuisance caused by sewage or sewerage plant effluent; (2) safeguard
public health; (3) cope with the long-term needs of the area; (4) maintain the quality of
receiving waters in terms of any standards which may be required by the Regional Water
Board; and (5) be acceptable economically."
The growth of the Motueka Borough has been quite rapid, and showed a 15 percent
increase at the last census. The scheme has been under discussion for some time. A number
of possible sites were investigated by the borough's consulting engineers after the site
originally chosen, which was part of the Anglican Whakawera Trust, was objected to by the
Bishop of Nelson in his capacity as chairman of that trust. As I have already indicated, the
Cawthron Institute was commissioned to prepare an environmental impact report on the
new site chosen, and it proved to be neutral on all counts. As a result, the Commission for
the Environment did not require an audit. Therefore, the report itself became an assess-
ment. Very few local objections have been made to the proposal.
Agreement on land acquisition has been completed, and the loan intention for $253,000
advertised. Despite the title of the Bill, there is no reclamation or in-filling. Most of the land
in question is above the ordinary high-water mark, although it is flooded by occasional high
springs. I think the need and purpose of the Bill are best summed up in a brief paragraph in
the Department of Health report, which states: "Construction of the oxidation ponds will
eliminate the present discharge of untreated sewage into Tasman Bay. The coastline in the
vicinity is used for the collection of shellfish and swimming, and elimination of the discharge
will represent a valuable improvement in the hygienic quality of the marine environment." I
wish the council well with the project it has undertaken.
Bill read a second time.

QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND NATIONAL TRUST BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill will substantially enact the Government's 1975 election manifesto promise to
establish a National Trust to ensure that sufficient open space is provided for the needs of
New Zealanders. The manifesto also stated that the functions of the trust would be: first, to
co-ordinate the separate land protection and recreational responsibilities of the National
Parks Authority, the Department of Lands and Survey, the New Zealand Forest Service, the
Historic Places Trust, and local and regional authorities; secondly, to define those special


## p. 4923 (#359) ###########################################

1 December
4923
Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust Bill
reserves or recreational areas that are of regional or national importance; thirdly, to
negotiate covenants with willing landowners to protect private land from the pressures of
urban or coastal development; and, fourthly, to negotiate the loan or lease of land for the
extension of parks, reserves, and walkways to ensure access to areas for recreation, sport,
and leisure.
The manifesto also stated that membership of the trust would be sought from individu-
als and bodies corporate, and contributions by the Government would augment trust funds
to allow the trust to purchase land. There will be duty concessions and subsidies from the
Government on donations made to the National Trust. In itself, the Bill is a further
illustration of the importance the Government places on the provision of a pleasant
environment in which all New Zealanders should live. Of equal importance, if not more
significance, is the fact that Her Majesty the Queen has agreed to have her name associated
with the trust in this her silver jubilee year. We know that Her Majesty and her family are all
identified as keen outdoor people.
The trust itself, in terms of the Bill, will have a board of 10 directors drawn from
representatives of the private sector—that is, there will be no Government officials with
direct membership rights on the board. The board members will include, however, represen-
tation from those organisations with a close day-to-day interest in land and in the mainte-
nance of sufficient open space. Those organisations, of course, include the Counties
Association, the Municipal Association, and Federated Farmers; our Maori people will also
be represented. Other members will represent New Zealanders who wish to become
financial members of the trust. There is also provision for the chairman and two other
directors to be appointed. They will be appointed having regard to their personal qualifica-
tions and background, and because of the contributions they can be expected to make to the
trust's activities.
The private nature of the trust has been decided on because there are many property
owners in the country who hold land worthy of preservation, but who are reluctant to deal
with Government departments. An important function of the trust will be co-ordination
between Government departments and other bodies with a responsibility for open space. In
recognition of this, provision has been made for representatives of Government departments
with open space responsibilities to attend board meetings, with speaking rights, but no vote.
It should be emphasised that the trust is not being established to administer or control
national or forest parks, public reserves, or that type of open space, but to act as an advisory
body on the preservation and protection of those and other open spaces. It will encourage
co-ordination between various land-administering agencies where such co-ordination is
desirable in the public interest.
I should also mention that concern was expressed to the select committee that some
confusion could arise in the minds of the people over the role of the Queen Elizabeth the
Second National Trust and that of the New Zealand Historic Places Trust. The Bill's
preamble clearly states the intention of the national trust. That plainly places the Bill outside
the functions of the Historic Places Trust, and for that reason the Historic Places Trust was
excluded from the provisions of the Bill. The Historic Places Trust operates nationally and is
primarily concerned with the preservation and restoration of buildings of historical or
architectural interest or value. It has other functions in relation to archaeological sites and
certain historic land sites. However, the prime management aim for that land is preservation
for historic purposes. That function takes it outside the scope of the National Trust, which
will be concerned with landscape protection and access to the countryside at large.
There can be no doubt that there is and will be increasingly a demand for use of our
available open space area. This is nowhere emphasised to a greater degree than in the
immediate vicinity of our major urban areas. The Government recognises the individual
landowner's right to continue to use rural land on urban fringes or along coastlines for
productive purposes. At the same time, the Government is keenly aware that these same
people, because of the economics of maintaining such land in productive use, are often
placed in the position where they have no other choice than to sell their land for urban
subdivision or for speculative purposes. Provisions in this legislation will enable landowners
to continue to use their land for its productive purpose. By way of an open space covenant,
landowners will be able to receive financial assistance from the National Trust to meet at
least some of the rating charges, thus ensuring that the land remains an open space.
It may be helpful to the House if I explain in more detail how the open space covenants
are to be negotiated. The covenant is simply an alternative to the outright acquisition of land


## p. 4924 (#360) ###########################################

4924
1 December
Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust Bill
when, for example, the requirement is to preserve a representative and aesthetically pleasing
area of existing landscape from some form of detrimental development. A covenant will be
for a specific period or could be in perpetuity, and can be registered against the land title. It
will be a purely voluntary matter. Landowners can approach the trust or vice versa. If either
party does not wish to negotiate, the matter lapses at that point. The question of the amount
of consideration to be paid will be dependent on the uses the landowner might forgo in
permitting the trust to take out a covenant. Public access, use, or even some development
may be involved, or alternatively the covenant may simply protect the land from detrimental
development. The Bill uses the words "treat and agree", and this has been inserted to be
deliberately flexible to allow both parties to come to any kind of mutually agreed arrange-
ment.
I do not propose to speak further at any length during this second reading debate.
However, I shall be moving one or two machinery amendments during the Committee stage
by way of a Supplementary Order Paper. I thank members of the Lands and Agriculture
Committee for their careful examination of the Bill and also those who made submissions to
the committee. I especially thank Federated Farmers for their initial and continuing support
of the principles contained in this new measure. I commend the Bill to the House.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): As the Minister said, this Bill establishes a national
trust to mark the silver jubilee of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Second. It continues the
work of Federated Farmers and, of course, implements the proposal set out in the National
Party's 1975 election manifesto, but the federation did have in mind, before the Bill was
introduced, what is commonly known as a "heritage trust". The federation welcomed the
Bill, and its recommendations have been incorporated in the proposition now before the
House. The Bill is in four parts, dealing with the trust itself, the functions and powers of the
trust, financial provisions, and miscellaneous provisions.
Part II, one of the most important sections, was substantially amended by the select
committee. The new subclause (3) of clause 21 states: "Nothwithstanding paragraph (b) of
subsection (2) of this section, where any land has been transferred to the trust by way of gift,
the board shall not dispose of that land by way of sale or exchange unless it has first offered
the land, on such terms and conditions as the board thinks fit, to the donor or (in the case of
a gift of Maori land) to the descendants of the donor." The new subclause (4) of clause 21
states: "For the purposes of subsection (3) of this section, the descendants of a donor of
Maori land shall be determined by order of the Maori Land Court." Briefly, that means that,
if the trust has no further use for the land which was originally taken, then such land is first to
be offered back to the original donors or beneficiaries, and thereafter the trust is empowered
to dispose of the land as it thinks fit. This significant provision will establish and consolidate
the trust on a firm basis.
The committee received 18 submissions, 17 of which supported the Bill. The one
exception was Mr Armitage, who, after some discussion with the committee, was able to
resolve his problems. I have much pleasure in supporting the Bill.
Bill read a second time.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 3)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill will have the effect of establishing the sixth Local Government
Commission since 1946. That year the first commission was set up under the Local
Government Commission Act, charged with the duty of reviewing the functions and districts
of local authorities and with the preparation of reorganisation schemes. It is a sorry record,
but very true, that the five commissions we have seen during the past 30 years have not really
achieved the purposes for which the commissions were established, despite their tremendous
cost of some $1.5 million in direct expenditure and an unknown sum in indirect costs
probably in excess of that. They have not obtained the degree of rationalisation in local
government that their architects were looking for.
Successive Governments have been careful to draft the terms of reference of all these
commissions in such a manner that there could be no ministerial or governmental pressure
influencing decisions in individual cases. Successive Ministers have been scrupulous in
declining all requests that they should endeavour to bring influence to bear. But successive
commissions, while they have approached local government reform quite correctly in terms
of the legislation under which they have operated, have tended, quite unintentionally I am


## p. 4925 (#361) ###########################################

1 December
4925
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
sure, to develop their own interpretations of the manner in which reform should be carried
out. Without exception, these interpretations have ended up at variance with the philosophy
of the Government of the day. The inevitable result has been a change to both the law and
the commission.
Any impartial analysis of the results of the work of the various commissions established
to undertake this task over the last 30 years must come to the conclusion that, under our
system of Government, people cannot be coerced into accepting changes to their local
political institutions that do not accord with prevailing public opinion, yet the procedures
under which all previous commissions have worked have led to this form of confrontation.
Whether we like it or not, anything to do with the restructuring of any governmental
organisation, and certainly anything to do with the restructuring of the political institutions
of local government, is an issue with which the Government and Parliament are vitally
concerned. The Government has a responsibility to ensure that what is done in this area is in
accord with its stated policy. No Government, whatever its party, would have it otherwise.
This Government's policy is quite clear. One of our election promises was that, in the
restructuring of local government, the views of the local community should prevail. We also
said that, in our opinion, the work of the Local Government Commission should be
complemented by a greater move towards voluntary reform on the part of local authorities
themselves. That is the National Government's policy.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Do nothing!
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: More will be done in the restructuring of local government and in
the creation of regional government in this country in the next 12 months than in any
previous 2 years.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: I refuse to believe it.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: This time next year the member will swallow his words. The
Government believes that the co-operation and help of local government itself should be
enlisted. It is a matter of great regret to me, and to my colleagues, that there have been so
many examples in recent months where public opinion has been so strongly opposed to the
commission's decisions, and that such a high proportion of those decisions have been either
successfully challenged in the courts or defeated at the polls.
It was, for instance, not difficult for anyone at all sensitive to public opinion to foretell
that the scheme brought down for the union of five local authorities in south Otago would
prove to be wasted effort, because it was likely to be voted out, as indeed proved to be the
case. It was not difficult to forecast that any suggestion that a regional scheme to link the
whole of the Central Otago region with coastal Otago as far south as Owaka and as far north
as Palmerston would generate widespread and vocal opposition-especially in the Central
Otago area; and, closer to home, we all know the reaction of the Horowhenua area towards
the suggestion that it be included in the proposed Wellington region.
Mr T. J. Young: By gee, the Minister has gone back on his word on that one.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I have not gone back on one word as regards local government.
What I was trying to do as Minister of Local Government was to strengthen local
government and bring local authorities together, not coerce them into something with which
they would not agree and which was bound to fail because it did not have the support of the
majority of people in the area. I do not intend the examples I have quoted to be taken as a
reflection on the integrity of the members of the present commission. They have, no doubt,
conscientiously applied the law as they saw it, but clearly their interpretation has not
reflected the Government's philosophy or wishes, or, for that matter, prevailing public
opinion. The only way to remedy this is to bring down legislation which clearly sets out the
Government's political philosophy, and to appoint a new commission which cannot be said
to reflect past attitudes and policies.
It is a matter of record that my predecessor, the Hon. Henry May, for whom I have a
great personal regard, was trying to go too far and too fast in imposing a new structure of
local government. People were just not prepared to accept what he himself described as
bulldozer tactics. In retrospect, perhaps the changes this Bill will make should have been
made much earlier, but I was hopeful that the existing procedures would have been applied
in a way that would not have attracted the degree of public opposition that has become
apparent. Perhaps I was hoping for too much in expecting the commission to change its
approach without a clear indication in the law that it should do so.
The chairman of the Local Government Commission has taken issue with me over one
of my remarks when I introduced this Bill. I said then that, pending the appointing of a new


## p. 4926 (#362) ###########################################

4926
1 December
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
commission as from 1 April 1978, I had asked the present commission to carry on in the spirit
of the Government's policies and wishes, and I said I was assured that it would do so. The

responsibility reposed in it by the Local Government Act, and that consequently its

Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Platitudes!
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Let me tell the member for Timaru that I will have the last say this
time next year, because no one can be permitted to opt out of regional planning-and under
this Government no one will be permitted to-but when the opposition is strong and extends
over substantial areas that could conceivably stand on their own, then some notice must be
taken of it; and that is exactly why the Government has taken this action. The Bill is
designed to ensure that due regard is paid to such views in the future.
I want to stress three points: the Bill does not sound the death knell of the restructuring
of local government as some critics-who should know better-have said; it does not spell
the abandonment of a Local Government Commission charged with restructuring local
government free of governmental or ministerial pressure in reaching individual decisions;
and it does not herald the discarding of the concept of regional government for matters
requiring a regional approach.
I have been astounded, and most disappointed, at the ill-informed statements made by
one or two people of some prominence in local government about the Government's actions
in bringing down the legislation. Their views reflect parochial attitudes, and are quite
contrary to the views of the Municipal Association and the New Zealand Counties Associa-
tion, which have a country-wide overview and agree with the action the Government is
taking. I hope Opposition members have read the statement issued by these two associations
published in tonight's Evening Post. I spoke to the Municipal Association today, and one
mayor who has been vocal in his opposition to the Bill will be making a statement later giving
his amended views.
The Bill is based on four main premises; first, it recognises that there is a need for local
government reorganisation and the development of the sensible regional structure based,
where practicable, on our existing territorial local authority boundaries; secondly, it recog-
nises that local government reorganisation, however desirable, cannot be brought about by
coercion—that has been proved over the past 50 years; thirdly, it recognises that to achieve
worth-while results there must be co-operation and a full commitment by the territorial local
government associations to work with the Government to produce a strong and more
effective local government system; and, finally, it recognises that to achieve these aims
procedures must be based on full consultation with the people concerned, and with regard to
public opinion.
If these basic premises are appreciated, it will be understood why the Bill provides for a
commission of three, with an independent chairman appointed by the Government, one


## p. 4927 (#363) ###########################################

1 December
4927
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
member nominated by the Municipal Association, and one by the Counties Association. It
will be appreciated also why the Bill provides for co-opted membership when a proposal
affecting an ad hoc authority is under consideration, and why provision is made for the
appointment of conciliators when dealing with reorganisation schemes. During the Commit-
tee stage I shall be introducing an amendment providing for up to two conciliators to be
appointed in any given case.
For regional schemes, the Bill states in effect that the commission is not to proceed with
the issue of a provisional scheme unless, after preliminary inquiries and consultations, it is
satisfied that there is reasonable public support for the scheme from the proposed region as a
whole. During the Committee stage I shall be introducing a minor amendment to the
proposed new section 19(4) to reinforce the Government's intention in this regard.
I repeat, for the benefit of Opposition members that the Government is not backing
away from the concept of regionalism. Regional development organisations are already in
being under the guidance of my colleague the Minister of National and Regional Develop-
ment. Regional planning is to be given a much needed boost. Experiments in the regional
operation of health services are to be carried out, and water and soil problems are
approached on a regional basis. One could go on. The united and regional councils that will
be set up under the Bill are a logical step in this process. They will be the basis on which
regional development of all kinds can eventually be built and on which much of the decision
making at present done at the central level can eventually be placed. The development of
regional government will proceed expeditiously.
The Bill recognises that there may still be some doubt about the extent of public support
or opposition for a scheme, despite the greatly improved consultative procedures. That is
why, in the case of local reorganisation schemes involving the union of territorial authorities
or boundary alterations, provision is made for a survey of electors to be taken to ascertain
the degree of public opposition so long as 15 percent of electors demand that this be done.
The National Government is allowing a small number of people in any community to ask for
the feelings of the electorate to be tested. In other words, the local electors will have the final
say, and if more than half of them object to a local scheme no further action will be taken. I
must emphasise here that I am speaking of reorganisation schemes as opposed to regional
schemes. By the end of next year 25 regions will be established.
It is important to note that in future the survey will be taken at an earlier stage than it
has been in the past, thus avoiding unnecessary expense and the engendering of undesirable
divisions in communities in which it is clear that the weight of public opinion is against a
proposed scheme. Obviously surveys of this nature are not appropriate to proposals for the
establishment of regions. The issues involved are too many and too varied to allow a simple
yes/no approach to regional proposals. That is why the Bill provides that the Minister, if he
thinks fit, may refer a final regional scheme back to the commission for reconsideration of
such of its provisions as he might specify. If the Minister does this he will, of course, be
working on feedback from the region concerned, and will be expressing to the commission
his reservations about some of its ideas.
If the Bill had been law when the organisation of regions in the Wellington district was
being considered I would have referred to the commission the question of whether Kapiti
should be included. However, the power of referral back of a final regional scheme is not a
power of veto. There is no way under the legislation by which the Government can veto any
scheme brought down by the new commission.
Mr T. J. Young: If the Minister's not satisfied-
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: If the Minister is not satisfied he refers the scheme back to the
commission and, after considering what the Minister has said, the commission will have the
power to go ahead with the scheme. Would the member for Hutt have forced the
Horowhenua and Kapiti regions into the greater Wellington scheme? Obviously he would
have.
The existing provisional regional schemes brought down by the present commission are
to be abandoned in any instances where the Minister so recommends, and a fresh start made.
The Minister is given the power in the case of the Horowhenua region, and the Otago
Central and Ashburton region-the Aorangi scheme-to refer the schemes back. I
appreciate that the Opposition does not like this point. The schemes can be referred back to
the new commission so that they can be started afresh, taking note of public opinion in the
area. Having visited the areas I know what the commission will find. It does not mean that
regional bodies will not be set up in those areas. The Government is committed to the

in administration, the high rates levied, and other consequences that have followed the need
to reorganise local government. It goes without saying that some toes are inevitably stood
upon whenever any reorganisation takes place.
We set up a Local Government Commission, comprising men from within the commun-
ity with widespread experience in many aspects of local government, to examine the position
and hear evidence not only from local body representatives but also from the people living in
the various areas, and to produce a provisional plan for further examination before it was
made final. That is the only way in which reorganisation of local bodies will be achieved in a
manner beneficial to New Zealand. We have already had experience of the type of
commission proposed in the Bill, and it was a failure because it accomplished nothing.
Indeed, it could do nothing because the two associations with representatives on the
commission could not agree on the solutions to any problems brought before it. As a result,
the problems were merely thrown in the corner, and local body reform languished. Because
of the failure of that type of local government commission, a select committee was set up in
1960 to look at the problems. We know that the Hon. Henry May, as Minister of Local
Government, grasped the nettle and moved ahead with a view to overcoming unnecessary
duplication. I know of no other Bill vitally affecting the constitutional structure of this
country that has not first been referred to a select committee, and I object very strongly to
those with knowledgeable views to put before the House being denied such an opportunity.

legislation has been handled by the Government.

Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): When I was interrupted about 20
minutes ago I was saying that the Racing Amendment Bill provides for the legalisation of
totalisator betting on greyhound racing for the first time. As from 1 August 1978, betting on
greyhounds will get away to a good start. It will be restricted initially to betting on the course
only. There will not be any off-course betting through the Totalisator Agency Board on
greyhound racing meetings either in this country or overseas—at least not initially. That will
be a matter for the future requiring further amendment to the principal Act, the Racing Act
1971.
When introducing the Bill, I said that it contained provisions that could be regarded as
momentous for greyhound racing. That sport has waited a long time for totalisator betting. I
am sure its followers will welcome this advance, which I hope and believe will do much to
help the sport establish itself on a better financial basis, and provide programmes that will be
attractive to its patrons. The Bill also expands the membership of the New Zealand Racing
Authority. It provides for the Greyhound Racing Association to be represented by one
member. It makes provision also for the New Zealand Standardbred Breeders
Association-which has emerged in recent years as a major body representative of the
breeding sector in trotting to be admitted as a nominating body for membership on the
authority. The association will participate in a joint nomination with other bodies in the
trotting code of one member.
I should like to express my thanks to the chairman and members of the Local Bills
Committee for the careful attention they gave to the Bill. The committee received 13 written
submissions on the Bill. This was not a great number, but I think it is fair to say that the Bill
was exposed to pretty searching scrutiny. I want to stress that, for it was put to the committee
that there probably would have been a good many more submissions had racing people—the
racing and trotting clubs especially-known about it. The committee was told that many of
the clubs neither knew that a Racing Amendment Bill was to be introduced this session, nor
had any idea of what would be in it. I find that quite extraordinary-in fact, quite amazing.
Of all the Bills I have had anything to do with in my time as Minister, I cannot think of any
other to which I have given so much prior announcement, or on which there has been so
much consultation with the parties principally involved.
On 16 July 1976, when addressing the annual meeting of the Trotting Conference at
Hamilton, I said that a number of amendments to the Racing Act were being contemplated.
I added that, because of the heavy legislative programme facing Parliament at the time, they
would not be dealt with in 1976, but it was my hope that they would be proceeded with in
1977. I told the conference even then of the main things the Government had in mind:
restricted totalisator betting for greyhounds, and attention to the membership of the Racing
Authority. My remarks were quite widely reported in the press. The next occasion I had to
address a racing gathering was a combined function of trotting clubs and kindred associations
of the Auckland province held at Alexandra Park on 11 October 1976, when I again
mentioned proposed amendments to the Act, and when again there was wide press
coverage.
I mentioned the matter once more in July of this year, when I addressed the annual
meeting of the Trotting Conference in Christchurch. This time, however, I was able to be
more definite. I told the conference that there would definitely be an amending Bill in 1977,
and I went into considerable detail as to what it would contain. Once again my address
received very good press coverage. Further to this, about 2 months ago I gave a special
interview to Mr Eric Benton of the Parliamentary Press Gallery, as a result of which he
wrote a very good special article giving a full forecast of what the Bill would contain. This
appeared in the daily press from one end of the country to the other. So much for
pronouncements.
Now for the matters of consultation. The New Zealand Racing Authority, which is the
statutory body set up to advise me on racing, was for some months deliberating on the
amendments it proposed to recommend to me. Both the conferences had two representa-
tives on the authority. But not only did they have that means of being kept informed, the
authority consulted directly with them and with the Greyhound Racing Association, and


## p. 4946 (#382) ###########################################

4946
1 December
Racing Amendment Bill
invited their comments on its proposals. Further than this, when all the proposed amend-
ments had been put into departmental draft form, I held a meeting in my office with the
presidents, some executive members, and the secretaries of both conferences. The chair-
man, deputy chairman, and secretary of the Racing Authority were also present. A specially
prepared explanatory memorandum on the amendments was tabled, and this was discussed
at length with and accepted in principle by the representatives of the conferences. After all
this consultation, it is astonishing that clubs should claim they had no knowledge of the Bill
or its contents, and, if the reason is that they were not informed by the conferences, then
surely that is something they should take up with the conferences.
I want to return to the point I made earlier, that the submissions received did lead to a
searching examination of the Bill, and the result, as members will see, is that the Local Bills
Committee has made a number of amendments to the Bill, which is, I am sure, the better for
what they have done. Clause 2 substitutes several new definitions for those at present in the
principal Act. This is necessary to make provision for greyhounds in totalisator races. A new
definition is included of a “restricted totalisator licence", and also a new definition of trebles
betting. Trebles betting is now a commonplace form of betting, which, however, was not
contemplated at the time of the passing of the 1971 Act.
Clause 3 provides for the membership of the New Zealand Racing Authority to be
increased from 9 members to 10, the additional member to represent the New Zealand
Greyhound Racing Association. It also provides for the deputy chairman to be appointed by
the Minister and not elected from among the members, as at present. This provision is to
ensure his independence from sectional interests. I direct attention especially to subclause
2(a) of clause 3, which makes provision for the New Zealand Standardbred Breeders
Association to participate along with two other bodies in trotting in the joint nomination of
one member of the racing authority. It was on this matter of joint nomination, which is
provided for in the principal Act, that the committee received most of its submissions.
At present, the Act provides for four bodies, two in racing and two in trotting, to be
paired for the purpose of nominating one member to be appointed to represent each pair of
bodies on the authority. Those bodies are the New Zealand Racing Owners and Trainers
Federation and the New Zealand Thoroughbred Breeders Association as one pair, and the
New Zealand Trotting Owners, Trainers, and Breeders Association and the New Zealand
Trotting Horsemen's and Trainers Association as the other pair. That provision, of course,
dates back to 1971. Since that time, however, another body-the New Zealand Stan-
dardbred Breeders Association-has emerged. Formed in 1972 with a membership of about
200, it now has a membership of more than 1500, and is the major body representing the
breeding sector in the trotting industry.
The association made a strong claim to the Local Bills Committee for representation on
the authority, but acknowledged that it would not be desirable for the authority to be
enlarged beyond the proposed membership of 10. If it had to share a right of nomination, the
association sought to share this with its counterpart body in racing, the Thoroughbred
Breeders Association, rather than with the Trotting Owners, Trainers, and Breeders
Association, and the Trotting Horsemen's and Trainers Association.
After much careful consideration, the committee rejected this proposition, which would
have meant that the Racing Owners and Trainers Federation would have to be associated
with two bodies representing the owning and training sectors of trotting. The committee
doubted that this would be a workable arrangement. Short of enlarging the membership of
the authority to give all the bodies I have mentioned their own individual representation,
and thus make the authority unwieldy in size, there seemed to be no harmonious solution.
The committee decided that in the circumstances it seemed best to keep racing bodies
associated together, and trotting bodies associated with sister organisations in that code.
The Bill, therefore, provides for the Standardbred Breeders Association to be admitted
as a nominating body along with the Trotting Owners, Trainers, and Breeders Association
and the Trotting Horsemen's and Trainers Association. Subclause (2) provides that in the
event of the nominating bodies not being able to agree on a joint nomination, the Minister
may require an election to be held among the membership. Clause 8 deals with the powers of
the Racing Authority, which in future will have direct powers to act in certain areas in which
at present it has only advisory powers, such direct powers being the determination of the
distribution of totalisator licences between racing, trotting, and greyhound racing.
Clause 9 provides for the Racing Authority to adjudicate in disputes between the
Racing Conference, the Trotting Conference, and the Greyhound Racing Association, and


## p. 4947 (#383) ###########################################

1 December
4947
Racing Amendment Bill
in such disputes between clubs and their national bodies as are referred to the authority by
those national bodies. It was submitted to the Local Bills Committee that clubs should have a
direct right of appeal to the authority. The committee believed, however, that it should not
detract from the authority of the conferences, and that they should continue to have the right
to determine what are in large part domestic matters. As to the fear that a genuine grievance
against a decision of either of the conferences or the Greyhound Racing Association would
not get past those bodies to the authority, I believe that as responsible national bodies they
would be sensitive to the criticism that would inevitably follow if they failed to refer to the
authority disputes involving strongly held resentment against its findings.
Clause 15 provides for the totalisator to be opened for betting on a maximum of 10 races
at a meeting, compared with the present maximum of 9. Clause 16 provides for the aggregate
number of racing permits, including those for restricted totalisator meetings, to be fixed
from time to time by Order in Council. The number of restricted totalisator licences for
greyhound racing is fixed initially at a minimum of 60, with 10 each for both trotting and
racing. As the number of full totalisator permits was recently increased by 33 each racing
season-12 extra for racing and 21 for trotting- I believe there is a need for a settling down
period to see how many restricted totalisator licences from the total minimum number of 80
specified for racing, trotting, and greyhound racing will be availed of, bearing in mind that
restricted totalisator clubs will still have the option, if they want to, of operating equalisator
betting rather than restricted totalisator betting. This is made possible by the amendments
effected to the principal Act by clauses 14 and 26.
The only other provision I wish to draw specific attention to is clause 32, which will
lower the legal betting age from 20 to 18. This, of course, is in line with other areas in the law
where there has been a similar relaxation. The other matters dealt with are mainly
machinery matters arising from the necessity to amend the principal Act to provide for
betting on greyhound racing, and to update it by recognising recently introduced new forms
of betting. Although the Bill is not a massive measure, as I said earlier, it is of much
importance, especially to greyhound racing.

In the main, members of both parties have agreed on the Bill. The select committee

In the background we have the McCarthy royal commission and, later, research into racing
