I shall not deal with the other clauses of the Bill. Other members who heard the
evidence presented to the select committee will deal with the provisions more fully.
However, I express disappointment that no provision is incorporated to ensure that a bettor
who backs a winner, no matter how hot a favourite it might be, received back the money he
has invested. The system adopted in New Zealand is different from that followed in
Australia and the Old Country. We work under what I would term a minus dividend system.
I know of nothing more galling than to back a winner and lose money. That does not happen
very often, and the dividends are usually fairly close to the original investment, but I have in
mind the occasion when Good Lord won a race at Feilding recently, and every bettor who
had placed money on that horse lost 15c in the dollar. That could not happen in Britain and
Australia, and it should not happen in New Zealand.
That subject was discussed in the select committee hearings, and the Racing
Conference-admittedly for some sound reasons-was very much opposed to a change from
the minus dividend system. It maintained that a change would break some of the smaller
clubs. I asked the conference to give the approximate annual cost of the scheme I favour, if it
was introduced, but I obtained no figures. However, the Avondale Racing Club said that it
wished to run a scheme itself, under which it would guarantee investors their money back,
but the conference would not agree to that proposal. The Avondale Racing Club representa-
tive said that such a scheme would cost about $600 or $700 over a period of 6 years—and that
amount is only pigeon feed to a club such as the Avondale Racing Club-but the conference
denied it the right to operate such a scheme. No wonder some people regard the conference
as undemocratic, and talk about making an appeal to the authority.
The fact that a vast number of punters with the TAB do not know what their fancy is
paying on the tote causes them to be very frustrated and disheartened. They actually have to
back a horse blindly. They want that horse to win, and then, when it does win, they
sometimes lose money. The days of the multiple brackets are gone; most of the small
dividends were paid when the winning horse was one of a bracket, and therefore the
prospect of the minus dividend has lessened, but surely a clause could be inserted in the Bill
to ensure that the backers of winners do not lose on their investment. I have raised this
matter in the House several times in the past few years, but with no success. However, I look
forward to an amendment being introduced within a year or so, setting up a small fund so
that this very desirable scheme can be operated. I conclude by saying that I am very pleased
that, in the main, both parties agree with the Bill.

NATIONAL PARKS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a second

membership of the Egmont National Park Board when the term of the present board expires

board members have been appointed, and bring it more into line with membership of other
national park boards. The Bill also deals with other amendments of a non-controversial
nature, the main ones being an increase in the penalties for offences, and more effective
powers for rangers
and park employees within the boundaries of all parks.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Interrupted debate on the question That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): When the House rose last evening I
was outlining the main features of the Bill. Now I want to turn for a moment or two to clause
17, which inserts a new section 84A in the Social Security Act to make it clear that the
granting of a social security benefit does not in any way restrict the beneficiary's rights to
maintenance under the Domestic Proceedings Act or any other Act. That is consistent with
the long-standing principle that the primary responsibility to support separated and divorced
wives and their children and ex-nuptial children rests with the father of the children rather
than with the taxpayer.
The Government's policy is to adjust the rates of social security benefits every 6 months
in accordance with movements in the consumer price index. This policy has been followed
since the Government took office, and clauses 18 and 19 validate the increases approved in
January and July of this year. Since the Government took office, benefit rates have been
increased in aggregate by $17.58 a week for married couples and $10.55 a week for single
beneficiaries. That represents an increase of 30.3 percent compared with the increase in the
cost of living, as measured by the consumer price index, of only 30.2 percent over the same
period.
The last clause I want to refer to is clause 21, which provides for the additional amount
of $25 to be paid for each dependent child for whom family benefit, orphan's benefit, or
child's war pension is payable in respect of the 4-weekly period commencing on 16
November 1977. These additional amounts, which were paid on 29 November, were aimed
at assisting families with their Christmas expenses, and at stimulating production. They will
be paid for more than 1 000 000 children, and are estimated to cost $25 million.
I want to refer briefly to Part II, which makes major changes in medical, hospital, and
other related benefits. Given the need to restrain Government expenditure, and bearing in
mind that these health benefits are patient benefits, there was a need to adopt a selective
approach when reviewing benefit rates. Also, there is a need to consider the possible impact
of one benefit on others when considering increases in benefit rates. Departmental proposals
about benefit increases were discussed first with the Medical Services Advisory
Committee a statutory body charged with advising the Minister of Health on matters
connected with social security health benefits-and, later, with representatives of the New
Zealand Medical Association. Both the nature and the amount of the variations to the
specialist and general medical services benefits have been fully agreed with the New Zealand
Medical Association
The additional cost of both benefits is estimated at almost $7 million in a full year-$5.3
million for the general services benefit and $1.5 million for the specialist benefit. Informa-
tion filtering through to the Department of Health, and subscribed to by the Medical
Services Advisory Committee, was that some families, particularly single-income families,
were experiencing some difficulty in meeting doctors' charges. It was therefore decided to
increase the general medical services benefit for children only, and to increase it to a level at
which it should normally equate or nearly equate the total normal charge of general
practitioners. In the negotiations that took place with the New Zealand Medical Association,
the association agreed that the prime need was to increase the benefit for children and also
undertook to recommend to the medical profession that any patient charge additional to the


## p. 4955 (#391) ###########################################

1 December
4955
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
new rate of benefit should be "nominal or minimal". That has been done.
The specialist benefit for an initial consultation has not been increased since its
introduction in 1969. That payable for subsequent treatment consultations has merely
followed the movement of the general medical services benefit. The original claim of the
New Zealand Medical Association, which would have involved additional expenditure of $3
million in a full year, demonstrated that in the opinion of the Medical Association a
substantial movement in rates was necessary. The additional $1.5 million available for the
specialist benefit represents about 60 percent of current annual expenditure on this benefit.
Again, a selective approach was clearly called for. The objectives in this selective approach
were, first, to encourage better patient care, particularly for those specialties attracting the
higher initial consultation benefit-that is, physician, paediatrician, psychiatrist, neurolog-
ist, and neurosurgeon.
It is important that the doctor should devote adequate time to seeking to establish a
diagnosis. The quadrupling of the benefit from $5 to $20 will encourage him to spend time
with the patient. Conversely, specialists should be encouraged to release patients back to the
care of general practitioners to treat patients once the diagnosis has been made. If specialists
choose to treat the patient, however, the benefit should not be higher than that attracted by
the general practitioner under the general medical services benefit system.
Secondly, it is necessary to assist child patients. As with the approach adopted for the
general medical services benefit, there is evidence that some parents, particularly in single-
income families, have difficulty in meeting doctors' fees. Once a general practitioner has
established that a specialist opinion is desirable, it is important that this should be obtained.
The $6.50 increase, from $3.50 to $10, in benefit proposed for the specialists attracting the
lower rates of initial consultation benefit will go some way to assisting in this, while the $15
increase for the "long" specialist should meet a reasonable proportion of the total fee.
The third objective is to assist specialist practice. As with other forms of private medical
practice, practice costs have risen substantially and now probably approximate 50 percent of
gross income. There is some reason to suppose that young doctors are not entering private
specialist practice, particularly general physicians, because the income derived is not
commensurate with the time and effort in attaining specialist qualifications and the costs of
establishing themselves in practice. If New Zealand is to have a balanced health service,
regard needs to be paid to ensuring that this form of private practice remains viable.

action in changing the maintenance and collection aspects of Government administration?
No action whatsoever has been taken against the errant father who leaves his wife to rear the
child by herself. About 90 percent of the country's domestic purposes beneficiaries are
legally receiving maintenance, or should be. Maintenance in these cases is intended to offset
the cost to the State of the benefit. However, because the present collection methods return
only between 40 and 50 percent of maintenance owing, the taxpayer has to foot the bill for
the rest.

SPEAKER'S RULING ON URGENCY
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: This may be an appropriate time for me to do what I offered
to do earlier on the point of order raised by the honourable member for Henderson. I have
had further discussions on the matter with my advisers, and I have thought about it myself.
Speaker's ruling 66/3, to which I refer first, says, "A point of order must be brought up at the
time it occurs, and not at a subsequent sitting of the House (or at first reasonable
opportunity)." The event that led to the point of order being raised was the interruption of
the proceedings of the House by the introduction of two members of the Japanese Diet, so
that would have been the appropriate time to raise the point of order. To imply that the
subject-matter of the point of order occurred at 10.30 p.m., when the honourable member
raised it, means that urgency did not begin to take effect until then. That is patently absurd,
of course, but if it were so the incident would not have had the effect of breaking urgency.
The point of order should have been raised at the first reasonable opportunity. Not having
been raised then, it was not properly raised later; so I would have been justified in ignoring it
as a point of order.
The list given in Standing Order 47 is not entirely exhaustive. For example, the making
of a statement by leave by a Minister is specifically allowed for, but there is no allowance for
the making of a statement by leave by a member. Although this matter is raised on a point of
order, which is covered by the Standing Order, the granting of leave to a member is not, if
one wishes to interpret the Standing Order in strict legalistic terms. But I am sure no
member would want that courtesy and concession to be denied to a member, and as far as I
know no one has ever claimed that such an interruption has broken urgency. Were I to have
upheld the point of order raised by the member for Henderson, I think that would effectively
have prevented the Speaker from ever again extending a customary courtesy to a visiting
fellow member after urgency has been taken, because that action is approved by the Speaker
himself and he would not wish to interfere in that way in the business of the House. The
introduction of visitors is a courtesy that does not involve the stating of a motion. No
member has a right to speak to it. The interruption to introduce distinguished visitors is in
the nature of a formal communication from the Speaker, and his actions are not open to
debate except by motion, and can therefore be taken to be outside the scope of the business
of the House.
The exclusions in Standing Order 47 (3) are all matters provided for in other Standing
Orders. The word "purpose" must relate to the business of Parliament. It must mean a
purpose contemplated by the Standing Orders-that is, a question or amendment, or a
question of order, as provided in Standing Order 166. Interruption of this kind was in the
nature of a hiatus in the business of the House, because this action is nowhere contemplated
under our Standing Orders. In any case, since the situation is not covered by our own
Standing Orders, I must fall back on Standing Order 2. There being no guidance from the
House of Commons, I go back to the common law rule of common sense, and I am sure that
common sense would not suggest that I should not have asked the House to extend a
traditional courtesy to distinguished visitors in that way.
The House adjourned at 12.50 a.m. (Friday).

to extend the session a little, or maybe take a break of a day or two, so that when we come to
the last day we will have everything in front of us, particularly that rather complex Bill on
which there is a free vote, and on which I imagine there will be some further printing to be
done to get a clean copy. We should get a clean copy of it before we finally pass it in
whatever form the House decides.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Lotteries for Performing Arts
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert)
asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Does he intend to conduct one or more special
lotteries, the profits from which would be made available to assist the performing arts?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): Under the present legislation, the
Gaming Amendment Act 1963, no provision is made for the conduct of national lotteries for
special purposes. However, this will be possible under the provisions of the Gaming and
Lotteries Bill now before the House, which is to come into force on 1 April next. At this
stage I have no definite plans for such special lotteries.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Will the Minister give sympathetic consideration to the plight of
the arts when he does get around to considering special purpose lotteries?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Naturally I shall have to discuss the question of special purpose
lotteries with the Lotteries Board of Control, but when the general question was raised
earlier I indicated that I considered it would not be inappropriate to conduct lotteries to
assist in the funding of projects such as the National Art Gallery. While specific capital
projects appear to be appropriate for special lotteries, general purposes such as providing
assistance to the performing arts would be of doubtful appropriateness. After all, the board
makes an annual grant of about $500,000 to the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council for general
purposes at the moment.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Then is one to assume that the likelihood of such a lottery for the
benefit of the performing arts is remote?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: As I mentioned, for general purposes it is remote, but for a
specific project that embraces the arts it is a possibility.

Housing Corporation-Vendor Mortgage Scheme
6. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Housing: In view of his
statement in the Dominion of 25 November that National's manifesto had mentioned that
lenders in the vendor mortgage scheme had to be approved and that the individual in the
case was not an approved lender, could he confirm that the Housing Corporation would not
allow the woman to take out a mortgage in her name but would approve a mortgage whereby
her solicitor's nominee company acted as her agent, and could he explain the reason for the
distinction?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Both the National Party's manifesto
and the 1977 Budget provided that for a vendor mortgagee to qualify for a tax rebate under
the vendor mortgage scheme the mortgage must be a guaranteed first mortgage. A
guaranteed first mortgage through the Housing Corporation is one administered by an
approved lender who has both the ability and facility to undertake loans on mortgage. In the
case referred to by the member, the woman can take a mortgage in her name, but, under the
vendor mortgage scheme, the loan to be guaranteed must be through a solicitor or a
solicitor's nominee company or other approved lender that has first satisfied the corpora-
tion's requirements under the guarantee scheme.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is the Minister aware that the solicitors have indicated that the
corporation had advised them that it would not approve of the lady as a lender in her own
name?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I am not aware that the corporation had advised the solicitors
that they would not approve of the lady as a lender in her own name. I am aware that
individuals are not approved by the Housing Corporation under the terms of its own scheme.
Of course, the mortgage could be in this lady's own name and simply administered by the
nominee company or by the solicitors, but I am advised that in this particular case the
solicitors, of their own choice, do not wish to be approved lenders.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is the Minister also aware that, in terms of the booklet on mortgage
guarantees which is deemed to be incorporated in the Act and comprises 15 pages, an
approved lender must also be able to provide valuation services, and that solicitors' nominee
companies are not in a position to provide such a service?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not know that I can answer all those questions, but I can
tell the honourable member that there is no difficulty in approving organisations such as
solicitors' nominee companies as approved lenders.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Queen Elizabeth Arts Council Amendment Bill (No. 2) 2 December
QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND AMEND-
MENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Queen Elizabeth
the Second Arts Council of New Zealand Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. In its
election policy statement the Government gave an undertaking that it would encourage the
practice and the appreciation of Maori and other Polynesian arts. The principal purpose of
the Bill is to provide for the establishment of a council for traditional Maori and other
Polynesian arts within the structure of the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council. The
Bill introduces a new Part IA in the principal Act to provide the structure and means to assist
in preserving the traditional arts of the Maori and other Polynesian peoples, and to
encourage the practice of these arts in the present day. I firmly believe that these traditional
art forms, springing as they do from an immensely rich tradition, will bring to today's society
more than just the re-creation of art objects. They should provide fresh enlightenment and
understanding to a society that has much to recover from the past. The arts of the
Polynesians are an integral and important part of their society. The membership of the
council will, therefore, be very important.
The Bill provides for maximum consultation in the appointment of council members. I
must consult the Minister of Maori Affairs. The Bill also specifically provides that I should
consider any nomination submitted by any person. I want to emphasise that this committee is
for the Maori and Polynesian people, and their policies, their enthusiasm, and their foresight
will be required to make it work. It is not something imposed on Maori and Polynesian arts
by an alien bureaucracy, neither is it something separate from the other New Zealand arts.
I must admit that I was concerned at the original proposals that a separate council from
other New Zealand arts be established. The council has been placed within the Queen
Elizabeth the Second Arts Council, because it has a major contribution to make to all the
arts in New Zealand. That is why the functions of the council, as set out in the Bill, link it so
closely with the main functions of the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council and its
community and regional councils. It would be wrong to make the council, and hence these
arts, separate from the practice of all other arts in New Zealand. The Bill provides that the
chairman of the council for traditional Maori and Polynesian arts will be a member of the
Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council, and that is the major reason for amending the
legislation. At the appropriate time I shall move that the Bill be referred to the Maori Affairs
Committee for recess study. It is likely that there will be differing views-for example, on
the definition of traditional arts, and on the scope of the council's work. I therefore believe
that all the views of those deeply concerned merit careful consideration. The Bill also
amends other aspects of a minor administrative nature. The definition of the Minister is
amended to read "Minister for the Arts". Provision is also made for administrative local
authorities to make a grant to enable a community arts council to undertake its functions.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): I was pleased to hear the Minister say that the Bill will go to a
select committee to enable submissions to be heard. I take it that the hearings will be open to
the media. The establishment of a council for traditional Maori and Polynesian art has a lot
of merit, but one or two matters need to be cleared up. We know that a certain amount of
money is given to the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council-the main council-and
that there have been many complaints that the council has not received even the minimum
amount of money it wanted. I think it received $100,000 less this year.
The council being set up is excellent, but it will not be much good if the money needed
to establish it and to finance its grants is to come from the overall grant made to the Queen
Elizabeth the Second Arts Council. Will a separate grant be given to the council, so that the
already low amount received by the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council will not be
depleted even further? The proposed new section 25A in the new Part IA inserted by clause 3
states: “. . .(2) The Council for Traditional Maori and Polynesian Art shall consist of the
following members: (a) One person who shall be appointed as chairman by the Minister; and
(b) Eight other persons who shall be appointed by the Minister." The only consultation will
be between the Minister in charge of the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council, and the
Minister of Maori Affairs. Would it not be more proper for the Minister to consult the New
Zealand Maori Council?
Mr Couch: He will.
Mr ISBEY: It does not say so in the Bill, which states that the Minister will consult the

WAR PENSIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): On behalf of the Minister in Charge of
War Pensions I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill gives legislative
effect to several adjustments that have been made to war pensions since December 1976.
The adjustments fall into two main categories: adjustments to war disablement and war
widows' pensions; and special payments and increases to war economic pensions, war service
pensions, and war veterans' allowances.
Adjustments to war disablement and war widows' pensions are made on the basis of
movements in the consumer price index. Under an agreement between the Government and
the New Zealand Returned Services Association these pensions are reviewed annually at
1 April each year. From 1 April 1977 the disablement pension for total disablement was
increased by $3.55 a week to $29.45 a week. Pro rata increases were awarded to pensioners
with a lesser degree of disablement. From the same date war widows received an increase of
$2.65 to $21.75 a week. The additional pensions for the severely disabled and clothing
allowances were also increased from 1 April.
The increases in disablement and war widows' pensions are further evidence of this
Government's commitment to meet the needs of disabled ex-servicemen and their depen-
dants. Most of those pensioners, disabled in wartime, are, of course, now well over the age
of 50, and it may be that their disability has deteriorated with increasing age. I urge
pensioners in this position who are receiving a pension assessed at less than 100 percent
disablement to approach their local social welfare office and apply for a review of their
disablement pension. Arrangements would then be made for them to be medically examined
and for the rate of their pension to be reviewed in the light of the medical report.
Other adjustments validated in the Bill are increases in war economic pensions, war
service pensions, and war veterans' allowances from 12 January 1977 and again from 27 July
1977. The increase in these pensions and allowances from 12 January 1977 was $3.64 a week
for married couples and $2.18 a week for unmarried persons. The allowances for children of
solo parent pensioners were increased by $1.48 a week from the same date. From 27 July
1977 the basic rates of these pensions were further increased by $4.84 a week to $68.84 a
week for married couples and by $2.90 a week to $41.30 a week for unmarried persons. War
orphans' pensions were increased to $21.65 a week, and the allowances for children of solo
parents who are on pensions were also increased again.
There has been some misunderstanding about the rights of persons receiving war
veterans' allowances or war service pensions to transfer to national superannuation. I want
to stress again that whether or not it is to their financial advantage to do so depends on the
individual circumstances of the pensioner, and any pensioner still in doubt about his best
course of action would be well advised to discuss his position with a departmental officer.
War veterans' allowances and war service pensions should not be confused with war
disablement pensions, which are paid regardless of financial circumstances to compensate
for a disability attributable to or aggravated by service with the forces. Disablement pensions
can be paid in addition to national superannuation, which means that a disabled ex-
serviceman who is over the age of 60 can receive full national superannuation as well as his
disablement pension.
A further adjustment validated in the Bill is the special additional payment made in
December last year to each income-tested pensioner. This additional payment was the
eqivalent of 1 week's payment of the recipient's income-tested pension or allowance.

IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. As members will be aware there has already been considerable debate on the Bill, both
at the time of its introduction and when it was reported back from the Labour Committee.
The Bill has been described as controversial. It should not be controversial, and would not
be controversial were it not for the number of misleading and even incorrect statements
about the contents of the Bill and what it is intended to achieve.
In essence the Bill is concerned with five things. First, it makes it necessary for a
temporary visitor who wants to work to hold a valid work permit; and if he works without
such a permit he commits an offence. To my mind there should be nothing controversial
about this provision. In virtually every country there is a system of work permits. For
instance, a person cannot enter the United States, Switzerland, or Great Britain as an
ordinary visitor and then obtain work without first obtaining permission; yet, apart from
people coming from Fiji, Western Samoa, and Tonga under the South Pacific work permit
schemes, virtually all persons coming to New Zealand as ordinary visitors can take up
employment without any further formalities. I need hardly remind people that the jobs taken
by such visitors might be jobs that would otherwise go to unemployed New Zealanders, or
possibly to people coming in legally under the Pacific Islands work permit schemes.
The Government will not be stopping all temporary visitors from working. That is
certainly not its wish. Many temporary visitors can help the New Zealand economy, as well
as themselves, if they are allowed to work here. Moreover, the Government recognises that
many of our young people go to countries such as Britain to work, to see the world, and to
gain experience. The Government, therefore, wants to allow young people from Britain and
elsewhere to come here and work on a temporary basis. But the issue of work permits will be
controlled, and the Government will not allow temporary visitors to New Zealand to hold
jobs that are needed by suitably qualified New Zealanders.
Secondly, the Bill makes it an offence to obtain an immigration permit, or extension or
variation thereof, by making false representations. At the present time it is an offence to
obtain a permit to enter New Zealand by making false representations. However, nothing at
present makes it an offence for a visitor already in New Zealand to obtain an extension to a
temporary permit, or to obtain permits such as re-entry permits by making false representa-
tions. That is obviously a loophole that needs to be closed.
Thirdly, the Bill will make it an offence for an employer to employ someone who he
knows does not have a permit that allows him to work. This is the part of the Bill that has
provided most comment, and on which there is most misunderstanding. We have heard
statements that employers will be acting as an arm of the immigration division, and that the
legislation will make it necessary for them to interrogate prospective employees to see if they
are entitled to work. Such statements are completely false.
Mr Malcolm: And irresponsible.
Hon. T. F. GILL: Yes, they are false and irresponsible. I want to make it crystal clear
that employers will not be required to interrogate workers to see if they are entitled to work,
nor will they be required to do anything they are not required already to do. The Bill
states-and it means what it says—that an employer will commit an offence if he employs or
continues to employ someone he knows is not entitled to work. He must know-not suspect,
or believe, or think. He commits an offence only if he knows that the person should not
work, but nevertheless goes ahead and employs him. Such legislation is extremely reason-
able. Under section 37(1) of the Factories Act it is an offence for an employer to employ in a
factory anyone under the age of 15 years. In other words, he commits an offence if he
employs someone who should not be working in a factory.
There is very little difference between that legislation and the provision contained in
clause 4 of the Bill. In speaking on this clause I should stress very strongly that the legislation
as presently worded is acceptable to the Employers Federation, which stated in its submis-
sion: "We acknowledge that for a person whose right to be in the country at all is controlled
by a permit, he should not seek or obtain employment or engage in any activity for gain or
reward except as specified in the permit. Were he to do so he would clearly be committing an
offence. We also acknowledge as a principle that an employer should not with deliberate


## p. 4982 (#418) ###########################################

4982
2 December
Immigration Amendment Bill
intention employ any such person who is committing an offence." That is also the Govern-
ment's view, which is reflected in the legislation.
Fourthly, the legislation allows the Minister of Immigration, if he thinks fit, to require a
person who is to be deported to pay the whole or part of the expenses associated with his
deportation, instead of the taxpayer footing the Bill as sometimes happens. This provision
needs little elaboration. If a person is to be deported for breaking our laws and if he is in a
position to pay the costs himself, I see little reason for the New Zealand taxpayer to foot the
bill. Fifthly, the Bill will enable a person ordered to be deported for an immigration offence
to appeal, if there are exceptional circumstances of a humanitarian nature, to the Minister of
Immigration for the deportation order to be revoked. If the Minister is satisfied in the light
of these circumstances that the sentence of deportation is unduly harsh or unjust he may
permit the person concerned to remain in New Zealand. This provision is probably one of
the most far-reaching advances in our immigration legislation. At the present time a person
convicted of being in New Zealand illegally is automatically sentenced to deportation,
irrespective of his personal circumstances.
I need hardly say that such a procedure can on occasion cause great hardship. The
provisions in clause 6 will remedy that. I do not see the clause being used lightly. If a person
is in New Zealand illegally he can expect to be deported; that will be the normal procedure.
If there are genuine humanitarian circumstances that make deportation unduly harsh or
unjust, then that person shall be allowed to stay.
I am sure that during the debate there will be misinformed criticism to the effect that the
appeal procedure should be handled in a different way. I have already heard suggestions that
the court should decide whether a person should be permitted to remain permanently in New
Zealand. That ignores the fact that circumstances of a humanitarian nature are highly
confidential and it is not fitting or possible to discuss them in a court of law. Moreover, it
ignores the fact that a decision to allow a person to stay in New Zealand is an immigration
decision and not a legal decision. This sort of suggestion has been made by people who have
been aware of the problem for years, but who until now have said nothing about it.
It is appropriate to mention at this stage that the Government proposes to introduce
legislation this session which will bring the deportation provisions of the Aliens Act into the
Immigration Act, and will establish a tribunal to hear appeals from any person who has been
ordered to leave New Zealand for offences other than immigration offences. Consequently,
the present Bill, together with the Bill to be introduced, will provide, for the first time,
comprehensive machinery to consider appeals from anyone who is being deported either for
immigration offences or other offences. The Bill to be introduced will be referred to a select
committee for recess study.
I shall now deal with the Bill clause by clause. Clause 1 relates to the short title and
commencement date. Clause 2 relates to visitors to the country, and makes it an offence if
they obtain employment or engage in any activity for gain or reward unless they have been
authorised to do so. Clause 3 is a machinery provision extending the present provision by
making it an offence to obtain by false representation an extension or variation of any permit
ssued under the Immigration Act. Clause 4 makes it an offence for an employer to employ
or continue to employ someone he knows is not permitted to work. Clause 5 makes provision
for the Minister of Immigration to require a deportee to meet various deportation costs.
Clause 6 gives the Minister of Immigration the power to allow a person convicted of an
immigration offence to stay in New Zealand if, in his view, there are exceptional humanita-
rian circumstances which would make it unduly harsh or unjust for the person to be
deported.

99
The general feeling in Western Samoa and Tonga is that New Zealand should have a
continuous, revolving system which encourages Island people to come here under a work
permit scheme. If they illegally settle here permanently, as they so often do, the overall
scheme will not be able to continue as in the past. I believe it is in the interests of Island
communities to have a strong movement of people coming to New Zealand under the work
permit scheme.
The member for Hutt asked whether preachers and evangelists brought to this country
would require permits under the provisions of clause 2. The department will issue permits to
such preachers, but there will always be the question of whether they require outside work
which would take employment opportunities away from New Zealanders. This will be the
overriding factor. I do not envisage any system different from the current one applying to
evangelists coming to New Zealand.
The member for Hutt also mentioned the industrial unrest that could result if this
legislation is passed. It is true to say that submissions made by the Federation of Labour and
others, including the employers, expressed concern that industrial disputes could result
because of an employer's actions. I do not believe that is correct. As the immigration
division of the Department of Labour will continue to handle the matter, I do not think the
argument is valid. I was surprised at the submissions made by the Federation of Labour, as I
thought it would have been concerned, since every person who comes to New Zealand
illegally and works puts a New Zealand worker out of a job. I thought the federation would
have been more co-operative. It did state, however, that it thought the immigration division
should be strengthened to take overall control, so that an employer would not be responsible
for seeing that people illegally in New Zealand were not taking jobs from New Zealanders.
Every New Zealander has a responsibility to co-operate; that is all the legislation requires.

Mr LUXTON: The proposed new section 19A in clause 4 of the original Bill stated:
"Every person commits an offence and is liable to a fine not exceeding $200, and, if the
offence is a continuing one, to a further fine not exceeding $20 for each day during which the
offence has continued, who engages or offers to engage in any type of employment any other
person who he has reason to know (a) Is required to hold a permit under this Act but does
not in fact hold one; or (b) Holds a temporary permit. . ." That provision was changed quite
considerably in line with the representations made.
It is now an offence for an employer who employs or continues to employ in any type of
employment any other person if he knows that that other person is required to hold a permit.
The employer has to know, rather than have reason to know. I believe that this meets the
requirements of the many people who came before the select committee. The Employers
Federation felt that this was necessary, and we have met its request and overcome the
problem. Indeed, the Employers Federation wanted the word "knowingly" inserted, rather
than the words "has reason to know".

immigration division to do its work and to enforce the Act as the Government would wish it
to be enforced in future. I believe it will be in everyone's interest to have a system that
continues to operate to the benefit of all.

Supplementary Questions Procedure
TUESDAY, 6 DECEMBER 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SUPPLEMENTARY QUESTIONS PROCEDURE
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: It may suit the convenience of honourable members if I rule
on two matters referred to me last week to which I said I would give consideration. The first
is the question of the priority accorded members seeking to ask a supplementary question.
Standing Order 311, which deals with the procedure to be followed in the Committee of the
Whole House, lays down the principle of alternation of calls, all other things being equal.
However, Standing Order 84 states that, at the discretion of Mr Speaker, supplementary
questions to elucidate an answer may be asked by any member. Therefore Standing Order 84
gives the Speaker absolute discretion in deciding who to call and, I presume, in what order.
I have also consulted Mr Speaker Jack. He informs me that he initiated the practice of
allotting the first supplementary question to the member who asked the question originally. I
think that has been the accepted practice, and it is one that I certainly have followed. It
seems to me that the logical extension of that principle is to allow any member on the same
side of the House as the member who asked the question to substitute for that member in
asking the first supplementary question if that member so desires. For example, there are
occasions on which the leader of either side of the House may seek the call to ask the first
supplementary question, in which case—providing, of course, the member who asked the
original question is prepared to yield to him—he will be the appropriate member to call.
That is the procedure I propose to continue to follow. It has been rather difficult to
determine from the journals what has happened in the past, because the reports do not show
whether a member who has sought the call first has been overruled.
ATTIRE OF MEMBERS IN CHAMBER
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The second matter on which I propose to rule now was raised
by the honourable member for Napier, who requested that members be permitted to remove
their jackets in the Chamber. As honourable members know, the Chamber is air
conditioned. I am informed that the air-conditioning plant has been installed progressively
since about 1972, but that it is still subject to change and to improvement, and I gather that
more improvements are likely to be made to it. Honourable members will notice that over
the weekend the green covering above the fanlights in the ceiling has been replaced. That
has had the effect of reducing at least the glare if not the heat.
I also point out to honourable members that the near set of fanlights has been changed;
the old leadlights have been taken out and experimental plastic ones have been put in, I
think as much for the safety of members as for their comfort. There has been some
suggestion that, in the event of some earth-shattering occurrence, the leadlights might come
down and do grievous bodily harm to those sitting beneath-and those sitting beneath
happen to be members, the Hansard staff, and the staff of the Clerk's office. I am led to
believe that the plastic material, if shattered, will just flutter down gently and not do so much
damage.
The air-conditioning equipment has been installed with the object of regulating the
temperature, but not the humidity. The object of the exercise is to keep the temperature
between 67°F and 69°F, whatever that is in Celsius; the equipment, like me, is not
sophisticated enough to handle that sort of equation, but normally it keeps the temperature
between 66°F and 70°F. However, I am told that the equipment cannot cope on those rare
occasions when Wellington turns on the heat without the wind to blow it away. I think one of
those very rare occasions occurred last week, and it probably led the honourable member for
Napier to raise the matter in the House and ask whether members could remove their
jackets. I discussed this matter also with Mr Speaker Jack, and his advice was that on the
rare occasions when members might suffer some discomfort it would be in the interests of the
decorum of the House if members kept their jackets on to maintain formal wear. I have no
desire to change that.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Auckland International Airport
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services: Can he confirm that the situation that will prevail on the opening of
the Auckland International Airport next month is that: (a) a piece of equipment costing
$50,000 and imported for the purpose of improving the airport's instrument landing system
will have been lying uncrated for 2 years; and (b) air traffic controllers serving the airport
will have amassed some 800 days' holiday time owing to them; and, if so, what steps does he
propose to take to remedy this situation?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
The equipment to which the member refers has been installed on a trial basis. Technical
problems have arisen, and I am not yet in a position to forecast when they will be resolved.
In the meantime, the equipment originally installed is still in use and is providing a
satisfactory service to the operators. It is correct that air traffic controllers serving the airport
will have an amassed sum of approximately 800 days' holiday time owing to them. The
primary reason for this situation is the decision of the State Services Tribunal on May 1976 to
give controllers an additional 8 days' leave per annum and the backdating of the implementa-
tion of that decision to July 1975. In addition, the tribunal approved a roster system which
had the effect of giving controllers an extra 16 non-working days per annum. The combined
effect of these decisions created a shortage of staff to meet the new rosters. The normal
training of controllers requires 3 years and, while the ministry has taken steps to increase
staff and has recruited adults with flying experience who can be trained in a shorter period, it
will be some months before it is possible to completely eradicate the leave backlog.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Has the department yet embarked on the research programme
into air traffic control which the State Services Tribunal, either in that decision or in another
one going back 2 years, then said was urgent in the interests of safety?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The ministry has embarked on looking at air traffic
controllers in general and the training that they need. One difficulty which I did not mention
in my original answer was that when topdressing work showed a downturn we were able to
train more air traffic controllers quickly because of their previous flying experience. When
the industry again showed an upturn, we lost those officers back to private industry.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

2. Mr. T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: In view of the

is used most economically?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): While long distance rail haulage is
more than twice as fuel efficient as long distance diesel truck haulage, it is not so easy to
generalise about the short-haul situation where shunting and inconvenient truck deliveries to
rail heads must be recognised. It is by requiring the road transport industry to pay its proper
costs for wear and tear on the roads, and by promoting fuel efficiency through the tax
system, that I believe we can have a transport sector that is an efficient and economical user
of resources.
Mr T. J. Young: Will the Minister introduce steps to monitor the effective use of fuel in

Farm Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme
3. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the report in
the Northern Advocate of 19 November 1977 that 45 farmers have already applied to the
Whangarei office of the Department of Labour to participate in the farm employment wages
subsidy scheme, and can he give the latest figures of the number of applicants applying in
Northland and the rest of New Zealand?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I have seen the report referred to by the
member for Hobson in the Northern Advocate of 19 November 1977 on the recently
announced farm employment subsidy scheme. As at Friday, 2 December 1977, 21 workers
had been placed with farmers in Northland and there were 62 vacancies for which workers
were being considered. At 2 December 1977 151 persons were working under the scheme
throughout New Zealand, and there were 201 unfilled vacancies for which workers were
being considered.
Mr H. N. Austin: Can the Minister give a breakdown of the number of females in the
scheme?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Nationally the figure was 23, and in the Whangarei district, which
I presume is the same as Northland, it was 1. The area employing the most females was
Gisborne, with six.
Hon. M. Rata: As the registered unemployed in Northland is estimated to be 12 percent
of the total registered unemployed, is the Minister satisfied that this scheme is sufficient to
deal with the problem; and, if not, what other schemes does he have in mind?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Accepting the member's figures, this scheme is but one of six or
seven alternatives offered in the Prime Minister's recent Financial Statement. The most
successful scheme by far, numerically, is the community work effort under the control of the
Minister of Internal Affairs. From memory, about 134 schemes, with multiple numbers of
people involved, have been approved in that field already.
Mr Elliott: Is the Minister aware that no tertiary students came forward for a Lands and
Survey block scheme proposal in the Dargaville area, just out of Whangarei, last week, and
so the department had to call on the unemployed register to fill that vacancy; in other words,
no tertiary students were available?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I am not aware of the details of that case, but I am aware of
complaints from employers who have not received answers to applications for certain jobs.
Mr Rogers: The Minister said that 45 farmers had applied for the subsidy and that 21
had been satisfied. Could he say why the other 24 farmers had received no reply to their
request?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I said that in Northland 21 workers had been placed, and that
there were 62 vacancies for which workers were being considered. I think the member will
appreciate that in "boss and one worker" or "boss and two workers" relationships everyone
must be compatible, and the department is making every effort to see that there is
compatibility. It is not the same as working in a factory.
Mr Rogers: If a farmer was prepared to take his own worker along, is it legal for him to
suggest to the Department of Labour that his worker would be suitable for the job, and
could the department employ him?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No. I give the member an absolute assurance that that is
debarred. The original annnouncement stated that the scheme applied only to workers over
and above the number he has employed at any time before.

Railways Workshops
5. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), on behalf of Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth), asked

equipment and rehabilitate workshops", and, if so, can he advise whether there is any
evidence available to support that claim?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways); Yes, I have seen the report
referred to by the member for New Plymouth, and I can assure him that the allegations are
completely unfounded. The Government is fully committed to the reorganisation and the
redevelopment of railway workshops. A workshops redevelopment working party, with joint
union and management membership, has been set up and has already made a number of
interim recommendations. One recommendation was for the urgent purchase of some new
equipment for the workshops, and now, just 6 weeks later, tenders have closed for this
equipment costing more than $1 million, and some has already been ordered. Last Thursday
the working party completed its field work of visiting railway workshops, and I will be
looking for the working party's full recommendations early next year.

being smashed up, so I cannot answer the question. However, some refurbishing is being
carried out.

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: In 1977, 20 apprentices were taken on at East Town, and

to Wanganui-which has increased from 402 recruited last year to 672 authorised this year. I
do not have any further information on the East Town workshops, but I was pleased to learn
this morning that additional tradesmen are being recruited.

Fish-Commercial Netting in Rivers
9. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Are there regulations
governing the placing of nets across freshwater rivers, such as the Wairau in Marlborough,
by commercial fishermen, and, if so, who is responsible for enforcement?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): It is lawful to fish for native species of sea
fish provided the net does not extend more than halfway across the width of the river.
Kawhai may be taken by this method, but not trout or salmon. The fisheries officers of the
Ministry are primarily responsible for policing this regulation.
Dr Shearer: Does the local acclimatisation society have any power?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: Acclimatisation society staff sometimes have Part I Fisheries Act
warrants and therefore may police this regulation. If acclimatised fish are netted, any
society's ranger can take action.

Economy-Department of Statistics Figures
10. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Statistics: Has he seen the letter
in the Dominion of 30 November, in which a certain Mr G. A. Chapman expresses his
concern at the use of balance of payments figures produced by the Department of Statistics,
and, if so, can he advise the House whether those figures are an "accepted measurement of
New Zealand's international economic performance", and whether, in view of Mr Chap-
man's obvious preference for the Reserve Bank overseas exchange transaction figures, his
department intends to continue publication of its own series?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics): I have seen the letter from Mr G. A.
Chapman, President of the New Zealand National Party. I agree that the Reserve Bank
statistics are more realistic because they measure cash flows for international economic
performance between New Zealand and the rest of the world. Balance of payments figures
include significant elements which do not affect cash flows; for example, the net retained
earnings of overseas-owned New Zealand companies, which for the year ended September
1977 made the current account deficit for the balance of payments about $156 million more
negative than the current account balance in the overseas exchange transactions. It would
include, too, imports of ships and planes financed on credit; for example, even the Penrod
rig and the Blue Whale vessel would be included as imports when they came into the country
and exports when they leave. This in no way rules out the requirements for balance of
payment figures to measure all reserves. The Department of Statistics will continue to
publish its own series as an accepted measurement.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister give the movement in the balance of trade as shown in the
overseas exchange transactions record and the overseas balance of payments statement for
the year ended September 1977?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is not related to the original question or answer. The
question sought information about the acceptability of two methods of publishing statistics.
That should be the basis of any supplementary question.
Mr T. J. Young: Is there any way the Minister can modify or correct either the
presentation made by the Department of Statistics or the Reserve Bank so that the picture is
more realistic and united?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No. It is accepted that there are two different ways of
measuring and they each have different components. One problem with the balance of
payments statistics from the department is that initially they are an estimate and not
necessarily precise. Over the years the department has refined its system. When the figures
are presented as estimates they are acceptable for use, and when finally presented they are a
generally accepted international measurement.
Mr Marshall: Can the Minister confirm that the balance of payments figures from his
department are more likely to be up-to-date than was the case earlier, and there is no longer
any necessity to depend on overseas exchange transactions figures for up-to-date accurate

statements of the country's position?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I do not believe there is any need for change, as the
member has suggested. It is a matter of utilising which set of figures is required. It is
generally accepted that in the immediate term the overseas exchange transactions figures are
more likely to be accurate, but both are needed to measure overall performance.

Accident Compensation-Doctor-Patient Relationship
11. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Labour: Can he advise whether
current Accident Compensation Commission procedures require a doctor to disclose
personal details of an accident or treatment directly linked to the name of an individual
patient, and, if so, is this a breach of the principle of confidentiality in the doctor-patient
relationship?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Section 146 of the Accident Compensation
Act empowers the commission to require a doctor to supply certain information relevant to a
compensation claim made by his patient. The information includes details of the injuries
seen or diagnosed by the doctor, and the treatment given. However, except with the
claimant's consent the commission cannot require a doctor to disclose statements made to
him by his patient. This is the only area in which the law of privilege protects doctor-patient
confidentiality in so far as the Accident Compensation Act is concerned.
Mr Malcolm: Has the Accident Compensation Commission required, as an administra-
tive procedure, doctors to give details of accidents for treatment directly linked with
individual patients?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I understand that the commission has recently asked doctors
seeking payment of more than $6.50 to give details of the injuries or the treatment given to
the patient.
Mr Malcolm: Has that request by the Accident Compensation Commission met with
opposition or support from the medical profession?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The question is in two parts. I have received complaints about the
former part of the question, but am not aware of any protest by the medical profession. I
have not received any communication from the profession.

E. C. T. Treatment, Lake Alice
20. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to ask the Minister of Health: Is it correct that
the only administrative preliminary to the administration of electro-convulsive therapy at
Lake Alice Hospital is a requirement that the patient sign a form stating "I have no objection
to receiving E. C. T. treatment"?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): This is not correct. Normal procedures are that
on admission to Lake Alice Hospital all possible forms of treatment, including electro-
convulsive therapy, are first discussed with the patient, and the likely outcome, benefits, and
disadvantages of each form are explained. Only after this is done does the patient sign a form
indicating the treatment to which he gives consent. When the patient is so disturbed that
discussion would be unprofitable, the treatment is discussed with or notified in writing to the
patient's next of kin. In the case of a child, treatment is discussed with the patient's legal
guardian and any others who have an interest in the child's welfare. If the patient or next of
kin object to any form of treatment, the psychiatrist in charge of the case, if he decides to
proceed, records his reasons why treatment should proceed and the fact that his reasons have
been discussed with another psychiatrist.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Could the Minister take steps to correct the information
disseminated by the Citizens Commission on Human Rights to the effect that the only
requirement is the signing of a form in the terms quoted in the question?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There is not much merit in correcting every claim that is made, and, if
one tried to, the press would not have room to print it. This one had not been brought to my
attention. If the member is prepared to send it to me, I should be delighted to take it up with
the hospital.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to

Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 2)
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. The Bill is a major and complex measure, with 250 new sections
to be included in the principal Act. A working party comprising departmental officers, a
recently retired town clerk, and a county clerk worked for some time to bring together this
major amendment incorporating the many new sections into the existing Municipal Corpora-
tions Act and the Counties Act. The proposals were the subject of detailed discussion with
the local government consultative group representing the Municipal Association and the
Counties Association, and we reached 99 percent agreement-if not 100 percent
agreement—with the working party and the consultative group before the Bill was
introduced into the House and referred to the committee.
It is understandable with a measure such as this that many people would want to make
submissions, and that the committee would be recommending many amendments as a result.
No other outcome could be expected in the light of the range and complexity of the subjects
covered. At a time when suggestions have been made that legislation is being rushed through
the House, I point out to honourable members and others who may be interested that all
those who wanted to appear before the committee and make submissions in support of their
view did appear, were given the opportunity to state their case, and were cross-examined by
committee members. Fifty-two submissions were made, and more than 20 of those who
made submissions appeared before the committee.
Most of the amendments relate to matters of a machinery nature. The work had been
well and truly done before the Bill saw the light of day. I do not propose to discuss the
amendments now, as the opportunity will occur during the Committee stage. I thank all
those who made submissions, many of which contained useful suggestions. It is pertinent to
observe that one or two of those who appeared told the committee that they had really to
delve into the fine print of the legislation to come up with worth-while submissions. I thank
the members of the committee who devoted so much time and effort to what was by any
standards difficult legislation to deal with-particularly the member for Oamaru, who
chaired the committee in the latter stages during my absence overseas. I thank also the
departmental officers and Mr McVeagh, parliamentary counsel, for the time and patience
they devoted to this complex legislation.

Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): Some unusual arrangements seem to have been
made, and I do not want to cut across them if it is avoidable. During the Committee stage
some parts of the Bill were opposed by the Opposition. I refer particularly to the
amendments, which really spelled out the different views of the Government and the
Opposition about this important Bill, which, of course, is part of the total package of
industrial law that has been before the House for some weeks. The wording of clause 3(2)
was opposed because Opposition members believe that if the court is to succeed, especially
with general wage orders, it is imperative that it is seen by the work force and the employers
to be paramountly concerned with maintaining living standards rather than the economy.
The amendments put forward as a consequence were defeated by the Government's
majority. Nevertheless, the Opposition believes that its approach to the matter is superior.
Although one cannot divorce the impact of wages on the economy, members on this
side believe that the court as such ought not to be seen as an instrument to sustain the


## p. 5007 (#443) ###########################################

6 December
5007
General Wage Orders Bill
economy, but should play its part in such a way as to maintain the confidence and proper
participation of the work force and employers in determining what is a fair and equitable
share, whatever the economy might be. When clause 6 was being discussed during the
Committee stage the Opposition moved that when making a general order the court should
give paramount importance to the maintenance and promotion of living standards so far as it
is within the capacity of the economy to sustain such an adjustment. This seemed to give the
court its proper priority rather than putting the economy ahead of the work force.
Opposition members consider that the court's job is to see that there is justice and
equity, whatever the economy. Too often the workers have thought that the conditions of
their employment, or wages, are the tools of Governments trying to adjust the economy. I
do not know whether that argument is acceptable, or non-debatable, but in human relations
what people think is sometimes more important than what the situation actually is.
Therefore, what appears to be a matter of semantics is a great deal more than that. It
establishes in the minds of the parties concerned that when they appear before the court it
will consider their position, not that of the economy, as being of paramount importance,
even though the economy must be taken into account.
Clause 7 provides a general right for the Combined State Service Organisations and
others-including the Minister of Finance—to be heard. If there is to be a Minister, we
believe that it should be the Minister of Labour, so that again the involvement is away from
those concerned totally with the economy, and so that the work force knows that its
Minister-the Minister of Labour-is involved. Also, it is important that the Department of
Labour should be concerned if a Minister is to be involved, because the department has no
other objective than the promotion of the best results from our industrial resources-the
work force and the capital involved. The argument sounds semantic; it is true that if it is the
Minister of Labour he will seek advice from the Minister of Finance and from his Cabinet
colleagues. I see no objection to that in a general way, although frankly I would rather no
Minister was involved at all; but if there has to be one it should be the work force's Minister,
the Minister of Labour.
The Opposition moved amendments along those lines in the Committee stage, but did
not have a great deal of success, because the Government has a different point of view and a
different philosophy. We think the Bill would have been improved if our amendments had
been adopted. Nobody would have been prevented from having a say, but the priorities
would have been put in the proper order, first, to maintain the living standards and to
promote the maximum well-being of the work force in so far as the economy can sustain it.
We think that would be better law. The argument in the Committee stage was not very
prolonged, because it was on a very high plane and was based on the differing philosophies
of the two political parties. We preferred our way, but the Government had the majority and
will have its way in the meantime.

## p. 5008 (#444) ###########################################

5008
6 December
Town and Country Planning Bill
We also heard the New Zealand Maori Council, the New Zealand Planning Institute,
the city of Christchurch, Federated Farmers, the New Zealand Catchment Authorities, the
city of Wellington, and the National Water and Soil Conservation Authority. The Municipal
Association and the Counties Association made history by combining their submissions to
the committee. The New Zealand Harbours Association, represented by harbour board
chairmen around the country, made submissions. Of the 237 submissions received by the
closing date, only 56 of the parties indicated they wanted to be heard, and many of them
were already associated with national organisations. The 38 submissions we heard came from
a wide cross section of the community.
Part I of the Bill has been reprinted, and clause 5 contains the major change. It was felt
by the committee that clauses 23, 25, and 26 would be better represented in local
government legislation. Clause 5, which stated that the regional or united councils should be
augmented by representatives from catchment boards, other local authorities, the Ministry
of Works and Development, and the Maritime Planning Authority, has been changed.
The Bill now provides that the united or regional councils shall themselves be planning
authorities, but that a committee of each council shall be an advisory committee to the
regional or united council. The committee shall include such members as shall maintain a
majority on the advisory committee, and also a member of each catchment authority, a
member of the Maritime Planning Authority, a member of the Maori Council, a representa-
tive of each local authority adjacent, a member of the Ministry of Works and Development,
and not more than three persons who are members of the united council appointed by the
united or regional council. At all times the regional or united council, as the planning
authority, shall maintain a majority. What it means, in effect, is that the regional or united
council, which comprises the elected representatives of the people, shall be responsible for
the planning that is provided for in the Bill.
Another major change is the proposed new clause 91A, which provides for the
establishment of Maritime Planning Authorities. The major harbour boards as constituted
under the Harbours Act 1950, will be able to carry out harbour and maritime planning in the
same way as if they were considered to be a constituent council. This entirely new suggestion
is recommended by the committee as an amendment to the Bill. There are two other special
provisions. One is that the Northern Regional Planning Authority be allowed to proceed in
the meantime, as it has already started.
A further amendment is a special provision for the Thames-Coromandel District
Council. In the 1974 Act covering local government, no provision was made to continue two
of the district schemes then in operation or the Coromandel district scheme, which was then
only provisional. There was no way in which they could have proceeded without either
starting the job all over again-representing a cost of between $75,000 and $100,000—or
asking for special legislation. It seemed appropriate to include special provisions in the Town
and Country Planning Bill so that the three schemes now incorporated into one can be
accepted as an operative district scheme. The schedules to Parts I and II have been
amalgamated, with some minor changes in places.
At this stage, I express appreciation of the work put into the Bill by many people. The
members of the select committee have been very co-operative, and they have done a
tremendous amount of work on the measure over the past 3½ months. Parliamentary
counsel, officers of the Ministry of Works and Development, the members of the caucus
committee, and many people throughout New Zealand have made a valuable contribution to
the legislation in one way or another. Although the Bill may still not be perfect, the changes
recommended will go a long way towards providing for a better planning system. I am sure
all members, and particularly Government members of the select committee, will agree that
the changes made will build a much improved planning system.

at the forefront of the summary of that body's representations. Almost universally, witnesses
who were allowed to go before the committee, and others whose written submissions

of the Bills the full attention required.
Another point made was the impossibility of balanced comment being made without
knowledge of the regulations. We hear that representation from time to time when Bills are
under consideration, and not much weight is given to it in the ordinary course of events.
People are told—and I think reasonably so that regulations are mechanical things and that
it is the policy material in the Bill that is important. These regulations are different. Again
and again we were told that they are, as we all know, an integral part of planning procedures.
The Town and Country Planning Regulations, as they stand, are virtually as important as the
existing 1953 Act, and so will the regulations be that are made under this Bill when it is
enacted. One cannot assess the operation of the legislation as a whole until one sees the
terms of the regulations. To take one instance, public notification is an essential part of town
and country planning-how to get to the people concerned notice of what is to be done. The
current series of legalistic material that fills the pages of newspapers on Saturdays is very
confusing to the citizen. I hope the new regulations will make provision for this to be
simplified. Until one can discuss that aspect, one does not know what steps the Government
proposes to take to get to the public the material contained in the legislation.

Town and Country Planning Bill
Mr BIRCH: Of the 51 submissions lodged, 28 were heard by the committee. Over 200
submissions were made on the Town and Country Planning Bill, and 40 were heard. More
importantly, the submissions tended to focus on points central to the Bill; for example, on
clause 5 dealing with the structure of regional planning authorities; on Part I, dealing with
the preparation of regional planning schemes; and on Part V, dealing with the constitution of
maritime planning authorities. An analysis of those submissions clearly showed that there
was little point in hearing over and over again verbal submissions on the same points. The
important points were in the written submissions. This may not apply to the Opposition
members on the committee, but certainly the Government members studied those written
submissions very carefully indeed, and the Bill has been substantially modified-in clause 5
in particular, but also in Parts I and V.
Mr T. J. Young: What about the power boards' submission?
Mr BIRCH: Clause 60, the main clause the power boards committee mentioned in its
written submission, has been modified. The select committee has been responsive to the
points made to it. I doubt whether any other Bill has had greater study in depth.
Mr Rogers: Oh! Come on now!
Mr BIRCH: I do not know whether the honourable member interjecting did this, but
Government members spent long hours outside of committee hearings considering the
submissions in depth so that when they went back to the committee they knew what had
been said and written. Some Opposition members on the committee were not good
attenders, but Government members endeavoured to maintain their attendance, do their
homework, and be responsive to the submissions, and this Bill reflects the submissions made
on it. Three aspects were essential to the submissions.
Clause 5 deals with the structure and form of the proposed regional planning authority
to administer regional planning. The original Bill proposed that a regional planning
authority be established as a separate corporate body, comprising a united or regional
council supplemented by persons appointed because of their special interest or ex officio
capacity. The committee considered it did not make sense to establish a new corporate body
simply to undertake regional planning. It took the point made by the Municipal Association
and the Counties Association that it was better to let regional government, in whatever
form, be responsible for regional planning, but that a regional planning statutory authority
should be established to which these other parties would be appointed. The Bill has been
amended accordingly, and we now have a regional planning committee rather than a
regional planning authority. That will set the structure for regional government, not only for
planning, but for the other functions regional government can be expected to undertake.
Another aspect that provoked widespread discussion, and again was central to the
submissions made by the principal parties to the committee, was the preparation of regional
planning schemes. Under the Bill's original form the Minister was required to approve
schemes, and to ajudicate on disputes between districts, regions, and central government.
The committee applied itself to these problems, recognising that there are three tiers of
planning; that is, national planning, which is the responsibility of central government;
regional planning, which should be the responsibility of regional government; and district
planning, which should be the responsibility of territorial local authorities. The new Part I
reflects those three levels of planning and the responsibility shared by the three tiers of
government.
Central to Part I is the settling of disputes between districts and regions, and regions and
central government. The committee decided that disputes between districts and regions
should be settled by an independent appeal tribunal. I think that is a common-sense
decision. When disputes arise between regions and the Crown, the Bill provides that the
Minister shall refer the dispute back to the regional planning authority. If the dispute
continues the tribunal will be asked to consider it, but the Crown reserves the right to decide
finally on matters of national importance or of significance beyond the region. I do not think
that anyone would disagree with central government's deciding matters of national import-
ance. If Opposition members do disagree with that principle they should read the Bill again,
because its emphasis is now different from the emphasis in the original Bill.
Finally, I want to refer to Part V of the Bill, which deals with maritime planning-a
concept that has not been included in any previous legislation. I do not think many people
would argue that it is not necessary to plan for the use of our harbours, waterways, and gulfs.
Already there is conflict about whether beaches should be preserved for swimming, and
places set aside for water-skiing and boating, and whether fish farming should have a prior
right to those areas. Part V deals with the problem of how this planning can best be done. It

maritime planning authority will be a matter to be decided by the two Ministers primarily
responsible. I support the Bill as reported back.
