that there should be a regional planning committee, and that every united or regional council
should have a regional planning committee, which shall be a committee of that council. That
has been provided for. Not less than three members of the united or regional council shall be
appointed by the council, which shall appoint a chairman, provided that the united or
regional council may appoint such of its members to constitute a majority of the members of
that committee. The united councils are concerned that regional planning committees will
not outnumber them as elected bodies. They have been given what they requested.
Clause 5(3) provides that a representative of each catchment authority, a representative
of any maritime planning authority in or adjacent to the region, a representative of each
local authority, and a representative of the Maori people in the region nominated by the
district Maori council will constitute a regional planning authority. That covers the request
made in the submissions by the Maori groups. The Bill goes a long way towards implement-
ing the interests of Maoris. The submissions wanted the Minister to be uninvolved in
regional planning, and to be brought in only in the national interest.
Members have criticised the Minister of Works and Development for not being present
during the hearings. He was kept in touch with the proceedings. He wanted the regions to
make their own decisions, and to have the teeth they have not had before. The submissions
indicated what was required, and the committee has recommended what is in the best
interests of the regions. I support the reporting back of the Bill.

GENERAL WAGE ORDERS BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a third time.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): It would be generally accepted by both sides of the House and
also by the Employers Federation and the Federation of Labour that there is a need to have
a general wage orders statute that complies with the demands of the situation. However,
during the Committee stage, it was discovered that the Labour Opposition and the
Government had conflicting opinions on how this matter should be dealt with. In particular,
we were not in accord over clauses 3, 6, and 7. Clauses 3 and 6 deal with the criteria that the
courts must take into consideration when determining a wage order. The Opposition
strongly believes that, if a court is established to adjudicate on a general wage order, it is of
paramount importance that the wage and salary earner have confidence in such a court.
We believe that clause 3 tends to undermine the value of the court in its deliberations,
and to impose on it an onus that is more properly the responsibility of the Government.
Clause 3(2) states that, "In making any such review the court shall give paramount
importance to the promotion of the economic stability of New Zealand." That same
consideration is set out in clause 6(1). The very fact that the first consideration of the court is
to give paramount importance to the promotion of the economic stability of New Zealand
undermines the rest of the criteria, undermines the confidence of the wage and salary earner
in the court, and, as I said earlier, places on the court an onerous duty that should be the
responsibility of the Government. That responsibility can be placed upon no one else.
During the Committee stage, the Opposition moved an amendment to clause 3, and a
consequential amendment to clause 6: "In making any such review, the court shall give
paramount importance to the maintenance and promotion of living standards, so far as it is
within the capacity of the economy to sustain such an adjustment." That would have given
balance to the criteria. Unfortunately, the Government rejected the amendment.
It is to be regretted that the Government did not follow previous legislation which,
among other criteria, asked that the court should take into account the economic conditions
affecting finance, trade, and industry. The words "paramount importance" were not
included, thereby putting all criteria on the same level. The rejection of the Labour
Opposition's amendment to clause 6 will mean endless trouble and strife during general
wage order hearings.
In the Committee stage dissension was caused by clause 7. Here again, the Opposition
considered that participating parties-the New Zealand Employers Federation, the New
Zealand Federation of Labour, and the Combined State Service Organisations—should have
confidence in the court, but clause 7 includes the Minister of Finance. This means a
completely new departure in negotiations between employers and employees, particularly
when a case is to be taken to the court. It undermines the value of bargaining, conciliation,
and arbitration between the two parties. With the intervention of the Minister of Finance, a
dictatorial aspect will be introduced that will undermine the free bargaining and negotiating
system between the Employers Federation and the Federation of Labour.
During the Committee stage the Opposition moved that the words, "the Combined
State Service Organisations and the Minister of Finance respectively" be deleted and
replaced with the words "and the Combined State Service Organisations respectively". The
Opposition did not want the physical removal of the Minister of Finance-it does not intend
that at this stage-but was attempting to prevent him appearing in the Arbitration Court in
his own right and acting as a party to prevent a proper hearing between the Employers
Federation and the Federation of Labour. That is the only point in this clause on which the
Government and the Opposition differ.
If the Government had accepted the amendment the Bill would have been much better,
and it would have had the confidence of all parties in conciliation and arbitration. The
country could then have returned to the established tradition of successful conciliation and
arbitration under the Arbitration Court, that was founded in 1894 and has successfuly
assisted in the growth and development of New Zealand. It is unfortunate that the
Opposition's amendments were not accepted. When the Bill becomes law it will cause
enormous strife between the parties.

FISHERIES AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That the Fisheries Amendment Bill
(No. 2) be introduced. This is a small Bill of 13 clauses. It makes a number of minor
amendments to the Fisheries Act 1908, and updates some provisions in the Act. It also
integrates amendments made by the Fisheries Amendment Act 1977, and the Territorial Sea
and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977.


## p. 5026 (#462) ###########################################

5026
6 December
Fisheries Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Most of the clauses in this small Bill are reasonably self-explanatory, but I should like to
cover a few in greater detail. Clause 4 deals with quotas. Earlier in the year, regulations
provided for a new concept of management of the snapper stocks in the Auckland area.
These came into effect after discussion with the industry, and included the placing of a
maximum quota of snapper to be taken by trawlers and Danish seiners from part of the area.
The need for the placing of such a quota was accepted by the industry. Since that time,
however, some doubt has surrounded the validity of placing a quota on this fishery, and the
Bill will clarify any doubts in that area.
Because of the rapid expansion of fishing and the fishing fleet, controls are required to
ensure that a continuing economic yield of prime species is sustained. We must also be able
to protect fish by imposing maximum landing tonnages on any species, or, in the case of
areas where various species are normally taken together, if one of the species is under stress
we must be able to protect it. Area and quantity controls will be necessary to obtain this
protection.
Clause 10 relates to the moratorium that can be exercised in controlled fisheries. As I
intimated earlier, the Fisheries Amendment Act was also passed this year. This Act provides
for the establishment of a fisheries licensing authority to hear applications for licences for
areas and/or species declared controlled species pursuant to that Act, and also to provide
terms and conditions for the control and exploitation of such species in such areas. As
members are aware, this is intended to protect any resource from exploitation beyond its
maximum sustainable or economic yield. The Act makes provision for the Minister to place a
moratorium on the issue of any further licences or fishing permits as an interim measure
before the declaration of a controlled fishery. Such a controlled fishery was declared earlier
this year in relation to the Nelson-Golden Bay scallop fisheries.
These moratorium provisions were expected to be of short duration, but, because it has
taken some time to set up the fisheries licensing authority, it will now take longer than
expected to settle the number of applicants who finally obtain licences. Consequently, the
Minister's powers have been amended to give him discretion to grant further approvals in
particular cases while the moratorium prevails. An example could be the case of an owner
who was already committed to building a new vessel for a fishery, and was then caught by the
moratorium and could not proceed in that fishery.
The new Part III of the Fisheries Act was integrated into the Act earlier this year, but it
is now considered that a much wider integration is necessary to ensure particularly that
powers of fisheries officers under the main Act are extended to cover Part III of the Act. It is
also proposed to ensure that the terminology used in the Fisheries Act is similar to that used
in the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977. It will also extend the powers
conferred on naval officers by the Fisheries Act to include all Air Force personnel who are
now taking a more substantial role in the policing of the 200-mile zone.
The Bill integrates several measures that are designed both to protect to the utmost the
immediate and long-term interests of New Zealand fishermen, and to enable progressive
expansion of the New Zealand fishing industry. The doubts regarding quota regulations
require clearing up as rapidly as possible for the immediate protection of the fish stocks.
Although the provisions of the Bill are of a minor nature, it is important that they are
enacted this session. This is particularly so in regard to the need to give the Minister
authority to grant additional scallop licences during the period of the existing moratorium.
For this reason, I do not intend to refer the Bill to a select committee. I do not believe it is a
difficult Bill to understand. It is one that will benefit the New Zealand industry.

STATE SERVICES CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of State Services): I move, That this Bill be
now read a third time.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I suppose that this Bill, which deals with the
conditions of employment and remuneration of our own employees, is one of the most
important that has been before the House. The Committee traversed the details of the Bill,
as well as individual clauses that had been the subject of a great deal of discussion between
the Government and the State Service unions. The Combined State Service Organisations
and the Government finally agreed in some form or other to about 55 of the 75 clauses.
I am one of those people who believes that this exercise was badly timed, even though I
appreciate that, having said what it did a couple of years ago to get elected, the Government
was perhaps hooked on a course it would have liked to avoid, but could not. This became
clear when we considered Part VIII. One or two earlier clauses are still a matter of some
concern to a group of Government employees who for many years have proved to be usually
helpful and anything but militant, though skilled in negotiation and well-resourced, as every
good trade union should aim to be. It is clearly known that the next Labour Government will
remove the penalty clauses, because, even in our recent experience in the House and
although the Bill applies to the public sector, the penalty clauses applying to the private
sector can only be said to have been a total failure.
The Opposition opposed these clauses during the Committee stage because they are
included in the Bill to give a cosmetic suggestion that the private sector and public sector
work force will come under the same penalties and the same sanctions that seem so dear to
the National Government, and have cost the country so dear in the field of industrial
relations. Even in the State sector the confrontation approach in legislation, and sometimes
in speeches outside the House, has cost plenty and has not really achieved what the people
were persuaded during the last general election would be achieved.
Although as a Parliament we now know that that propaganda is a failure in practice, in
Part VIII of the Bill we are going through the farce of enacting legislation that will be very
difficult to apply in any circumstances, and can only promote industrial disharmony. It is bad
news, and represents a move towards the sort of industrial relations that have proved
unsuccessful and costly in disputes. In the Western World this kind of sanction is gradually
being rejected by more enlightened societies.
I now refer in some detail to clauses 63 to 75—which again show the principal difference
between the parties in the House on the approach to those other New Zealanders known as
State servants. They are not a foreign race; they are not an alien group; they are our
employees. In anyone's language their record as servants is beyond reproach. We sometimes
wonder why Parliament does not get the respect it is entitled to get and should get.
Sometimes it does not earn that respect, and Part VIII is one of the fundamental reasons. In
my view, State servants are not the kind of people who need the sanctions and penalties
provided for in this part of the Bill.

not to follow the procedures set down clause 70 makes provision for penalties to be imposed.

New Zealand had the sixth worst strike record in the world in 1976. That was recorded
by the International Labour Organisation, and was referred to in the Committee stage. The
information was published in London on 23 November. The position in New Zealand is
three times as bad as it is in Britain, but not yet as bad as it is in Australia under a
Conservative-Liberal Government, despite the enactment of legislation containing penal
provisions applicable to the private sector. The Government now proposes to relate these
provisions to the public sector. Our record has deteriorated since the penal provisions were
applied to the private sector. They have not worked, and there is no justification for applying
them to the public sector.

Government is amending its own legislation by inserting Part VIII and Part IV. If it went

of the CSSO and the Opposition. Clauses 76 to 86 are also taken from the 1969 legislation. I
want to put the record straight, because the member for Piako tried to leave the impression
with the House and the country that the Government was merely carrying forward
legislation that was passed by the Labour Government. That is quite incorrect.

between the Government and the Combined State Service Organisations did not take place.

provisions of the Bill. At no stage have they signified their agreement with Part VIII; they
are totally opposed to it, and rightly so.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I am gratified to hear that both sides of
the House support the view that almost all the provisions of the Bill, which replaces the State
Services Remuneration and Conditions of Employment Act 1969, were agreed between the
Committee on the State Services and the Combined State Service Organisations. It is right to
point out that the parties, after 10 months of harmonious negotiation, disagreed on Part VIII
only, and it might be as well to indicate what that part does. It provides that legislation can
be brought into force if necessary. The Minister is empowered to call a compulsory
conference in the case of industrial disruption, and to appoint a committee of inquiry. It
contains provisions regarding industrial disruptions in certain essential public services,
including the supply of electricity. Who wants to be imperilled by industrial strife? It includes
the working of any railway service, transport service, fire service, and air service, the
operations of hospitals, of welfare institutions under the Social Welfare Act, and of penal
institutions under the Department of Justice.
Surely everybody wants to be certain that wherever and however industrial strife is
caused the country will not be left in want of energy or control, which could imperil society
as a whole. This is written into the Act-although the Combined State Service Organisations
did not agree that it should be—and it can be called upon should the need arise. That is the
simple provision that the Labour Opposition wants to divide the House on. I believe that
most New Zealanders would say that this is a prudent provision, even though they hope the
need for it will not arise. On that basis, the National Government is quite confident that the
Bill should go forward as it now stands, knowing that it serves the public interest. Members
on this side are quite happy to see the House divided by the Labour Opposition, if it wants to
persist in its peculiar attitude that industrial legislation should have no penalties.

Most of the arguments put forward by the Opposition have turned out to be a sheer

past-who deliberately employs, as a source of cheap labour, people who are illegally in the
country. The Bill seeks to do away with the possibility of advantage being taken of a person

community. It is for the benefit of employers and the people who work for them. It will
prevent the abuses of rack renting and underpaid jobs. New Zealand has been more
generous than most countries in the matter of overstayers, and that past generosity has,

attitude. It has now become necessary, in the interests of good relations with our Pacific
neighbours and in the interests of overstayers themselves, to take a more practical view-

The Opposition has some very strong reservations about some of the Bill's provisions.

overstayers made up as follows: 965 from Western Samoa, 942 from Tonga, 443 from the
United Kingdom, and 260 from the United States. The overstayer problem, which this Bill is
to solve, is worsening under the administration of the present Government. The Bill reflects
the worsening employment position, and if the Government implemented a policy of full
employment I believe there would be no need for the Bill.
Clause 2 amends section 14 by inserting a new subsection (2a), which requires that
every work permit "shall be issued subject to the condition... that the holder, while in New
Zealand pursuant to the permit, shall not seek or obtain employment, or engage in any
activity for gain or reward, of any type without the consent of the Minister, which shall be
endorsed on the permit." The proposed new subsection (2B) sets a fine not exceeding $200
for a person breaking that requirement, with a continuing fine not exceeding $20 for every
day during which the offence continues. When will the Minister give his consent? Will it be at
the time of issue of the work permit? Will the conditions have to be made abundantly clear to
every person from, say, the United Kingdom, who intends to have a working holiday in New
Zealand? What will be the position of a visitor to New Zealand under the visa abolition
agreement who decides when he arrives here that he would like to work? Can the conditions
on his entry permit be changed in this country to enable him to take up employment? No
Government speaker has clarified that point.

the Government intend to exempt Australian visitors from work permits? Employers will
have difficulties in vetting applicants for jobs and in ensuring their nationality. How can an
employer know the status of a person seeking employment? The latest statistics show that for
the year ended March visitors working temporarily totalled 8468, and that for the period
between April and August this year 3188 visitors had temporary work permits—an increase
of 508 over the 1976 year. What number of visitors' work permits will the Minister issue
under clause 2? He has power under clause 2, and the House is entitled to know how far he
will go in issuing visitors' work permits.

the department ensure that all visitors are told about their responsibilities before they come
to New Zealand, or on their arrival? If a visitor knows the law he is more likely to observe it.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-URGENCY
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That urgency be accorded formal
business, the introduction of Bills, the Supplementary Order Paper on Ministers' replies to
questions, reports of select committees, the Committee stage of the Immigration Amendment
Bill, the Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust Bill, the Local Government Amendment
Bill (No. 3), the Racing Amendment Bill, the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill, and
the National Parks Amendment Bill, the second reading of the Electoral Amendment Bill, and
the third reading of the Appropriation Bill and the Appropriation Bill (No. 2). I take that
course so that the House can see what is before it. It may mean that we shall have to sit late
to go right through that amount of business. We do have to sit late one night in the year and
it seems to me that this is the appropriate night.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I know that there is no
discussion on this.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: No discussion at all.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I wish to raise a point of order. I refer to items 8 and 9 on the
Order Paper. It is normal in Parliaments based on Westminster democracy for the Appropri-
ation Bill to be the last normal business of a session, but we are being asked now to debate
Orders of the Day 8 and 9, both Appropriation Bills, with a significant amount of business to
follow them. It is traditional for the Crown not to be refused supply in the old technical term
"until after redress of grievances" which, in modern parlance, means after all legislation has
been passed. In the past, after the third reading of the Appropriation Bill, Bills have
occasionally been brought in for consideration in the recess, and valedictories and matters
like that have been discussed, but not formal business of Parliament. In this instance, a series
of Bills follows the two Appropriation Bills. I exclude from what I am saying the last three
Bills on the Order Paper. We know that the Prime Minister proposes to take the Contracep-
tion, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill after other business has been concluded, because it is
substantially a matter of private business, but there are 14 items of Government business,
and we are given no indication as to the Prime Minister's intention on them. My point is that
this procedure shows at best, a lack of concern for parliamentary tradition and, at worst, a
complete contempt for parliamentary tradition. I submit that this is an inappropriate
occasion for the Prime Minister to have moved urgency in the way he did.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I cannot see that there is a point of order,
Mr Speaker.

speak to it as though it were a point of order.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not know what the Deputy Leader of the Opposition is
worried about. I have taken advice on this matter, and it is perfectly in order. There is no
point of order. As the Deputy Leader of the Opposition said, it has been customary, and
indeed notice was given that business will be taken after the Appropriation Bill this year.
There are two Appropriation Bills, but, as members will know, it is the second one that is
debated in a broad general debate, usually during the last night of the session, but not
invariably, and it does not have to be. I thought we should do it tonight because I have had

MASSAGE PARLOURS BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Massage Parlours Bill
be introduced. The Bill expresses the Government's concern about the growing feeling
shared by the community and the police that many so-called massage parlours in our cities
are merely fronts for people seeking to make a living from prostitution and drugs. The way in
which some of these establishments are run often makes it difficult, if not impossible, for the
police to obtain sufficient evidence that criminal offences are occurring. It is thought,
therefore, that the normal methods of law enforcement are inadequate, in the absence of
provisions that would be largely unacceptable, to deal with the problems created by massage
parlours.
To control the activities of persons operating massage parlours, the Bill provides that
every person operating such a business shall obtain a licence to do so from a magistrate, and
that every employee offering massage must obtain a certificate of approval. Every place
13.


## p. 5062 (#498) ###########################################

5062
7 December
Massage Parlours Bill
of business must be under the supervision of an approved manager. No licence or certificate
of approval shall be issued to any person who, within 10 years of applying for approval, has
been convicted of any offence involving prostitution or drugs, and, before issuing a licence or
a certificate of approval, a magistrate must be satisfied that the applicant is a proper person
to hold a licence or a certificate of approval. Professional masseurs such as physiotherapists,
are exempt.
A copy of every application for a licence or a certificate of approval must be served on
the police, who have the right to appear before a magistrate to oppose the granting of the
application. This provision will allow the police to assist in ensuring that only those who are
proper persons to do so operate or work in massage parlours. The Bill also makes provision
for the revocation of licences and certificates of approval on specified grounds, including
convictions for offences involving prostitution or drugs.
A further and most important measure of control is contained in the provision allowing
the police to enter and inspect any premises licensed as a massage parlour, and to enter with
a search warrant any premises in which it is reasonably suspected that the occupier is
carrying on the business of operating a massage parlour without a licence. Provision is made
for a person who has been refused a licence or a certificate of approval to appeal against that
decision to the Supreme Court. Appeal rights are provided also for licensees or approved
employees whose licence or certificate of approval has been revoked or suspended under the
disciplinary provisions of the Bill. It is thought that the licensing provisions of the Bill,
together with the police powers of entry and inspection, will go a considerable way towards
ensuring that people operating massage parlours keep within the law. The Government
recognises that a number of massage parlours are operated for proper purposes, and it is felt
that there is little in the Bill that will adversely affect such establishments, and much that will
aid enforcement of the criminal law. At the appropriate time I shall move that the Bill be
referred to the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): As the Bill is to be sent to the
Statutes Revision Committee there is no need for much discussion on it now. Every member
who has been a member of Cabinet will appreciate the concern the police have expressed on
this matter. The explanatory note to the Bill states that the Bill provides for the licensing of
massage parlour operators, and for the scrutiny of their managers and staff. Is this to be a
personal function of the Minister of Justice, or a duty to be shared by selected colleagues? In
serious vein, there is a delicate line between the examination of legitimate businesses and
businesses that are covers for illegal operations. I assure the Minister that the Opposition
will support any attack on the latter. Definition of a massage parlour will be difficult. Clause
3 attempts to define what is not covered by that term. The fact that an act of massage is
performed in a sports club is no guarantee that it is legal, yet sports grounds and sports clubs
are exempt from the provisions of the Bill. A satisfactory definition will be difficult to find,
and I think problems will arise.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I want to carry the point about definition made
by my colleague a little further. The definition of physiotherapy is set out in the
Physiotherapy Act 1949, which was reprinted last year. It set out in some detail the criteria
that must be met before a person can register under that Act. The Minister doubtless knows
that there is an association of people who might be called masseurs and masseuses. I
understand their organisation is an incorporated society. It has approached the Government
from time to time for recognition at a level substantially below that for registration under the

JOINT COUNCIL FOR LOCAL AUTHORITIES SERVICES BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Joint Council
for Local Authorities Services Bill be introduced. This is a relatively short but very important
Bill for local government. It provides for the setting up of a 20-member council comprising
equal representation from employer and employee interests in local government. The
general purpose of this joint council will be to foster and promote the development of an
integrated career service for local authority administrative, professional, technical, and
clerical officers. The Bill results from joint representations to the Government by the main
local authority employer associations, local government unions, and officer groups. It
represents a major initiative on the part of these interests, and it has been the subject of a
great deal of negotiation and discussion between the employer and employee groups and
Government officials.
The specific functions of the joint council are set out in clause 11. It will be the function
of the council to promote the training of local authority employees, to encourage and
promote study and courses of study in local government, to encourage local authorities
within the scope of the joint council to carry out job evaluation exercises, and to carry out
these exercises itself for the purpose of establishing job relativities between local authorities.
In addition, the joint council will have power to investigate and make recommendations in
three areas crucial to the eventual emergence of a local government career service, and also
to the future responsibilities of the joint council itself. These relate to the provision of a
system of national supervision in matters affecting employment in local government, the
provision of machinery for the regular consideration and fixing of mandatory national salary
scales for occupational classes within local government service, and the fixing of national
conditions of service for local government.
The Bill also enables the joint council to make recommendations to the Higher Salaries
Commission about the salaries of officers in the top local government positions that are at
present fixed by that commission. In this regard, the joint council will have the same rights
vis-à-vis a higher salaries commission as are given to the hospital medical officers advisory
committee and the University Grants Committee. This is an important provision that will
have a particular bearing on any future responsibilities of the joint council in determining
salaries for top positions in local government.
The joint council will be a body corporate with members appointed by the Minister of
Local Government on the respective nominations of the local authority employer organisa-
tions and the unions and officer groups specified in the schedules to the Bill. There will be 10
employer members and 10 employee members, and the council will elect its own chairman.
The Bill will make the usual provisions for the operations of a statutory body, and the joint
council will have power to engage its own staff. Clause 20 empowers the joint council to levy
the local authorities specified in the second schedule to the Bill, to finance its activities. The
basis of the levy is not set out in the Bill. This will be prescribed by Order in Council once the
joint council has been set up and has been able to assess what funds it will need, and how
these can be raised through a levy system.
The Bill is the first step towards a more far-reaching system for fixing salaries and
conditions of service in local government. The setting up of the joint council will be a most
important step in achieving more effective co-ordination, and in providing the basis for the
emergence of an integrated local government career service.
However, as a further development of the joint council's responsibilities, the local
authority interests have also sought certain pay-fixing powers for the joint council. In brief,
these involve a delegation from the Higher Salaries Commission to the joint council of the
responsibility for fixing the salaries of most of the top positions in local government,
authority for the joint council to prescribe salary scales for local authority officers not
covered by awards and collective agreements, and power to fix basic conditions of service
within local government. While negotiations with the local authority interests have made a
good deal of progress, in the time available it has not been possible to finalise the extent of
the joint council's powers in this pay-fixing area.
There are still many important and complex issues yet to be resolved. The Government,
however, is keen to see that the progress achieved to date, and the value of bringing together
the local authority employer and employee interests in a joint council, should be recognised.
The negotiating local authority employer associations, unions, and officer groups have


## p. 5065 (#501) ###########################################

7 December
5065
Joint Council for Local Authorities Services Bill
agreed to legislation setting up the joint council going ahead on the basis now set out in this
Bill, and, for the time being, leaving aside the question of the council's pay-fixing respon-
sibilities. These will be discussed with the joint council once it has been set up; and it is
intended that the council's powers in this area will be the subject of further legislation early
in the next session. In the meantime, the joint council will be able to begin its operations,
and, in particular, will be in a position to make recommendations to the Higher Salaries
Commission in time for the general review of higher salaries to be carried out by the
commission at 1 April next year.
In view of the fact that the major employer and employee groups have been consulted
and support the joint council concept, and also the desirability of establishing the joint
council so that it can commence operations early in the new year, it is not proposed to refer
the measure to a select committee.
The Bill does not interfere with the existing rights of individual local authorities to
employ their own staff, but it will provide the basis for local authority officers to be part of a
more unified local government service. As Minister of Local Government, I am convinced
that this will be in the interests of achieving a strong and effective system of local
government. The joint council will have an essential part to play in this.

TOKELAU (TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE) BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That the Tokelau
(Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone) Bill be introduced. The political leaders of
Tokelau have formally requested New Zealand to replace the 3-mile territorial sea and 9-
mile fishing zone around Tokelau with a 12-mile territorial sea and a 188-mile economic
zone. In effect, the Bill does for Tokelau what Parliament recently did for New Zealand with
the New Zealand Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act. Tokelau's capacity to
develop, manage, and exploit the fishery resources of its economic zone is at present limited.
However, such small entities as Tokelau should benefit from the services offered by the
proposed Pacific Regional Fisheries Agency.
The principal species of fish that it will be concerned with are highly migratory species,
such as tuna, and the licence fees that foreign fishing vessels are expected to pay to catch
tuna in Tokelau's zone will probably constitute the main practical benefit for Tokelau arising
from the implementation of the Bill. The provisions are modelled, as closely as circum-
stances in Tokelau permit, on the recent New Zealand legislation. As the principles in both
Bills are practically the same, I need not cover them again. The Bill leaves some of the
detailed provisions for fisheries management and enforcement to be dealt with by regula-
tion.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): Opposition members do not object to the introduc-
tion of the Bill, but there are some distinct differences between the Bill and last year's
legislation. For example, the definition of migratory fish does not include turtles, which
would be of interest in the Tokelaus. While the intention is to provide for the Tokelau
Islands the same legislation as is now applicable to the exclusive economic zone in New
Zealand, certain features that apply only to the Tokelaus should be taken into account. It
will be recalled that concern was expressed last year about the way in which the zone might
be policed, and comments were made about the issue of field glasses. Since the Bill is being
introduced now, presumably for recess study-or is it to be passed immediately?
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: Yes.
Hon. M. RATA: I am sorry that is the case. Is there some urgency? An opportunity
should be given to members to understand the needs of the Tokelauans, as the island is
infrequently visited by members, who should learn something about it from the Island
Affairs Committee. Tokelau is not easy to get to, and the opinions of departmental officers
would be of interest. On 10 December 1976, an Act was passed into law by the House.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: With various changes.
Hon. M. RATA: Yes, and I must admit some of the circumstances here are different.
There are some marked differences in interpretation, the method. of policing the area, and
by whom. If the Minister could answer those questions, the Opposition sees no reason for a
lengthy discussion of the Bill at this stage. Presumably the Bill has been introduced on
advice, but is it so necessary to pass the legislation before the House rises, probably next
week? I believe it will be doing the area concerned an injustice to pass the Bill at this late
stage of the session, especially when most of the previous relevant legislation, which has
been in force for about 12 months, is contained in the new Bill. I suggest that the Minister
refer the Bill to a select committee for recess study so that any support needed by him to
ensure that the Tokelau people are able to benefit from the changes contained in this
legislation will be given without hesitation.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I listened to what the
honourable member had to say, and it is true that legislation was introduced last year, at the
request of the Tokelau people, to establish a 3-mile territorial sea and a 9-mile fishing zone.
The Tokelau people have now asked for a 200-mile economic zone to be established in
concert with zones being established not only by New Zealand, but also by Fiji and other
member countries of the South Pacific Forum. The Tokelau people want to have the zone
established by the end of March, so the Government is meeting their request. I take the
point made by the honourable member for Northern Maori that there are differences. Of
course there are. The absence of a continental shelf in the Tokelaus makes a difference
between the two Bills, because some of the provisions in the New Zealand legislation are

1. Mr FENTON (Hastings) asked the Minister of Education: What are the percentage

effort will be required to construct and develop the supply system. It is therefore not possible
at this time to say when Paraparaumu will be reticulated for natural gas.

Silverstream Hospital Rehabilitation Centre
14. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) asked the Minister of Health: How many patients
can be catered for at one time in the Silverstream Hospital rehabilitation centre, and how
many patients are at present being assisted by the centre?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I assume the honourable member is referring to
the geriatric day hospital at Silverstream Hospital. This day hospital is planned to cater for
12 patients at a time, but it has accepted 14. At present there are 6 in attendance. The
number varies greatly according to the number requiring treatment who are referred by the
general medical practitioners of the area. It must be stressed that this is not just a social
centre. It is a day hospital providing active treatment for patients in the community who
require some form of physiotherapy or occupational therapy. The Silverstream Hospital also
has a 20-bed rehabilitation ward that takes in patients, mainly from the Hutt Hospital, who
require an intensive rehabilitation programme. It also provides short-term intermittent relief
to families who are caring for a disabled person at home. The ratio between the two groups
varies. At present, 7 rehabilitation patients are in the ward.

Maui Development-Capital Cost
15. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Finance: What is the capital
cost of the Maui development to New Zealand, and how is this reflected in its balance of
payments?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The latest published estimate of the
final cost of the Maui project released by Maui Development Ltd on 4 November is $998
million. The capital cost of developing the Maui field is reflected in higher imports of capital
goods and equipment, and higher figures for short-term capital flows used to finance these
imports.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Can the Minister indicate how the capital cost might be reflected in
this year's balance of payments-in actual figures?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, because the question is too indefinite. There is a
difference between balance of payments and the measure normally used-the overseas
exchange transactions. Hundreds of millions of dollars are involved. We estimate, when the
development is concluded and the Maui gas comes on stream in the first half of 1979, an
improvement in our balance of payments on the overseas exchange transactions basis of the
order of $150 million a year. That is the most exact round figure I can give, and it is subject
to variation in either direction, because it is a very difficult calculation to make in advance.
That is the order of magnitude when we stop paying for major capital works and start
recouping the benefit from Maui gas taking the place of imported oil. A little later on we
shall be getting into the Maui B development, when the picture will change again.

freedom of movement within the aircraft. The Boeing 737 has been certificated by the

URGENT QUESTION
Scrapping of Railway Carriages
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Railways, as an urgent
question: Will he order work to cease on the scrapping of railway carriages being carried out
at Marton until satisfied that these coaches-which I am informed include ex-North Island
and South Island main-trunk first-class carriages and sleeper coaches-cannot be repair and
refurbished for further rail passenger use?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways): The demolition of condemned
rolling stock near Martin should be no secret to the member for Timaru, because this work
started in 1972 under the previous Labour Government. This remote site was chosen to
minimise disturbance to the environment through noise and smoke. Some former main-
trunk passenger stock is included in the present programme, but these are extremely old
wooden-framed carriages, which are more than 40 years old, and their condition is such that
satisfactory repair or refurbishing for passenger use is completely out of the question. The
wooden frames are burned as the most efficient means of disposal, and all steel components
that are not reusable-and some are-are sold for scrap. I see no reason whatever to order
this work to cease.

CLUTHA HYDRO-ELECTRIC SCHEME-NOTICE UNDER STANDING
ORDER 89
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received the following
letter from the Senior Opposition Whip on behalf of the Junior Opposition Whip: "I propose
to move today that the House be now adjourned for the purpose of discussing a definite
matter of urgent public importance. This is the decision of the National Water and Soil
Conservation Authority which is chaired by the Minister of Works in granting water rights to
the Crown for the development known as scheme F for the hydro generation of electric
power.
"This decision has been made in the face of opposition from local bodies in Otago and
from orchardists whose enterprises are detrimentally affected by the decision. The authority's
decision runs counter to commissions of inquiry that the Government has set up in past
months which have endorsed scheme H and rejected the scheme that is now approved by the
National Water and Soil Conservation Authority. The decision of the National Water and
Soil Conservation Authority means the destruction of long established apricot producing
land which is important to the welfare of the district and involves those apricots which are
brought into earliest production in the country and for which there are large export sales.


## p. 5077 (#513) ###########################################

7 December
5077
Urgent Question
"It is also noted that the stability of Cromwell could be affected by this decision and
there is very deep concern expressed by His Worship the Mayor of Cromwell, Mr Anderson,
on behalf of the citizens of that town. It is believed that the decision of the National Water
and Soil Conservation Authority in granting water rights to this extent is neither in the best
interests of the region nor of New Zealand. The decision of the National Water and Soil
Conservation Authority under the chairmanship of the Minister of Works appears to run
against the best available evidence. This is a matter which involves the administrative or
ministerial responsibility of the Government in that a Minister is chairman of the authority
which made a decision in face of widespread opposition."
This application was received within the time prescribed by Standing Order 89, and
clearly conforms with two of the criteria set out in Standing Order 90, in that it refers to a
particular case of recent occurrence, and involves the administrative or ministerial responsi-
bility of the Government. The third requirement set out in Standing Order 90 is that the
matter proposed to be discussed requires the immediate attention of the House and the
Government. In determining this question, I think it is relevant to consider a number of
factors. The National Water and Soil Conservation Authority, established under the Water
and Soil Conservation Act 1967, is not a court of record, so no considerations of sub judice
under Standing Order 183 arise. However, the authority is a quasi-judicial tribunal of
competent jurisdiction.
I note that the decision in respect of which this application to move the adjournment of
the House relates is subject to appeal, and that development on the dam is subject, among
other things, to the outcome of any such appeal. It appears that an appeal may be lodged
with the Town and Country Planning Appeal Board within 28 days of the decision.
It seems to me that it would be in exceptional cases only that the House would wish to
debate the decision of a quasi-judicial body taken in the exercise of its statutory functions,
especially when that decision is subject to an appeal. I do not believe this to be an
exceptional case, because, as far as I know, the hearings and appeal procedures are being
conducted in accordance with the law passed by Parliament. An exceptional case could
perhaps be one in which there was sufficient evidence reported of improper procedures
being followed; in which case, of course, that, and not the dam, would be the issue. For this
reason, I rule that the matter does not at this time require the immediate attention of the
House and the Government, and I must, therefore, regretfully decline the application of the
member.

(25/11/77)
Radio New Zealand-Offices at Levin and Mt. Maunganui
17. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Were the branches of Radio
New Zealand at Levin and Mt. Maunganui opened for purely commercial reasons, and, if so,
when is it expected that the additional advertising revenue generated by these branches will
be sufficient to cover the total operating cost of each branch?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: I am informed by the
Broadcasting Corporation that Radio New Zealand's objective in opening branch offices in
Levin and Mt. Maunganui was to strengthen the contact and mutual sense of identification
between the towns involved and the stations serving them. Each such branch office provides
a base for servicing current advertisers and canvassing new business, for the prompt and
comprehensive coverage of newsworthy local events, and for close liaison with the commun-
ity in all those activities in which radio can play a part. The branches were not established,
therefore, for purely commercial reasons. However, in both cases, projected additional
advertising revenue is expected to cover the total operating costs within the first year of
operation.
(25/11/77)
East Timor-Debate at UN General Assembly
18. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What were
the reasons for the New Zealand delegate at the UN General Assembly Colonial Committee
voting against giving the Fretilin a chance to present a second case on their desire for an
independent East Timor?


## p. 5083 (#519) ###########################################

7 December
5083
Questions and Replies
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The question of hearing
the Fretilin representative for a second time was a procedural matter unrelated to the
substance of the East Timor resolution itself. On 8 November the chairman of the fourth
committee closed the general debate on a number of items, including East Timor, on which
the Fretilin representative had spoken. The committee also agreed to defer consideration of
the specific item on Timor and the resolution relating to it for 2 days. The following day, on 9
November, the request to hear Fretilin a second time was made. The New Zealand
representative took the view that, with the closure of the general debate and the deferral of
the specific item, there was no procedural justification for hearing Fretilin at that particular
time. Had Fretilin sought to speak on 10 November when the committee resumed considera-
tion of the item and the related resolution there would not have been the same procedural
impediment, and he would have been heard without objection. New Zealand's vote against
hearing Fretilin a second time in the fourth committee's general debate does not signify any
change in the Government's attitude towards the events in East Timor. As in previous years,
New Zealand abstained on the Timor resolution when it was put before the committee on 10
November; 46 other countries also abstained, including Australia and Britain.

(29/11/77)
Primary School Site, Birkenhead
22. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: (a) When was the new
primary school to serve the Chatswood area of Birkenhead designated by agreement with
the Ministry of Defence for defence land in the Kauri Point area; (b) when was the
agreement broken and by whom; (c) what steps has the Department of Education taken to
acquire land at another site, and at what cost; and (d) when is work likely to commence on
the school?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: In 1969 informal discussions took
place between officials of my department and the then Navy Department, which controlled
the Kauri Point Defence Reserve, concerning the transfer of 5 acres to the Department of
Education for primary school purposes to serve the Chelsea area (Chatswood Estate) of
Birkenhead. No formal agreement was reached at these meetings to transfer the land, but
there appeared to be general acceptance that a site could be made available from the defence
reserve subject to the Department of Education obtaining satisfactory assurances from the
Navy Department concerning safety factors in relation to the ammunition storage areas. No
such assurances were subsequently given by the Navy Department, although the Auckland
Education Board, on its own initiative, lodged a town planning requirement with the local
authority to designate a school site on the defence reserve. In October 1973, following
further approaches by my department, the Ministry of Defence advised that it could not
make a school site available as the land was required for defence housing following the
reorganisation of the armed services and the use of Kauri Point as a facility for the three
armed services. Subsequently efforts were made to obtain another site, and further represen-
tations were made to successive Ministers of Defence for the release of the defence land. In
February 1975 the Minister of Defence in the previous administration decided that the Kauri
Point land must be retained for defence purposes. This was confirmed by the present
Minister in February 1976. The decision was also endorsed by the Prime Minister when the
matter was referred to him earlier this year. In May 1976 I approved the placing of a town
planning requirement over an alternative school site of 7 acres in the Chatswood subdivision.
The requirement was placed by the Auckland Education Board in June 1976, and, although
objections to the designation of the land were made initially by the Birkenhead Borough


## p. 5085 (#521) ###########################################

7 December
5085
Questions and Replies
Council and Chatswood Estate Ltd, the objections were later withdrawn. The Ministry of
Works and Development, on behalf of my department, is currently negotiating with
Chatswood Estate Ltd for the purchase of the land. As the purchase price will include
compensation for development work already undertaken by the developers and is still
subject to negotiation, it is not possible to give an indication of cost at the present time. Until
the purchase of the site is completed and planning of the buildings commenced I am unable
to say when work is likely to commence on the school.

Music and Drama Blocks for Schools
25. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: How many modified S.
68 music drama blocks have been constructed within the last 3 years, and, in view of
criticisms made of them, are any further modifications being made to these blocks?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Since November 1974, one
modified S. 68 music drama block has been constructed. This block, which was originally
designed as two music rooms, was modified to contain one music room and one drama room.
During the same period the following blocks were completed: three S. 68 music blocks each
containing two music rooms, and one S. 68 drama block containing two drama rooms. A
further S. 68 block containing two music rooms is under construction. A number of other
blocks of similar type have been designed by private architects. My department has recently
received criticism of some of these rooms, and action is being taken to rectify the problem.
The criticisms received relate in particular to the acoustic properties of the music rooms. The
rooms were designed with acoustics suitable for performing and listening to music, and, as
such, have not proved to be entirely satisfactory for traditional classroom teaching. The
modifications authorised for the existing blocks are intended to make the acoustics within
the rooms suitable for both speech and music. My department is to set up a working party to
examine the accommodation requirements of music in secondary schools, and this may lead
to some revisions of standard music room plans.

Radio-Citizen Band Emergency Channel
28. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Postmaster-General: Will he allocate or designate a
channel for emergency use by citizen band equipment and those licensed to use it alongside
the existing channels in the 26.400 MHz to 26.600 MHz band?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: Because of demands on the
limited radio frequency spectrum resources, further channels cannot be made available for
citizen station operation unless the present band is rechannelled with narrower spacing
between frequencies. This aspect is at present under consideration, but may necessitate
equipment changes which must first be discussed with radio equipment manufacturers.
Should rechannelling be practicable, the designation of a frequency for emergency use would
be considered. As there are at present only seven channels in the citizen band which are
freely available for use by all users (now some 17 000) it is considered impractical to


## p. 5087 (#523) ###########################################

7 December
5087
Questions and Replies
designate one of these solely for emergency use. However, there would be no objection if
citizen band users, by mutual consent, designated a particular channel to be used for
preference in emergencies. This is already done in some areas. In this connection the Post
Office proposes to notify all citizen station licensees of the desirability of co-operating to the
extent possible during emergencies by refraining from making any transmissions which
would interfere with the emergency communications.

Mt. Ruapehu-Early Warning System
38. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Lands: Has he read the article
entitled "Radio System and Warning Device an Urgent Need on Mt. Ruapehu" in the
Evening Post of 9 November, which states that the National Parks Authority was responsible
for the delay in not approving funding for an early warning system on the mountain, and, if
so, is the statement true, and, if it is, what was the reason for the delay?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: Yes, I have read the article referred to
and I can assure the member that any implication that the National Parks Authority was
responsible for the delay in approving the necessary funding is not correct. After the 1975
eruption on Mt. Ruapehu renewed interest in a warning system led to the Tongariro
National Park Board calling for a detailed report and preliminary costings. These reports
required considerable investigation and were not available until June 1976, when the park
board submitted a case to the National Parks Authority. At its meeting on 28 July 1976 the
authority authorised an approach to the Government for a special grant of $116,300 for a
volcanic warning system and essential radio back-up for Mt. Ruapehu. The Government
endorsed the expenditure in May of this year as part of the 1977-78 new policies review. The
newspaper article refers to the biggest problem being the amount of technical work needed
to design the system and the warning equipment to enable tenders to be called, and I have, in
fact, already taken this matter up with the Minister of Works and Development. Progress on
the VHF radio back-up system is proceeding satisfactorily, and at present the park board is
discussing details with the favoured tenderer.
(17/11/77)

Postal Service
41. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Has he seen the report in
the Christchurch Press of 8 November 1977 in which the chairman of the Malvern County
Council claims that it had taken 8 days for a copy of the council agenda sent to him by mail to
travel the 16 km distance from Darfield, and, in view of the claim that the situation has
worsened recently, what does he propose to do about it?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: I have seen the report. The
agenda posted to the chairman of the Malvern County Council should not have taken 8 days
to be delivered and the Post Office can only speculate as to how this happened. One
possibility is that the item concerned was sorted incorrectly, as mistakes do occur on
occasions. The incidence of these is a microscopic part of the total mail handled. Mail posted
at Darfield up to 4.30 p.m. Monday to Friday would normally be available for delivery in
surrounding areas, including Hororata, the next day. Tests of transit times for mail posted at
Darfield have recently been carried out but have failed to indicate any problem.

Organic Cyanide Levels in Kernels of Stone Fruit
44. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: Is there any evidence
that significant levels of organic cyanide are present in the kernels of other stone fruits in
addition to the apricot, and, if so, does the Department of Health intend placing a similar
ban on their sale in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The kernels of other stone fruit, such as
cherries and peaches, contain the cyanide compound amygdalin. As with apricot kernels,
provided these kernels undergo treatment to inactivate the cyanide compound, there is no
objection to their sale in New Zealand. However, the Department of Health is not aware of
any kernels, other than those of apricots, being offered for sale here.

Employment and Pay Between Christmas and New Year
54. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Labour: Is there anything to
prevent employers laying off staff 2 weeks prior to Christmas to avoid having to pay them for
the 4 days between Christmas and New Year, and has an employer any obligations if he re-
employs the same workers during January?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied on behalf of the Minister of
Labour: There is nothing to prevent any employer terminating the services of an employee at
any time provided he is justified in doing so and complies with the provisions of the relevant
award or collective agreement on termination. If a worker is unjustifiably dismissed the
personal grievance provision of the Industrial Relations Act would have application. Most
awards and collective agreements and the Factories Act 1946 provide that workers become
entitled to payment for any statutory holiday if they have been employed at any time during
the fortnight ending on the day the holiday occurs. Any worker not employed during the
period does not become entitled to payment for any such holiday. If any dismissed worker is
re-engaged after the holidays the employer would have no obliagation in respect of the
statutory holidays involved, but that is subject to the condition that the worker would qualify
for payment if he were employed at any time in the 14 days before the statutory holiday.

Sulphide Discharge in Waiwhetu Stream
67. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister for the Enviroment: Has he seen
the article "More Fish Killed in Waiwhetu Stream" in the Evening Post of 10 November
which contains a report of the deaths of thousands of herrings from sulphide poisoning, and
can he indicate whether any progress has been made in identifying the source of the sulphide
discharge?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Enviroment) replied: I am aware of the statement in
the Evening Post of 10 November. The sulphide that caused the death of the herrings
originated in water pumped out of excavations close to the stream. The excavations are in
land that was once salt marsh, and the sulphate originating from the earlier marine
enviroment has been reduced to sulphide. The contractors are now aware of the potential
hazard to fish as a result of their pumping activities, and steps are being taken by the
Wellington Regional Water Board to control this unusual form of toxic discharge. The water
board has now provided facilities for all the industrial wastes to be passed into the trade and
waste sewer rather than, as hitherto, directly into the Waiwhetu Stream.

Economy-Balance of Payments
82. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of Finance:
What action does the Government intend to take immediately to correct the deterioration of
New Zealand's balance of payments situation, which has now been revealed as extending
over the two quarters of the current financial year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance) replied: The Government is
acting continually to improve the balance of payments both in the immediate future and in
the longer run. The Government's policy of domestic restraint has reduced the demand for
imports. The latest figures from the Government Statistician show that forward orders for
imports have dropped. This means we can expect a reduction in import volumes in the next
few months. The Government has also taken active measures to boost the export drive. The
livestock incentive scheme is providing a basis for sustained growth in primary exports.
Incentives have been extended for non-traditional exports, including services. Policies have
been set in train to stimulate the development of efficient import replacement industries and
to accelerate the development of indigenous energy resources.

Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry)
replied on behalf of the Minister: "I am advised by the Secretary of Trade and Industry that
the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974 provide for an appropriate reduction in a

production. When the fall in world coffee bean prices is reflected in the total cost of the
product of the domestic coffee manufacturer an appropriate reduction in price will be
required."

Arapawa Island Goats
100. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Forests: Has he any informa-
tion to suggest that the goats on Arapawa Island are genetically similar to the "rare old
English breed" of goat which is now extinct in Britain?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: I do not know whether they are all
extinct, actually. It has been claimed that the feral goats inhabiting Arapawa Island are the
descendants of an old English breed of goat brought to New Zealand by Captain James
Cook, but there is no firm evidence to confirm this assertion. From information supplied by
the Rare Breeds Survival Trust of England, it is known that if the original Arapawa goats
were liberated by Captain Cook they probably would have been a native British breed.
These goats have now been largely supplanted by modern milking breeds, although a few
still remain in the British Isles. It is possible that the Arapawa goats are descended from the
native British goat, but the history of these animals is not so precisely known, and therefore
any claim of uniqueness can neither be rejected nor upheld.
(23/11/77)

School Leavers-Subsidised Apprenticeships
103. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he received a
letter from the Hokianga-Bay of Islands development committee on a subsidised apprentice-
ship scheme for school leavers, and, in view of the increasing difficulties school leavers are
having in finding suitable work, will he ensure that the proposal receives prompt and
favourable consideration?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: I have received a letter from the
Hokianga-Bay of Islands development committee suggesting that the Government subsidise
apprentices' wages to encourage eligible employers to take on more apprentices. As the level
of work available in each industry, rather than the wages payable to apprentices, is the main
determinant of the number of new apprenticeship contracts, there is no certainty that the
suggested subsidy would result in an increase in the number of apprenticeships available for
school leavers. Furthermore, because of the holiday season and the normal recruitment
period, it will not be possible until well into February to ascertain the exact number of young
people who actually leave school and do not obtain jobs. Should the situation at that time
require the implementation of further measures to provide employment for school leavers I
will ensure that the suggestion is given consideration.

Oil Exploration, Great South Basin
104. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), asked the
Minister of Energy Resources: Can he indicate what quantities and volumes or combinations
of quantities and volumes of oil, condensate, or gas would constitute an economic productive
field if discovered more than 100 miles off shore in the region of the Great South Basin?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied: It is not possible to give a
precise answer to this question as no oilfield or gasfield has been developed in the depth of
water in which Kawau, for example, is being drilled. Present indications are that for an
oilfield to be economic it would need to be of a similar size to the larger North Sea fields,
which have daily flow rates of more than 300 000 barrels a day. The structures at present
being drilled have this potential. At this stage, in terms of current technology, it is not
considered that a gasfield or a gas-condensate field would be economic to develop.
(23/11/77)

Regional Development-Plant Depreciation Rates
106. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland
Revenue Department: Has he seen the report in the two Dunedin newspapers of 12
November in which the Labour candidate for Dunedin North is reported as advocating
special depreciation rates for plant and machinery as part of regional development policy,
and can he confirm that these are in being as a result of the 1976 National Government
Budget?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department)
replied: Yes, I have read the reports, and find them rather surprising. In 1976 the
Government enacted legislation providing for a number of investment allowances specifi-
cally designed to encourage regional investment. These were: the regional development
allowance of up to 20 percent; the export production allowance of up to 20 percent; the
industry development allowance of up to 40 percent; and the farming and fishing allowance
of 40 percent. These investment allowances, which are of course in addition to the first-year
depreciation allowance of 25 percent, have the effect that the overall write-off for taxation
purposes over the life of the plant and machinery may amount to more than its cost price. I
should have thought it would be difficult to beat that as an example of incentives for regional
development.

activities such as hangis and tramping trips. Trade training officers from the Department of
Maori Affairs pay frequent visits to the institute to discuss progress and, where necessary, to
advise tutors. The Vocational Training Council Polynesian advisory officers and a Samoan
officer from the Industrial Training Service work closely with the institutes.

Native Plants Protection Act
108. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Lands: Are there any plans to
review the Native Plants Protection Act 1934?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: There are numerous statutes such as the
Reserves and Domains Act, the National Parks Act, the Land Act, the Trespass Act, the
Police Offences Act, and the Forests Act which, in addition to the Native Plants Protection
Act 1934, give a measure of protection to native flora. A degree of protection is also
suggested in the draft provisions of the Town and Country Planning Bill. The Nature
Conservation Council is preparing a submission to me on the question of a review of the 1934
legislation and, if the present legislation requires revision, particularly in so far as
endangered plants are concerned, this will be undertaken.

likely to be considered by any review committee?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: I have seen the article referred

structure of the consumer price index will be undertaken by an index revision advisory
committee during 1978.

Wanganui Computer Centre
141. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert), on behalf of Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson)
asked the Minister of Justice: Can he confirm that local authorities are now expected to
supply to the Wanganui Computer Centre extensive details of those prosecuted for minor
offences, including the failure to register dogs and the infringement of building bylaws, both
before and after conviction, and will he advise the extent of the details required and if any
assistance will be provided for the paper work involved?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The local authorities initiating
prosecutions have been asked to supply personal information about defendants in the same
form as has been given for many years by the Police and the Ministry of Transport. The
information, which includes the sex, date of birth, and place of birth of the defendant, is
used to assist in the identification of the defendant in the Wanganui Computer Centre system
and to maintain the integrity of the record in that system. The honourable member will be
aware of the concern to ensure that the information stored in the Wanganui Computer
Centre system is accurate so that it may be used for future law enforcement purposes. There
has been no insistence that this information be provided to registrars, and if local authorities
are unable to provide it this does not in any way prevent them bringing the prosecution.
However, the availability of this information will assist courts should they have to take
enforcement action to collect any fine that might be imposed, and as most of that fine is paid
to the local authority there is ultimate benefit to the authority if it is able to supply the data.

Maori Infant Mortality Rates
144. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen the statement
in Time magazine of 22 November in which it is stated that Maori children "have one of the
highest infant mortality rates in the world, and, according to Maori psychologist Donna
Awatere, one in every four dies before his first birthday", and, if so, can he say whether this
is correct?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Yes, I have seen the statement in Time
magazine. The statement is both incorrect and irresponsible. In 1975, the latest available
figures, the Maori infant mortality rate was 20.5 per thousand live births, not 250 as the
statement claims. From World Health Organisation statistics, a comparison of 61 countries
studied reveals that 21 countries, or 34 percent, have a lower infant mortality rate than
Maoris, and 40 countries, or 66 percent, have a higher mortality rate.
(25/11/77)
State House Waiting Lists

either (a) changes have been made since November 1975 to the criteria used to determine

interpretation of these criteria have been much more rigidly enforced in order to exclude
many thousands of people who have a need for rental housing?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: Since November 1975 there has
been no change to the criteria used to determine whether or not people should be included
on the corporation's rental house waiting lists. These criteria have not been any more rigidly
enforced.
(25/11/77)
Electricity Tariff Differential, South Island
146. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East), on behalf of RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North),
asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Has he seen the reports in the two Dunedin
newspapers of 12 November in which the Labour candidate for Dunedin North advocates an
electricity tariff differential for the South Island, and, if so, is such a proposal at present
under consideration, and what relationship does it bear to possible national distribution and
pricing of LPG when Maui gas becomes available?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) replied: I have seen the report referred
to. The question is being considered along with other energy policy proposals to see whether
a case really exists on economic, regional, and social grounds. One of the inescapable
implications of such a differential would be a logical application of the same philosophy to
coal, petrol, diesel, and Maui LPG pricing. This could more than offset any electricity price
advantage to the South Island. Whether such differentials in pricing are really desirable is
questionable.

Lead Exposure
161. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn), asked the Minister of
Health: Is it a fact that more than three-quarters of the lead process workers temporarily
suspended last year because of lead exposure came from two factories in the Hutt Valley,
and, if so, what is the explanation for this?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: It is a fact that more than three-quarters of
the lead process workers temporarily suspended last year because of lead exposure came
from two factories in the Hutt Valley. Workers are suspended as a result of routine testing
and before any risk to their health occurs. The number of suspensions is an indication of the
care with which the supervision of lead process workers is undertaken in those factories
where exposure to lead fumes and dust is known to be present. This concentration of
workers at risk is because one of the two factories involved produces 65 percent of all the
lead batteries and 100 percent of all the heavy industrial batteries used in New Zealand.
Also, the number of firms engaged in lead processing, the number of persons under
supervision, and the number of examinations are greater in the Hutt health district than in
any health district.

Coal Mines-Reduced Expenditure on Development
165. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines: What is the justification
for reducing the Mines Department vote by $1,660,000 for plant and equipment, $2,340,000
for the development of mines, and $1,000,000 for stripping, excavation, and surface
restoration, when the Government is claiming that it is giving the highest priority to the
development of indigenous energy resources?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied: The reductions in the Mines Department
vote were not made to constrain expenditure but to adjust the allocation of moneys to a
figure in keeping with the expenditure that is expected to come to charge in the 1977-78
financial year. Of the programmed expenditure of $9,559,000 on plant and equipment there
is an expected 1977-78 expenditure shortfall of $1,660,000 which will come to charge in the
1978-79 financial year. The main cause of this is that many of the items are of overseas origin
involving longer than expected lead times both in calling tenders and obtaining deliveries. Of
the 1977-78 programmed expenditure of $19,713,000 for the development of mines, there is
an expected shortfall in expenditure of $2,340,000 that is attributable mainly to unexpected
and unavoidable delays in the Huntly coal mining project. Extremely wet conditions in the
Waipuna opencast mining area prevented the operation of heavy machines, with the result
that expenditure in the 1977-78 financial year is expected to be $1 million less than
estimated.
