Employment of Farm Cadets
184. Mr WETERE (Western Maori) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Has he seen the
article in the Auckland Star of 9 November 1977 headlined "Not much hope for farm boys",
and, if so, is it true that not enough farmers are prepared to employ farm cadets this year and
that some boys will miss out?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture) replied: I have seen the article
referred to. The Auckland Federated Farmers farm cadet scheme selects and accepts cadets
throughout the year. The main intake is in January of each year, and while at times it is not
possible to place everybody during January boys accepted are placed as soon as possible
within a month or two following. At the moment the number of farmers offering to employ
cadets is only slightly down on previous years, and it is not expected that there will be any
real problem in placing all the boys.

Waterfront Industry Commission Administration Fund Levy
189. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the
recent announcement by the Waterfront Industry Commission that the national administra-
tion fund levy has been reduced by 15 percent, can he advise what this levy is designed to
cover and how it has been possible for it to be reduced?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The national administration fund levy
covers payment of waterside workers' guaranteed wages, annual and statutory holiday pay,
temporary inter-port transfer costs, the cost of running amenities, and capital expenditure
authorised under the Waterfront Industry Act, all administration expenses of head and
branch offices, pay offices and bureaus. It has been possible to reduce the commission's
national administration fund levy at this time, because by agreement with the New Zealand
Waterside Employers Union of Employers, the Container Terminal Operators Association,
and the Harbours Association of New Zealand, the commission's funds have been built up
since the previous levies were fixed on 2 February 1976. The level of funds available to cover
any possible redundancy situation and long service leave commitments is now considered to
be quite adequate.

Yesterday the Minister of Labour left to attend an OECD conference in Paris, and it is
fitting to reflect that he has left the country in a state of relative industrial calm. That is a
tribute to a Minister who is prepared to get close to the parties to any dispute that is referred
to him, and it is a tribute also to the moderate forces in our community. However, we should
all consider seriously the industrial madness we have witnessed in recent times. I have said
many times, both inside and outside the House, that New Zealand is well served by its trade
union leaders and management. However, we sometimes have occasion to observe some
fault on either side. People are often too quick to turn to industrial action and the threat of a
strike to solve their problems. I have always held the belief that people should decide their
own futures, and a recent visit to the Republic of Cyprus has reinforced that view.
This comes through in the attitude of myself and the Government, and the Minister of
Local Government's attitude to restructuring local government by taking into account the
people's views. We find madness in our midst, and that is brought to our attention by the
headline in this evening's Evening Post, "Woolstores men may ban exports". Many members
have observed in the past that the world does not owe New Zealand a living. One has only to
travel overseas to realise how small a population New Zealand has-3,200,000 people. It
would be of little comfort to us if New Zealand disappeared below the waves, but the rest of
the world would not be too upset about it. People might grieve for an hour or two, but they

Opposition members have, however, expressed reservations regarding the proposal. In both
cases I have asked the Ministers involved to discuss the clauses in question with the
Opposition spokesman involved in the hope that agreement can be reached before the
Committee stage of the Bill.
The draft Supplementary Order Paper also proposes a number of detailed amendments
to the clauses, all of which were unanimously recommended by the committee. A new date,
better related to the payment of tax, is proposed in clause 3 for the payment of accident
compensation levies. A revised clause 14 would limit to specific situations and circumstances
the power of the Commissioner of Apprenticeships to delegate his powers to any other
officer, Clause 63 amends the Medical Practitioners Act by permitting the appointment of a
"lay observer" to the medical practitioners' disciplinary committee. As drafted, the clause
requires that such an observer be a person “of eminence and distinction in the community";
the committee recommends the deletion of these unnecessary words.
A minor
drafting amendment, consequent on the passing of the Land Valuation
Proceedings Act earlier this year, is proposed to clause 93, which relates to Rotorua town
lands. Clause 107 would permit trustee savings banks to operate their own imprest accounts;
a minor drafting amendment makes it clear that such accounts can be operated by the bank
itself on its own accounts,
There was initially some reservation about clause 108, which also amended the Trustee
Savings Bank Act, by extending the definition of New Zealand Government securities to
provide for the inclusion of such other securities as may be approved by the Minister of
Finance. The draft amendment, approved by the committee, would require that such
approval be now given by a formal regulation. The committee considered that the maximum
monetary penalty that could be imposed for disciplinary matters by the Valuers Registration
Board pursuant to clause 114 was too low, and, with the concurrence of the board,
recommends that
Finally, Ish this be increased from $500 to $1,000.
4
note that the committee also considered draft amendments to three
other statutes other than those included in the Bill as introduced. The first authorises the
Broadcasting Corporation of New Zealand, with the consent of the relevant local authority,
to erect and maintain relay stations on roads or streets or road or street reserves and
authorises the local authority to give such consent. The second amends the Machinery Act to
enable control to be exercised over amusement devices such as ferris wheels. Both of these
amendments were unanimously agreed to by the committee. The third proposed amendment
is to the Quarries Act and amends the law restricting the employment of women and young
persons in or about a quarry or tunnel. Although this would be an implementation of an
International Labour Organisation Convention, the committee has some reservations
regarding the provision and, again, I have asked the Minister to discuss the matter with the
Opposition spokesmen on these matters.
I should like to thank the many departmental officials and parliamentary counsel, and
particularly counsel in charge of the Bill, Mr Hurrell, for the assistance they gave to the
committee in its consideration and deliberation on the measure.

ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill now be read a
second time. There are three new provisions in the Bill, which I believe are not contentious:


## p. 5144 (#580) ###########################################

5144
7 December
Electoral Amendment Bill
one increasing allowable election expenses to candidates, one extending the meaning of
"ordinarily resident in New Zealand" to 18-year old children of public servants overseas,
and one important new clause regulating the publication of advertisements on behalf of
individual candidates. Otherwise, this short Bill virtually completes the undertaking given by
the National Party 2 years ago to repeal a number of provisions that were pushed through by
the then Labour Government in the 1975 Electoral Act against the wishes of the National
Party in Opposition, which we then gave notice we would repeal on becoming the
Government.
Much of the Bill simply restores the principal Act to the form it took prior to 1975—that
is, to the form of the Act under which the 1972 election was conducted. As that election was
won by the Labour Party the suggestion made that this measure will provide for party
advantage is plainly absurd, and I hope it will not be raised again. Before I proceed to a
consideration of the clauses I ought to refer to another bit of misinformation on the Bill that
has been bandied about, and point out that since 1967 five of the eight amendments to the
Electoral Act were agreed to unanimously by the House. The 1967, 1969, 1971, 1972, and
1974 amendments were all enacted with the agreement of members on both sides of the
House, but the then Labour Government used its substantial majority to force the 1975
amendment Bill through the House against the wishes of the Opposition.
I shall now discuss the clauses. The 1975 amendment Act provided that candidates who
were school teachers or university lecturers could receive remuneration for supervising
students preparing for examinations if the supervision took place in the period during which
the candidates would otherwise be required to take unpaid leave of absence. The amend-
ment was basically designed to avoid as far as possible any disruption to students studying for
examinations at the time of an election. It resulted from the submissions of the Association
of University Teachers of New Zealand to the 1974-75 Electoral Act Committee of the
House. However, the Department of Education found that, as far as school teachers were
concerned, the 1975 amendment caused difficulty and confusion. I believe that was borne
out by Mr McDavitt in his evidence to the select committee on behalf of the Values Party.
Accordingly, the Government has determined that the 1975 amendment should apply to
university staff only, which was the basis of the originating submission to the 1974 select
committee, and that is provided for in clause 2.
Clause 3 merely amends the statutory meaning of "ordinarily resident in New Zealand"
to include the children of public servants outside the country in the course of their duties.
That amendment is a necessary consequence of the lowering of the voting age to 18 years,
and Opposition members indicated in the select committee that they will support it. Clause 4
restores the residency requirement in an electoral district from 1 month to 3 months for voter
registration purposes in line with the stance taken by the National Party when in Opposition
in 1975. The fifth clause disqualifies from voting those persons convicted of offences and
detained in penal institutions. The National Party could see little merit in the enfranchise-
ment of such persons in 1975, and has taken this opportunity to restore the law to its
traditional position on this matter.
The requirement set out in the 1975 amendment that a list of polling places and
candidates be sent to voters prior to an election is removed by clause 6. The Act, of course,
requires the returning officer to advertise both the names of all the candidates and the
polling places. Perhaps I should repeat that, because there has been some misunderstanding
about it. The Act requires, and will continue to require, the returning officer to advertise
both the names of all the candidates and the polling places.
Clause 7, which relates to special votes, has caused some misunderstanding and
confusion. It has been possible in the past, and still is possible, for persons who voted in the
ordinary way in a past election to cast a special vote at the next election if their names have
somehow been omitted from the roll. The effect of clause 7 is to repeal the provision inserted
in 1975 that permits a person to vote if he is entitled to be registered, but is in fact not
registered, if he believes on reasonable grounds that he is or should be registered as an
elector.
It became quite clear at the last general election—and, of course, that was conducted
under the administration of the Labour Government-that this provision caused consider-
able confusion and led some people to think that they were entitled to vote without having
made any effort whatsoever to have registered as an elector in their electoral district. As I
said on introducing the Bill, the Chief Electoral Officer found it was difficult indeed for
returning officers in the last general election to determine whether an applicant for a special
vote had reasonable grounds for believing he was or should have been registered as a voter.


## p. 5145 (#581) ###########################################

7 December
5145
Electoral Amendment Bill
The Government, when the Act was so amended in 1975, made it clear that it believed that
this provision should be repealed.
Clause 8 increases the maximum amount of election expenses from $2,000 to $4,000.
Clause 9 repeals the 1975 amendment that allows loudspeakers to be used in public places
between 9 a.m. and 8 p.m. on any day other than Sunday in the month preceding polling day
despite any local bylaw to the contrary. There are two basic points of view on this matter.
The first is that all parliamentary candidates should have the same rights in respect of the use
of loudspeakers for the period leading up to a general election. This view was propounded by
the member for Roskill on the introduction of the Bill. The second point of view is that the
right to control the use of loudspeakers is a function that has been properly vested in local
authorities so that they can determine what is best for their areas in line with the wishes of
their local body constituents. The Government, as we stated in 1975, believes this to be the
correct view, and has acted accordingly.
Clause 10 is an attempt to lay down more precise rules in relation to election
advertisements. At present election expenses are expenses incurred by or on behalf of a
candidate, and advertisements, published in support of a particular candidate but without his
knowledge, do not constitute part of his election expenses. It is, therefore, open for a third
party to spend a considerable amount on behalf of one candidate if it is done without the
authority of that candidate. Clause 10(1) restricts this possibility by making it an offence to
publish an advertisement to promote a candidate without the candidate's consent. As a
result of recent English case law, an advertisement urging electors not to vote for one
candidate constitutes an advertisement promoting the remaining candidates. This will be
prohibited under the clause unless the remaining candidate authorises its publication.
Subclause (2) of clause 10 makes it quite clear that an advertisement at the national level
is not to be regarded as part of a candidate's election expenses unless it relates solely to the
candidate for a particular electoral district. The advertisement must, of course, also be
authorised by him. This will ensure that advertisements at the national level in respect of
party leaders or more than one candidate will not fall within the restrictions made on each
candidate at electoral level as to election expenses.
Clause 10 is not designed as a comprehensive measure to regulate all election advertise-
ments. It does, however, represent an attempt by this Government to set out some
guidelines for such advertisements. I believe it to be useful in this respect while recognising
that more comprehensive measures may be required. However, that is a matter for a
fundamental review of our electoral laws which I should like to undertake when reason
requires and resources permit.

​Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The Electoral Amendment Bill makes history,
because, for the first time in the history of New Zealand, a Government has sought by

previous electoral Bill was designed to extend the franchise. This Bill restricts it.
First, I want to register my outrage at the handling of the Bill in Parliament. Never have
we seen a worse abuse of the parliamentary system. The Bill was introduced on 3 November.
Despite its constitutional importance, it received no advance publicity, and Government

provision, such as voting rights for prisoners, was emphasised, but the real purpose of the

invalid, as provided for in clause 7, has carefully been ignored. Although the Bill was sent to
a committee, submissions opened and closed in less than 2 weeks. The committee heard
evidence and rammed the Bill through on the same day without any warning to Opposition
members. The committee hearings on this Bill were a complete and utter farce. The Bill is
not the result of parliamentary committee hearings. It is the result of secret National Party
caucus decisions.
The importance of the Bill cannot be overstated. K. J. Scott, in his book on the New
Zealand constitution-and that is very relevant to this Bill-stated at page 6: "The only
other Act that could be regarded as the constitution is the Electoral Act 1956. Like the
Constitution Act, it resembles what are called constitutions in other countries both in
constitutional importance of the subject matter and the facts of the matters covered in it." In
other words, we are changing the constitution of New Zealand when we have urgency and
are off the air. In any other parliamentary democracy that in itself would be sufficient to lose
the Government the next election. The democratic ideal can be summed up in one sentence;
"Government is government by all the people for all the people of all the people." That
principle can be summarised in the simple word "freedom", which National Party members

say they believe in.
Never before in the history of this Parliament has the restriction on the right of citizens
to vote been sought. When this Parliament was formed over 130 years ago only people with
substantial property could vote. The franchise was first extended to all men, and then we, as
a Parliament, made history by extending the vote to all women. While past Governments,
fearful of electoral prospects have attempted to alter boundaries—and in 1934 one Govern-
ment even put off an election-no Government has ever taken away a citizen's vote once it
has been granted. All electoral Acts have been designed to give votes to more citizens, to
make our elections fairer, and to make voters better able to understand what they can vote
for. By this legislation, the third National Government, for purely party political reasons,
has sought to destroy that fine record. This was the only Parliament that could claim that
such a record had existed for 130 years.
We should not be under any illusions about the effect that clause 7 will have. This Bill is
not whether prisoners can vote. That is a red herring if ever I heard of one. In its submissions
the Values Party said—although it might have some difficulty in proving it—that from its
experience prisoners voted National anyway. This has nothing to do with whether or not
local authorities will control loudspeakers. That is another red herring. This Bill is about a

Mr McLay: An exaggeration.
Mr PREBBLE: That figure is not an exaggeration. It is an understatement. For the

wanted it, and their votes were not counted. Those votes were disallowed because they were
not on the electoral roll. A further 14 916 people who were not on the roll at the last election
cast their votes, and their votes were counted under provisions which we are now repealing
in clause 7.
During the committee hearings I conceded that I was not completely happy with the way
the provisions of clause 7 worked at the last election. Under that clause the votes of 44 937
New Zealanders who took the trouble to vote were not allowed. That number is three times
higher than the valid vote in my own electorate. The overall statistics are even worse. The
total number of disallowed votes at the last election was 76 252. Those people who voted for
New Zealand the way they wanted it cannot understand how we ended up with a National
Government, because they were not told that their vote had not been allowed. I am sure that
if each one of them were told that his vote had not been counted the outrage would be so
great that we would not be doing what we are going to do off the air tonight.
The total number of disallowed votes at the last election equals the total valid vote in the
Auckland Central, Franklin, King Country, Manawatu, and Porirua electorates. The
turnout at the polling booths at the last election was low, and I believe that at the next
election the votes of 100 000 New Zealanders who vote for New Zealand the way they want it
will be disallowed because of the tighter provisions of this clause. Anyone who believes in
democracy will not be happy about that.
When one considers that 341 000 New Zealanders who were on the roll at the last
election did not vote, one should start to question whether Parliament is a democratically
elected body. That figure is half the total vote the National Party received. Those figures add
up to the simple fact that our voting system is too complex, and that thousands of New
Zealanders are losing their right to vote because of the bureaucracy of our electoral system,
unnecessary form filling, and complex technical rules that even returning officers do not
understand. Our total valid vote is only 1.6 million people. More than 300 000 New Zealand-
ers do not vote, and on top of that about 7 percent of the total vote is disallowed every
election. When one realises that a swing of only 3 percent can change a Government, one
realises also just how complex our electoral laws are.
I subscribe to the philosophy of Al Smith, the perennial American Democrat candidate,
who has said that there is nothing wrong with democracy that more democracy cannot fix. I
believe there is nothing wrong with out electoral laws that more democracy could not fix.
This problem is not unique to New Zealand. It occurs in every democracy, but responsible
Governments have tried to solve the problem.

Carter "it is proposed to remove unnecessary and unfair barriers by creating a method of

appears to support the idea that Maoris should be able to enrol on either the Maori or the
general parliamentary rolls, whichever they choose. Indeed, I believe that should be
encouraged.
According to the Government Statistician, the total number of Maoris for electoral

electorate, 44 789 in the Western Maori electorate, 34 728 in the Eastern Maori electorate,

Maoris in the Northern Maori electorate have shifted from the electorate or have moved and
failed to fill in another registration card. It is clear that a considerable number have failed to
return the enrolment card. I gathered from what the Minister of Justice said that the
Government has no intention of requiring the electoral office to initiate a campaign to re-
enrol electors throughout New Zealand.
I believe that the Bill provides a good opportunity for initiating some changes, but I
consider it has been introduced simply because of political vindictiveness. However, I shall
not go into my reaons for saying that, as I stated them in an earlier debate on the Bill.
Certainly the provisions in the measure are not of great moment. The Prime Minister went to
great lengths this evening to tell us of the large number of people that do not vote, and of the
large number of voters who had their votes invalidated because they were not on the
electoral roll. What provision in the Bill will correct either of those problems? If measures to
overcome them are not taken at this stage the Government will fail a lot of people, and
particularly Maori people, in a period when important transitional changes are taking place.
The future of Maori electorates depends very much on the changes made in the
transition, and I believe these should be measured more accurately. That is why Opposition
members are pleading that the electoral procedures be tightened and corrected as much as
possible. It is extremely important that they should be. The member for Whangarei may be
interested to know that more than half of the 4000 Maoris in Whangarei who could vote in
the Northern Maori electorate will probably vote in his electorate. I welcome their
opportunity to do so, if it is what they want to do. About the same number of Maoris in the
Northern Maori electorate will probably vote in the Bay of Islands electorate. I shall
welcome that too, if that is their choice. If a person does not have a choice he will feel
aggrieved, and will not vote at all.
At this point I am not pushing my own political party, but, in the interests of all Maoris
and the electoral rights of all New Zealand citizens, it is important that some changes be
made. On 23 March 1977, the Minister of Justice advised me as follows: "The legislation
provides explicitly that once the choice is made, it cannot be changed until the next re-
enrolment after the 1981 census, and there is no allowance for mistakes." According to that
advice the Minister acknowledges that a mistake had been made. What steps is he taking to
correct such mistakes? As the Government has not objected to Maori people having a choice
as to which roll they want to be enrolled on, why does he not take steps to correct the
anomalies, either in the Act or in the regulations. If we set aside the higher number of non-
voters arising out of circumstances not relating to the Bill before the House, a considerable

Hon. R. J. TIZARD: I suggest to the member for Waitemata that a proper recording of

section at the city council office, yet he did not find his name on the supplementary roll. So
that person is denied a vote.
Under the existing law such a person would be entitled to a special vote, claiming that
he or she had made every effort to get on the roll and was reasonably entitled to expect that
the name should be on the roll. However, under this legislation we find that unless the name
is on the roll the voter is not entitled to a vote. Contrary to the views of some members of the
House, I stress that this was not the action of a person ignorant, or careless, of the rules. It
was considered action twice taken by a person who knew the rules, someone who was an
active participant in voting procedures and who had been actively engaged in securing other
persons to vote on behalf of a political party. Still, under the terms of this amendment he is
not entitled to vote. A further technicality disqualified that person.
Had the name been on the parliamentary roll at the same address the applicant would
have been entitled to a vote, but there had been a shift within the city area and within the
same general election roll, and therefore not even on that ground could the vote be allowed.
It was not a matter of neglect or carelessness on the part of the applicant that disqualified
him from a vote. That is what the original amendment by the Labour Government was all
about. We wanted to make sure that people who sought the vote had an opportunity to vote.
We have dismissed some of the claims that have been put forward. We have heard that
having a period of 1 month's residence would mean rigging of electorates. That was replied
to by the member for Wanganui, who told us that in Australia that system had been
operating for almost 70 years, and, as far as we know, had never led to an instance of an
electorate influenced by the movement of voters. I wonder where any party in this country
would find sufficient electors to move them around, or the finance to do so, particularly to
keep them for a month in an electorate in sufficient numbers to influence the result. The
proposal for 1 month's qualifying period was simply a means to ensure that more people
were entitled to vote by an ordinary vote. It was an attempt to overcome the number of
applications for special votes because people had moved from a district in which they were

Appropriation Bill
APPROPRIATION BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now read a
third time. This is the last general debate of the parliamentary session. It has become the
custom for the debate to be led off by the Government, but it is not necessary that that
should be so. Tonight I propose to lead off the debate, because I am concerned about the
Opposition's tactics during the session-the tactics it has used inside and outside the House
of denigrating the country and talking down the New Zealand economy.
For some years I have made no secret about the fact that New Zealand is facing its
greatest challenge since World War II. With the increase in the price of oil in 1973 and the
events that followed, New Zealand's terms of trade deteriorated by 40 percent. I know of no
other country where the terms of trade have deteriorated by a higher percentage. It has been
agreed at international conferences that it is not the Third World, but the developed primary
producing countries that have received the greatest blow from the increase in oil prices.
There is no doubt that Third World countries have taken a blow as the rich have become
richer and the poor become poorer, but the developed primary producers, of which New
Zealand is one, have received the greatest blow.
Terms of trade mean the relative price we receive for our exports as against what is paid
for imports. If our terms of trade have deteriorated by 40 percent that means it takes that
many more bales of wool to buy an imported tractor. Purchasing power was 60 percent of
what it was before. That is something that the people of New Zealand are now beginning to
understand, but I remind you that it happened at the end of 1973, when a Labour
Government was in power and when the present Leader of the Opposition was Minister of
Finance. During 1973 that Labour Government had let the brakes off in spite of warnings
from the National Opposition. It had used up the reserves that we had painfully accumulated
between 1967 and 1972-painfully accumulated to the point that at the end of 1972, for the
first time in our history, our external reserves were greater than our overseas debt. We were
a creditor nation.
That disappeared in the first year of the Labour Government, and it will be many years
before we get back to that position again. So when the OPEC countries increased the price
of oil for the first time, and when they increased it subsequently to about five times the 1972
price, the profligate Labour Government, with the present Leader of the Opposition as
Minister of Finance, had squandered the reserves and the Government was in no position to
meet the circumstances that then developed.
The New Zealand Institute of Economic Research has today released its quarterly
predictions. The institute says that the onslaught we are experiencing is likely to bottom out
in the second half of next year. There is nothing in the report that is essentially different from
what I have been saying day by day, week by week, month by month, and year by year since
1973-nothing. But while the Labour Party was in power it denied it. Since it has been in
Opposition, of course, it has preached a sermon of doom. Let me go back to 13 November
1973. The New Zealand Institue of Economic Research stated: "The balance of payments is
forecast to deteriorate markedly during the coming year as import payments continue to
rise." Import payments were going to continue to rise because the Labour Government, with
the member for Tasman as Minister of Finance, had excessively stimulated the New Zealand
economy. A few months later, on 7 March 1974, the New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research stated: "The prospects for 1974-75 are for continued strong inflation, a marked
deterioration in the balance of payments, and a slackening in the rate of growth of
production." We had a rate of inflation of 5.5 percent in 1972 under the National
Government, 10 percent in 1973 under the Labour Government, and 12.6 percent in 1974
under the Labour Government.
The Monetary and Economic Council stated in May 1974: "The New Zealand economy
will face serious problems if the current account deficit continues to increase during 1975-76.
The appropriate steps to obtain overseas finance should be taken now." In other words,
"Government, get out and start borrowing if you can find anyone to lend to you." The
Government did. It found someone to lend to it at about 9.5 percent, and borrowed $400
million in 1974, when the present Leader of the Opposition was Minister of Finance. As
recently as today, he was saying that we have borrowed more, knowing full well that what we
borrowed recently was to repay the $400 million that he borrowed in 1974, but we borrowed
it at two-thirds of the rate of interest that he had to pay, because we are now a triple A
nation, top line of credit in the world-which the Labour Government could not have got
when he was Minister of Finance.


## p. 5162 (#598) ###########################################

5162
7 December
Appropriation Bill
I was interested when a banker in the United States 2 or 3 weeks ago said to me, “I do
not know New Zealand, but your credit is good. Your credit is better than the credit of
Australia." And it is. The Australian economy should be stronger than ours, as they have
more resources, but the fact of the matter is that the market says that our credit is better than
that of Australia—and that is the best independent compliment that can be paid to the
economic management of New Zealand at present.
Let us come back to the Leader of the Opposition when he was Minister of Finance. In
the New Zealand Herald of 23 October 1974 we read: "New Zealand has one of the
strongest currencies in the world, a sharp change from a few years ago', the Minister of
Finance, Mr Rowling, said in Auckland yesterday." The strongest in the world! He upvalued
it twice, but a year later he had to devalue it and a year later he had to devalue it again, until
it was well below the value when he took over as Minister of Finance at the end of 1972. I
quote from the Auckland Star of 14 November 1973: "Rowling sees boom going on next
year. The Minister of Finance, Mr Rowling, believes the sustained high economic growth in
New Zealand during the past year can be maintained in the coming year. He believes the
country is heading for considerably improved price stability and reasonable balance between
supply and demand in 1974."
When he took over, the consumer price index was going up by 5.5 percent. In his first
year he nearly doubled it to 10 percent, and in his second year he more than doubled it to
12.6 percent, while telling the public there would be continued price stability. On 8 January
1974 an article in the Evening Post stated, under the heading "Finance Minister plans early
Budget, expects good year": "In the expert opinion of the Minister of Finance, Mr Rowling,
1974 will be a good year for New Zealand, and that is notwithstanding the difficulties faced
in 1973 in the energy crisis. 'I believe a very sound foundation was laid during 1973, a
foundation which will allow for considerable expansion in New Zealand in the future,' said
Mr Rowling today”.
Did he know he was deceiving the people, or was he ignorant of the fact that at that very
time New Zealand was moving over the precipice that has caused us so much concern and
anxiety ever since? I think his advisers knew, although I do not know whether he accepted
that advice. On 8 April 1974, 3 months later, it was stated in the Dominion that: "Rowling
sees no grounds for depression talk", and "In spite of an extra $200 million a year in oil
costs"-it is now $400 million extra-"and a deteriorating balance of payments situation, the
Minister of Finance, Mr Rowling, is still confident there is no depression looming ahead for
New Zealand." And so it goes on.
I have mentioned those old quotes tonight, because I want to sheet home the
responsibility for New Zealand's present economic difficulties to two sources: first, the
natural source the increase in the price of oil, and the 40 percent decline in our terms of
trade, which any Government had to face—and, secondly, the one that we did not have to
face-the incompetence, the negligence, and the culpability of the Labour Government,
which, in the face of that challenge, did nothing but borrow and hope-not my term, but that
of the chairman of the Monetary and Economic Council. The previous Minister of Finance
and Prime Minister did nothing, but said that the economy would turn around internation-
ally.
I went to the public on a policy of putting the economy straight, and got rid of a lot of
the clever young men such as the member for Manukau and his colleagues. I will go to the
public again next year on exactly the same policy-face the facts; do not shy away from
them. I believe that New Zealanders are prepared to back, a Government that faces the
problems heaped upon us by international events, and nothing that I have seen in the last
2 years will change my mind. When we have a weak, do-nothing leader of a political party, who
in Government hopes it will come right-borrows and hopes-and in opposition criticises, I
do not think the people will do anything more than they have done in the last 2 years. Every
time there is a poll the Leader of the Opposition slumps further in the public esteem—and he
deserves to. He was given a task and he was given the opportunity at a time of crisis in our
history. He failed miserably, and the ordinary New Zealander has judged him and found him
wanting. There is no way that people will ever have him leading the country again.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Even at this time of the
morning the House might have expected the Prime Minister to take the opportunity in this,
the last wide-ranging debate of the session, to give some indication as to how he proposes to
lead the country out of the mess he has created over the last 2 years. Rather than that, he
chose to once again attempt to apportion the blame to other people; that has become a
characteristic of the Prime Minister and his Government.

I want to take a moment to protest at the time and the nature of the debate. It has been

sacking of the five members of the Local Bodies Commission, Highet emphasised the need
for greater consultation and for the new commission to acknowledge public opinion in areas
affected by reform proposals. Similarly-in acknowledging the need to improve the structure
of local government-the National Party's 1975 election manifesto promised to 'maintain a
democratic local government structure with clearly defined responsibilities, acting in co-
operation with central government but with a minimum of central government interference'.
It gave the glib assurance, too, that in the restructuring of local government, the views of the
local community should prevail'. The Government is now making nonsense of those words.
The Town and Country Planning Bill gives central government an even greater role than
now in planning responsibilities, and ignores five years of advice from such bodies as the
Holmes Task Force, three committees on local body finance and the Local Government
Commission that central government devolve its power to local bodies, enabling them to set
their own priorities.
"The Bill drastically overhauls the structure of town planning throughout New Zealand
and fundamentally affects every citizen. Most important, it erodes individual rights by-for
example-giving councils new and unprecedented delegated authority, and by making the
Minister, rather than an independent tribunal, the final authority in certain circumstances.
Setting up a select committee to hear public representations on the Bill was a sham—the
Government had made it clear it wanted the complex measures (132 pages in draft form) to
be passed through all stages this session. When the select committee began hearings, 222
submissions had been received plus 56 representations on one clause, and more were to
come. In its first six meetings, the committee dealt with 18 submissions, and by November
10, it had heard about 40. It decided then to hear no more . . . ".
The Town and Country Planning Bill as it stands is undoubtedly improved, but by how
much nobody in this House knows, nor how far it meets the representations of the people
who came to give evidence to the committee, because we will not know, and cannot know
until we are able to send copies of the Bill as reported back to the people who made
representations. We will not be able to do that today, nor tomorrow, and probably not next
week, by which time the Bill will be well on its way to being passed, if not passed in its
entirety. The result will be that the parties affected and interested by the legislation will have
imposed on them terms of which they know nothing before they come into operation. To call
this open Government or participation by the community or an exercise in democracy is to
make a mockery of the term, and this is a typical example of the manner in which the
Government has decided it shall rule the country rather than govern the country.

THURSDAY, 8 DECEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Social Welfare-De Facto Relationships
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Will he confirm
that a letter was sent to Beth Furmage in May on behalf of the Social Security Commission
by the Director-General of Social Welfare, apologising for the fact that a declaration was
sought from Mrs Furmage concerning her relationship with a male friend?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The answer is no, as to the best of
my knowledge there was no such letter.
Mr Marshall: Can I take it that the Minister is now also saying as clearly as he has said
before in the House that no such declaration has ever been sought from Mrs Furmage?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The Social Security Commission, in cases in which a benefit has
been cancelled because a woman is living in a de facto relationship that is not denied, can
invite the parties to make a statement about the nature and extent of such association to
assist the commission in deciding whether there is an entitlement to a benefit. However, it is
not the policy to seek a declaration asking the parties to alter the nature of their association.
Mr Quigley: Can the Minister confirm that Mrs Furmage's case was declined by the
Social Security Commission, and an appeal was made to the Social Security Appeal
Authority, which upheld the commission's decision and declined the payment?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Following the cancellation of this woman's benefit she twice
appealed unsuccessfully to the Social Security Commission. She then appealed unsuccess-
fully to the Social Security Appeal Authority. She has now appealed on a technical point of
law to the Supreme Court. I am advised by the Crown Law Office that that restricts further
questioning, because the matter is sub judice.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: If no such letter was sent to the lady herself, was any letter of that
type sent to her solicitor or to anyone else on her behalf?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Not that I am aware of. I can see no reason why an apology
should be sent. The woman has appealed to two judicial bodies. Her appeals have been
rejected by both those appeal authorities, and there is no reason in the wide world why
either of them should apologise.
Mr Marshall: I am not sure, from the Minister's reply to my first question about how a
declaration can be sought from people in these circumstances, whether he meant that such a
declaration had been sought in the first place from Mrs Furmage.
Hon. H. J. WALKER: If it so wishes the commission may invite a couple who have been
charged with living in a de facto relationship-and if the woman is still seeking a benefit-to
write to the commission and tell it the extent of their association or relationship, but the
commission does not, as has been claimed by some people, tell anyone how often he or she
can sleep with someone else or have sexual intercourse with someone else. Those charges are
not true.

Stock Incentive Scheme

Student Drinking
7. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the report in the Waikato Times of 26 November
headlined "Schools stop sports over drink abuse", in which the principal of one Hamilton
secondary school is reported as claiming that "secondary school overnight sports fixtures are
becoming a thing of the past-because of student drinking", and, if so, is there any action
that can be taken to prohibit the use of action photographs of young athletes to promote
alcoholic liquor, such as the one that appeared in the Timaru Herald on Wednesday,
2 November, of a secondary school boy aged 16 years, which was used without his or his
parents' permission?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have seen both the article and the
advertisement referred to by the honourable member. As far as I am aware, nothing in the
law prohibits the use of such photographs without the consent of the athlete. However, it
may be that the advertisement is in breach of the code of practice drawn up by the New
Zealand Liquor Industry Council in 1973. The code states that liquor advertising should not,
by use of any illustration directly or by innuendo, encourage drinking by young people under
the legal age either directly or by implied example through linking liquor with identifiable
heroes or heroines of the young. In addition, the code states that all models in liquor
advertisements should appear to be over the age of 20. I should add that one of the functions
of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council established last year is to make recommendations

to me about the advertising of liquor and the need to regulate or in any way restrict any such
advertising. I suggest that the honourable member take the matter up with the council.

question is the subject of a protest and an investigation by his department?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have said that I have seen both the article and the
advertisement. To my knowledge this is the first time the matter has come into my hands.
Travel Tax
8. Mr KIRK (Sydenham), on behalf of Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast), asked the
Minister of Finance: Has he read the editorial in the New Zealand Herald of 11 November
entitled "Travel tax in disfavour", which states, "The tax is believed in the travel industry to
have encouraged travellers to take money out of the country or use credit cards to buy travel
while overseas so as to avoid the extra charge. A tax that has such an effect diminishes its
own usefulness", and, if so, as a result of this and other criticism is he considering the
removal of travel tax?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Reserve Bank statistics give no
evidence that travellers are deliberately evading the travel tax in the ways alleged by the
newspaper editorial quoted by the member. Most travellers prefer to have all their travel
arrangements completed before leaving New Zealand. By doing so they avoid difficulty in
arranging onward bookings, problems with possible fluctuations of exchange rates, and the
likelihood of having to meet increased travel fares while overseas. The member's criticism of
the travel tax is, therefore, quite unfounded, and the Government has no intention of
removing the measure.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that the Minister of Tourism was quoted in the
Christchurch Star of 4 October as having said: "The Minister of Tourism, Mr Lapwood, said

Pea Aphid
11. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
asked the Minister of Agriculture: Has any progress been made in determining how the
highly destructive pea aphid Acyrthosiphon pisum reached New Zealand, what control
measures are planned, and how widely distributed is the aphid at present?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): The pea aphid referred to by the
honourable member closely resembles the blue-green aphid, and mixed populations occur in
New Zealand. The blue-green aphid was first identified in New Zealand in late 1975, but it
was not until this year that entomologists confirmed the presence of two species. There is no
indication of how either of these aphids appeared in New Zealand. The blue-green aphid
arrived in Australia about the same time, and it arrived in the United States of America 2
years earlier. Neither of these countries has been able to explain the sudden arrival of this
native of Manchuria.
Roading, Terrace Tunnel, Wellington
12. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) asked the Minister of Works and Development:
What was the commencement year and original estimated cost of the Terrace tunnel on the
Wellington motorway, and what is the present estimate of the cost of completion?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The construction of the
Terrace tunnel was commenced in late 1974 at the then estimated cost of $8.87 million. The
present estimate of the cost of completion is $12.35 million.

had been placed in employment on farms under the farm employment wage subsidy scheme
by the Department of Labour. The age groups of those placed are as follows: under 18 years,
47; 18 years to 20 years, 50; 21 years and over, 54.

restrictions placed?

COAL MINES BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): I move, That the Coal Mines Bill be introduced.
The purpose of the Bill is to consolidate and amend the Coal Mines Act 1925 and its
numerous amendments relating to coal prospecting and mining. The present coal mines
legislation is 52 years old, and has been amended no less than 26 times. It no longer meets
the needs of a rapidly changing and developing industry at a time of significant demands in
the energy field. The Bill updates the legislation, and provides the means for the regulation
of today's coal mining industry to promote greater efficiency in the development and use of
New Zealand's coal resources. It also brings many licensing and other coal prospecting and
mining procedures into line with those applying to minerals under the Mining Act 1971.
It is vital that we as a nation make the best and most efficient use of all our energy
resources. We must, therefore, ensure that our coal resources are wisely used, and that each
coal mining operation is considered not only on an individual basis but also in relation to its
place in the overall scheme of things. One of the features of the Bill is that the legislation will
now regulate the mining of privately owned coal as well as coal owned by the Crown, by
requiring the grant of a licence by the Minister of Energy in all instances. Too often in the
17-Vol. 416


## p. 5188 (#624) ###########################################

5188
8 December
Coal Mines Bill
past there has been mining of coal by both private enterprise and the State which has not
made the best use of the resource. It is clear that in many cases past practices are not
acceptable, and that we must ensure that we do make the best use of the coal resource in the
future without unduly disturbing the environment.
In this measure, the Government is mindful of the limited extent our our coal resources
and the frequently fragmented nature of land ownership. Members will be aware that to
assist with energy planning the Government has already commenced a programme of coal
prospecting that will eventually range over the whole country. The Government should be in
a position to regulate the development of coal deposits discovered during this programme.
The proposal is not intended to prevent private coal mining, and, I emphasise, does not
provide for the Crown to take over ownership of land or coal. In fact, the Bill provides that
private owners will still have to give consent or make agreements before a coal prospecting
or mining licence can be granted, and it further provides that the owners are entitled to any
revenue from any activities that are so licensed. In the Bill, too, is a clause that allows the
Minister to assist private enterprise in coal prospecting and mining proposals by way of
grants, loans, subsidies, or in any other way he thinks fit.
The provisions relating to the licensing of coal prospecting and mining operations are
significantly updated, with more emphasis being laid on the need for applicants to satisfy the
Minister of Energy that the proposed operations will have every chance of success and will
result in the best use of the coal. The Bill requires that before a coal mining licence is granted
the nature and extent of the coal resource is indicated, that a programme of work is
prepared, that markets are available for the coal won, and that environmental safeguards are
adequate. Such steps taken before any commitment is entered into must reduce the chances
of failure and ensure that all proposals are adequately researched and are consistent with
national energy policy or planning requirements.
Concurrent with the updating of the licensing structure are changes affecting regulation
and safety requirements of the industry and the well-being of those employed in it. This is
important, as more sophisticated methods are introduced progressively to obtain the greatest
possible percentage of coal recovery. There is in the Bill a clause providing that owners of
coal mines must accept responsibility for ensuring that their mines are worked in accordance
with the legislation. If they delegate these statutory responsibilities, they must take adequate
financial and other provisions to ensure that this requirement can be complied with. There is
no equivalent section in the present Act.
As an aid to constructive planning, the Bill provides that the mine manager of every
underground coal mine must submit to the secretary copies of plans for each mine, showing
its proposed development, before any work is undertaken. Another change concerns the
regular medical examination of all persons working underground. At present, medical
examinations are required only for winding-engine drivers. The new Bill still requires these,
but requires also that everyone employed below ground has a medical examination every
year if under 20, and every 2 years if 20 or more. Similarly, every person must be medically
examined at the coal mine owner's expense prior to employment below ground. Such a
requirement can only be in the best interests of employees and employers alike.
Throughout the world the need for research into alternative forms of energy and the
better use of existing energy resources has never been more evident, and we in New Zealand
share the world's concern at a shrinking resource. The Bill recognises the importance of this
research by giving statutory backing to the levy by which the Coal Research Association of
New Zealand is financed. The Bill sets the levy initially at 10c a tonne on all marketable coal
mined. Under the present Act, a levy of 7.5c a tonne is also paid by coal mine owners on all
marketable coal and lignite recovered, and this is lodged to the credit of the Coal Mining
Districts Welfare and Research Council. The Bill continues this levy, but renames the
council the Coal Mining Industries Welfare Council, and whereas previously some of the
council's funds were used in research, this will not now be the case. Instead, a greater
proportion of the council's funds will go towards the provision of retirement allowances for
those who work in the industry. The other purposes to which these funds apply are
unchanged.
Finally, the Bill sets out in detail the items to be covered by regulations. These, too, will
be updated, and in many cases expanded. This is an important and very necessary
consolidation of the coal mining legislation. Once enacted, it will have the effect of
revitalising an all-important industry, at the same time regulating the extent and manner of
its growth to be in accord with the national interest. Because of the significant changes the
Bill makes to the present legislation, and the wide interest likely to be shown in its

provisions, I propose that it be referred to the Commerce and Mining Committee for
consideration during the forthcoming recess.

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): First, the levy placed on coal and other forms of
energy last year, with effect from this year, is unrelated to those levies referred to in the Bill.
The $1.50 a tonne levy on lignite and $2 a tonne on coal is strictly an energy resources levy.
The honourable member will be aware that this year more than $40 million is being spent on
proving our energy resources in one way or another-oil, geothermal, or coal. The
programme for coal proving must somehow be financed from the public sector, and this is
one very appropriate source of revenue for that type of work. The coal proving programme
is likely to take between 12 and 15 years to complete, and in today's money terms, could very
well cost $40 million during that decade or decade-and-a-half.
The two specific levies referred to in the legislation relate to welfare and research and
do not affect the scene very much. The legislation formalises the research levy which has
been paid voluntarily by nearly everyone concerned. The welfare levy has grown out of the
history of coal mining, and not only helps good industrial relations but also represents one of
the ways in which the industry can make a small but proper return to those who have devoted
their careers to it.
The mines inspectors have powers to ensure that mines are safe. Apart from the powers
that directly concern safety, not aesthetic qualities, I understand that only town planning or
local body regulations apply. I see the provisions of the Bill, as amended, as giving the
Minister power to ask a developer of coal to comply with certain requirements right through
the programme of development up to and including the eventual abandonment of the field,
so that it is restored in a reasonable manner to a satisfactory environmental condition. It will
take some time to bring those mines already operating into the arrangement. I understand 5
years is the transition period.
Obviously the requirements of future mining activity could be much more specifically
set out than would be possible for those mines being developed at present. However, I
believe that when representatives of the industry give evidence before the select committee
we will find that they are anxious to co-operate to ensure that the legislation not only works
but works well. After all, the legislation is not introduced to make life difficult for the
industry, but rather to make sure that there is a rationalisation of the use of our coal
resources and their development in such a way that they have a suitable market. In a number
of parts of New Zealand, at present and in the past, coal has been developed without close

is the procedure that has been applied for consolidating titles, for instance, so that a mine
might be operated. One of the problems in this business is that even an entitlement at the
surface of the ground might be very inconvenient in terms of the relationship of the coal
underneath, and it is necessary at times to have some power by which the properties can be
brought together, or a piece of property can be brought in with another piece, so that coal
reserves can be developed. In this respect the Bill is breaking no new ground.

MARINE RESERVES AMENDMENT BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-
tee to present the report of the committee on the Marine Reserves Amendment Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I am also directed
to report that the committee recommends that the Minister of Fisheries introduce a
Supplementary Order Paper containing an amendment to increase the number of members
of a management committee of a marine reserve by up to two members, and to make any
consequent amendment to the Act. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The Lands and Agriculture Committee received submissions from nine groups repre-
senting a wide range of views. Although the Bill is only a small one comprising four clauses,
it generated widespread interest, particularly because of the establishment of a marine
reserve around the Poor Knights Islands in the Hauraki Gulf, and the area of seabed and
water surrounding that area, which has worldwide significance for its biological fish life and
recreational area.
The various representatives who presented submissions supported the provisions of the
Bill, and many took the opportunity to recommend to the committee that the principal Act
of 1971 be amended in certain respects. Many of their recommendations had a lot of merit.
The committee had to consider whether to recommend the inclusion of additional amend-
ments, other than those which arose from consideration of the Bill's provisions, but it
decided to confine its report only to the submissions it received on the Bill. It therefore
recommends only two small changes. The first is that a new subsection (3)(b) be inserted in
clause 2 so that an additional condition may be inserted in a notice to include the word
"species". The second is that clause 3 be expanded to permit authorised fishing until a
management committee is appointed to implement a management scheme. The committee
felt that the suggested amendments to the principal Act should be brought forward by way of
a Supplementary Order Paper, a course of action which the committee agreed upon. The
Supplementary Order Paper will be explained by the Minister, either during the second
reading or in the Committee stage.

MAORI PURPOSES BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I am directed by the Maori Affairs
Committee to present the report of the committee on the Maori Purposes Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table.
The committee heard evidence that related primarily to clause 5, which was concerned
with expanding the powers of incorporations to areas in which they may invest any funds.
The committee amended the Bill to make it clear that the Maori Land Court, after receiving
an application from an incorporation following a general meeting of the owners, could, if it
decided it was proper, grant any incorporation investment powers to pursue any activity
under section 27. There was some uncertainty in this area, so we made the position clear,
and the committee unanimously decided on the attached amendments. Although there was
some suggestion that the powers were not wide enough, the committee did not accept the
suggestion.
Motion agreed to.
MAORI LAND ALIENATION
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I am directed by the Maori Affairs
Committee to present the report on the petition of Mrs Whina Cooper and 1760 others
praying that there be no further alienation of Maori land. The committee recommends that
the petition be referred to the Government for inquiry. The committee has taken this
unusual course because it is a unique petition that directs its attention at the large number of
Acts passed by the House.
During the hearing of evidence it became clear to the committee that the prayer of the
petition, on which it had to make its recommendation, did not reflect the evidence put
forward by the petitioners when they appeared before the committee. The referral of the
petition to the Government for inquiry will make it possible for the Government to attend to
the points in the petition that can be resolved by Parliament. Members of the committee
were impressed by the obvious concern by witnesses about the loss of Maori land, but agreed
with the petitioners that laws should not be passed to prevent totally the alienation of Maori
land. I move, That the report do lie upon the table and be referred to the Government for
inquiry.
I should like to thank the House for granting leave for a limited debate on the report.
Members of the committee have sought this dispensation because the petition is important to
Maori people in particular and to all New Zealanders in general. Members will recall that the
petition was presented to Parliament at the end of the Maori land march. The committee
heard a lot of evidence, and every member was impressed by the sincerity of the witnesses.
Members of the committee spent 2 days earlier this year hearing evidence at the Mangere
marae, and I take this opportunity to thank again the people responsible for the marae for
granting us every possible facility while we were there. In its prayer to the House the petition
asked for changes in two substantive matters. First, it asked "That an enactment of
Parliament which enshrines the spirit and intendment of this Memorial shall incorporate in it
the protective principle of entrenchment whereby it shall not suffer repeal or amendment
without the assent of the Maori people, such assent to be forthcoming by the expression of a
majority of all those persons eligible to vote as Maoris in a National Referendum." I am sure
that all members will agree that such a provision would create some difficulty, and would be


## p. 5196 (#632) ###########################################

5196
8 December
Maori Land Alienation
a radical departure from the normal method of changing our laws. It would not be feasible to
delegate to a section of one group of New Zealanders the right to vote on whether or not a
law should be changed.
Secondly, the prayer of the petition asked "That all pernicious clauses in every Statute
of the present day or in new Statutes in the future, which have the power to take Maori
Land, Alienate Maori Land, Designate Maori Land, or Confiscate Maori Land, be
Repealed and never to be administered on the remaining Maori Land at the present day, and
whereas Management, Retention and Control remain with our Maori People and their
Descendants in Perpetuity." If the Government were to accept that proposal, after recom-
mendation from the committee, no Maori land could be sold in perpetuity. The committee
was unanimous that it could not refer that proposal to the Government for action, either
favourably or in any other way.
As the evidence accumulated, it became obvious that there were some matters on which
the petitioners wanted action to be taken. These matters were summarised by Matakite as
follows: that there should be an elected Maori Land Commission composed entirely of
Maoris, given the function of protecting remaining Maori land by proposals to the Govern-
ment on legislation appropriate to multiple-owned land and by generally supervising the
protection of Maori land. The Maori people can make their views known to the Government
in a number of ways, and the committee was not convinced that it should recommend this
action.
The next proposal was that there should be encouragement by law for the return of
some land to its former Maori status, and an exchange of land for Maori land taken for
public works. The committee agreed that this was a matter on which the Government could
take action. The third proposal was for the protection of multiple-owned land against a sale
for rates and similar charges. The committee envisaged difficulties in enacting that principle.
The next proposal was for the protection of historic and sacred places as reserves-that is a
proposal on which progress should be made. The next proposal was for the establishment of
Papa Kainga to enable homes to be built in country areas. Some progress has been made on
this issue already; it is primarily the responsibility of local government. The final proposal
was that Maori members and advisers should be introduced to regional planning authorities
and similar bodies. That principle is being adopted at the moment, but the petitioners
emphasised the desirability of that course.
The petitioners outlined to the committee about 15 Acts and more than 60 clauses that
they considered to be pernicious in some way to multiple-owned Maori land. An extremely
careful scrutiny of these clauses would be needed before any action was taken. I should
remind the House that action has been taken on some of these matters already, and the
Town and Country Planning Bill covers some of the points that concerned the petitioners. At
all times the committee worked constructively to meet the wishes of the petitioners, to clarify
the major points of concern, and to see whether the petition could be recommended to the
Government for possible action. The committee's job was not easy, because from time to
time there was some contradiction. I thank all members of the committee for the way in
which they attended to their responsibilities, and I place on record the committee's thanks to
the Matakite organisation for the way it presented its evidence to the committee. Witnesses
were courteous and well informed, and presented their evidence in a commendable manner.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): As the member representing Mrs Whina Cooper,
members of her group, and the people who took part in the land march, I thank members of
the Maori Affairs Committee for the courtesy and the hearing they extended to the people
who presented submissions.
On 13 October 1975, Parliament saw the views of the Maori people expressed in the
strongest terms ever seen in our history. The principal aim of the land march was to draw
attention to the fact that the Maori people felt they should be taken for granted no longer,
and should never have been taken for granted. Maori people have close associations with
their land. History has shown that in the name of public interest the Crown has confiscated
more than 2 500 000 acres of Maori land, has bought more than 22 000 000 acres of land in
the South Island, for which payment was not made until a century later, has not settled
justifiable grievances, and has passed Acts that have deprived Maoris of the ownership,
management, and control of their land and, therefore, of their destiny. These historical
facts, rather than the actions of the Government of the day, were responsible for the march
to Wellington.
The House should make a declaration that New Zealand, as a multicultural society,
cannot permit Maori land holdings to fall below their current level. Maori land holdings are


## p. 5197 (#633) ###########################################

8 December
5197
Maori Land Alienation
small at present, and must now be built on. Maori land is part of a distinctive life style—that
is what the dispute is about.
For many years the Maori has used courtesy, petitions, and other expressions to draw
his fellow New Zealanders' attention to his determination to hold his place in society. Those
attempts were not successful; consequently they decided to place the matter before the
House by marching and presenting a memorial.
The last attempt to alter the Maori life style was in 1967, when an Act was passed
further depriving the Maori of his powers. That legislation, coupled with another major
public Act, has had an adverse effect on the Maori population. The Rating Act, the Town'
and Country Planning Act, and the Public Works Act-to name just a few-have all had an
eroding effect on Maori life and the Maori community. The Maori people have refused to
tolerate these moves and have petitioned that their opinions, judgments, and attitudes
should be reflected in the statutes.
I support the resolution that the petition be referred to the Government for inquiry, as it
will have an effect on 41 public Acts. It is 2 years since this matter arose, and the House
should act expeditiously.

Maori looks at it as his turangawaewae, his personal interest; even if it is only a post hole, it
is a place to stand.

Government we will amend the Town and Country Planning Act." He got to the heart of the

As long as the House addresses itself likewise to the problem, looking to the future to
see whether it can pick up the problems, attend to them, and ensure as far as possible that
there are no "pernicious" clauses relating to multiple-owned land, the petition will have
been the success that those who started it and saw it through believe it should be. With the
interest and co-operation of both sides of the House, we can make considerable progress. I
thank all members of the committee for the attention they paid to the petition.
Motion agreed to.

HAWKE'S BAY CATCHMENT BOARD EMPOWERING BILL
Mr CHRISTIE (Napier): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill will
enable the board to rectify errors caused by the issue of erroneous certificates of adjusted
values. The events leading up to the need for the Bill are that section 159 of the Rating Act
1967 provides for valuations to be adjusted when any special purpose authority makes and
levies rates, and when, under the Valuation of Land Act 1951, current valuation rolls for all
such constituent districts did not take effect on the same date. This adjustment is more
frequently termed the equalisation of values.
In 1975 the board received a request to apply to the Valuer-General, through the branch
manager, Napier, for an adjustment of valuation. In due course a certificate setting out the
total adjusted values for each constituent district was received. The constituent districts are
the cities, boroughs, and counties, or parts thereof, in the board's district. Subsequently,
some local authorities expressed concern at the increased level of rating in their districts.
It was later found that there had been a transposition of valuations between two
authorities. This error affected all rates levied throughout the board's district. Schedule 1
sets out those districts that were overrated, and schedule 2, those that were underrated. The
error was not apparent because the certificates were issued on land values this year for the
first time. Previously, they were issued on unimproved valuations. Had the unimproved
valuation system been used, it is possible that the comparison with valuations for previous
years might have revealed the error.
As no existing legislation makes provision for the issue of an amended certificate the
board's original levies on its constituent local authorities could not be varied. The Wairoa
Borough Council referred the matter to the Ombudsman. Subsequently, the Department of
Internal Affairs informed the board that some of the inequities arising from the 1975
certificate could be rectified by a local Bill designed for the purpose; hence the reason for
this Bill.
Bill read a second time.
