NOXIOUS ANIMALS BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. When the Bill is finally passed it will be known as the Wild Animal Control Act. The
management of introduced wild animals in New Zealand has always been a controversial
issue. From the early years of this century, Governments have been criticised by farmers and
forest owners concerned about the damage caused by introduced wild animals. As well,
there has been almost continual concern about the high rates of soil erosion in many major
catchments and other areas, and the contribution to that erosion by browsing and other
noxious animals has been recognised. Conversely, recreational hunting organisatons have
strongly opposed any efforts to regulate recreational hunting.
Furthermore, in the last two decades we have seen the development of the commercial-
isation of the recovery of wild animals. It is probably a gross understatement to say that
pressures in this area have often found the law and the ability to implement it somewhat
lacking. In fact, the industry was reaching a stage—as all members of the House well know—
where, in places such as Fiordland, a New Zealand type of "Wild West" situation was
emerging.
An indication of the extent of the controversy over matters related to noxious animals
or wild animal control is that, in the 20 years since the Forest Service assumed responsibility
for the control of these animals, there have been five official inquiries touching on the
matter. The difficulty for the legislator is that the situation from area to area is quite
different throughout New Zealand. The Bill now before the House goes a long way towards
resolving some of the long-standing difficulties. Not only does the Bill, as reported back,
have a new name, but, more importantly, it embodies several new principles. In fact, it
brings radical changes of direction in several fields.
For the first time control, not eradication, is the general objective. I stress that control is
the general objective, because in some areas-national parks, scientific, and special
areas eradication is still necessary. Obviously, however, there could still be practical
problems in pursuing that policy in some areas. The Bill does not attempt a single-answer
solution; it acknowledges that different areas require different treatment. There is no


## p. 5204 (#640) ###########################################

5204
8 December
Noxious Animals Bill
question that in areas such as national parks and areas where water and soil conservation
values are threatened every effort will be made to continue to reduce animal numbers.
We still have with us specific problems in the control of wild animals in what is described
as the wapiti area of Fiordland National Park. Members who are familiar with the situation
in the Ruahine Ranges will know that, to give the vegetation any chance at all to recover, the
deer population must be drastically reduced, and that there are large erosion-prone areas
where total eradication must be the policy. So much of the undergrowth of the beech forest
there has been eaten out that the understorey is like a hollow shell. The southern Ruahines
are indeed in a very fragile state.
On the other hand, the Bill makes, for the first time, legislative provision for the setting
aside of recreational hunting areas. Obviously these can be only in places where water and
soil conservation is not at stake. Provision has been made for individuals as well as
organisations to comment on proposals for recreational hunting areas; a recreational hunting
advisory committee is to be set up to advise the Minister. A major change in principle is the
dropping of the word "noxious", about which there has been considerable controversy over
the years.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: A very good move.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am glad to know I have the support of the member for Timaru,
who has a lasting interest in this field of Government legislation and responsibility. Some
difficulty was encountered in finding an alternative name. We were faced with the task of
finding a suitable word to describe animals that are both hunted and farmed and which, as
well, can be major pests. The word "feral" was considered seriously, but that word is not
understood by a wide range of our population. Generally the term "wild animal" was
considered more appropriate.
The Bill also contains important provisions for the regulation of helicopter hunting, or,
more specifically, the regulation of wild animal recovery operations on Crown-owned
land-and that includes national parks. The select committee has agreed to the Forest
Service licensing operators to take animals. The Bill also provides for zoning for wild animal
recovery operations by commercial operators. The Forest Service will be responsible for
licensing all operators, regardless of the tenure of the land over which they propose to
operate.
The most significant aspect of this part of the Bill is the provision for tough penalties
against those who offend. The size of the fines that can now be imposed on those who break
the law are substantial, and will, I believe, act as a suitable deterrent. The procedures in the
Bill will, I hope, bring some order and calm to what is often a very volatile situation. The
licensing and penalty clauses will ensure that we get some sort of order, and I would hope
complete order, out of what has been chaos.
The Bill also contains tough new measures relating to trespass. It is important for many
farmers, because it gives special protection to landowners. The Bill makes it clear that
hunters must have authority to be on land before they hunt, kill, or capture wild animals. If
permission is not obtained, any person who carries out the act of hunting, killing, or
capturing, acts unlawfully. The Deerstalkers Association expressed concern that these
provisions adversely affect recreational hunters who trespass inadvertently. However,
Federated Farmers and the Deerfarmers Association strongly supported the measures
contained in the Bill.
I want to refer specifically to clause 37, because there was considerable objection to
some parts of it. It has now been amended. Originally, this clause provided that, when a
person was found in circumstances where a reasonable presumption could be made that the
person had committed or intended to commit an offence, the liability was on the alleged
offender to prove his innocence. The clause now provides that, if any person is found with a
firearm, or other means of hunting, on land where wild animals are usually present, this shall
be evidence from which the court may infer he was hunting. This is, in itself, a substantial
strengthening of the present Act.
The Bill is much needed, and it will become increasingly important because of the
control it will exercise over the game industry. In recent times this industry has developed as
an extremely valuable earner of overseas fund, and is, without doubt, an industry in its own
right. The provision for the regulation of commercial hunting and wild animal recovery,
together with the control of recreational hunting, is one of the main thrusts of the Bill. The
other main features are, as I have mentioned, the co-ordination of hunting and control
measures, and the action to be taken to prevent the damaging effects of wild animals on
vegetation, soils, waters, and wildlife. I compliment the select committee on its bipartisan

While the Bill is aimed to update the principal Act, I think by and large we have been

Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this

Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: It is!

The select committee received about 39 submissions, and in its deliberations was greatly

The Bill makes provision for the control of introduced wild animals, as they will now be

Complementary legislation to amend the Air Services Licensing Act 1961 to require

New Zealand has about 113 deer farms, 97 holdings breeding deer and other animals for

The committee has recommended that the title of the Bill be changed to the Wild

The committee supported a change to clause 4, which sets out the purposes of the Bill.
The new clause states: "(1) This Act shall apply to all land, having regard to the provisions of
any Act applying to the land, and shall be for the purposes of controlling wild animals
generally, and of eradicating wild animals locally where necessary and practicable, as
dictated by proper land use. (2) This Act shall be administered, having regard to the general
purposes specified in subsection (1) of this section, so as to (a) Ensure concerted action
against the damaging effects of wild animals on vegetation, soils, waters and wildlife; and (b)
Achieve co-ordination of hunting measures; and (c) Provide for the regulation of recrea-
tional hunting, commercial hunting, wild animal recovery, and the training and employment
of staff." I am pleased that these provisions have been so clearly spelt out to make the intent
of the Bill very clear.
I am particularly pleased that the Bill provides for action to be taken against the
damaging effects of wild animals on vegetation, soils, waters, and wildlife. Over many years
we have seen damage done to our mountain lands; under the provisions of the Bill we can be
assured that adequate control measures will be adopted. I give the Bill my full support
because of the close scrutiny given to it by the Lands and Agriculture Committee. The Bill
will benefit deer farming and other wild animal industries, and at the same time will protect
mountain and hill country land from the ravages and the proliferation of wild animals.
Dr WALL (Porirua): Although the Bill reflects a bipartisan approach, it is unfortunate
that the land-owner interests of the Government have been reflected in some of its
provisions. As I have spent much of my leisure time and also have been employed in the
back country, I cannot let the Bill pass without protesting at what will result from its
provisions. People will be put in danger because of the nature of the back country and the
people in it.
When legislating for the back country we are legislating for people who will meet in twos
and threes, miles from anywhere, and who will walk or march for a whole day away from
human habitation-that is not uncommon in the southern part of New Zealand. The Bill
gives Forest Service officers likely to be in the back country extraordinarily sweeping
powers, and it also gives rights to land owners, which, compounded with the powers given to
those officers, could become extremely onerous. Events will take place before few, if any,
witnesses other than the participants.
To me this is dangerous. After events that will be misdemeanours under this legislation,
people might take violent action to protect themselves or their property because they are so
remote from legal processes available in the rest of the country, and because no witnesses are
present. For that reason I see great danger in the Bill's stringent provisions. Instead of
promoting good order in lonely and wild places, the Bill will cause disorder.
I draw the House's attention to one or two matters that have given me considerable

Idiosyncracies in landowners and residents in the back country are not uncommon. An
innocent climber walking over the land may be ordered off by a landowner. The climber may
have a rifle with him to shoot himself a feed, not because he is deerstalking. After words with

property, the local landowner jacks up the presence of his friend the forest officer. Under
the Bill, the Forest Service officer has the power to take the climber's rifle, his motorcar, and
anything else on him, and to hold those articles for 12 months without reference to any court.

MUNICIPAL CORPORATIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill was generally welcomed on its introduction. Its principal
operative clause, clause 2, is an important one, and represents a significant step forward for
the Government's energy conservation policy. Its effect is to require the thermal insulation


## p. 5210 (#646) ###########################################

5210
8 December
Municipal Corporations Amendment Bill
of new residential buildings for which building permits are issued on or after 1 April 1978. It
achieves this end by requiring borough and city councils to make bylaws that will apply to
building permits, under which the insulation standard will be enforced.
The full insulation of residential buildings is clearly in the national interest. It will
provide savings in future energy requirements and energy supply capacity. At the same time,
those who are building new homes will benefit. The Government will lend up to $400 interest
free over 4 years to cover the cost of insulation. This sum is sufficient to insulate the average
New Zealand home. The home owner will eventually recoup his investment in the form of
reduced heating bills. Nationally as well as individually the capacity for savings is great.
Fewer than 8 percent of all occupied dwellings have both wall and ceiling insulation. Only
one new house in five has wall insulation to an accepted standard installed. We cannot afford
to miss the advantage offered by new construction to insulate residential buildings
adequately.
I explained when introducing the Bill that the bylaws made by councils under this
legislation will have their effect through each council's building permit procedures. It is
expected that most, if not all, councils will adopt the standard prepared by a committee of
the Standards Association, which sets out the minimum thermal insulation requirements for
residential buildings. This standard has been approved by the Government. During the
introduction of the Bill, it was asked how a single standard can be applied to the whole
country when it is obvious that climatic conditions and heating loads vary widely. This, I
think, is simply a matter of learning to walk before we run. The New Zealand standard will
give satisfactory savings in all conditions.
It is desirable that the standard be as straightforward as possible in the early stages. A
variety of regional or even local standards would create difficulties for manufacturers,
builders, building inspectors, and others in accommodating differing requirements to
different local conditions. If this were the situation, it is likely that further delays in the
insulation of new buildings would have to be accepted while, for example, climatic zones and
their requirements were determined. I mention that local bodies will be free to frame bylaws
requiring a higher level of performance if they wish, and, of course, the Standards
Association intends to review its own code as experience is obtained with insulation and new
building and insulation practices.
Some doubt was expressed about the ability of local authorities to frame and adopt
suitable bylaws by 1 April 1978, as required in the Bill. There will be sufficient time to act.
The maximum period for the completion of the special order procedure for the adoption of
bylaws is 70 days from commencement. Many councils, however, have adopted the New
Zealand Standard Model Building Bylaw, NZSS 1900 Chapter 4, and thereby have largely
met the requirements of this legislation. All they will require is the formal approval of the
Minister of Energy so that they can enforce the bylaws. The model bylaw has been amended
to relate to the newly developed insulation standard issued by the Standards Association.
Councils that have not adopted that model bylaw will have no difficulty in framing a bylaw
based on that model. I am sure of that. The matter has been discussed with the Municipal
Association, which agrees that the time available, although short, is adequate.
I emphasise that a long process of consultation has marked the progress of this
legislation from the beginning. Local authorities, Government departments, the building
industry, professional associations, and research organisations were represented on the
Standard Association's building and civil engineering sectional committee that drafted the
new standard. I am confident that this thorough preparation will ensure the success and
continuing public acceptance of this very necessary legislation.
Clause 3 makes a consequential amendment to the principal Act arising from the Land
Valuation Proceedings Amendment Act 1977. The effect is simply to place the jurisdiction in
land valuation matters, previously exercised by the Administrative Division of the Supreme
Court, with the land valuation tribunals established under that Act.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill is one of a series to consolidate and revise the Local
Government Act 1974, the Municipal Corporations Act 1954, the Counties Act 1956, and
other legislation affecting territorial, local and regional government. A second Bill, which
will deal principally with land subdivision and roading, will, I hope, be printed and ready for
introduction at the end of the session for recess study. The final instalment should be ready
for introduction and enactment next year. When finally brought together, these measures
will provide a long overdue and modern codification of a major portion of the law relating to
local government, and the Counties and Municipal Corporations Acts will disappear from
the statute book.
The desirability of having a code of law common to all territorial authorities-counties,
cities, and boroughs-has become more apparent as the years have gone by. Differences in
the electoral franchise between municipalities and counties have gradually disappeared until
they have become almost non-existent. They will be completely non-existent when this Bill
becomes law. Many other earlier dissimilarities between the Acts applying to rural and
urban local government have also been steadily reduced in recent years. Indeed, even when
one refers to the physical characteristics of local districts, it is now highly misleading to
regard county government as applying only in the rural context, or to speak of municipal
government as applying to only urban areas. We have municipalities containing urban areas
as large as some counties, and we have counties responsible for urban areas the size of a city.


## p. 5212 (#648) ###########################################

5212
8 December
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Clearly, the law affecting our local government system needed to be revised and recodified.
This Bill, and the other measures I have mentioned, do just this.
When the Government was elected, not only did it promise to consolidate the Municipal
Corporations and Counties Act, but it also said in no uncertain terms that it believed in
maintaining a democratic local government structure with clearly defined responsibilities,
acting in co-operation with central government, but with a minimum of central government
interference. The Bill gives meaning to this philosophy. Throughout its preparation we have
been mindful of the need to clearly define responsibilities in broad terms, but at the same
time special care has been taken to give local authorities the utmost discretion to act within
those terms. In many cases, this discretion is far wider than it ever has been in the past, and
gives meaning to the term "local government".
Some of the local authorities that made submissions to the Local Bills Committee
suggested that procedures in the Bill should be more precisely spelled out. In effect, they
were saying they would prefer less discretion. However, the Government believes—and I
know that most local authorities believe-that the Government's present policy of allowing
the elected representatives of local people to exercise more initiative on their own account is
the correct one. As Minister I certainly intend to continue with it.
The Local Bills Committee received more than 50 submissions, and while there was
some criticism of the time available to prepare submissions to the committee, in my opinion
this was not justified. It is of course always the first claim by anyone who does not like
something a select committee is to consider to say that he has not had sufficient time to study
it. An extension of the time for hearing submissions would not, in my opinion, have led to a
better Bill. After all, the Local Bills Committee allowed sufficient time to hear everyone
who wished to appear before it. I take this opportunity to record my appreciation of all those
who made submissions. Many of the changes made stemmed directly from their experience.
I want now to speak about some of those changes.
The provisions for the constitution of regions and regional and united councils are very
much as they were introduced. The intent of the legislation is that there should be united
councils for most regions, because it is in this way-by nominating the members of the
regional body—that constituent authorities can best participate in regional planning and
regional projects generally. A change has been made to the appeal procedure dealing with
representation on elected regional councils. The Bill as introduced re-enacted the previous
law giving the Local Government Commission the role of arbiter in the event of any
constituent territorial authority not being satisfied with its representation as determined by
the regional council.
Members will recall that last year a decision of the commission purporting to generally
review representation on the Auckland Regional Authority as a consequence of one appeal
was set aside by the court. As a result of representations arising from this case the Local Bills
Committee has changed the Bill to make it quite clear that the commission has the authority,
when determining an objection by any constituent authority, to carry out a full review of
representation on the regional council. That is the only important change made to the
regional constitutional provisions.
Some amendments were made to the provisions applying to the establishment of district
councils-the term used primarily to facilitate the union of a borough and a county where the
resultant new district is really neither one nor the other. It is interesting that the district
councils already in existence seem to be functioning well as they overcome their teething
problems-so much so that at least one county containing a former borough wishes to adopt
district council government. The Bill as introduced permitted this to be done. It was put to
the committee that the opposite should also be provided for-that a district council should
be able to revert to borough or county council status if it wished to do so. The submission
was not accepted. The committee felt that once a council made a commitment to adopt
district council status it should stand by it. This will ensure that a decision to adopt this status
will not be taken lightly, and once it is taken there should be reasonable stability; otherwise,
one could foresee a yo-yo situation.
The Counties Association suggested that a county council should not be given the
authority to abolish riding elections and to substitute either elections at large or elections
based partly on ridings and partly at large as the Bill provides. The riding system for county
elections is admittedly traditional. It is well entrenched. But today it is quite anachronistic
when applied compulsorily to the urban county situation, in Waimairi, for instance. There is
no reason why an elected county council should not decide its own system of election, just as
can be done by any municinal council. Indeed, such an approach is fully in keeping with the


## p. 5213 (#649) ###########################################

8 December
5213
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 2)
philosophy I mentioned earlier, that discretion on issues such as this should be with local
councils. I would not expect many county councils to abandon riding elections, but the
committee felt that no really sound reason why a council should not determine this matter
for itself had been advanced. It could not accept the submission on that point.
The term of office of a county chairman is another issue of some moment to the
Counties Association. The county chairman is the odd man out in the local government area.
He is the only leading citizen who is elected by his council for 1 year. All mayors and other
chairmen of bodies of any consequence hold office for 3 years—a period which is long
enough to contribute towards the maintenance of a reasonable degree of continuity of
administration. Under the annual election system, the office of chairman tends to become
regarded by some councils as a reward for services rendered, or a "your turn next" type of
office. In any case, it does not help continuity of administration.
The Bill as introduced provided for the county chairman to be elected by his council for
3 years. The committee has not changed this provision, although it gave careful considera-
tion to representations made by the Counties Association following a resolution of its last
conference. The committee could not see any reason to distinguish between the term of
office of a county chairman and that of other chairmen or mayors. However, I do not think
this provision should come into force immediately. After all, it is only a few weeks since
county councils held their annual meetings and elected their chairmen for a 1-year term. As
the Counties Association said to me only this morning, many of those people may not want
to continue in office until after the 1980 elections, and it would be quite wrong to compel
them to do so.
I hope the member for Porirua is listening to what I am saying, because, unfortunately,
owing to the very short time, I have not been able to advise him of this small amendment,
but I am sure he will agree with it. I quite agree with the Counties Association, and
consequently I propose to introduce in the Committee stage a Supplementary Order Paper
that will continue the present method of annual election of county chairmen until the 1979
election. This means that the election of county chairmen for 3-year terms will operate from
the 1980 elections. I hope the member will agree that that was a wise course to take.
Over the years there have been many representations seeking authority to pay non-
council members of committees for attendance at committee meetings, as if they were
council members. It has always seemed to me to be rather unfair that a person who is
appointed to a council committee because of his expertise and special knowledge should not
receive any recompense whatsoever, while the council member sitting alongside him should
be paid as a councillor. I know that in the past there were problems involved in removing this
anomaly, stemming mainly from the composition of some hundreds of fire committees.
However, those bodies went out of existence a year or two ago, thus removing the last
impediment to treating all council committee members alike. The Bill enables all ordinary
committee members, whether elected councillors or not, to be paid the same attendance
rates, provided of course they are not officers of the council.
Finally, I make a brief reference to one or two changes made by the committee to united
councils. The committee has amended the Bill to make it quite clear that as far as possible
the staffing and administrative requirements of united councils are to be provided from the
administering authorities' own resources. This, of course, was the original idea, but the
committee felt it was not made sufficiently clear in the Bill as introduced. By arrangement
with the committee on the Bill, several provisions introduced in the Town and Country
Planning Bill relating to works and other activities necessary to implement a regional
planning scheme have been transferred from that Bill to the Local Government Amendment
Bill, where they are more appropriately placed. I know that this further stage in the review
of territorial local government legislation will be welcomed by those who must work within
its framework. Of course, the Bill does not do everything everyone has asked for; that would
be impossible. But it does, in my view, represent a considerable improvement to the present
law. I thank the members of the Local Bills Committee for their work on the Bill. It was a
long Bill. I want to thank particularly the Opposition members for the way they co-operated
with Government members throughout.

Counties have continued to operate the old anachronistic system, in which voting rights
depend on the value of the land owned. That system was abandoned by central government
almost 60 years ago, and it has not applied in municipalities for a long time. The one man
one vote system is accepted almost universally throughout the English-speaking world, but it
still does not apply to the counties in New Zealand. The wealth of the landowner or the size
of the property owned by a ratepayer determines the worth of his vote and may make it far
more powerful or valuable than the vote of the man down the road. That it an anachronistic
electoral system. As I have said, every English-speaking country in the world has moved
away from it, but the National Government is now extending it to cover the municipalities.
The only excuse can be that the counties did not want to lose it.
Whereas previously no assumptions could be made in the determination of wards in a
municipality, because all municipalities have been operating under modern electoral systems
for at least 50 years and it would have been unthinkable to divide the districts up on any
other basis than that one man should have one vote, clause 56-obviously at the request of
county interests-will now change the position. I consider this a very backward step.
Subclause (3) provides: "For the purpose of giving due representation to the several wards,
the council shall have regard to the population"—that is, the modern universally accepted
concept of one man, one vote. However, to keep in with the friends in the counties, the
backwoods men also decided that the council shall have regard to the "rateable value, and
area of each ward, and such other additional factors or combination of factors as the council
considers relevant".
The Opposition does not have just an airy-fairy theoretical objection to the proposed
electoral system. One has only to think of the application of that principle to the city of
Wellington, and realise the effect it would have to appreciate that. If the factors mentioned
are to be compulsorily taken into account and Wellington was divided into wards, the people
would no longer have equal voting rights-as they do now whether they live in Lambton
Quay, Karori, Island Bay, Miramar, or any other suburb. Under clause 56(3) the man who
has a penthouse in Lambton Quay or lives in The Terrace will have the rateable value of his
property taken into account in determining the value of his vote. When one thinks of the low
population and the high rateable value of land between the harbour and The Terrace and
between Thorndon and Oriential Bay, one can readily appreciate how much more valuable
the vote of a landowner in those areas would be than would be the vote of someone living in
Newtown, Island Bay, or Karori. Therefore, I emphasise that our objection is not merely
theoretical. In the legislation the Government put through the House last night it disfranch-
ised people-

FISHERIES AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. Its purpose largely is to make machinery amendments to the Fisheries Act 1908 in
relation to the Fisheries Amendment Act 1977 and the Territorial Sea and Exclusive
Economic Zone Act 1977. The Fisheries Amendment Act 1977, which was deliberated upon
by a select committee and arose from requests from the fishermen's associations and the
Fishing Industry Board, created a new Part III to the Fisheries Act 1908, and provided for
the declaration of "controlled fisheries". In order to ensure that this new part of the Act may
be effectively controlled, the existing powers and protections of fishery officers in Part I of
the Act are being integrated into Part III.
Part III of the Fisheries Act has provision for the Minister to declare a moratorium on
licences and fishing permits for any fishery named in the schedule. On 14 July 1977, at the
request of the industry, such a moratorium was declared on the Nelson-Marlborough scallop
fishery. Since that time, representations have been made by fishermen to the ministry, the
Fishing Industry Board, and myself that the moratorium should not be completely inflexible.
The moratorium was originally proposed as a short-term, interim measure, but experience
has shown that more time will be needed before the final number of units to be licensed in
the fishery can be investigated and decided upon. Consequently, the Bill provides for the
Minister to have some discretion in the issue of further licences while a moratorium is in
existence.
Since regulations were passed earlier this year placing a quota on the Hauraki Gulf


## p. 5216 (#652) ###########################################

5216
8 December
Fisheries Amendment Bill (No. 2)
snapper fishery, some doubt has arisen as to their validity, and the Bill is intended to remove
any possible ambiguity. The industry was in agreement with the placing of this quota. It is
intended to amend the terminology of naval officers to conform with that in the Territorial
Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977, which was deliberated upon by a select
committee, and to extend their powers to include air force personnel who are now taking a
larger role in the policing of the 200-mile zone.
The provisions of the Bill, which have been discussed with and agreed to by the Fishing
Industry Board management, are as follows. Clause 1 is the short title, and integrates the Bill
with the Fisheries Act 1908. Clause 2(2) outlines the definition to assist in the placing of
quotas on a species of fish or on a group of species commonly caught together and which may
be regarded as a unit for the purposes of modern conservation and management, and should
be read in association with clause 4, which provides for the placing of quotas on any fishery.
Clause 3(1) makes fishery officers appointed under Part I also fishery officers under Part III.
Subclause (3) ties the terminology of naval officers etc. in with the Territorial Sea and
Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977, and also gives them authority under Part III.
Clauses 5, 6, 9, 11 and 12 apply existing powers and protections of fishery officers in
Part I to Part III. Clauses 7 and 8 tie the terminology of New Zealand's armed forces in with
that used in the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977. Clause 11 gives the
Minister discretion to permit further licences or permits to be issued during a moratorium.
This will in no way interfere with any final decision of the Fisheries Licensing Authority.
The measures I have outlined are largely of a machinery nature, but are of some
importance, and it is necessary to implement them this year. They have the support of the
Fishing Industry Board and will be of benefit to the industry.

JOINT COUNCIL FOR LOCAL AUTHORITIES SERVICES BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in speaking to
the Bill. As I explained when it was introduced, it is a relatively short but important Bill for
local government. It is an empowering measure to set up a joint council of 10 employer and
10 employee members covering a wide range of local authorities. The general purposes of
the joint council are to establish machinery to secure the largest possible measure of joint
action for the consideration of salaries and conditions of service in local government, and to
promote and develop the concept of an integrated local government career service.
The functions of the joint council will relate to the administrative, professional,


## p. 5219 (#655) ###########################################

8 December
5219
Joint Council for Local Authorities Services Bill
technical, and clerical employees in local government-those employees generally referred
to as being white-collar workers. At present, employment in the local government sector is
very fragmented and unco-ordinated. Not only is this so between the various classes of local
authorities-for example, between the municipalities and, say, the power boards-but in
many cases even within a particular class. In some cases, employees are covered by awards
and, as these usually include a maximum salary bar, a number of employees fall outside the
scope of those awards. In other cases, a separate in-house agreement for a particular local
authority has been negotiated, and this brings a much wider range of employees within the
scope of the agreement. So we have some local authority employees covered by a general
award, others covered by a specific in-house agreement, and others who are not covered by
any award or agreement. The top positions are, of course, subject to the jurisdiction of the
Higher Salaries Commission.
While there is some uniformity in pay scales and conditions of service in the awards, on
the other hand the in-house agreements tend to reflect the particular requirements and
structure of the local authority concerned, and can differ markedly between authorities.
Overall, little regard is paid to the interests of developing a more unified local government
career service, and in many cases there is no portability of conditions of service when an
employee moves from one local authority to another. Given this fragmented picture, both
the Minister of Labour and I were only too pleased to respond in a positive way to the
initiative from the main local authority employer associations, unions, and officer groups
when they submitted joint proposals for bringing about more co-ordinated machinery for
fixing salaries and conditions of service in the local government sector. As I explained when
the Bill was introduced, the setting up of the joint council is the first step towards the
ultimate objective.
In his remarks on the introduction of the Bill, the member for Porirua referred to the
need to avoid setting up another body that will only further complicate the wage and salary
relativities between the State, private, and local government sectors. Because of this need,
the Bill does not, at this time, specify the joint council's powers in pay fixing. During the
introduction of the Bill, I outlined the three areas in which the local authority interests have
sought pay-fixing responsibilities for the joint council. The first involves a delegation from
the Higher Salaries Commission to the joint council of the responsibility for fixing salaries of
certain top positions in local government. The local authority interests have proposed that
the joint council should eventually assume this responsibility, but it is accepted that the
Higher Salaries Commission should retain responsibility for determining the top salaries for
the major local authorities, and that any salaries fixed by the joint council would have to be
related to those fixed by the Higher Salaries Commission.
The Government's attitude is that once the joint council has been set up and has shown
that it can operate effectively, an extension of its powers in this way can be considered. In
the meantime, and to give the joint council the opportunity to gain experience in this area,
the Bill gives it power to make recommendations to the Higher Salaries Commission about
the salaries of officers in top positions in local government. The enactment of the Bill this
session will enable the joint council to exercise this power in time for the next general review
of top salaries by the Higher Salaries Commission as at 1 April 1978.
The second aspect of the council's pay-fixing responsibilities concerns the prescribing of
salary scales for local authority employees not covered by an award or agreement. However,
before any powers can be exercised by the joint council in this area there must be a clear
definition of its jurisdiction, particularly over the existing arrangements under which awards
and collective agreements are negotiated. The third area for which local authority interests
have requested powers for the joint council is in prescribing basic national conditions of
employment, including the portability of those conditions between different employing
authorities. This is certainly an area where there is scope for improvement, and the
portability question is essential to the eventual emergence of a more unified local govern-
ment service.
As I have already indicated, it has not been possible to finalise negotiations on these
matters in time for this Bill. However, officials of the departments concerned-the Depart-
ment of Internal Affairs, the Treasury, the State Services Commission, and the Department
of Labour-will have further discussions with the joint council on those three issues as soon
as the council is established early in the new year. As already indicated, it is intended that
the joint council's powers in the pay-fixing area be the subject of further legislation early in
the next session.
I do not think it is necessary to comment further on the Bill at this stage. I should like to

TOKELAU (TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE) BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. As I indicated when I introduced the Bill, it will replace the existing 3-
mile territorial sea and 9-mile fishing zone around Tokelau with a 12-mile territorial sea and
a 188-mile economic zone. As honourable members know, Parliament has already enacted
legislation for New Zealand in the New Zealand Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic
Zone Act. This is now being done for Tokelau. The circumstances of Tokelau and New
Zealand are not the same, as was observed by the member for Northern Maori when the Bill
was introduced. For that reason two separate Bills are being enacted. It should be
emphasised however, that in principle the differences are minor.
The important point is that the Bill establishes a 200-mile economic zone for the benefit
of the people of Tokelau, and that it is based as closely as possible on the present New
Zealand legislation. Clause 2 is the interpretation clause. Clause 3 extends Tokelau's
territorial sea from 3 miles to 12 miles from the base line. During the introductory debate the
member for Northern Maori asked why the definition of fish in clause 2 had been altered
from the definition in the present legislation, and asked whether it would include turtles. It is
questionable whether whales and turtles should be dealt with in this Bill, or whether they
might be more properly included in some more appropriate legislative vehicle that would
control the taking of marine life other than fish. I have been advised that the matter can be
dealt with under New Zealand legislation by regulations. The Bill deals with those species
for which a sustainable yield is established and where a sustainable yield can be allocated.
Clause 6 prohibits fishing by foreign craft inside the 12-mile territorial sea, and provides
penalties for foreign fishing craft that infringe the zone. Clause 7 establishes an exclusive
economic zone extending 200 miles seaward of the base line of the territorial sea. The
principle here, of course, is exactly the same as it is for the New Zealand legislation. Clause 8
makes provision for the Governor-General to make regulations relating to the control of
foreign fishing craft within the exclusive economic zone. Members will note that this clause
will permit the same penalties to be imposed for infringements of Tokelau's zone as are
provided for in our own legislation. Clause 9 provides that offences in the economic zone
shall be deemed to be committed in Tokelau.
Clause 10 declares that the foreshore and the bed and subsoil of the internal waters,
territorial sea, and exclusive economic zone are deemed to be and always to have been
vested in the Crown. Clause 11 empowers the Governor-General to make general regula-
tions in respect of Tokelau's territorial sea and economic zone. Clause 12 sets out the powers
of law enforcement officers over foreign fishing craft within Tokelau's maritime zones.
Clause 13 places the onus of proof on a defendant to establish that he held a licence at the
requisite time, and clause 14 repeals the Tokelau (Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone) Act that
we set in place last year. This legislation supersedes that Act.
As I said at the time of its introduction, the Bill makes provision for the establishment
for the benefit of the people of Tokelau of an exclusive economic zone and territorial sea in
precisely the same way as a zone was established for New Zealand. It is done at the request
of the people of Tokelau, and will provide, with the setting in place of the zone, for the


## p. 5221 (#657) ###########################################

8 December
5221
Tokelau (Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone) Bill
effective use of the South Pacific Fishing Agency as an agency to harmonise policies for the
taking of fish in the area. I can really add nothing to that. It is a simple piece of legislation,
but I am sure that the people of Tokelau will derive a benefit from it, even if the benefit is
nothing more than the fees that will be charged for licences for those who are licensed to fish
in the area.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): Just as the Opposition supports
the principle of the exclusive economic zone for New Zealand, so does it accept New
Zealand's responsibility for the Tokelaus, particularly, as the Deputy Prime Minister said,
because the Tokelau people requested New Zealand legislative action to protect their rights.
I do not think there is any need to say much more than that, except that we hope—and I echo
the sentiments expressed by the Deputy Prime Minister in this-that the people of the
Tokelaus will be able to derive some direct economic benefit as a consequence of the passage
of the legislation.
Bill read a second time.
TOWN AND COUNTRY PLANNING BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. The 1953 Town and Country Planning Act and this Bill have been
the subject of detailed consideration, first by the review committee that reported in 1973,
later by the Government and its caucus committee, and more recently by the select
committee on the Bill. The original proposals for the Bill have been considerably refined.
This was made necessary by the changes to the local government legislation, which had a
direct bearing on the matters contained in the Bill. It was also necessary to take account of
the points raised in the many submissions made to the select committee. It has been possible,
nevertheless, to retain most of the basic recommendations of the earlier review
committee-namely, that more effective links be created between planning at the various
levels, national, regional, and local; that third party rights to participate in planning be
broadened; and that the provisions of the Act be simplified and made more easily
understandable.
The basic system of local planning has to a large extent been retained. The 1973 review
committee found that this system was sound and well suited to New Zealand conditions. It
has also proved to be flexible and adaptable. The planning procedures have, however, been
simplified in the Bill, and this reform should remove the confusion and ambiguities that
resulted from the numerous amendments to the 1953 Act. For example, it is proposed that
the rights of objection and appeal be simplified and made consistent throughout the Bill.
These changes will be welcomed by the public and by local authorities, and will be of
considerable assistance in the preparation and administration of district schemes.
The importance of the Bill, and the interest it has aroused, were indicated by the large
number of submissions received by the select committee. The Bill was first introduced on 24
August, so it has been before the House for almost 4 months. This has allowed sufficient
time for the Bill to be studied, and for the amendments required to be prepared by the select
committee. The major changes are in the field of regional planning, with consequential
changes in both the district and maritime planning provisions. The Bill is a particularly
important one, affecting as it does the rights and obligations of the people of this country as
well as those of the Crown and regional and local authorities. The Bill provides that the new
Act will come into force on a date to be fixed by Order in Council. It is the Government's
intention that the Act should come into force on 1 April 1978. This will enable the
regulations, which in town planning have more than usual importance, to be prepared
following consultation with bodies directly affected, particularly the local government
associations.
The select committee on the Bill considered some 240 submissions, and from these, as I
anticipated when introducing the Bill, worth-while changes have been proposed. When
adopted, these should greatly improve this important measure. I appreciate the work done
by the committee and the efforts made to have the Bill dealt with expeditiously. I am
grateful, too, to the people and organisations who presented submissions, and for the
interest they displayed.
Clause 3 of the Bill deals with matters of national importance: the preservation of the
coastal environment, the avoidance of the encroachment of urban development on good
farm land, and the prevention of sporadic urban development in rural areas. The Bill
provides, in addition to these principles, for further matters to be recognised as being of
18*


## p. 5222 (#658) ###########################################

5222
8 December
Town and Country Planning Bill
national importance: the conservation, protection, and enhancement of the environment,
the wise use and management of New Zealand's resources, the avoidance of unnecessary
expansion of cities, and the relationship of the Maori people and their culture to their
ancestral land.
Major changes are proposed to the part dealing with regional planning, and it is
proposed that the present Part I in the Bill be deleted and a new Part I be substituted. The
new Part I meets the views expressed in many submissions, and brings the regional planning
provisions into line with the changes made by the Minister of Local Government in the local
government legislation. The changes will mean that the function of regional planning will be
carried out by the united and regional councils constituted under the Local Government Act
1974. This is in accordance with the Government's policy on local government, and accords
with the stated views of the Municipal Association, the Counties Association, and the
various territorial local authorities.
The proposals now contained in the Bill provide a better system of regional planning.
Clause 6, as proposed by the select committee, requires a united or regional council to
establish a regional planning committee. The committee will be comprised of members of
the united or regional council sufficient to constitute a majority, representatives of catch-
ment authorities, maritime planning authorities, other local authorities, the Maori people of
the region, and the Crown. The committee's functions will be to advise and assist a united or
regional council in preparing and implementing a regional planning scheme. Clauses 7 and 8
provide for the appointment of subcommittees. Clause 7 enables a land resource advisory
committee to be set up as a subcommittee of the regional planning committee. This fulfils
one of the promises made in our manifesto, and illustrates the Government's concern that
land must be considered a national resource.
Clauses 11 to 16 deal with the preparation and approval of regional planning schemes.
Briefly, these clauses are designed to allow the widest possible public participation in the
formative steps of a regional planning scheme. Provision is made for the planning tribunal to
conduct an inquiry and report on any dispute between a local authority and a united or
regional council. As soon as the matters between a local authority and the united or regional
council have been resolved, the scheme is referred to the Minister. The Minister is now
restricted in making recommendations to the united or regional council to matters of
national importance and having significance beyond the boundaries of the region. There is
provision for further interchanges of views between the Minister and united or regional
councils, and provision is made for the scheme to be then approved by the Governor-
General by Order in Council.
Clause 17 provides that the Crown, and every local and public authority, shall adhere to
the provisions of a regional planning scheme, and that in the event of any conflict between
the provisions of a regional scheme, district scheme, or maritime planning scheme, the
regional scheme will prevail. This provision effectively links national and regional planning,
and, through the regional planning scheme, to district and maritime planning schemes, and
contrasts with the existing provisions under which regional planning schemes were designed
simply as a guide, and were provided in isolation from national policies.
Clauses 23 to 26 provide transitional arrangements to deal with existing regional
planning authorities, which will continue in existence, and operate their schemes in accord-
ance with the provisions of the present 1953 Act. However, when regional planning
authorities are so reviewed, they will have the same force and effect as a regional planning
scheme under the Bill. Generally, regional planning authorities are envisaged as only
transitional bodies, and it is provided that in the event of the constitution of a united or
regional council the functions of a regional planning authority will be transferred to the
council.
Part II deals with the control of development in districts in which there is no operative
district scheme. Part III provides for the preparation, changes, and reviews of district
schemes. The select committee recommended that clause 32, headed "Contents of district
schemes", be reworded to further simplify matters relating to district schemes. The rights of
the public to object and appeal, both on matters being included in district schemes and
on applications made during the administration of a scheme, have been clarified and
broadened. The provisions relating to public utilities such as pylons, power and telephone
lines, and pipes, have been clarified. Councils have been given certain powers relating to the
location of utilities. The procedures for making applications to councils have been simp-
lified. Councils have been provided with powers to delegate to committees, commissioners,
or council officers. It is hoped that these changes will streamline the handling of planning
matters, and reduce the costs both to the council and to the applicant.


## p. 5223 (#659) ###########################################

8 December
5223
Town and Country Planning Bill
The maritime planning provisions contained in Part V are new. It is intended that
maritime planning will be undertaken only in those areas where there are serious conflicts in
the use of water. It is also intended that an existing authority, such as a harbour board or a
council, be appointed the maritime planning authority. The select committee has recom-
mended that where a maritime planning area is wholly within the limits of a harbour board,
then that board shall be appointed the maritime planning authority. The committee has also
recommended that a new clause be inserted, providing for each maritime planning authority
to constitute a maritime planning committee, the majority of which will comprise members
of the body appointed the maritime planning authority. However, there will be representa-
tives of other local authorities and the Crown, and provision will be made for the
appointment of other people with special knowledge. The committee's main role will be to
advise on the preparation of a maritime planning scheme. The principal function of a
maritime planning authority will be to prepare a maritime planning scheme, and, in keeping
with the rest of the Bill, wide rights for public involvement are provided. For the first time
the Crown is now bound to follow through procedures set out in this part of the Bill,
although exceptions are provided to cover emergencies.
Clause 113, requiring outline plans of works to be submitted to the tribunal, is new. The
plans cover matters such as the height and shape of buildings, the finished contours of the
site, and parking provisions. This provision will enable councils to have a say in these matters
and empower them to request changes. If their requests are not met they have a right of
appeal to the tribunal.
Part VII contains the compensation provisions, which remain unchanged from the
present Act. The clauses dealing with the planning tribunal are contained in Part VIII.
Briefly, the present Town and Country Planning Appeal Board has been reconstituted as the
planning tribunal, and the respect the present boards have earned from the public and those
associated with planning is reflected in the increased status and standing accorded the
tribunal. Furthermore, the jurisdiction of the board has been extended and the tribunal will
fulfil a very important role in environmental planning under the new Act, together with its
related responsibilities under other legislation.
I am confident that the careful consideration of the framing of this legislation and the
constructive changes proposed by the select committee as a result of the wide-ranging
submissions received have resulted in a good Bill. It creates for the first time a coherent
system of national, regional, and local planning. It strengthens regional planning and
updates and improves the sound system of local planning established by the 1953 Act. As I
said in my introductory speech, no legislation can guarantee good town planning; all it can
do is to provide a workable and acceptable framework in which planning can flourish and
serve the community well. I believe we have largely achieved that objective with the Bill now
before us. It puts town and country planning on a sound footing for the years to come.

The Bill is the first full review and consolidation of the Town and Country Planning Act
and its amendments. The committee was asked to combine the principal Act and its
amendments, and it has returned the Bill now before us. The Bill promotes a much closer
relationship between national, regional, and local government. In recent weeks new local
government measures have been passed, and the amendments made to the Town and
Country Planning Bill will go hand in hand with those measures. The importance of regional
government must be plain to everyone. Regional government must set up an organisation
representing the people, and this will be done under clause 5 in Part I.
Changes have been made to the original Bill. Clause 5 now provides that the elected
people will be the planning authority, but that the committee of that authority shall be the
advisory planning committee, which will be augmented by catchment boards and a wide
range of interested groups. It is worth pointing out which groups can be represented on the
committee. The council must maintain a majority, and one of its members as chairman. The
committee will have a representative from each catchment board, the Ministry of Works and
Development, and the Maori community, or a member approved by the Maori Council.
Opposition members have not given the Government credit for having widened the
committee to include Maori interests-historical, cultural, social, and otherwise. The
Government has taken a tremendous step in planning by including many interests.
District planning is the next step down, and there has been no change in the structure of
those councils. I have seen press releases in local newspapers that stated that people were
afraid that their local government bodies-county councils and catchment boards—would go
out of existence. That will not happen, because there will be no change in the structure of
local community councils. Provision is made for public participation in planning at an early
stage, and the public will be invited to put forward ideas and to take part in planning.
The member for Henderson mentioned the environmental issues. The Bill gives
environmental groups the opportunity to put their views forward for consideration. In many
cases the Crown is bound to follow specified procedures for public works, and provision is
made for full rights of objection and appeal. The maritime planning section is new. Clause
91A provides that the major harbour boards, as defined in the Harbour Boards Act 1950,
may establish planning committees which will consist of members of the harbour boards with
one of those members as chairman, and maintaining sufficient of their own members to
maintain a majority. The committee may also appoint representatives from adjacent
authorities. They may also have two representatives from the Crown, and three others with
interests in harbour and maritime planning.
Clause 164 makes provision for the problem faced by the Thames-Coromandel District
Council, caused by an omission from the 1974 Local Government Act passed by the Labour
Government. The Act prevented the council from carrying forward an uncompleted
planning scheme. If provision had not been made in this Bill, it would have cost the council
between $50,000 and $100,000 to do the job all over again. My people in that area will be
very pleased with the important provision in clause 164. The Bill also contains provision for a
land resource advisory committee, which can call upon a wide variety of interests to give
advice to the local planning authority on the best use of land. The Maori people will be
involved in the planning committee.

## p. 5237 (#673) ###########################################

8 December
5237
Town and Country Planning Bill
When we consider what the Bill will do we should reflect on whether we as a
Parliament, are doing our job properly, or whether in fact we are being dictated to by the
Executive.
The Town and Country Planning Bill, in essence, decides what priorities will be given to
land uses. It states, in effect, that a man or a woman cannot use his or her own property as he
or she wishes, but must use the property as a community council, a tribunal, or maybe the
Minister directs. I seem to remember that it was stated during the election campaign—if it
has not been often stated at other times-that the National Party represented a property-
owning democracy. The Bill is in essence opposed to that concept. It actually takes away the
owner's right and gives it to someone else.
We accept that there is a need for town and country planning, and we accept that the
owner's individual rights are being taken away so as to preserve the right of a man to be able
to enjoy the use of his house without having a factory put next door or a rubbish tip across
the road, or without discovering to his horror that he is suddenly next door to a new
supermarket car-parking area. Those threats to the enjoyment of his property are in fact
greater than the possible effects of the Town and Country Planning Bill.
I point out, however, that a zoning change to one's home can in some cases be
disastrous. Because of the effects of the Bill, some people will find that their homes are to be
zoned in a way they will be most unhappy about. If we, as a Parliament, are to protect the
legitimate rights of people, it is only right and proper that the Town and Country Planning
Bill should reflect those rights; but I am not confident that the Bill will do that—not because
I do not believe that I would be able to work the Bill out if I spent enough time studying it,
but because I know that as a member of Parliament, I have not enough time to do that.
I know that the local authorities in my area have not had sufficient time to consider the
Bill, and I know also that the community councils and others interested in town planning
have not even seen it. Yet tonight we are passing it into law. It is a safe prediction—in fact, it
is a certainty-that it will cause a number of injustices. Individual New Zealanders will
suffer, not because the Bill is complex but because a Bill that was 5 years in preparation was
considered by a select committee for only about a month and then rushed through all its
stages in the House.
We, as a Parliament, should reject such a procedure. It is the constitutional duty of
Government back-benchers to act as watchdogs over the Executive. Instead they are acting
more like spaniels. They should be standing in the House and saying firmly, "As members of
Parliament, we will not be directed. We will make sure that the Bill is considered properly,
and that it is sent back to the select committee for further consideration."
Mr Brill: What don't you like about it?
Mr PREBBLE: I do not like it because, as a member of Parliament, I have not been
given the opportunity I believe I am entitled to.
Mr Brill: You don't understand it.
Mr PREBBLE: That is right. I am confident that the member for Kapiti does not
understand it either. In fact, I know the chairman of the select committee does not
understand it, because I listened to his rambling explanation. As members of Parliament, we
should refuse to pass legislation until we are completely confident that it has been given very
thorough examination, that all submissions have been heard and carefully considered, and
that the Bill will withstand a most searching review. I have no doubt that the Town and
Country Planning Bill will be subjected to considerable examination after it has been passed,
and I believe we will be even more severely criticised than we have been recently by an even
greater number of Supreme Court judges, who will comment that the legislation must have
been passed by a committee of 87 members at a quarter to 12 at night. That is exactly what is
happening.
Mr Brill: What's wrong with that?
Mr PREBBLE: I am sure the member for Kapiti knows that it costs a great deal of
money to take an individual town planning case to a tribunal. Why should New Zealanders
be required to take a case before the court only to find that an error has been made, not by
the local body, the tribunal, or the Supreme Court, but by Parliament itself, which passed
the legislation in an extraordinarily stupid manner. The public has every right to kick the
Government, as it has kicked it in the past month, about the way it is enacting legislation. I
hope the kicks will grow even harder, but I stress that the only way one can kick against the
measure before us is to kick the National Government out of office.
I have no doubt that many people will complain to me in the next few months about the
town and country planning legislation. When they do I shall tell them why it is faulty: the Bill

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Auckland International Airport Rescue Craft
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services: What steps is he taking to ensure that if the rescue craft at Auckland
International Airport is ever called on to rescue passengers and crew from an aircraft down
in the Manukau Harbour it will be able to reach shore again?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
If the marine rescue services at Auckland International Airport are called out they are able
to return without problem. The hovercraft would be first on the scene, and would be used as
a platform from which to rescue survivors. This appliance carries four 25-man life rafts,
which can be used in addition to aircraft rafts and slides. Backup services are provided by
two 16 ft outboard powered inflatable rescue craft known as "Z" boats. These craft carry
inflatable 10-man life rafts, and are used to assist in search and rescue operations. When the
hovercraft is out of commission for maintenance, the "Z" boats are used.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is it not a fact that when the hovercraft was recently brought out
after lengthy inactivity it took the concerted efforts of two tractors and a ditch digger to pull
it to shore?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I can neither confirm nor deny that. However, the
honourable member can accept my word that no aircraft can operate unless efficient rescue
craft are available. The same type of rescue craft is available in Wellington and Auckland.
Auckland Medical Aid Centre
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen the
article in the magazine Humanity (November issue) entitled "Clinic Fails to File Reason"
relating to the fact that some abortions carried out at the Auckland Medical Aid Centre in
1976 were for no stated reason, and, if so, is any prosecution to follow?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Minister of Health replies as
follows: "I have seen the article referred to, and I have made inquiries about the centre's
compliance with section 140A(2) of the Hospitals Act, which requires records of all abortions
performed, and the reasons for them, to be sent to the Director-General of Health. The
National Health Statistics Centre is currently investigating this matter. In reply to the
member's query about a prosecution, I should point out that no provision for penalties is
made under the. 1975 amendment to the Hospitals Act."
Mr D. M. J. Jones: In view of the fact that no prosecution will follow an abortion, how
can the Minister differentiate between this and abortion on demand?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I do not feel competent to answer that question, but if the Act is
not being complied with then either an amendment to the Act or a regulation is required to
ensure that the provisions of the Act are met.

Educational Institutions—Child Care Centres
7. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the
Government's policy of encouragement to adult students, many of whom are married
women, to return to schools, how can he justify his department's recent circular discouraging
the establishment of child-care centres at educational institutions?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Minister of Education
replies as follows: "My department's recent circular did not discourage the establishment of
child care centres at educational institutions. It was designed to clarify the department's
responsibility for the benefit of those controlling authorities seeking to establish child care
centres. Providing that educational controlling authorities can meet the conditions specified
in the circular there is nothing to prevent the establishment of such facilities."
Mr Marshall: Will the Minister confirm that the circular dated 9 January on behalf of
the Director-General of Education began: "The department is concerned at increasing
numbers of child care centres established at educational institutions", and would the
Minister not confirm that that is not exactly encouragement?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes, I can confirm that the circular starts with that sentence,
but it is designed to point out to educational institutions that in going into such development
they must be aware of the department's difficulties. The accommodation must be surplus to
requirement. The department cannot make funds available nor can the teaching staff be
involved in running the system. It is only fair that the educational institutions should be
aware of the limits of the department's authority.

Cardiac Failure-Causes
10. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: Could he outline,
giving percentages, the major causes of cardiac failure in New Zealand in (a) males and (b)
females?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Minister of Health replies that
the major causes of cardiac failure in New Zealand are ischaemic heart disease, otherwise
called coronary artery disease, and hypertensive heart disease, which is associated with high
blood pressure. Rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease, and other sundry causes
make a relatively small contribution. Actual percentages as to total deaths are not readily
available and would be difficult to assess, because hypertension and ischaemic heart disease
often co-exist.
Miss Dewe: Could the Minister say whether coronary heart disease is more common in
males than females, and does he have any figures relating to age?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Ischaemic heart disease is more common in males than in
females, particularly in the younger age group.

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The fact is that there is a difference of opinion as to the
