CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): I am directed by the Social Services Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. I want to thank all who made submissions, and to stress that all
submissions, whether large or small, were equally treated. Witnesses were advised that they
could be invited to clarify their submissions, and the contributions made by the smaller
groups and people with smaller petitions were very valuable. I thank the members of the
committee for their co-operation and the contribution they made. The experience and
interest of committee members from both sides of the House played a great part in ensuring
that the Bill could be reported back today.
Some Opposition members reserved their decisions on several of the clauses, and their
position was respected. No doubt they will elaborate further on the points they made. There
was total agreement with the principles of the Bill, and genuine concern for the welfare of
the people who would be affected. The method of implementing the legislation can be a
matter for debate. Although some of the suggestions made in the submissions were at
variance with the committee and the Minister, they might well have to be looked at again in
the future. No evidence came forward to suggest that moves other than those made by the
Minister would be effective or acceptable at this time.
The recent murders committed by youthful offenders, and the dilemma facing the courts
and the country today with the differentiation of a person's chronological years, played no
small part in this proposed legislation. A child of 13 years of age and another of 14 years and
1 day are treated differently when charged with manslaughter or murder, and this presents a
problem. I do not think the problem will be solved easily or quickly but, unfortunately, it
must be dealt with. It is not suggested that the legislation solves all such problems, but it is
necessary to deal with them. I think the public expected it of the committee, and I am certain
that we must regard it in this light.
Some critics said it was a retrogressive step. However, although generalisations have
been made, no evidence has been forthcoming to show that the more modern views result in
a lessening of crime. Legislation dealing with such matters will always be open to amend-
ment and adjustment. A degree of flexibility is most essential, because it affects and involves
the conduct of society. This is important, because the legislation is a process of individual
soul searching. It is easy for us to say where responsibilities should lie.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! Is the honourable member reporting on the proceed-
ings of the select committee, or is he giving a second reading speech? I presume that will
come later.
Mr DOWNIE: I could very well be getting on to second reading material. I will come
back to the points of the Bill. I merely wish to make the important point that the committee
met in the same atmosphere of co-operation that existed in 1974 under the chairmanship of
the member for Porirua when the original Bill was before the House. While the original Bill
was a good one, these amendments are of considerable significance.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): I want to record the Labour Opposition's apprecia-
tion of the Government's agreement that the Bill be referred to the select committee; it gave
an opportunity to examine rationally what was being proposed. The consideration of the Bill
was not easy in the present circumstances. There is a considerable amount of disquiet in the
country because of matters involving young children. Unease was expressed at the provisions
of clause 5, and the best way to deal with unusual and tragic circumstances. Clause 5
provides for the charging of persons aged 10 to 13 years with murder or manslaughter, and it
is hardly surprising that 16 of the 17 submissions presented sought to retain the status quo,
while one submission called for the reinstitution of capital punishment.
Unfortunately, time did not permit all those interested in this important matter to be
heard by the committee. There has been some publicity about Dr Sutherland and members
of his group. Despite his strong feelings, his integrity and interest in the affairs of children or
those in great need are in no way questioned.
One of the difficulties is that the Act was promoted primarily in the best interests of


## p. 5250 (#686) ###########################################

5250
9 December
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
children, and it has been said that the proposals of clause 5 contravene the very spirit of the
Act. Next year the Royal Commission on the Courts will report to the Government. I
contend that clause 5 should be discharged pending the outcome of that report. The
circumstances covered by the Bill are tragic, and the Department of Social Welfare does not
know exactly what to do with young people placed under its care and responsibility after the
laying of a complaint of this nature, rather than a charge. The clause seeks to introduce an
element of deterrent.
Charges of murder or manslaughter against children would be dealt with by the
Supreme Court, as are charges against adults. I do not believe that the Children and Young
Persons Court is the place to deal with them. I think the matter could have been discharged,
and that it will have very little effect on the existing circumstances. There is considerable
sympathy when children are involved, and there is a great deal of unease. It might be
preferable to set the matter aside until the royal commission has reported on its intensive
studies, and then make a judgment rationally in a way that will fulfill the public's
requirements and demands. Perhaps all we are doing in moving now is simply providing the
public with its pound of flesh, but we are endeavouring to see that justice is served and seen
to be served.
Is the Supreme Court the best place to deal with children involved in serious crimes? I
am only a lay person, but I believe that the number of these tragedies over the past 20 years
has been small. That of course, should not mean that we do not do something about the
matter, but we must deal with it appropriately and give a young person who is charged an
opportunity to clear his name. The committee has dealt with it as best it can, but I have the
greatest reservation about whether clause 5 should proceed at this stage. Clearly, the
Government will serve the interests of young persons and the public, and the interests of
justice, better if it awaits the outcome of the report of the Royal Commission on the Courts
before deciding on the appropriate body to deal with these unusual and tragic circumstances.
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): I listened with interest to the comments of the
member for Northern Maori. I am sure he would agree that the submissions to the select
committee were not given in emotional terms, but were presented factually and after much
consideration. They came from groups and individuals with wide experience in dealing with
youthful offenders or young persons alienated from their home or social environment. One
of the most impressive submissions came from a little-known Christchurch-based group
called Six-A. We are legislators and we are required to take into account the realities of
certain social factors and prevalent forces. I would be the first to admit, as did the member
for Northern Maori and the member for Pakuranga, that these instances are tragedies.
Most of the submissions concentrated on clause 5, which does represent a departure
from the principle of the Children and Young Persons Act 1974, in that a child—as defined,
between the ages of 10 and 13 years-cannot be convicted of a criminal offence. We have
had to consider the possibility or probability of prosecutions in cases of murder or
manslaughter. The law abounds in cases in which fairly arbitrary limits have to be drawn,
and I think those who appeared before the select committee admitted that. While on some
occasions, perhaps, differing from the Government or the wording of the Bill on how this
could best be done, nevertheless they conceded that an arbitrary limit had to be drawn. It
was recognised that murder and manslaughter, even when committed by the most youthful
of offenders, still constitute the two most serious crimes; therefore it is defensible to place
them in a special category.
Another point highlighted by the submissions was the problem of providing adequate
security. Clearly that must be resolved, and it was encouraging for the committee to be

MARINE POLLUTION AMENDMENT BILL (NO. 2)
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to provide the financial means of dealing with oil
pollution in maritime areas. Until now the finance for dealing with this very real hazard to
New Zealand's marine environment has come from two sources. Harbour boards bear the
cost of providing equipment and materials to deal with clearing up limited quantities of oil
spilled within harbour limits, and the Government, through the Ministry of Transport, is
responsible for dealing with spills that occur elsewhere. In all cases the cost of cleaning up oil
spills is a liability on the offending party if that party can be identified.
The Bill provides for levying ships on the basis that potential polluters should pay for
the purchase of a national stockpile of equipment and materials, as well as the costs of
cleaning up spills from unidentified sources. Clause 1 specifies the short title. Clause 2
empowers the Minister of Transport to direct a harbour board to deal with any oil or
pollutant that has been discharged or has escaped into a harbour. Where harbour boards are
unable to recover the costs of the clean-up from the person responsible for the oil spill the
board will be reimbursed from the proceeds of the new levy. The legislative provisions for
imposing the levy are contained in proposed new Part IIIA of the Marine Pollution Act. The
proposed new section 29A deals with the interpretation of various terms used in this part.
Honourable members will note the definition of "contributing ship", which applies only to
ships larger than 100 gross tons. The proposed new section 29в empowers the introduction of
the detailed scheme by Order in Council, and specifies the principles upon which the scheme
will be based, including the maximum rate of the levy. The machinery for collecting the levy
is to be similar to that for collecting light dues and will be relatively easy to administer.
In formulating the scheme there was considerable discussion about whether the levy
should be based on the tonnage of a ship or on the tonnes of oil carried by each ship. The
scheme that has emerged is a compromise between the two views. It is based on a ship's
tonnage, but a factor of five times has been built in for ships carrying a cargo of more than
2000 tonnes of persistent oil in bulk. The factor of five times emerged from a study of the
records of oil spills in our harbours and around our shores over the last few years. The spills
occurred equally from tankers and other ships, but tankers form only one-fifth of the
tonnage of shipping using our ports. It is also accepted that tankers are more likely to pump
washings from their tanks into the sea. The Government considers that it would not be
feasible in all cases to impose a direct charge on the owner of the oil, nor would it be possible
to base the charge on the tonnes of oil on board at a particular time. Greatly increased costs
would be associated with attempting to collect the levy for the tonnes of oil on board a ship,
particularly, for example, foreign fishing vessels and tramp ships. It is worth noting that the
levy on ships for the payment of light dues to maintain the coastal navigational lights and the
Australian oil pollution levy are both based on the ship's tonnage.
The levy will be collected annually, except for vessels that trade overseas. They will
have the option of paying either annually or for each voyage. Provision is made for a partial
or total refund of the levy to cover circumstances where ships pay in advance and then
change their trading patterns, so becoming liable on a different basis. The levy will apply to
all ships of more than 100 gross tons entering New Zealand ports, whether they are foreign
going, home trade, or fishing boats. The only exceptions will be ships to which the Marine
Pollution Act does not apply, such as naval vessels, exempted ships entering New Zealand


## p. 5257 (#693) ###########################################

9 December
5257
Marine Pollution Amendment Bill (No. 2)
ports for emergency purposes only, and vessels owned by harbour boards that provide
equipment to cope with oil spills within the harbour limits.
The maximum levy for all ships other than ships carrying a cargo of more than 2000
tonnes of persistent oil will be an annual rate of 60c for each gross ton. For an overseas ship
paying on the basis of individual voyages the maximum levy will be 2c for each gross ton on
the first port of entry and 1c for each gross ton for each subsequent port of entry on that
particular voyage. In line with the principles recently outlined the maximum levy will be five
times the normal rate where a ship carries a cargo of more than 2000 tonnes of persistent oil
in bulk. Although the Bill specifies the maximum rate for the levy, which would bring in
approximately $1.2 million a year, it is intended to charge only half the maximum rate when
the levy is introduced by Order in Council in April 1978, thus bringing in approximately
$600,000 in the next financial year.
To give honourable members some idea of the charges that will result from the levy, I
can inform them that a container ship of 33 000 gross tons paying on a per voyage basis will
be required to pay $300 at its first port of call and $150 at its next port of call. A trans-
Tasman roll-on roll-off ship such as the Union Hobart, which has a gross tonnage of 4375,
would have the option of paying on a per trip basis, in which case the payment would be
about $44 for the first port and $22 for each subsequent port, or $1,312 on an annual basis.
The advantages of paying on an annual basis accrue if a vessel is making more than 20 trips to
and from New Zealand in a year, and calling at more than one port in New Zealand. There
are few New Zealand fishing boats over 100 tons. The amount that a fishing boat of 100 tons
will be required to pay is $30 a year.
The new sections 29c, 29D, and 29ɛ contain further administrative provisions. They
make it clear when the liability to pay arises, who is liable, and that a vessel may be detained
if payment is not made. The new section 29F requires money raised by the levy to be paid
into a separate account within the Public Account, the account to be called the Oil Pollution
Trust Account, and details the uses to which the money may be put. The money levied can
be used to refund all expenditure incurred by the Crown for preventing and controlling oil
pollution, including the costs of training personnel and acquiring equipment. The Ministry of
Transport expects substantial expenditure of about $1.3 million over the next 3 years on
equipment and dispersant to deal with oil spills. The fund will be used to cover the cost of
cleaning up an oil spill when the money cannot be recovered from the offending party.
Neither of these provisions limits either the Crown or harbour boards from making every
effort to find the person responsible for the pollution, and from enforcing the liability
provisions contained in the Marine Pollution Act.
The new section 29c establishes an oil pollution advisory committee to advise the
Minister on various matters relating to the oil pollution levy, including what the rate of levy
should be for each forthcoming year. I shall shortly be calling on the shipping and oil
industries, and the Harbours Association, to nominate representatives for the advisory
committee. The new section 29н, 291, and 29, provide for the change of the use of a ship,
offences against this part of the Act, and the recovery of levies.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): This is not a large Bill, it is not a controversial Bill,
but it is a very important measure for New Zealand. I feel that certain things should be said
on this occasion about pollution and the moves being made to minimise and control it. The
Bill deals with the means of raising the money to cope with oil pollution. Ships entering New
Zealand ports will be levied. The money will be paid into the Oil Pollution Trust Account
and used for the purposes set out in the new section 29F. An oil pollution advisory committee
will be set up under the new section 29G. The Opposition has no objection to that.
This is the second amendment to the Marine Pollution Act this year, and it is not
unexpected. The Act was originally introduced in 1974 by the Labour Government after I as
Minister had picked up the draft legislation and original proposals of my predecessor.
Successive Governments have taken the issue seriously, and have ensured that we have the
best possible marine pollution legislation because of our geographical position as an island
country. The Marine Pollution Act replaced the Oil in Navigable Waters Act 1965, and
expressed general compliance with the international convention proposed by IMCO. At that
time New Zealand was up with the world leaders, and this Bill is a step towards ensuring that
we remain in that position.
Primarily the focus is on internal waters, including territorial sea, harbours, estuaries,
and so on. As an island nation, New Zealand must at all times be conscious of how
vulnerable it is to potential marine pollution, and we have good reason to ensure that the
best possible practical marine environmental legislation is in force. Our coastline extends


## p. 5258 (#694) ###########################################

5258
9 December
Marine Pollution Amendment Bill (No. 2)
more than 3000 miles, and is subject to prevailing onshore winds and sea action. We know
about this, and that is why we place such importance on this legislation. Our extensive
coastal interests and fisheries must have as much protection as possible from potential
marine pollution. This means not only spillage of disaster proportions; all spillages, because
of our geographical position and isolation, can be quite disastrous.
The Bill applies to overseas ships coming to New Zealand, as well as to our own ships
and fishing vessels. It is pertinent to refer to the New Zealand universities law reform report
of 1974-75, surveying marine pollution legislation. The Bill is in line with that report, which
stated that the nature of marine pollution makes it appropriate that the development of
statutory law should follow the development of international law. It is an international
problem. Pollutants discharged in international waters may move to threaten coastal
interests. Pollutants discharged in national waters may move to infect international waters,
and other national territories, and vessels that discharge pollutants within national waters
may be outside the registry of the affected coastal state, presenting international ramifica-
tions even if the pollutants remain within those national waters. That means that ships
visiting New Zealand are liable for spillages resulting from their operations here if they cause
damage to our shore, our fisheries, or our coastline.
It is pertinent to remind the House of the growing loss of shipping tonnage. According
to Lloyds' register, in the 6 years to the end of 1974 there was a loss of 2400 ships, or about
6 000 000 tons of shipping. There has been an average loss of 377 ships a year, some of which
were small fishing boats. In every case there was a possibility of spillage and pollution. The
losses included large oil tankers. We have every reason to be concerned, and the marine
insurance publication stated in July 1977 that the lost tonnage exceeded 1 000 000 a year for
the fifth time. We must be concerned about the possibility of and our vulnerability to
pollution from these sources.
It is important to work closely with Australia. When the Bill was introduced, I asked the
Minister about the possibility of transporting chemicals between Australia and New Zealand
should a spillage affect either country. In 1974 I was fortunate enough to have the
opportunity of looking at a demonstration of anti-pollutant chemicals in Brisbane with the
late Secretary for Transport. We were impressed with the progress being made there. I hope
that the Minister's department has kept up with developments in Australia, and worked
closely with the people there. One can get from Auckland to Sydney or Melbourne as
quickly as to Invercargill. It is imperative that the anti-pollutants held here and in Australia
are known and available to either country in the event of a spillage.
I asked the Minister to clarify a possible wording anomaly about the liability of the
owner and the master of a vessel, and whether the schedule of fines and levies applied
equally to both. There could be some misunderstanding, and I hope when the Minister
replies he can indicate whether he proposes to clarify this point in the Committee stage.
It is not clear how the Oil Pollution Advisory Committee to be set up under section 29G
will tie in with the existing New Zealand Committee on Pollution of the Sea by Oil, nor is it
clear how the Oil Spills Action Committee, as described in a Cabinet-approved contingency
plan for dealing with oil pollution, will dovetail in. I am not saying we have too many
committees, but there appears to be a danger that too many committees could be set up in a
vital area in which we must know exactly who is in charge in the event of a spillage. Certain
organisations might believe they have control when that is not the case.
I refer to the contingency plans and the role of the on-scene controller under the
proposed scheme. It is stated that the on-scene controller will be the nautical adviser or the
deputy nautical adviser or such other persons as the director of the marine division or his
deputy may appoint. What is the role of the on-scene controller if a marine spillage is
involved in conjunction with a civil defence operation? Does the civil defence controller
come under the authority and jurisdiction of the on-scene controller covering marine
pollution? There is a very real possibility of a major oil spillage occurring, and we must know
who is in charge, who has the control, and who has the authority. Nothing would be worse
than to have this occur, and chaos prevail, but with several committees active in one area
that is a very real danger. We have the New Zealand Committee on Pollution of the Sea by
Oil in operation, and the Oil Spills Action Committee, and the Oil Pollution Advisory
Committee is to be set up. I think I can see their roles clearly, and the Oil Pollution Advisory
Committee does not appear to cut across the other two committees; but with a conglomera-
tion of committees we cannot afford the possibility of confusion in the event of marine
pollution.

## p. 5260 (#696) ###########################################

5260

Road User Charges Bill
ROAD USER CHARGES BILL
[With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time of the Minister of
Transport be extended.]
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I thank the House, and will try
not to take longer than necessary. I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. When I
introduced the Bill, which is an important one, I made general comments on its provisions,
and the effect it would have on the road transport industry. I also mentioned that it had its
origins in the Budget announcement earlier this year. I shall now go through the Bill in
greater detail, and explain to members how the new road taxation system will operate.
Before I start, however, I shall spend a moment describing the present complex and
disorganised system of road taxation, which comprises annual licence fees, heavy traffic fees,
petrol tax, and a mileage tax for diesel-driven vehicles. As a system, it can best be described
as unco-ordinated, as the vehicles which cause the most wear and tear on our roads are not
paying an equitably high proportion of taxation. In effect, smaller, lighter vehicles, such as
light trucks and cars, are subsidising heavy vehicle operators.
This piecemeal collection of revenue is also unsatisfactory to the National Roads Board.
The effect of inflation and the consequent steep increases in costs in relation to a fixed rate of
tax per litre of petrol, as well as the effects of the oil crisis and consequent measures taken to
reduce oil imports and conserve energy, have been difficult to cope with. The impact of these
factors on roading revenue has been severe. For the past 3 years, extra funds have had to be
made available to the board from the Consolidated Revenue Account. Clearly this patching-
up process—if it can be called that—is most unsatisfactory, especially as it affects National
Roads Board planning.
Members are no doubt aware that all counties and municipalities depend heavily on the
National Roads Board's funds for at least half the finance required for the maintenance and
upgrading of every street, road, and highway they administer. Our State highways provide
the arteries for our communication and transport systems to flow freely, effectively, and
smoothly. Members do not need me to stress the importance of the country's roading
system. A major objective of the Bill is to provide the National Roads Board's fund with
adequate finance on an assured basis to enable the board to put forward a yearly-and I
emphasise yearly-programme for expenditure based on the following 3 years. The Bill will
rationalise the unsatisfactory way in which road taxation is collected and put to use.
As I said when I introduced the Bill, it was announced in this year's Budget that the
road taxation system would be revised and implemented from 1, April 1978. Members will
note that the key section of the system-the charge for the distance licence-will apply from
1 April 1978. At that time also, the present mileage tax which is imposed on diesel-driven
vehicles on the basis of a declared mileage will be abolished, as well as heavy traffic fees.
Sales tax on vehicles, as announced in the Budget, will reduce by 10 percent to 13
percent in April 1978, and by 10 percent a year after that until 1 April 1980, when it will be
fixed permanently at 10 percent. This progressive reduction will fit in with the increases
which will be imposed by the distance charge. I emphasise again that the total tax payments
by the industry for each year will not be greater than would have been payable had the
present taxation system continued. Petrol tax will remain, but for vehicles over 3 1/2 tonnes
which are wholly petrol driven there will be a rebate of 9.7c per litre, since they will also be
paying the distance charge.
I will now give details of just what these road user charges will be like, and how they will
be calculated. As I have already said, the new system is based on the charges made for the
compulsory purchase of a distance licence. The distance licence will be available in multiples
of 1000 km, and the charge will reflect the gross laden weight of the vehicle, the axle
configuration and number of wheels, the necessity for the roading system to provide passing
lanes of sufficient surface strength for heavy traffic, and the provision of road painting,
lighting, and other such costs. The operator will nominate the maximum weight at which he
intends his vehicle to operate, and the charge for the distance licence for that vehicle will also
reflect this.
The level of charges has been determined bearing in mind that for a certain percentage
of the time vehicles will be partially laden only, and in some cases empty. I understand that
the calculation was made on the basis of 55 percent of loading. This method of calculation
sounds pretty complex, and it is. What it does is to reflect as nearly as possible the true costs
each heavy vehicle imposes on our roads. Thus, the principle that users who impose the most
costs on our roading system pay the most tax towards the upkeep of roads has been
incorporated in the calculation.


## p. 5261 (#697) ###########################################

9 December
5261
Road User Charges Bill
The bulk of the heavy transport industry will be included in the category of those
required to pay the distance charge. The distance the vehicle travels must be measured
accurately for the system to work. All vehicles and trailers over 3 1/2 tonnes using distance
licences will be required to have a hubodometer. The hubodometer is sealed and will have to
be fitted to a non-lifting axle on the left side of the vehicle, so that it may easily be read from
the roadside. The distance licence will contain the beginning and end hubodometer readings
of the distance for which the licence is valid. Hubodometers will be read at 6-monthly
intervals by Ministry of Transport vehicle inspectors as a check against declared readings,
and whenever the vehicle is inspected on the roadside by the Ministry's traffic officers.
Inability to equip the total fleet prior to 1 April 1978 will not jeopardise the introduction
of the distance charge, as an approved distance-measuring device is defined to include the
conventional cable-driven distance recorder. By 1 April 1978 all vehicles, including sepa-
rately registered trailers and semi-trailers of a maximum gross laden weight exceeding 3 1/2
tonnes, which are not at present fitted with a conventional cable-driven distance recorder,
will be fitted, and it is expected that this will have to be extended by 1 July 1978 to include all
vehicles over 10 tonnes.
Earlier, I said that the operator of the vehicle must nominate a maximum weight for his
operations. Should he wish to exceed this weight maximum on his distance licence, a
supplementary licence in multiples of 50 km will be necessary, for which the rates over the
distance will be higher, but reflecting the increased costs imposed on the roading system by
his increasing the weight of his vehicle. If an operator wished to raise the maximum weight
permissible on his vehicle permanently, he would purchase a new distance licence calculated
at a correspondingly higher rate, and receive a refund for any unused portion of his original
distance licence.
The licences for which these road user charges will be paid will be available at Post
Offices, and the full amount will have to be paid, but schemes for payment in advance and
bulk purchase are being developed. There will be a small administration fee for each
individual transaction.
I said earlier that most heavy vehicles will require distance licences. For vehicles which
carry out most of their operations off the road, a licence to cover a certain period of time will
be purchased, rather than one based on distance. Vehicles such as front-end loaders, mobile
pile drivers, asphalt mixing and paving plant, and several other types, would all cover less
than 1500 km per annum on the road. The charge for the time licence is calculated in much
the same way as for the distance licence, but at a much lower rate, reflecting the smaller time
spent on the road. Some other vehicles, such as farmers' tractors, forklifts, traction engines,
and others like these which do extremely limited road running, will be exempted from the
provisions of the Act by regulation, as, compared with other vehicles, the costs they impose
on the system are minimal, as we all know.
Operators of vehicles will have certain responsibilities concerning these licences. The
first is to ensure that the vehicle has the correct licence if it is being operated on the road. An
operator must ensure that a working hubodometer of an approved type is fitted to the
vehicle. He must ensure that the vehicle displays the licence sticker on the left hand side of
the windscreen. The licence must contain certain particulars, such as the registration number
of the vehicle to which it relates, and each trailer. The serial number of the hubodometer and
the axle weight rating must be included. As well, the start and finish readings of the
hubodometer are required. Where any of these things are incorrect or absent, an offence is
committed, and the Bill before the House contains provisions for fines of up to $1,000 for the
driver and $5,000 for the operator responsible for the vehicle in respect of each offence. I
have spoken at some length on the road user charge system, but it is important for members
of the House to understand it fully.
I have been disappointed at the publicity which has caused so many people to
misunderstand exactly what the Bill is all about. I shall now give a brief description of the
provisions in the Bill. [Interruption.] I thought members would be interested in listening to
the details of the Bill, but I can see that a few are making a joke about it. This is a complex
measure and an important one. Clause 2 contains definitions. Clause 3 states that the Act
shall bind the Crown. Clause 4 creates certain exemptions from the system. Petrol-driven
vehicles with a gross laden weight of less than 3 1/2 tonnes are exempt, as are trailers of less
than 3 1/2 tonnes.
Clause 5 is the key operative clause in the Bill. It states that motor vehicles to which the
Act applies cannot be on the road unless they are licensed under the Act. Clauses 6 to 13
provide for three types of licence-distance, time, and supplementary-and contain provi-


## p. 5262 (#698) ###########################################

5262
9 December
Road User Charges Bill
sions relating to the application for the issue of and payment for those licences. Clause 8
contains one matter that I have not yet mentioned. The Heavy Motor Vehicle Regulations
will still apply. Thus, for particular operations, such as the transport of over-dimensional
loads, the requirement for the permit from the local authority will still continue. The
supplementary licence will be endorsed to show that a permit has been issued. In this
particular case, the maximum and minimum hubodometer readings will not be required on
the supplementary licence, as it is not possible to predict accurately the exact readings in
advance when purchasing the licence.
Clauses 14 to 18 relate to refunds where one type of licence supersedes another or where
there has been off-road travel. There is also provision for other types of refunds. For vehicles
with distance licences which operate off the road some of the time, refunds will be made on
the basis of the declared off-road distance travelled. Clause 19 details the manner in which
the licence is to be displayed on the vehicle. Clauses 20 and 21 concern the alteration of rates
for licences and the effect that new rates have on existing licences. Clause 23 creates offences
associated with operating a vehicle on a road without the required licence, and other lesser
offences in relation to interfering with licences, making false statements, and so on. Clause
24 authorises the making of regulations concerning the display of licences, the fitting of
hubodometers, and other related matters. Clauses 25 to 30 make consequential amendments
to the Transport Act 1962 relating to enforcement and motor spirit duty refunds, and also
repeal mileage tax and heavy traffic fee provisions. Clauses 31 to 34 amend and add
provisions to the National Roads Act, and relate to the financing of road works.
The first schedule enumerates those types of vehicles that require a distance licence.
The second schedule does the same for the time licence-namely, off-road vehicles. The
third schedule prescribes charges for distance, supplementary, and time licences. The way in
which the National Roads Board distributes its funds is not affected by the Bill. The basis for
the collection of those funds, however, is changed markedly, as I have described. The Bill
contains amendments to the National Roads Act and adds provisions to establish a 3-yearly
forward programme of estimates of expenditure by the National Roads Board. Each year the
next year's budget will be submitted to the Minister of Works and Development. If the
National Roads Board wishes to increase the road user charges as detailed in the third
schedule by more than 20 percent it must request the approval of Parliament.
When I introduced the Road User Charges Bill I mentioned that, in the course of the
many discussions held between Government officials and representatives of the transport
industry, concern was expressed that a liquidity problem might arise during the period
immediately before 1 April, because the charges are payable in advance. I pointed out then,
as I have on many occasions since, that the Government has temporarily relaxed the present
taxation burden on the road transport industry by reducing by 50 percent the heavy traffic
fees due for payment on 1 December 1977, for the quarter ending 28 February 1978. The
requirement to pay any heavy traffic fees from the end of February onwards will be
completely removed. These measures should ease the cash-flow problems that some
operators could face through the introduction of the road user charges system. I also remind
members that the system will be phased in as the sales tax payable on heavy vehicles is
phased down. The charges will not be at their intended level until 1 April 1980, at which time
the sales tax will be 10 percent.
At this stage I should like to say a word about the differences I expect the system to
make to the operating costs of the heavy road transport industry. Calculations made, using
the rural road transport industry in the Manawatu as an example, showed that average
operating costs would rise by approximately 3.5 percent.
Mr Rogers: And the rest.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I repeat, they will rise by approximately 3.5 percent-and
that was an extreme case. I can see the member for Onehunga shaking his head. If he has
other examples he can present I should like him to give them to me, so that I can have them
analysed.
A further example-a study made or a substantial firm with a fleet of vehicles based in
Wellington, carrying out both long haul and city operations-showed that operating costs
would rise by about 0.15 percent. I am satisfied that those rises are within an acceptable
margin. I have pointed out before that, although the total tax burden on the industry will not
rise by more than it would under the present system, some operators can expect rises in costs
due to the ironing out of inequalities in the old system. To put it bluntly, as I said earlier, I
believe that the owner of a motorcar pays more than his share at present, and the operator of
a big rig pays less than he should, if one takes into account the damage caused to our roads.

All farmers operating their own vehicles, and ancillary transport operators should save.
For example, a wholly petrol-driven 4-tonne farm truck would save between 4 and 5 percent
on its annual operating costs, plus the $25 heavy traffic fee. A 5-tonne diesel-driven truck
would save about 2 percent per annum in that way. Ancillary transport operators will save
slightly more than a similar licensed transport operator, as the amount paid at present by
way of heavy traffic fees is higher.
The transport committee of Federated Farmers has calculated that in extreme cases of
remoteness from freezing works and fertiliser suppliers, such as in the King Country, the
West Coast, and Central Otago, a farmer will face increases in annual costs for using licensed
transport operators of an average of about $400 per annum. On the other hand, in the case of
farmers operating their own farm trucks on the road, these costs will be offset by the saving
of about $250 on each vehicle.
Bus and coach operators are in rather a different position. Their costs will rise, due to
the fact that their vehicles are not subject to sales tax reductions, as they pay none at present.
These operators are levied at a rate of 34 percent only on the present petrol and mileage
taxes, and the rebate and abolition of these taxes respectively will not have the same effect as
it will have on the rest of the industry. The Government has agreed to review the position
relating to urban passenger transport operators, and to consider whether any relief is
necessary.
Concern has also been expressed by the road transport industry over the fact that
payment is, in effect, to be made in advance. Operators can see themselves caught in a
situation where it is not possible to foresee and obtain the particular kind of licence which
could be necessary. This would be especially true of supplementary licences. I appreciate this
concern and sincerely hope it has been allayed by the following measure. It will be a special
defence, in the course of legal proceedings concerning an offence of operating a motor
vehicle on the road without the appropriate licence, if the operator can satisfy the court of
two things: first, that it was not possible to obtain the licence at the time when the need for
the licence was reasonably foreseeable, or at any time thereafter; and secondly, that the
appropriate licence has been purchased subsequently to cover a particular journey. Where
the case is one in which that special defence clearly applies, a prosecution will not even be
commenced. We can see a case, especially over a weekend, when an operator whose licence
has run out gets an extra job with sheep, and has an overrun. Provision has been made for
that.
I am quite satisfied that the system of road user charging contained in the Bill is a good
one, and that from the operators' point of view it will introduce rationality and a satisfactory
degree of equity into the collection of funds to finance our vital roading system. It will also
provide a far more satisfactory, assured income than the previous system provided for the
National Roads Board. I am very happy indeed that the present system is being overhauled,
and I think that the system I have described just now will be with us for many years to
come-but I should add that there will be anomalies for a long time, and whoever happens to
be Minister of Transport will have to amend the legislation from time to time.

Here is an extract on road transport taxation taken from the 1977 Budget: "The wear

## p. 5267 (#703) ###########################################

9 December
5267
Road User Charges Bill
on everything to do with the road transport industry. He said, "Let us not confuse", then he
did his best to confuse everybody. He knows that many road transport fees are pre-
paid-heavy traffic licence fees, ordinary licence fees, and the tax on petrol as well. The Bill
is a good one. It is part of a package deal, and the member for Timaru was most unfair in not
making that clear. That package deal will be a distinct advantage to the transport industry.
The member did not mention the relief and flexibility that will result from the extension
of the road limit to 150 kilometres; nor did he say that the increased revenue for the National
Roads Board will result in better roads. The Bill gives effect to the Budget announcement of
a road-user charging system for financing the maintenance and improvement of the roading
system through the agency of the National Roads Board.
For a number of years it has been apparent that the system introduced in 1953, based
largely upon petrol taxes, heavy traffic fees, and mileage tax, has not been satisfactory. The
reasons are, first, the effects of inflation on the roading cost index-this has doubled in the
last 5 years; and, secondly, the oil crisis, which has led to heavy taxation of petrol, and has
stabilised petrol consumption and hence roading revenue. As a result, roading revenue has
not kept pace with costs and the work on roads has therefore fallen away in real terms. It was
necessary, therefore, to provide additional finance by way of grants from the Consolidated
Revenue Account, and in 1975 the previous Government made $16 million available. In
1976, the National Government provided $21 million, and in the current financial year has
made an additional 1c a litre in petrol tax available to the Roads Fund as of right, amounting
to about $20 million--augmented by the recent grant of $10 million; a total of $30 million
added to roading revenue in the current year.
The member for Timaru said nothing about the assistance the Government has given to
the roads board. The Labour Government had a sorry record of assistance, and I believe the
National Roads Board welcomes the opportunity this measure will give it of doing the job it
is supposed to do, not merely providing for maintenance, but carrying out the designed
amount of new work. Real improvements, particularly those that require advance planning,
have not been possible, simply because the annual grant system gave no assurance of finance
2 or 3 years ahead. The Bill provides that assurance to all roading authorities. It is a new deal
for roading, because once the distance charges are set the level of finance is assured, at least
at that level. The objective of the Bill is to apportion correctly to the users the costs they
create in the maintenance and improvement of the roading system.
Users fall into two categories. First there are private cars and light vehicles, which
create traffic volumes and therefore require adequate road widths to accommodate them.
Secondly, there are heavy transport vehicles, which require strong road surfaces and heavy
structures to handle their weight without damage. Roading engineers are able to allocate
roading costs broadly into those two categories, and that allocation is the basis of the
Bill-the basis of what a road engineer thinks, not a politician who is trying to make capital
out of a Bill that will do much for the country.
Clause 5 requires all vehicles, including trailers, of a gross weight of 3.5 tonnes and
over, to possess a distance licence. This will be paid for at a rate that depends upon the
weight and configuration of the vehicle, and takes into account the number of axles that
spread the weight of the vehicle and its cargo over the road surface, as well as the space it
occupies. The rate will be charged per kilometre of distance covered-hence the term
"distance licence", which has been worked out by people who have given a lifetime to road
engineering and know what they are doing.
The scale of charges incorporated in the third schedule is based upon the budget for the
current financial year; it is calibrated to recoup $44 million in distance charges from the
heavy-vehicle traffic compared with the total budget for the National Roads Board of about
$144 million this year. The correct allocation would be $60 million from heavy vehicles, but
the Government has stated that it does not intend to increase the tax burden on the industry
as a whole. The member for Timaru did not say anything about that. Consequently, a
transfer of finance from the Consilidated Revenue Account, at present estimated to be about
$16 million, will be made to honour this promise in the next financial year.
Other measures include a reduction of sales tax on heavy vehicles from 40 percent to 10
percent, spread over the next 3 years, abolition of heavy traffic fees-which are already
being phased out-and the abolition of mileage tax on diesel-powered and other non-petrol-
using vehicles. We heard nothing about that from the member for Timaru. While the
distance charge will be levied on all heavy vehicles, they will not be required to pay petrol tax
as well. This is to be refunded in much the same way as special rebates are granted at
present. Diesel-fuelled vehicles and other non-petrol-driven road vehicles will pay the


## p. 5268 (#704) ###########################################

5268
9 December
Road User Charges Bill
distance charge as set out in the third schedule. The main purpose of the Bill is to provide
adequate and assured finance for the National Roads Board. The Bill therefore amends the
National Roads Act.
Clause 32 requires the board to submit a forward road programme to the Government
by 31 October each year, together with an estimate of the revenue derived from various
sources to meet the programme, and it is to be set out for 3 years ahead. Of course it will be
reviewed annually thereafter. The Government will consider and approve a programme
level in the terms of its manifesto to provide appropriate finance for roading and bridging
construction and maintenance. My departmental roading engineers will then arrange for the
appropriate allocation of costs and calibration of distance charges, and the petrol tax
required to finance the programme. Provision is made in clause 20 for the rates of licence
fees to be altered by regulation, so that if Parliament is not in session the requirements can
be met within the statutory limit of the 20 percent variation. This does not mean that all
charges will go up by 20 percent, but it does provide for the variation of individual scales by
20 percent according to the nature of the programme of work. Some provision must be made
for roading improvements and cost escalation above the existing programme level.
Clause 28 provides for variations in the amount of motor spirits duty to be credited to
the Consolidated Revenue Account by Order in Council. This will provide the flexibility
required to adjust road taxation to the approved needs of the National Roads Board, and
will provide a firm amount of revenue for the 3-year programme. The administration of the
scheme will be carried out by the Minister of Works and Development. The forward road
programme will be developed for the National Roads Board's approval and for submissions
to the Government, and will include the calibration and handling of the scale of road
distance charges, the keeping of various records and statistics, and the refunding or rebating
of petrol tax and distance charges.
Enforcement and policing are matters for my colleague the Minister of Transport. We
have worked very closely on the preparation of the legislation. Reference has been made to
anomalies in the scheme, and much has been made of them. With a new scheme of this
nature, on the user-pays principle, some anomalies may arise because there has been no
experience of the scheme. [Interruption.] Surely that makes common sense; we admit we
have no experience with such a scheme. When anomalies arise, the Government will shape
up to them and resolve them in spirit of co-operation.
For instance, the distance charge set out in the third schedule is a graduated charge
based on vehicle type and weight. The Road Transport Association wanted to be charged
according to the maximum weight that a vehicle could carry. The scheme is designed to allow
vehicle owners to nominate the maximum weight for the period of the licence to be issued,
with provision in clause 7 for supplementary licences for carrying heavier weights for limited
distances. In the Government's view this is a fairer scheme, since it encourages operators to
make the most efficient use of their vehicles while being charged only the amount for a
specified weight. This is hardly an anomaly, but it does indicate the Government's anxiety to
be fair in levying the distance charge and relating it as closely as possible to road costs.

million-a record. The National Roads Board finalised its detailed programme this week
after considering the recommendations of district roads councils, and, in accordance with
clauses 35 and 36, the board will advise district roads councils of the approved programme
early in the new year. It will authorise the carrying out of the works in accordance with that
programme in ample time for local authorities to plan their works and to determine their
rating structure for the next financial year so as to raise their share of the costs. It will also
enable the contracting industry and those concerned with the design and construction of
works to be informed and to have adequate time in which to prepare for the programme of
works ahead.
This is a businesslike way of doing things, and is a considerable improvement on the
present system of financing the National Roads Board. The road-user charge will then
provide, together with petrol tax from lighter vehicles, the means for the National Roads
Board and all the roading authorities to plan with confidence their maintenance and
improvement programmes for the country's roading system. Because it is a user-pays system,
the more the roads are used the greater will be the revenue available to pay the costs-and
the charges will be based on costs, not on petrol consumption.
There have been complaints about the prospect of transport costs rising. Some of them
will rise, because heavy transport has not been paying its share of roading and maintenance
costs. But some transport charges will be reduced-in the lighter truck category-because
the lighter trucks have been paying more than their share of roading costs. The member for
Timaru said nothing about that. [Interruption.] The distance charge will be less than the
petrol tax to be rebated, so operators of these lighter vehicles will find their operating costs
reduced. That is what the Bill is about-a road-user charge correctly related to roading costs.
If concern has been expressed about anomalies in the proposed system, it is proper to
point out the anomalies of the present system. Mileage tax for diesel vehicles, for example,
has not been related in any way to roading costs since it was first instituted more than 40
years ago. Heavy trailers pay only a fixed fee, which is unrelated to road use. More
anomalies in the present system could be quoted-for example, heavy traffic fees have not
been changed since 1963. Two diesel vehicles paying mileage tax at present could pay the
same, but one could have twice as many axles as the other, with half the road wear. The
licensed industry pays less than the present taxes paid by other heavy transport operators.
The Bill will correct these and other anomalies.
All road users will in future pay equitably for road use. Again, that is the purpose of the
Bill-to introduce a user-pays system. Heavy traffic fees produce a small proportion of the
National Roads Board's revenue. Together with mileage tax, and an assessed proportion of
petrol tax, plus estimates sales tax on heavy vehicles, the transport industry is this year
paying about $64 million in taxes, but the lighter vehicles pay more than their share while
heavy vehicles pay less. The scale of charges in the third schedule of the Bill has been
calibrated on the basis of the assessed present taxes paid by the industry.
Now that the level of the roading programme for the next year has been fixed at $160
million, we will be able to calculate the heavy transport share, take into account the 10
percent sales tax remission, and recalibrate the charges to produce the required revenue,
taking into account the higher level of the programme for next year. The third schedule will
therefore be amended by Order in Council, as provided in clause 20, to provide for the next
year's programme. This will be validated by amending legislation next session, which will
produce an opportunity for further debate on these measures.
To ease the burden on heavier vehicles, the scales have been weighted in their favour so
that they will not pay their full share until sales tax is finally phased down to 10 percent in
1980, by which time the full road-user charges will be payable. By that time, also, there will
be a proportion of turnover in the heavier vehicles, thereby enabling a number of owners to
obtain the benefit of the reducing sales tax. It would be very easy to select a distance charge
that has increased significantly and play it up for all it is worth, ignoring the fact that it is a
true cost of road use, and ignoring the benefit of reduced sales tax, which can be easily
overlooked, as it is a cost that will not have to be paid. [Interruption.]
There will also be a tendency to ignore improvements in the roading system. They will
also lead to increased charges, but will be of immense benefit to the heavy transport
industry. The Government freely acknowledges that increased user charges mean an
increased acceptance of the responsibility to upgrade the roading systems-including the
strengthening and renewal of bridges-that will be of great benefit to the heavy transport
industry, enabling it to make a more economic use of the transport fleet by gradually
removing class II restrictions, and the weight restrictions that apply to numerous bridges.

Road User Charges Bill
Hon. R. L. Bailey: The National Roads Board engineer would not agree.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I do not know the particular engineer, but the National
Roads Board is represented here, and, because the answer is technical, I obtained the
information from its officials. The member for Timaru referred to the Road Transport
Association. It had presented four examples, with increases ranging from 1 percent to 17
percent, but there were several errors in the RTA's assessment of those operators, the main
ones being: (a) sales tax changes had not been included—this has been found out since the
discussions on the Bill started several months ago; (b) in some cases, off-road running by
trailers had not been excluded from the analysis; (c) in the 17.4 percent case, the RTA had
assumed that the vehicle operator would take out a distance licence for 40 tonnes for each
vehicle, but the legal limit is only 39 tonnes-in other words, the law does not entitle an
operator to carry more than 39 tonnes. The revenue figures showing rate increases of
approximately 17 percent were based on 1976 figures.
These factors have a considerable impact on the examples given. The increases would
change as follows: take, for example, a medium-sized rural carrier, with 19 trucks and 12
trailers. The increase would be approximately 2.6 percent, not the 4.4 percent claimed by the
RTA. Another example is that of a large rural carrier, with 51 trucks and 39 trailers. The
increase would be about 3.6 percent, not 5.3 percent. One member referred to a specialist
bulk carrier with five tractor units and nine trailers, and the vehicle averaging about 100 000
km per annum. The increase would be about 8.5 percent; not 17.4 percent as claimed by the
RTA. Members will see that these figures present an entirely different picture.
The member for Timaru contended that farmers would pay more. Well, the transport
committee of Federated Farmers estimated that most farmers will, in fact, pay less for their
cartage. Their concern is for farmers who are a long way from suppliers or markets. In
extreme cases, farmers—say, those in the King Country-may have to pay $400 per annum
more for long-distance cartage. I covered the situation in my opening remarks when I said
that if it were found that some were being unjustly treated we would deal with such
anomalies.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Federated Farmers are complaining bitterly.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: All the way through I have admitted that there will be
extreme cases. The member for Timaru also raised another matter that has been covered
more or less in the answer I gave about the farmers. This Government undertook to abolish
what was commonly known as the 40-mile limit. We have done so. We undertook not to
overload the industry any more than it has been overloaded. We have said right through that
road users will pay in line with the damage caused to the roads the National Roads Board
helps to maintain. That is the whole principle behind the Bill.
There could be anomalies. I mentioned the worry about long-distance hauling for
farmers in areas such as the King Country and parts of Southland. It is all very well for
members opposite to say, "Take the Bill back." If we did that with every item of legislation
we would have been home months ago, because most of the Bills we put through are
amending Bills. We have come as close as we can in this. We have faced up to the problems.
We brought in a Bill, which is something that the Labour Government was unable to do with
three Ministers and an Under-Secretary. They finally gave it away. I am certain that the
person who will profit most is the one who has to pay-the consumer.
In conclusion, I should like to read a letter that I am quite happy to show to the
Opposition spokesman on transport. I will not name the firm but will just read portions of
the letter: "I have now had the time to assess your decision to open the competitive limit
with rail to 150 km. . . . After 2 months' work under the new regulations my company enjoys
levels of productivity never before achieved. We have customers happy with the service
enjoying a freight reduction of 27 percent, and we are making reasonable profits. There are
many anomalies: mainly the old problem of those outside the limit. Provided the Govern-
ment is prepared to willingly work on the anomalies, then I am quite happy. Congratulations
for doing your job well and making a positive decision resulting in a practical and valid
compromise.

Ministerial Statement
TUESDAY, 13 DECEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
RATU DAVID TOGANIVALU
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have much pleasure in informing members that the Hon.
Ratu David Toganivalu, Minister of Labour and Immigration and Industrial Relations of
Fiji, accompanied by the Minister of Justice, is within the precincts of this Chamber. I am
sure that members would desire that he be welcomed and accorded a seat on the floor of the
House on the left of the Chair.
The Hon. Ratu David Toganivalu, accompanied by the Minister of Justice, entered the
Chamber and took a seat on the left of the Chair.
MINISTERIAL STATEMENT
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): With the leave of the House I wish to
make a statement. On 28 October 1977 I announced the introduction of measures to ensure
that spending would not decline and that business confidence would be maintained. In
confirming yesterday that almost all of these policies were already in effect or close to
implementation, I said that the Government would be continuing to monitor the economy
closely and would take action as necessary.
The business community is currently in a difficult liquidity position as demand has not
been sufficient to prevent a further build-up in stocks-thus tying up cash resources.
Production cuts have continued to occur as firms have tried to reduce inventories; and
employment opportunities have been limited. Many businesses have a 31 March balance
date, and in these cases the second instalment of provisional tax will be payable on 7 March
1978. This tax obligation necessitates a build-up of business cash in the interim to enable the
obligation to be met. While the mini-Budget measures will be of considerable assistance, it is
clear that some additional action is necessary to alleviate the effects of the liquidity squeeze
on businesses.
The measures I am announcing today will give immediate relief as they will release some
of the tax payment reserves for other purposes in the businesses concerned. These businesses
that will not qualify will benefit indirectly from the increased spending power injected into
the commercial sector. The new policy will be implemented by an amendment to the Income
Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2), which is still to have its third reading. A Supplementary Order
Paper for the consideration of the Committee of the Whole House will be distributed.
The main points in the new measures are: the assistance will take the form of a
deduction against taxable income for 1977-78 and will apply to non-incorporated organisa-
tions as well as companies; the tax relief, which is intended to alleviate the problems of stock
build-up, will be calculated at 5 percent of the opening stock values of businesses for the
1977-78 year-this means, for example, that for companies with a 31 March balance date the
base will be stock values at 1 April 1977; the relief will be available against all tax due in the
1977-78 year, and hence will allow a refund for businesses with early balance dates which
have already made their second provisional tax payments; the relief will generally be
available to manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers, and will apply to manufacturers' work
in progress; the assistance will not be available for farming and agricultural businesses, or for
other types of businesses entitled to adopt standard values for trading stock, for construction
businesses, for mining or quarrying concerns, or for oil companies. Certain organisations
that have a special basis of taxation may also be wholly or partially excluded.

for "correct" is in order. However, it is not in order to suggest that an honourable member
has been deliberately telling untruths, or part of the truth, because that suggests he has been
lying, and we are not permitted to make that sort of suggestion. Although I took the words
to be borderline and did not stop them, it would have been better if they had not been
used-certainly not in commenting on a ministerial statement.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Industry-High Priority Activities
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert), on behalf of Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Hender-
son), asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: (1) When were details of the high priority
activities scheme announced in the Budget on 21 July 1977 made known to businessmen; (2)
how many of them have qualified for export incentives under the scheme; and (3) in what
general categories of industry have incentives been awarded and in respect of which
countries?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade): No details of the high priority
activities scheme have, to date, been made known to any businessman.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As a great deal of publicity was given to the matter in the Budget,
and subsequently, why has action not been taken?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Priority is being given to the establishment and implementa-
tion of the procedures, so that an appropriate announcement can be made as soon as
possible.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As the first announcement was made in the July Budget, how can
the Minister, in all sincerity, suggest that high priority has been accorded this matter?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I can simply assure the honourable member that that is so.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Was the scheme included in the Budget even without either the
department or Cabinet having any knowledge of how it would operate?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: No. The honourable member cannot take that out of what I
have said.
Community Youth Programme, Hamilton
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Recreation and Sport: How
many applications have been made from Hamilton under the recent youth in the community
scheme, how many have been approved, and how many young people are involved in these
applications?
Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Recreation and
Sport): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Recreation and Sport. Of the 18 applications
received, 14, involving jobs for 64 students, have been approved so far.
Hospital Board Social Workers and PSA
3. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) asked the Minister of State Services: Would he
advise when he intends to recognise the Public Service Association as the appropriate
employee organisation to represent hospital board social workers in view of the fact that a
recent ballot overwhelmingly favoured membership of the PSA?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of State Services): The Minister has always
made it clear that he would not intervene in this matter until he had evidence of an attempt
by both parties-the Public Service Association and the present recognised service organisa-
tion, the Society of Hospital Employee Organisations-to reach some measure of agree-
ment. When the PSA wrote to him describing the conditions in which the ballot had taken
place, insufficient evidence that it was under mutually agreed conditions was provided.
Consequently, on 2 November the Minister wrote seeking the PSA's agreement to his
referring its letter to the Society of Hospital Employee Organisations, and seeking the
society's comments on it, before he further considered the matter. The PSA has not yet
written to concur with his proposed action.
Overseas Funds from Tourism
4. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Tourism: What is the projected
revenue in overseas funds from tourism in 1977, and how will this compare with other means
of earning export funds?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): The Reserve Bank travel receipts for the
year ended October 1977 were $167 million, an increase of 10.2 percent over the previous
year. Using this as a basis, an estimate for the calendar year 1977 could be $173 million.
These figures exclude the earnings of Air New Zealand. Tourism exceeds the export
earnings of cheese, milk powders, and timber, and is approaching the export earnings of
butter, $206 million, and paper and wood products, $213 million.

Primary Schools-Manual Training Facilities
6. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Education: Is it correct that
Lincoln Heights Primary School, Hobsonville Primary School, Whenuapai Primary School,
Massey Primary School, and Royal Road Primary School, with classes up to form II, are to
be deprived of manual training facilities next year, and, if so, why did this situation develop,
and what urgent steps can be taken to restore the schools to their current position?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the Minister
of Education. It is not correct to say that the five schools mentioned will be deprived of
manual training next year. Rapid roll growth at the Bruce McLaren Intermediate School,
where manual training facilities have been used to complement those at the Henderson
Manual Training Centre, has resulted in that school's facilities no longer being available.
Alternative arrangements are being made to meet the manual training requirements of
pupils at the five schools.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Can the Minister outline the alternative arrangements?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Broadly, there are two possibilities. The board is exploring
the possibility of accommodating manual classes from the five schools at one or more of the
intermediate or high schools in the district; and it is also looking at the possibility of
establishing a temporary manual training school.
'National Superannuitants—Additional Tax
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: How many letters were sent to national superannuitants about the payment of
additional tax, how much did it cost to send the letters, and has he any evidence that the
immediate cash payments to superannuitant beneficiaries are being reduced?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department):
Three hundred and ninety thousand national superannuitants were advised by mail of the tax
position if they have taxable income in addition to national superannuation. The cost of this
service was approximately $45,000. The letter suggested that, where an end-of-year tax
liability would arise, superannuitants might consider having the amount of tax deduction
adjusted to a level that would cover it. It is unlikely that very many have done so, because it
would apply to the 1 April 1978 tax year.
Mr Rogers: Is the Minister aware that the letters sent by the Inland Revenue Depart-
ment were received before the letters sent by the Department of Social Welfare; and,
therefore, will his department be more efficient than the Department of Social Welfare?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sure both departments have the interests of national
superannuitants in mind.

Energy Levy
9. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Has he seen
the reported comments in the December issue of Gas News by the Chairman of the
Auckland Gas Company, Mr A. G. Wilson, in which he urges the withdrawal of the energy
level and is reported as stating that "an energy pricing policy could be effective in regulating
demand but a pricing policy should also encourage a change from the use of overseas oil to
indigenous natural gas", and will he confirm that conversions to indigenous energy sources
could be restricted by the retention of the energy levy?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I have seen the comments referred
to. The energy pricing policy allowed for incentive margins for coal and natural gas over
industrial fuel oil. It has been complemented by the immediate tax write-offs announced in
the 1977 Budget for conversions to natural gas and new plants run on natural gas, with the
associated sales tax refund. The adequacy of the incentives is being kept under continued
review. Evidence to date suggests that natural gas is in fact very competitively priced.

State Services Staff, 60 and Over
11. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn), on behalf of Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau), asked the
Minister of State Services: Is there any general instruction, either long-standing or recent,
concerning the employment of staff aged 60 years and over?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of State Services): The State Services
Commission has a long-standing policy on the employment of people aged 60 and over. The
Public Service Regulations 1964 provide that anyone who joined the Public Service after 1
August 1964 shall retire at 60. People who joined before that date can retire after 40 years'
service—that is, either superannuation service or actual service-or at age 60 if they have
already completed 40 years' service. A person who has not completed 40 years' service may
remain until he has done so or to age 65, whichever is the earlier. Temporary employees can
be employed after age 55 and through to age 65. Their continued employment is reviewed
annually, and they are retained only if there is no one suitable for appointment to the
position who is eligible for appointment to the permanent staff
Whale Kill Quota
12. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Did New
Zealand representatives take part in the decision made in Tokyo, and outlined in the
Dominion of 7 December, to increase the whale kill quota for sperm whales in the Northern
Pacific from 763 to 6444, and what is New Zealand's official view of this decision?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): The decision to increase the
quota for sperm whales in the Northern Pacific was taken on the basis of a recommendation
to that effect from the Scientific Committee of the International Whaling Commission. The
committee, comprising whale scientists from both whaling and non-whaling countries, held a
special session in Sydney from 21 to 25 November to consider new scientific data on North
Pacific sperm whales. The result of those deliberations was a recommendation to the
commission at its special session in Tokyo last week to increase the quota. New Zealand
supported the committee's recommendation.
Dr Shearer: In view of Dr Paul Spong's statements during his recent visit, as reported in
the press, can the Minister indicate whether the recommendation was a unanimous one?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The recommendation was made by the scientific committee.
I am sorry, I cannot tell the honourable member what each scientist recommended, but that
was certainly a recommendation made by the scientific committee to the commission.

Wages Subsidy for Building Trades
19. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Labour: Could he indicate whether it

employment districts of the Department of Labour where unemployment levels are higher
than the national average. At 2 December the scheme was providing employment for 155
workers. It is scheduled to run for 6 months, until 10 February 1978. The scheme is available
to all employers in the private sector in the aforementioned employment districts. However,
the Public Service with certain exceptions, the armed forces, and local authorities, are
specifically excluded. All persons in the aforementioned employment districts who have
been registered as unemployed for more than 4 weeks and are in receipt of unemployment
benefit are eligible under the scheme. The scheme will apply to full-time workers only.

wages subsidy being extended to cover apprentices in the building trade?

apprentices.

them to take on apprentices.
