likelihood that some of those eligible for benefits will not receive payment before Christmas.
This matter received coverage in various television news programmes yesterday, and has
also received attention in the printed media. I enclose examples for your perusal.
"I submit to you that this application falls within the requirements of Standing Order 89
for three reasons. Firstly, it is clearly a particular case of urgent public importance, when the
Department of Social Welfare may not be able to process applications quickly enough to
avoid the very real hardship that may arise for families without income over the Christmas
and New Year period. Secondly, the fact that there are only eight business days remaining
before the commencement of the Christmas and New Year holiday period makes the matter
one which requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government. Thirdly, the
matter clearly involves the administrative responsibility of the Government. Yours sincerely,
A. J. Faulkner, M.P."
In his letter the honourable member referred to two matters that, in his opinion, require
the immediate attention of the House and the Government. These are-and I quote from
paragraph 2 of his letter-"the inability of the Department of Social Welfare to cope with
the sudden increase in applications for unemployment benefits and the likelihood that some
of those eligible for benefits will not receive payment before Christmas". The member
attached two newspaper excerpts to his letter. The one from the Dominion of 10 December
makes no reference to the subject-matter of these assertions. This article refers only to the
unemployment statistics, and of course the honourable member will recall those are not of
themselves sufficient cause for the adjournment of the House under these Standing Orders.
The excerpt from the Auckland Star of 12 December begins: "Auckland and
Christchurch will get most of the temporary Social Welfare Department staff to cope with
the increased rush of unemployment applications." There is no statement in the article that
the department believes it will be unable to cope with the increase. For this reason I am not
satisfied, on the material supplied to me, that there has been a "particular case of recent
occurrence” within Standing Order 90 which requires the attention of the House and of the
Government, as the first assertion made by the member in his letter is not borne out by the
newspaper articles. In respect of the second assertion quoted above, the member is referring
to events which he expects to occur in the future. Perhaps I should refresh honourable
members' memories about the two assertions-"the inability of the Department of Social
Welfare to cope with the sudden increase in applications for unemployment benefits . . .”
and the report in the newspaper which states that "Auckland and Christchurch will get most
of the temporary Social Welfare Department staff to cope with the increased rush of
unemployment benefit applications." The second assertion is the likelihood that some of
those eligible for benefits will not receive payments before Christmas. In respect of the
second assertion the member is referring to events which he expects to occur in the future.
Obviously this cannot constitute a case of recent occurrence, and so is not within the terms of
the Standing Orders.
I emphasise that I have reached my decision on the material supplied by the member. If
he has any further evidence substantiating his assertion that the department is unable to cope
with unemployment benefit applications, I will be happy to look at it, and reconsider my
decision if necessary. I regret, therefore, that I cannot accept the member's proposal to
move the adjournment of the House for this purpose.

CONTRACEPTION, STERILISATION, AND ABORTION BILL
The Order of the Day for further consideration in Committee of the Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill having been called,
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) said: I move, That the Order of the
Day for further consideration in Committee of the Bill be discharged. I have consulted with as
many members as I can on the several sides on this issue to see if there is not some way in
which Parliament can decide in a responsible and orderly fashion what it will do. I thank
those several members on both sides of the House and on the many sides of this issue who
have been good enough to find common ground on the procedure we might follow to make
our way through this question and its resolution in the most orderly fashion possible.
I have this recommendation to make to the House, and I do so in speaking to the motion
that the Order of the Day for the further consideration in Committee of this Bill be
discharged. In terms of establishing the feelings, the mood, and the will of the House I
believe we can reduce the matter to about five key questions. The first is, do we want the
Bill? When that is decided then I believe the next question should be, what form of Bill do
we want? We have in the range of amendments and the sequence in which they are set out in
the Bill and were registered, as it were, with the Clerk of the House a modus operandi that is
workable and should enable us to find out what Parliament's will is with the least confusion
and the maximum expedition. Nothing I am saying about procedure will affect any member's
opportunity to take any stand on any question.
First of all, does the House want the Bill? I remind members that the Bill was not
suggested by either political party, but arose out of the recommendations of a royal
commission upon which no member of Parliament sat. The Bill spans two Governments and
crosses an election. It has been the subject of considerable debate and comment, much of
which has been critical, and no one in the House would suggest that the Bill will pass in its
original form. If the Bill is discharged that would end the matter for the present time. If it is
not discharged it would be clear that it is the will of the House that the debate proceed, and
that Parliament agonises its way to an answer.
The member for Franklin, the member for Southern Maori, and the member for
Birkenhead, who are the proposers of the major groups of amendments, support my
suggestion that if the Order of the Day is not discharged the House should proceed to clause
31A, which stands in my name and is the proposal to replace the panel system with two
doctors. A proposed amendment by the member for Birkenhead-
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Would the Minister of Energy Resources come back to the
motion that the Order of the Day be discharged. We do not need to have a discussion on the
contents or the merit of the Bill. No discussion should take place now that could more
properly take place in the Committee of the Whole House. The House has already given its
approval to the Bill in principle by agreeing to the second reading. Of course, it is still open

Hon. G. F. GAIR: Although not wanting to transgress, I do want to explain to my

Clause 11c. No sterilisation operation within 1 month of request.
(1) No registered medical practitioner shall perform an operation of sterilisation within 1 month

5.21 p.m.
Clause 12. Reports on sterilisations.
(1) Every registered medical practitioner who performs an operation of sterilisation shall, within
1 month thereafter, forward to the Director-General of Health a report of the operation giving the
following particulars:
(a) The reasons for the operation:
(b) The age, sex, marital status, race, and number of children of the patient:
(c) Whether the patient stayed in hospital for 1 or more nights:
(d) Whether the operation was performed post-partum:
(e) Where the operation was carried out pursuant to an order of the Court made under section 10
of this Act, that fact.
(2) No such report shall give the name or address of the patient.
(3) Every registered medical practitioner who fails to comply with subsection (1) of this section,
or contravenes subsection (2) of this section, commits an offence and is liable on summary
conviction to a fine not exceeding $100.

Clause 13. Conditions relating to sterility not to be attached to loans.
(1) It shall be unlawful for any person (in this section referred to as the lender)—
(a) To require any other person (in this section referred to as the borrower), or the borrower's
spouse, as a condition of granting any loan, to undertake to become sterile; or
(b) To refuse to grant any loan to the borrower merely because the borrower or the borrower's
spouse is not sterile.
(2) Every person who suffers any loss by reason of any act or omission rendered unlawful by
subsection (1) of this section shall be entitled to recover damages from the person responsible for
the act or omission.
Mr BRILL (Kapiti) moved to add to the side heading the words "or employment"; to
insert after the word "lender" in subclause (1) the words "or any person acting or purporting
to act on behalf of the lender"; to delete from paragraph (a) of subclause (1) the word
"section" and to substitute the word "subsection"; to insert after subclause (1) the following
subclause:
(1A) It shall be unlawful for any person (in this subsection referred to as the employer), or any
person acting or purporting to act on behalf of the employer,-
(a) To require any other person (in this subsection referred to as the employee), or the
employee's spouse, to undertake to become sterile as a condition of granting employ-
ment of any kind, or any conditions of work, or fringe benefits, or opportunities for
training or promotion or transfer; or
(b) To refuse to grant any such employment, conditions, benefits, or opportunities merely
because the employee or the employee's spouse is not sterile.

Clause 15. Term of office of members of Supervisory Committee.
(1) Subject to the succeeding provisions of this section, every member of the Supervisory
Committee shall hold office for a term of 3 years, but may from time to time be reappointed.
(2) Any member of the Supervisory Committee may resign his office at any time by written
notice given to the Minister.
(3) Any member of the Supervisory Committee may be removed from office at any time by the
Governor-General on the recommendation of the Minister for disability, bankruptcy, neglect of
duty, or misconduct, proved to the satisfaction of the Minister.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) moved to delete the word "Minister" in
subclause (2) and to substitute the words "Speaker of the House of Representatives, or to
the Prime Minister if there is no Speaker or the Speaker is absent from New Zealand"; to
delete the words "on the recommendation of the Minister" in subclause (3) and to substitute
the words "upon an address from the House of Representatives"; and to delete the words ",
proved to the satisfaction of the Minister" in subclause (3).
Amendments agreed to, and clause as amended agreed to.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) moved to insert the following new
clause:
15A. Manner of appointments-(1) If any member of the Supervisory Committee dies, or resigns
his office, or is removed from office, the vacancy thereby created shall be filled in accordance with
this section.
(2) If any such vacancy occurs at any time while Parliament is in session, it shall be filled by
appointment by the Governor-General on the recommendation of the House of Representatives:
Provided that if the vacancy occurs less than 2 months before the close of that session and no such
recommendation is made in that session, the provisions of subsection (3) of this section shall apply
as if the vacancy had occurred while Parliament was not in session.
(3) If any such vacancy occurs at any time while Parliament is not in session, the following
provisions shall apply:
(a) The Governor-General in Council may appoint a person to fill the vacancy, and the person so
appointed shall, unless his office sooner becomes vacant, hold office until his appoint-
ment is confirmed by the House of Representatives:
(b) If the appointment is not so confirmed within 2 months after the commencement of the next
ensuing session, the appointment shall lapse and there shall be deemed to be a further
vacancy in the membership of the Supervisory Committee.
New clause agreed to.

Clause 23. Applications for licences.
(1) An application for a licence may be made by-
(a) In the case of a hospital under the control of a hospital board, the Superintendent of the
hospital; or
(b) In the case of a private hospital, the licensee; or
(c) In the case of any other institution, by the person for the time being in charge of the
institution.
(2) Every application shall-
(a) Be addressed to the Supervisory Committee; and
(b) Be in the prescribed form; and
(c) State which type of licence is desired; and
(d) Be accompanied by the prescribed fee.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources) moved to delete the words "Supervis-
ory Committee" from paragraph (a) of subclause (2) and to substitute the words "Director-
General of Health".
The ACTING DEPUTY CHAIRMAN declined to accept the amendment on the ground
that it was inconsistent with clause 17 as amended.
12.25 a.m.
Clause 24. Grant of licences.
(1) On receiving an application for a full licence in respect of any institution, the Supervisory
Committee shall grant such a licence in respect of that institution only if it is satisfied-
(a) That there are, in the institution, adequate facilities for the accommodation of patients for
one or more nights; and
(b) That there are, in the institution, adequate surgical and other facilities, and adequate and
competent staff, for the safe performance of abortions; and
(c) That there are, in the institution, adequate accommodation, surgical and other facilities, and
competent staff to provide treatment and care of patients suffering complications arising
while they are awaiting, undergoing, or recuperating from an abortion; and
(d) That the person who will be the holder of the licence if the application is granted is a fit and
proper person to hold such a licence.
(2) On receiving an application for a limited licence in respect of any institution, the Supervisory
Committee shall grant such a licence in respect of that institution only if it is satisfied-
(a) There is a need for a or another licensed institution in the area in which the institution to
which the application relates is situated; and
(b) That there are, in the institution, adequate surgical and other facilities, and adequate and
competent staff, for the safe performance of abortions; and
(c) That adequate arrangements have been made with any other hospital or institution for the
transfer of any patient suffering complications arising while she is awaiting, undergoing,
or recuperating from an abortion to that other hospital or institution for treatment and
care; and
(d) That the person who will be the holder of the licence if the application is granted is a fit and
proper person to hold such a licence.
(3) Notwithstanding anything in subsection (1) or subsection (2) of this section, on considering an
application for a full licence, the Supervisory Committee may, with the consent of the applicant,
grant a limited licence if it is satisfied in respect of the matters specified in subsection (2) of this
section but is not satisfied in respect of the matters specified in subsection (1) of this section.
(4) Subject to the provisions of sections 29 and 30 of this Act, the decision of the Supervisory
Committee in respect of every application for a licence shall be final.
(5) Where the Supervisory Committee refuses to grant an application for a licence, it shall, if
requested to do so by the applicant, give to the applicant a written statement of its reasons for
refusing the application.

1.16 a.m.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin) moved to insert the following new clause:
33. Supervisory Committee to set up and maintain list of certifying consultants-(1) The
Supervisory Committee shall set up and maintain a list of registered medical practitioners (in this
Part of this Act termed certifying consultants) who may be called upon to consider cases referred to
them by any registered medical practitioner and determine, in accordance with section 37 of this
Act, whether to authorise an abortion.
(2) Before drawing up the list, the Supervisory Committee shall determine the minimum number
of certifying consultants required to ensure, so far as possible, that every woman seeking an
abortion has her case considered expeditiously, and shall make that number of appointments in
accordance with this section. Thereafter, the Committee shall keep that number under review, and
shall from time to time make such further appointments, or revoke such number of appointments,
as it considers necessary to meet any change in the circumstances.
(3) Having determined the number of appointments to be made, the Supervisory Committee
shall consult with the New Zealand Medical Association, and may consult with any other
professional or other body, before determining whom to appoint.
(4) In making appointments to the list, the Supervisory Committee shall ensure that the
following requirements are met:
(a) At least one half of the total number of appointees shall be practising obstetricians or
gynaecologists, and the list shall be marked in such a way as to indicate which of the
appointees are so qualified:
(b) There shall be a sufficient number of appointees practising in each area of New Zealand to
ensure that every woman seeking an abortion can have her case considered without
involving her in considerable travelling or other inconvenience.
(5) In addition, in making such appointments, the Supervisory Committee shall have regard to
the desirability of appointing medical practitioners who hold views in relation to abortion generally
that are compatible with the tenor of this Act. Without otherwise limiting the discretion of the
Supervisory Committee in this regard, the following views shall be considered incompatible in that
sense for the purposes of this subsection:
(a) That an abortion should not be performed in any circumstances:
(b) That the question of whether an abortion should or should not be performed in any case is
entirely a matter for the woman and a doctor to decide.
(6) Every appointment to the list of certifying consultants shall be for a term of 1 year, but the
Supervisory Committee may reappoint any practitioner on the expiry of his term.
(7) The Supervisory Committee may at any time, at its discretion, revoke the appointment of any
certifying consultant.
1.21 a.m.
Mr LANGE (Mangere) moved to delete the words "who hold views in relation to
abortion generally that are compatible" from subclause (5) and to substitute the words
"whose assessment of cases coming before them will not be coloured by views in relation to
abortion generally that are incompatible".

Clause 35. Supervisory Committee to appoint or approve counselling services.
(1) For the purposes of this Part of this Act, the Supervisory Committee shall from time to
time-
(a) Appoint suitably qualified persons to provide counselling services for persons considering
having an abortion; or
(b) Approve any agency for the provision of such counselling services.
(2) In appointing or approving persons or agencies for the provision of counselling services under
this section, the Supervisory Committee shall have regard to the following matters:
(a) A counselling service may be conducted in the same building as the Abortion Review Panel
conducts its work:
(b) Every counselling service should be directed by an experienced and professionally trained
social worker, who may or may not be the Counselling Supervisor of the Panel:
(c) That suitably trained lay counsellors may also be used where there are insufficient profes-
sional social workers:
(d) Every counsellor should be thoroughly familiar with all relevant social services and agencies,
and able to advise patients, or refer them to appropriate agencies for advice, on
alternatives to abortion, such as adoption and solo parenthood.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin) moved to delete paragraph (a) of subclause (2); and to delete the

Clause 36. Procedure.
Clause negatived.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin) moved to insert the following new clause:
36. Procedure (1) Every registered medical practitioner who-
(a) Is consulted by a woman who wishes to have an abortion; or
(b) Proposes to perform an abortion on any woman if the abortion is authorised under this Part
of this Act-shall, if requested to do so by the woman, refer the case, in accordance with
the procedure for the time being prescribed by the Supervisory Committee, to any 2
certifying consultants (of whom at least 1 shall be a qualifed obstetrician or gynaecolog-
ist) with a request that they determine, in accordance with section 37 of this Act,
whether or not to authorise the performance of an abortion.
(2) On referring a case to any certifying consultant, the practitioner shall submit to him, in
writing,-
(a) A statement that the woman is pregnant and seeks an abortion; and
(b) A statement of the ground or grounds on which she seeks an abortion; and
(c) Such other information as may be prescribed from time to time by the Supervisory
Committee.
(3) As soon as practicable after a case is referred to him under subsection (1) of this section, each
certifying consultant shall consider the case and shall, if requested to do so by the patient, interview
her; and at any such interview she shall be entitled to be accompanied by her own doctor.
(4) The woman's own doctor and the proposed operating surgeon shall be entitled (with the
woman's consent) to make such representations and to adduce such medical or other reports
concerning the case as he thinks fit to each certifying consultant.
(5) Every certifying consultant may, in considering any case, consult with any other person
(whether or not a registered medical practitioner) as he thinks fit in order to assist him in his
consideration of the case, but he shall not disclose the woman's identity to any such person without
her consent.

3.27 a.m.
Clause 37. Determination of case.
(1) If, after considering the case, the 2 members of the Panel who are medical practitioners are of
the opinion that the case is one to which any of paragraphs (a) to (e) of subsection (1), or (as the
case may require) paragraph (a) or paragraph (b) of subsection (3), of section 187A of the Crimes
Act 1961 applies, they shall forthwith issue a certificate in the prescribed form authorising the
performance of an abortion.
(2) If those members are of the contrary opinion, they shall refuse to authorise the performance
of an abortion.
(3) If one of those members is of the opinion that the case is one to which any of the said
provisions applies and the other of those members is of the contrary opinion, they shall refer the
case to another registered medical practitioner for his opinion, being a registered medical
practitioner who is on the list of deputies maintained under section 33(3) of this Act.


## p. 5323 (#759) ###########################################

13 December
5323
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
(4) If that other registered medical practitioner is of the opinion that the case is one to which any
of the said provisions applies, the member of the Panel who is of the same opinion shall issue a
certificate in the prescribed form authorising the performance of an abortion.
(5) Every certificate issued under this section shall be forwarded to the holder of the licence in
respect of the licensed institution in which the patient intends to have an abortion, and a copy of
the certificate shall be forwarded to the patient.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin) moved to delete from subclause (1) the words "two members of

Clause 54. Meaning of "unlawfully".
54. Meaning of “unlawfully”--The principal Act is hereby amended by inserting, after section
187, the following section:
"187A. (1) For the purposes of sections 183 and 186 of this Act, any act specified in either of
those sections is done unlawfully unless, in the case of a pregnancy of not more than 20 weeks'
gestation, the person doing the act believes-
"(a) That the continuance of the pregnancy would result in serious danger (not being danger
normally attendant upon childbirth) to the life, or to the physical or mental health, of the
woman or girl; or
"(b) That there is a substantial risk that the child, if born, would be so physically or mentally
abnormal as to be seriously handicapped; or


## p. 5328 (#764) ###########################################

5328
13 December
Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
"(c) That the pregnancy is the result of sexual intercourse between-
"(i) A parent and child; or
"(ii) A brother and sister, whether of the whole blood or of the half blood; or
"(iii) A grandparent and grandchild; or
"(d) That the pregnancy is the result of sexual intercourse that constitutes an offence against
section 131 (1) of this Act; or
"(e) That the woman or girl is severely subnormal within the meaning of section 138 (2) of this
Act.
"(2) The age and the social and economic circumstances of the woman or girl concerned, while
not in themselves grounds for any act specified in section 183 or section 186 of this Act, may be
taken into account in determining, for the purposes of subsection (1) (a) of this section, whether
the continuance of the pregnancy would result in serious danger to her life or to her physical or
mental health.
"(3) For the purposes of sections 183 and 186 of this Act, any act specified in either of those
sections is done unlawfully unless, in the case of a pregnancy of more than 20 weeks' gestation,
the person doing the act believes-
"(a) That there is a substantial risk that the child, if born, would be so physically or mentally
abnormal as to be seriously handicapped; or
“(b) That the miscarriage is necessary to save the life of the woman or girl or to prevent serious
permanent injury to her physical or mental health.
"(4) Where a registered medical practitioner, in pursuance of a certificate issued by a Panel
under section 37 of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977, does any act specified
in section 183 or section 186 of this Act, the doing of that act shall not be unlawful for the purposes
of the section applicable unless it is proved that, at the time when he did that act, he did not believe
it to be lawful in terms of subsection (1) or subsection (3) of this section, as the case may require."
Dr WALL (Porirua) moved to insert after the word "girl" in the proposed new section

Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill
In this part of this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,-
"Abortion" means a medical or surgical procedure carried out or to be carried out for the
purpose of procuring the premature expulsion from the mother of an embryo or fetus
after implantation, otherwise than for the purpose of inducing the birth of a fetus believed
to be viable or removing a fetus that has died:
"Abortion law" means every provision of-
(a) Sections 14 to 48 of this Act; and
(b) Sections 182 to 187A of the Crimes Act 1961:
"Approved counselling service" means any person or agency appointed or approved by the
Supervisory Committee under section 35 of this Act:
"Contraceptive" means a substance or device or technique intended to prevent conception or
implantation:
"Family planning clinic" means any clinic established by or affiliated to
(a) The New Zealand Association of Natural Family Planning Centres:
(b) The New Zealand Family Planning Association:
(c) A Hospital Board:
(d) Any other association or agency approved for the purposes of this Act by the
Minister of Health by notice in the Gazette:
"Holder", in relation to a licence issued under this Part of this Act, means-
(a) In the case of a hospital under the control of a Hospital Board, the person who is
for the time being the Superintendent of the hospital, whether or not he held that office
when the licence was issued:
(b) In the case of a private hospital, the person who is for the time being the licensee
(within the meaning of section 118 of the Hospitals Act 1957) of the hospital, whether or
not he held that office when the licence was issued (under this Part of this Act):
(c) In the case of any other institution, the person who is for the time being in charge
of the institution, whether or not he was in charge of it when the licence was issued:
"Hospital Board" means a Hospital Board constituted under the Hospitals Act 1957:
"Institution" means any hospital, clinic, or other premises in which it is proposed to perform
abortions:
"Licence" means a licence issued under this Part of this Act:
"Licensed institution" means an institution in respect of which a licence is for the time being in
force under this Part of this Act:
"Panel" means an Abortion Review Panel appointed under section 33 of this Act:
"Private hospital" means a hospital in respect of which a licence is for the time being in force
under Part V of the Hospitals Act 1957:
"Secretary", in relation to the Supervisory Committee, means the officer of the Department
of Justice for the time being acting as Secretary of the Committee:
"Supervisory Committee" means the Abortion Supervisory Committee constituted under
section 14 of this Act.

Securities Advertising Bill
WEDNESDAY, 14 DECEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SECURITIES ADVERTISING BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Securities Advertising
Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill, which I propose to ask the House to refer to the
Statutes Revision Committee for recess study, is to consolidate and amend the law relating
to the raising of investment money from the public. The Bill follows a series of financial
collapses in recent years, which have drawn attention to the need for legislation to give a
greater degree of protection to the public. Commercial entities have been offering to the
public an increasing variety of investments. As well as being asked to invest in the usual
types of securities, such as shares and debentures, the public has been asked to invest in
contributory mortgages, hire-purchase paper, bills of exchange, and a number of quasi-
syndicates. Collapses have occurred mainly in investment in these less usual types of
securities-investment that has not yet given rise to similar duties and responsibilities as
apply to the usual types of investment.
The Bill defines securities in a very wide sense, and, generally speaking, it will require
commercial entities offering securities to the public to do so by way of a registered
prospectus, to appoint an independent person to look after the interests of investors, to keep
and disclose adequate financial information, and to be subject to official scrutiny. Precedents
for the duties and responsibilities I have just mentioned are to be found in the Protection of
Depositors Act 1968, the Syndicates Act 1973, and those provisions of the Companies Act
1955 that relate to prospectuses. The Bill will repeal those enactments and provisions that
deal with particular types of entities, and instead will constitute a virtually comprehensive
source of statute law on the duties and responsibilities that arise when an entity offers
securities to the public.
Put another way, the Bill represents activity-based legislation that will deal with this
area of law as a whole, so that there are no inconsistencies in its regulation and development,
and, more importantly, it will remove the present opportunity for disreputable promoters to
operate in less well regulated areas.
In drafting the Bill, consideration has been given to those recommendations of the
MacArthur committee on the Companies Act 1955 relating to prospectuses. There has been
wide consultation in the legal, accounting, financial, and commercial sectors on the purpose
and scope of the Bill, and the response has been very favourable. In a Bill of such wide
application it has been necessary to vest in the Registrar of Companies wide discretions and
powers, subject, of course, to appeal to the Supreme Court. I know that many have
suggested that there is a need for an independent commission for commercial affairs to
exercise this appellate jurisdiction and other functions. Although the Government has
appointed an interdepartmental committee to study the matter, I would welcome submis-
sions to the Statutes Revision Committee commenting on the need for such a commission
and its functions in relation to the Bill.
I emphasise that risk is an inseparable part of investment, and the Bill in no way
purports to alter that. But I do not regard as legitimate that part of the risk attributable to
irresponsibility or mismanagement. The Bill is aimed at redressing the balance in favour of
the investor who, in many of the financial collapses in recent years, has had little or no way
of ensuring that his investment has been responsibly and properly managed.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Bill is overdue-I had better not say long
overdue, or the Minister will make the obvious response. However, he will recall that when I
had his responsibilities I did advert to the topic on several occasions, and referred to the
difficulty of definition which, while not insuperable, posed a great many problems. I am sure
the Minister has found the same difficulty in resolving them. It is only as a result of lengthy
study that these problems have been resolved, I imagine-or I hope they will be resolved in
the Bill, which I have had only the briefest opportunity to glance at.

done in July 1975. I for one would be interested to learn whether it has made any progress,

FENCING BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Fencing Bill be
introduced. The Bill gives effect to the recommendations contained in the Property Law and
Equity Reform Committee report on the Fencing Act 1908 that the 1908 Act be repealed and
replaced with a completely new enactment. That report was presented to the then Minister
of Justice in June 1972, and the present Bill substantially follows the draft Bill appended to
the report. The Property Law and Equity Reform Committee took the view that there were
certain existing provisions in the Act that were not concerned with rights and obligations of
adjoining owners in respect of fencing matters, and recommended, therefore, that these
provisions be omitted and, if not obsolete, be included in more appropriate legislation. It is
also worth mentioning that the Property Law and Equity Law Reform Committee's report
considered and made certain recommendations on the then existing section 26A of the
Fencing Act 1908 relating to trees on boundaries, but these reform proposals have now been
attended to in an amendment to the Property Law Act.
The general principle in the 1908 Act is that occupiers of adjoining lands not divided by
a sufficient fence are liable, if called upon, to contribute to the cost of erection or repair of
fencing. This principle has been an integral part of the legislation since 1895 when the Act
was first passed, primarily to regulate obligations between rural landholders. Now, however,
with the Act applying equally to urban and rural properties, some modification of that
general principle is necessary. Accordingly, the Bill retains the general approach to the
principle of fencing liability, but restricts the obligation imposed on tenants to those having a
tenancy of 10 years or more. In this, the Bill differs from the draft Bill appended to the
report, in which the term of tenancy contemplated was 12 months. The Bill has, however, a
clause protecting agreements that may be entered into betweeen parties, and it is important
to note that the right of adjoining owners or occupiers to settle fencing matters by agreement
is not affected, and the Bill is generally drafted to encourage settlement of disputes by
agreement.
Another important change that the Bill introduces is the concept of an “adequate
fence". This has been defined as a fence that "as to its nature, condition, and state of repair
is reasonably satisfactory for the purpose that it serves or is intended to serve". This change
from the definition of "sufficient fence" in the present Act will allow for a more flexible
approach to be taken to the whole question of fencing, especially as changes in fencing
trends and uses occur. The new definition will be more adaptable, and, whereas under the
present Act the definition of sufficient fence is linked to the schedule of fences, this Bill does
not have a provision similar to the existing section 8, and the types of fence appearing in the
schedule are set out as an aid to conveyancing only.
Whereas the 1908 Act distinguished between the erection of a new fence on the one
hand and the repair of an existing fence on the other, the Bill does not make this distinction.
Under this Bill the liability is to contribute to work-which is defined to include both
erection and repair of fences. The notice required to be given is more specific than under the
existing Act, and includes an estimate of cost. Another important addition to the notice is
the explanatory note setting out the effect of the notice and the consequences of non-
compliance. The Bill sets out detailed rules for service of notices, and also sets out clearly the
procedure to be followed once notice has been given, and when there is a change of occupier
after a notice or cross-notice has been given.
Jurisdiction remains with the magistrate's court, and the Bill details the questions the
court may hear and determine. The Bill does not apply to Crown land except in certain
limited circumstances, and the distinction that the present Act makes between Maori and
European land has been removed. Finally, I intend to move that the Bill be referred to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee for recess study.

IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I move, That the Immigration Amendment
Bill (No. 2) be introduced. The Bill will rationalise criteria and procedures relating to the
deportation of persons convicted of criminal offences by bringing the deportation provisions
of the Aliens Act into the Immigration Act, and by applying the same provisions to aliens
and Commonwealth citizens. At present, Commonwealth citizens who are not New Zealand
citizens can be deported if they are convicted within 5 years of their arrival in New Zealand
of a criminal offence punishable by a term of imprisonment of at least 12 months. On the
other hand, an alien can be deported irrespective of how long he has been here. In neither
case is there provision for an appeal against deportation.
The Bill provides for all non-New Zealand citizens, aliens and Commonwealth citizens
alike, to be deported only if convicted of a criminal offence within 5 years of their arrival in
New Zealand. It will also establish a deportation review tribunal, to which a person can
appeal on humanitarian grounds if they have been ordered to leave New Zealand after
having been convicted of a criminal offence. If the tribunal considers that it would be unduly
harsh or unjust to deport the applicant from New Zealand, and it would not be contrary to
the public interest to allow the person concerned to remain in New Zealand, it will be able to
quash the deportation order.
The Bill also makes provision for the deportation of non-New Zealand citizens who
constitute a threat to national security or public safety. It will allow persons who are not
granted a permit to enter New Zealand to be held in custody if they cannot leave New
Zealand the same day and if they are likely to commit an offence or be a threat to public
safety if they are not held in custody. It also clarifies the powers of arrest exercised by a
police officer under the Immigration Act. Machinery clauses include consequential repeals
and minor amendments to the Immigration Act, and repeal the Aliens Act 1948. The Bill
comprises eight clauses, and it is my intention that it be referred to the Statutes Revision
Committee for consideration during the recess, and that the hearings be open to the news
media.
Clause 1 relates to the short title; clause 2 is an interpretative provision; clause 3
provides for persons who are refused permission to land in New Zealand to be detained
pending departure; and clause 4 repeals Part IV of the Act and substitutes a new part
relating to the deportation of all persons, both aliens and Commonwealth citizens, who are
convicted of a criminal offence. It also provides for the deportation of persons who
constitute a threat to national security, or who may be a threat to public safety. Provision is
also made in the clause for the setting up of a deportation review tribunal to hear appeals
against deportations ordered following criminal convictions, and for the tribunal to be
enabled to quash a deportation order when it is satisfied that it would be unduly harsh or
unjust to deport the person concerned. It also makes provision for persons who are to be
deported because they constitute a threat to public safety to appeal to the Supreme Court.
Clause 5 introduces a provision to clarify the powers of arrest exercised by a police
officer. Clauses 6 and 7 are consequential drafting provisions. Clause 8 adds new third and
fourth schedules to the principal Act to set out the administrative and procedural provisions
relating to the deportation review tribunal.

fact, the situation of the Commonwealth citizen remains exactly as it has always been. A
Commonwealth citizen always could be deported if convicted of an offence carrying a
sentence of imprisonment of a year or more within 5 years of his arrival in New Zealand. We
have brought aliens out of the Aliens Act into the Immigration Act. Previously, an alien
could be deported at any time but, the time limit has now been reduced to 5 years after his
arrival. In effect, a Dutchman is treated no differently from an Irishman, for example.
Aliens will now receive equal treatment with Commonwealth citizens.

The proposed new section 22(3) includes the phrase "for any other reason". When you

NEW ZEALAND PORTS AUTHORITY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the New Zealand
Ports Authority Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill will amend the New Zealand Ports
Authority Act 1968. Perhaps at the outset I should indicate that, at the appropriate time, I
shall be moving that the Bill be referred to a select committee for recess study. In its 1975
election manifesto the National Party stated that, "National believes that an effective
National Ports Authority is necessary for harbour planning and development and accord-
ingly will review the Act and amend it where necessary." I have stated publicly on several
occasions recently that it was my intention to introduce amending legislation before the end
of the current session. I am now in a position to do this. The New Zealand Ports Authority
Amendment Bill has been drafted following consultations with the Ports Authority and the
Harbours Association. The views of interested parties, both within and outside the Govern-
ment, on the changes proposed in the legislation have also been sought and considered. The
aim of the Bill is to clarify the functions of the Ports Authority, especially in relation to the
national ports plan, to extend the Ports Authority's powers in certain areas, and to clarify the
aspects of the procedures now being followed by the authority.
Basically, the aim is to give the New Zealand Ports Authority increased jurisdiction. It
has been said that the Ports Authority lacks teeth. The authority was established in 1968 to
exercise a certain degree of control to ensure rationality in the development of our ports
from an overall national point of view. The Bill before us today is designed to increase the
degree of control that the Ports Authority has over the expenditure of money on harbour
facilities and equipment. The contents of the Bill are important to the port and shipping
industries. They should be given every opportunity to consider and comment on them and,
although the interested parties have already had the opportunity for comment on the
principles, as I said earlier, I propose to send the Bill to a select committee for recess study.
With that in mind, I shall now give members a very brief description of the clauses.


## p. 5347 (#783) ###########################################

14 December
5347
New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 is concerned with definitions of "harbour works" and
"national ports plan". Clause 3 amends the principal Act to empower the chairman, or a
member, or the chief executive officer of the Ports Authority duly authorised by the
chairman, to issue summonses and to undertake other steps preliminary or incidental to
proceedings being taken by the authority. Clauses 4 and 5 amend the functions and
procedures of the authority. Clause 4 revises the obligation of the New Zealand Ports
Authority to prepare a national ports plan. As with the change to the definition of "national
ports plan" I referred to earlier, the aim is to make it clear that the plan will be of a
continuing nature for the progressive development of ports and harbours.
Clause 5 reviews the provisions in section 12 of the principal Act that relate to
consultation by the Ports Authority before reaching a decision on any proposal relating to
the national ports plan. Clause 6 deals with the control of capital expenditure. The clause
will extend the Ports Authority's powers to cover all harbour works whether or not they are
carried out by a harbour board, and will further extend its control to cover large items of
plant and equipment to be used in ports when the authority considers that their use would be
of significance to the national ports plan. Clause 7 gives the authority the power to examine
lease documents. This provision is designed to provide a check on leases for berths or back-
up areas to ensure that sole user rights do not preclude a potential user from taking
advantage of under-utilised facilities.
The Bill I have just described makes amendments to the procedures, functions, and
powers of the Ports Authority to enable it to provide what this Government believes to be
the necessary degree of rationality and co-ordination in the onward development of ports
and harbours in New Zealand.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 4)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local
Government Amendment Bill (No. 4) be introduced. This Bill represents a further stage in the
major task of revising and amalgamating the Municipal Corporations Act and the Counties
Act, and other legislation related to territorial local government.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Just messing about with local government again.

tant innovations, especially relating to land subdivision. Among other things, for example, it
provides for a levy for reserve purposes on major capital urban development where no actual
land subdivision is involved. It also recognises new concepts of urban development and the
desirability of a common approach to cost sharing throughout the country. It also binds the
Crown. The Bill is of such a nature that it is certain that various interests associated with land
subdivision and urban development will wish to have a good deal of time to examine it and to
make submissions. Accordingly, I propose to move that it be referred to the Local Bills
Committee for recess study. In fact, I promised this to the Municipal Association and the
Counties Association. It is a big Bill, and it is important.

Foreign Seamen's Act-Enforcement
1. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Transport: Have there been
many occasions recently when it has been necessary to enforce the provisions of the Foreign
Seamen's Act 1860, or the present Act under which the regulations exist, against a seaman of
Hamburg or the North German Confederation?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): There have been no recent
occasions when it has been necessary to enforce the provisions of the Foreign Seamen's Act
1860, or the present Act, under regulations existing against seamen of ships registered in
Hamburg or the North German Confederation.
Hon. M. Rata: I take it that the Minister intends to tidy up the Acts and regulations that
are no longer applicable?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The ministry is reviewing the matter at present, and any
unnecessary Acts or regulations will be removed.
Roading-Assistance to Waitemata City Council
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Is
he aware that the Waitemata City Council requires financial assistance with the reconstruc-
tion of Swanson Road, Swanson, and will the National Roads Board be able to assist the
council?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): At its last meeting the
National Roads Board approved assistance to the Waitemata City Council in 1978-79 for
upgrading Swanson Road. A subsidy of $3:$2 was granted and will involve $158,000 of board
funds.
Electricity-Combined-cycle Power Stations
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Electricity: Does he propose
that district heating will be associated with the new combined-cycle power stations to be
erected in Auckland, and, if so, will he ensure that the stations will be built in areas where it
will be possible to use the waste exhaust heat in new homes designed to make proper use of
district heating?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity): Before any decision is taken, a more detailed
study of the economies of district heating will be made as part of further siting studies for
new combined-cycle plant proposed for the Auckland area. A preliminary survey shows
greatest promise for commercial and industrial rather than domestic load.
Hon. F. M. Colman: The Minister spoke about the need for further surveys. What sort
of timetable does he envisage before reaching a decision on this type of extended use?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I hope that the studies at present under way on the first site will
mature within, say, the next 18 months, or perhaps sooner. The appropriate district heating
application will depend upon the sites that are most appropriate to begin with—for instance,
if one was at Westfield, an early application would be logical.
Mr Lithgow: Is it true that New Zealand is probably one of the countries that could lead
the world in combined-cycle power station development?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is true that New Zealand will be near the forefront. A number of
combined-cycle plants in the United States and Europe have been running long enough to
convince us that they could be developed as reliable base-load stations. However, the scope
and scale of the plants it is proposed to apply in the Auckland area will represent a significant
new development in combined-cycle generation.

$11.23 million.

Wool Marketing Corporation Intervention Price
9. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition), on behalf of Mr BRUCE
BARCLAY (Christchurch Central), asked the Minister of Agriculture: Is it correct that the
Government, through its representative on the Wool Marketing Corporation, took the
initiative which led to the lowering of the wool intervention price, and was this based on a
desire to receive overseas funds without undue delay?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The answer to both parts of the
question is no. The proposal to lower the corporation's market intervention levels was
decided on by the directors of the Wool Marketing Corporation at their meeting on 6
December. Growers and growers' nominees form a majority on the directorate of the
corporation. Therefore, any decision requires the support of some at least of the grower
representatives. The Government did not influence any of the directors in the way they
voted on the question. The reasons for the reduction of the intervention levels have already
been given by the corporation's secretary through the news media, and the chairman of the
corporation had an article in this morning's Dominion. Those reasons did not include
considerations in relation to any desire to obtain overseas funds without undue delay. Such
matters do not come within the statutory concerns of the corporation, whose object is to
obtain in the interests of growers the best possible long-term terms for New Zealand. I was
not in the country when the decision was made.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: At the time the decision was taken were the corporation's finances
such that it would have had to get either his approval or that of the Minister of Finance to
raise funds to maintain existing intervention prices?

ROAD USER CHARGES BILL
On the question, That the Road User Charges Bill be referred to a select committee,
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) said: At the conclusion of the second reading
debate last Friday I moved that the Bill be referred to a select committee for recess study,
and that the proceedings of the committee be open to accredited representatives of the news
media. During the second reading debate the Opposition registered very strong objection to
the Bill and to the fact that the Road Transport Association and interested parties had not
been given adequate opportunities to make their views known to the Government and to
officials.
The first schedule urgently requires reconsideration. At present it specifies vehicle types
in terms of the number of axles, but fails to give effect to the Government's intention of
ensuring that road user charges reflect road usage and the likelihood of road damage. Many
anomalies have been identified, and, if the first schedule is not changed, it will fail to reflect
road usage adequately. A number of speakers from this side pointed out the need to identify
each distinct type of heavy motor vehicle according to a formula which will more accurately
reflect road usage than the present formula, which is based on the number of axles. One
anomaly pointed out on a number of occasions was the differential in road damage resulting
from trucks with wide-spaced axles and those with narrow-gauge axles.
The member for Heretaunga drew attention to the New Zealand roading director's
confirmation that, if a vehicle's axles are close together, that causes one flexing in the road,
while two or more spaced axles cause less road wear than one heavy flexing and, therefore,
less damage. The member for Marlborough disputed that assertion, but the Opposition has
expert advice that its information is corrrect and that the information given to the member
for Marlborough and other Government members is incorrect. This is one of our strong
reasons for urging the Government to send the Bill to a select committee for urgent
reconsideration, so that the matter can be thrashed out after expert witnesses have been
heard. It can then decide who is right so that equity will prevail and the road tax will fall, as it
should, on people operating configurations of rigs and transport doing most damage to our
roads. The Road Transport Association has said all along that it is willing to pay a fair share
of road tax, and we have no reason to doubt its sincerity.
Some people believe-and there are good reasons for this-that the charges set out in
the schedule will not fall equitably, because a great mistake has been made in the
calculations worked out by the officials. I am certain they would not have done that
deliberately, but the only way the mistake can be rectified is for expert witnesses to give
evidence to a select committee of representatives of both parties.
Because there is a limit to the amount a road can bend at any one point, two axles close
together cannot evenly carry as much weight as do two axles spaced apart. For instance,
vehicle type 17, loaded to 14½ tonnes, will bend the road to the same extent as one spaced
twin-tyred axle vehicle loaded to 8.2 tonnes; but the present first schedule fails to recognise
that. This was only one of eight examples given by the member for Heretaunga, the member
for Grey Lynn, the member for Onehunga, the member for Hutt, and the member for
Otahuhu-and time did not permit our giving all the examples we had. Vehicle type 16
causes more wear than vehicle type 17.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! The honourable member is giving us a second reading
speech. He has just told us that the information had already been given during the second
reading debate. It is proper to make only passing reference to illustrate the point he is trying
to make that the Bill be referred to a select committee so that expert evidence can be heard

needed if we are to have an equitable road tax system, something we certainly do not have in
the Bill as it now stands.
In yesterday's New Zealand Herald the country's largest dairy company, the New
Zealand Co-operative Dairy Company, pointed out to the Government-which seems
determined to railroad this Bill through the House-that it will cost it an additional $386,000
in taxation for its enterprises. More than 5000 farmers in the South Auckland and Waikato
regions will be seriously affected by the provisions of this Bill simply because until now the
Government has refused to allow the detailed consideration which the measure deserves.
The prepurchasing of licences, accompanied by the appropriate road user charges, will
impose a strain on the cash flow of companies dealing in heavy motor vehicles.
The present Bill requires distance charge payments to be made monthly in advance of
the receipt of money for work performed. The liquidity problems of rural operators in
particular will be greatly accentuated. There is every reason to believe that it would be far
more equitable to allow distance tax to be paid quarterly and to have quarterly reconcilia-
tions. The machinery is set up. No reason has been given why this system cannot operate.
We believe that the road transport operators and the users of transport, be they primary or
secondary industries, have a right to know why quarterly reconciliations would not work
equitably and fairly. That is the reason for seeking to refer the Bill to a select committee-all
those anomalies could be ironed out.

problems have not been sorted out. I regret that the Bill came in so late. I said that when it
was introduced, and during the second reading. I know everyone will say that we are in the
last stages of the session, so we should let the Bill go through and see what happens-but we
know what will happen. The Road Transport Association knows what will happen. Both the
association and the Opposition have done an exercise, particularly in relation to the first
schedule. We know that there are errors, and, knowing that, we would be failing in our duty
as an Opposition if we did not point them out to the Government to ensure that road
transport operators and the users of road transport will not suffer because of increased
charges resulting from the passage of this Bill-a Bill that will not ensure that taxation falls
equitably on all members of the road transport industry. We urge the Government to
reconsider this very seriously indeed, and to refer the Bill to a select committee now.
If select committee hearings cannot be held until early next year, then the Government
should suspend the Bill's passage and keep existing taxation in operation until matters are
settled. A bridging system could operate. The Government will be failing in its duty if it does
not accept the Opposition's suggestion that the whole matter be considered by a select
committee. We will co-operate with Government members to ensure that road transport
operators and road users have a taxation system that falls fairly on all of them, and to ensure
that no anomaly exists regarding the additional impost being levied on transport operators
and users of transport.

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The point raised is certainly an interesting one. Standing
Order 230 reads: "A Bill having been read a second time shall be ordered to be committed to
a Committee of the Whole House on a future day”—that is one option-"or, alternatively,
on an appropriate resolution, the House shall refer the Bill to a Select Committee." As
honourable members will recall, the House took urgency on Friday. The Minister obtained
the call to reply to the debate at 2.25 p.m., and concluded his reply at about 2.35 p.m. or
shortly thereafter. That was the end of that debate; the Bill had then been read a second
time. The options open to me were to declare the Bill set down for committal next sitting
day and the reference to "next sitting day" indicates the place in which it is to go on the
Order Paper on the next occasion it is printed, which would have been Tuesday,
yesterday—or to permit the alternative procedure to be followed. In fact, that alternative
was adopted by the House in that an appropriate resolution was moved to refer the Bill to a
select committee.
Although arguments as to why the Bill should go to a select committee may have been
advanced during the second reading debate—and I am not disputing that—the point is that,
as distinct from the motion to refer a Bill to a select committee after the introduction debate,
when the debate is taken together with the debate on the motion to introduce the Bill, we
allow references to the fact that the Bill should be referred to a select committee. The two
debates are taken together, although two separate motions are put afterwards. If the House
decides it would like to send the Bill to a select committee after the second reading, that is a
separate motion and a separate debate. Not only is a separate motion put, but there is a
separate debate preceding the separate motion.
The question I have to decide is whether the Bill, having been read a second time on
Friday and on that occasion the motion having been moved, that it be referred to a select
committee at a later date or forthwith, presumably the motion could not have been put then
because we had urgency for Orders of the Day down as far as we went, which was, I think,
that Bill only. It ended on the second reading of that Bill, not on a motion to refer it to a
select committee which, as I said, is a separate motion. Debate on that was not allowed,
because we had exceeded the time allowed for normal business of the House on Friday, and
we were in urgency time. No further business could have been discussed at that time.
Obviously, the debate had to be set down for resumption on the next time the Order Paper
came up, which was yesterday.
The Road User Charges Bill was shown on yesterday's Order Paper as "Road User
Charges Bill-that the Bill be referred to a select committee". As honourable members,
know, it was not taken yesterday, and came up as the first Order of the Day today. I have to
decide whether the Bill-having been read a second time on Friday and the motion having
been put then to refer it to a select committee-should more appropriately be referred to the
Committee of the Whole forthwith or to the Committee of the Whole next sitting day.

of the Bill not being referred to a select committee, there is no requirement in the Standing
Order for it to be referred to the Committee of the Whole on a future day. My presumption,
therefore, is that it can be referred either forthwith-presently, today--or on a future day.
That is why I would take the pleasure of the Minister in charge of the Bill as to whether he
wishes it to be so referred. Had it been desired that the Standing Orders should provide that
the Bill should be referred to the Committee of the Whole House on a future day in the
event of the motion to refer it to a select committee being defeated, I am certain the
Standing Order would have been explicit on that matter; but it is not, and I believe a certain
degree of discretion is allowed. The sensible thing would be for the Bill to be referred for
committal presently. The Road User Charges Bill, therefore, is referred for committal
presently.

NOXIOUS PLANTS BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Noxious
Plants Bill be introduced. The Bill arises from a report of a committee on noxious weeds
administration that was established by the former National Government in 1972. The
committee reported to the Labour Government in 1973. Its recommendations have been
widely accepted as a blueprint for change in noxious weed control. Because of the extent and
significance of the proposals, and the desirability of consolidating all noxious weeds
legislation, it has been decided to replace both the present Noxious Weed Act and the
Nassella Tussock Act and to combine their provisions in the new Bill.
The Bill establishes a Noxious Plants Council to define policy and guide administration.
It will have an independent chairman, and the Department of Lands and Survey, the Forest
Service, the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, the Municipal Association, and commer-
cial and technical interests will each have a representative. The Counties Association and
Federated Farmers will have two members each. The council will decide which noxious
plants should be in class A or class B, and will recommend to the Minister of Agriculture the
forms and procedures for financial assistance that are warranted. The two nassella tussock
boards will be retained as now constituted. The Noxious Plants Council has been constituted
to ensure the active involvement and committal of those most directly concerned with
noxious plants and their control.
It is intended to promote a planned approach to noxious plant control, both nationally
and locally. As well as the national council, there will be eight regional co-ordinating
committees, each to cover a region of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. The
chairman is to be the ministry's regional advisory officer, with representatives from the
Department of Lands and Survey, district noxious plants authorities, and each province of
Federated Farmers. The functions of the committees will be to co-ordinate all noxious plants
administration within their region, and to recommend classifications and procedures to the
Noxious Plants Council. Territorial local government will remain responsible for noxious
plants control and administration. The district noxious plants authorities to be formed will be
the local authorities in the various regions—or, in some circumstances, an amalgamation of
two authorities.
The Crown will be bound by the new Act-something I am sure that many landowners


## p. 5372 (#808) ###########################################

5372
15 December
Noxious Plants Bill
bordering Crown property will welcome-with land-holding departments responsible for
financing and undertaking their own control programmes in co-ordination with each other
and the Noxious Plants Council. Noxious plants will be classified into class A or class B.
Government assistance through the Noxious Plants Council would cover the cost of class A
eradication—a very small number of dangerous noxious plants-and, where considered
necessary and warranted, assist in the control of class B noxious plants and the subsequent
follow-up. As well, the council will be expected to initiate research and action for early
control, particularly of aquatic weeds, which have been uncontrolled under the present
legislation.
It is desirable to put noxious plants into two categories-classes A and B, because
different species need different methods of control and eradication. The cost of eradication
is also different. Government assistance for class A plants would be for immediate eradica-
tion, and the follow-up work would be left to the owner or occupier. Many of the noxious
plants under the class B category could be different in different regions. This, of course, is
already enshrined in present structures. People who are interested or involved in this work
will be aware of the various committees set up under the main agricultural Act at present in
operation. The legislation puts the control mechanism we are all familiar with into a different
form.
The Bill is important. As the cost of the eradication of noxious weeds is high, both to the
individual and to the nation, it is desirable to have the most efficient method of control. The
committee set up in 1972 considered that the proposals in the Bill-which follow the
committee's 1973 recommendations-provide the most logical and sensible methods of
approach to this work. Because of the widespread interest of farmers, landowners, and local
authorities in the legislation, it is proposed to refer the Bill to the Lands and Agriculture
Committee for recess study.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Minister, of course, is aware of the pressure that
both he and I have been under to have the Bill introduced. He will also be aware that
because of that pressure I suggested to him that there was still time for the legislation to be
introduced this year and to be referred to a select committee. I am glad the Bill is going to a
committee, because it is of major importance to our primary industry and the country.
The other major factor is the obligation of the Crown to eradicate noxious weeds. I have
had a quick look through the Bill, and the noxious plants in classes A and B do not appear to
be named. I am sure that people making representations to the committee will ask about
that, because it is important to primary industry. Under this legislation, the Nassella Tussock
Board will be put on a better basis. The Opposition welcomes the Bill, and looks forward to
hearing from interested parties. I have no doubt that the points made by the committee
which considered all these matters will be further elaborated on during the select committee
hearing.

on Crown and Maori land shall fall to the responsibility of the Department of Lands and

Lands and Survey co-ordinate activities on Maori land rather than Maori landowners
accepting their responsibility to eradicate noxious weeds? Why can the Government not deal

No one is opposed to this legislation, but the best way for the Government to achieve its
aim is to ensure that landowners realise their responsibilities. I am sure the committee will
look at how this might be done. An area of land, which it does not own, cannot be vested in
the Crown, unless it wants to pay for eradicating noxious weeds. The Government seems to
consider that communal ownership of land is of secondary importance. It is not. Discussions

further, and a removal order was served. I am told that the person concerned has appealed
against the order and a hearing is set down for 30 January. As this is entirely a question of

Government makes and enforces its own laws on entry and residence.

Racism in Justice Department
3. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Mr McLAY (Birkenhead) asked the
Minister of Justice: Has he seen the article in the Christchurch Star of 28 November 1977 in
which Dr O. Sutherland of the Auckland Committee on Racism and Discrimination claimed

was better qualified than those appointed, and, if so, can he advise whether this claim is
correct?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Yes, I have seen the article to which the
honourable member refers. The claim made by Dr Sutherland has been the subject of
consideration by the Royal Commission on the Courts and the subject of a formal complaint
to the Race Relations Conciliator. The position referred to in the newspaper article is that of
a bailiff in the magistrate's court in Auckland. I can assure the honourable member that,
following a full investigation of the allegations made by Dr Sutherland, the Race Relations
Conciliator found no evidence at all to support any allegation of racial prejudice in failing to
appoint the Nuiean to the position. In fact, a Fijian Indian was appointed to one of the
vacancies.

countries, such as the Islands, and as the Niuean Government is so desperate for manpower

Justice Department-Responsibility for Judges' Materials
6. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), on behalf of Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Hender-
son), asked the Minister of Justice: Is there any reason why his department should not accept
full responsibility for providing judges with the materials necessary for the discharge of their
duties?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I presume that the honourable
member's question may have been prompted by an article in the Northern News newsletter of
the Auckland District Law Society on the amount available for the upkeep of the judges'
library in Auckland. My department does accept this responsibility. The procedures for
funding the separate judges' libraries differ from centre to centre. In Auckland a grant has
been made since 1958 towards the cost of books. There has been no way of knowing in
advance how much the society will claim for this purpose. As recently as 1975-76 the amount
claimed was only $900. It rose suddenly to $3,000 in 1976-77. For the present financial year,
the amount allocated in my department's estimates is $3,500, and the department is naturally
unwilling to overspend. The situation is recognised as being unsatisfactory, and from 1 April
next the department will take over direct responsibility for maintaining the judges' libraries
and relieve law societies of their responsibility in this regard. Every effort will be made, after
consultation with Their Honours or persons nominated by them, to obtain adequate funds
for the purpose. Obviously, however, as with all heads of expenditure, a certain amount

want, but there is a limit. We shall certainly ensure that they are provided with essential
material, but I cannot guarantee that they will get everything every one of Their Honours
thinks is desirable.
Mr Prebble: Does the Minister's confirmation that restriction on Government funds is
the reason mean that the National Government does not accept as part of its responsibility a
duty to see that judges have all the money they consider is necessary to give justice to New
Zealand citizens.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The member is quite wrong. I have already told the House
that from 1 April next the Department of Justice will take over direct responsibility for
maintaining the judges' libraries and relieve law societies of their responsibility, and that
every effort will be made, after consultation with Their Honours or persons nominated by
them, to obtain adequate funds for the purpose.

National Superannuation Payments
11. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: When will
widows' benefits be paid fortnightly and directly into a banking account?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Widows' and other long-term social
security benefits are at present paid 4-weekly, and there are no facilities for direct crediting
of those benefits. However, it is intended to bring the payment of all long-term benefits into
line with national superannuation and family benefits, which are currently paid fortnightly
and for which there is already provision for payment directly into bank accounts. It is
expected that the new payment system, which will include the payment of widows' benefits,
will be fully operative by the end of 1978.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: What is the proportion of benefits at present paid directly into a
bank account?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: As I have said, direct crediting is available for only two benefits.
About 50 percent of all family benefits is paid directly into bank accounts or other savings
accounts, and about 50 percent of national superannuitants have their benefits paid directly
into bank accounts. It is gratifying to note that the number of national superannuitants who
have their money paid directly into bank accounts is increasing.

Migration Statistics
13. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Immigration: Can he confirm that an
examination of migration statistics under the category "New Zealand residents departing for
a period of 12 months or less" and "New Zealand residents returning after a period of 12
months or less" indicates that there are more people returning under these categories than
there are departing, and, if so, can he indicate whether the corollary is also true—that is, that
a number of New Zealand residents who claim to be departing "permanently" in fact do not
do so, but return to New Zealand under a different statistical category within 2 years of their
departure?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): In the year ended September 1977 the
number of New Zealand residents returning after an absence of 12 months or less was
265 752, although only 262 365 New Zealand residents were recorded as departing with the
intention of staying away less than 12 months. The difference of more than 2000 was similar
to that in the previous year. In each of the past 7 years this pattern has been evident. It is
correct to conclude that many New Zealand residents who claim to be departing perma-
nently, or for more than 12 months, in fact return within 12 months.
Mr Malcolm: Can the Minister say whether the difference between the number of
people returning to and departing from New Zealand is greater during the summer
months-for example, at the end of March?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The number of people returning to New Zealand tends to reach a
peak before Christmas, and the number of people departing tends to increase about the end
of March as people leave to miss the New Zealand winter and enjoy a European summer.
Mr Malcolm: As the present system of collecting immigration statistics from the cards
people fill out is producing an anomaly in the figures, has the Minister considered using a
more accurate way of calculating the figures, or changing the categories shown on the card?
Hon. T. F. GILL: New departure and arrival cards are being designed, but this will not
materially alter the position. Compiling the statistics presents no problem-the additions are
done correctly, as is the recording of the information. The problem lies in the information
supplied by the person filling in the card. From time to time complaints are made that many
skilled people are leaving New Zealand. Everybody who fills in a departure card and relates
it to their employment has some skill. If the cards are not kept simple, people become bored
and just tick the card all the way down. The system is fallible, but it is the best we can do.
Other countries face the same problems, and we must learn to live with them.
