PUBLIC EXPENDITURE COMMITTEE-ANNUAL REPORT
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I am directed by the Public Expenditure Committee to present
the annual report of the committee. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. I want to
comment briefly on the content of the report. The committee has had a full year, and has
touched on some important and interesting subjects. Part I deals with the action taken on
previous committee recommendations, and contains comments from departments on prog-
ress made in implementing Public Expenditure Committee recommendations in past years.
The committee felt strongly that there has been some undue delay in actioning past
recommendations, some of which are outstanding from 1970. It is intended to introduce
follow-up procedures next year to ensure that more rapid and effective action is taken by
departments.
Part II of the report deals with the investigations of the full Public Expenditure
Committee. The committee carried out detailed investigations, as it did last year, into the
administration of major Government departments, and those selected for examination this
year were the Department of Internal Affairs, the Department of Social Welfare, and the
Railways Department. The committee found the standard of administration generally
satisfactory in the first two departments, particularly financial management, which is its main
interest. However, the committee gained the impression that the financial procedures of the
Railways Department are out of date and need upgrading. Recommendations are made
accordingly in the report.
The committee also examined its own procedures, and reports on three important
aspects: (1) as a continuation of the closer liaison being developed with the Controller and
Auditor-General, the committee will have available to it from next year a full-time audit
officer, who will assist the committee during special investigations; (2) the committee intends
to extend its activities into certain areas of local authority administration to the extent that
this is permitted by its terms of reference; (3) the committee has studied and clarified its
power to obtain information from officials.
Part III of the report deals with the reports of subcommittees, and the full report of two
subcommittees are contained in this part of the report together with interim reports from two
others. The subcommittee on pillaging has almost finished its inquiry, and the motion moved
by the Deputy Prime Minister today will allow that report to be published during the recess.
A subcommittee under the chairmanship of Hon. R. L. Bailey is investigating the Kaimai
Tunnel. This subcommittee will sit during the recess, and its report, if completed, will be

RODNEY COUNTY COUNCIL (MAHURANGI HARBOUR) VESTING AND
EMPOWERING BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. I extend my sincere thanks to the Local Bills Committee for the consideration it
gave to the Bill, and I appreciate that its decision was not an easy one. The Bill provides legal
authority for the reclamation work necessary for setting up oxidation ponds in the
Mahurangi Harbour, pursuant to the Rodney County Council's sewerage scheme. The
committee has recommended that the Bill proceed, but that it should come into effect on 1
February.
The committee was caught between two opposing groups, and was asked to decide a
highly technical matter, with large issues at stake, and with very little time for deliberation.
On the one hand, the committee had an obligation to the Rodney County Council, which in


## p. 5383 (#819) ###########################################

15 December
5383
Rodney County Council Vesting and Empowering Bill
turn has a statutory obligation to provide sewerage services, and had taken a lot of trouble to
canvass local opinion in a genuine endeavour to find an acceptable solution. On the other
hand, the committee felt it had an obligation to the Snells Beach Ratepayers Association,
which provided specific and well-prepared alternative proposals involving a land irrigation
method of disposal. The scheme has an immediate environmental attraction and is claimed
to be economically attractive.
In recommending that the Bill should not come into force until 1 February the
committee recognised the worth of the submission presented by the Snells Beach Ratepayers
Association. In the report to the Rodney County Council the chairman of the Local Bills
Committee stated: "I also refer to the submissions put forward by the Snells Beach
Ratepayers and Residents Association, which in my opinion were easily the most detailed
and comprehensive I had heard from any individual or group on local legislation, and this
was one reason for the course of action proposed by the committee in its rider."
The committee could have recommended that the Bill not come into force until some
date to be decided by Order in Council, but it felt, justifiably, that that would be less than
fair to the Rodney County Council. The committee has recommended that the Bill come into
force from 1 February, but with the following rider: "That the attention of the Rodney
County Council and the Snells Beach Ratepayers and Residents Association be drawn to the
proposed amendment to clause 1, which provides for the Act to come into force on 1
February 1978, in the hope that both parties may have further discussions on the merits of
the comprehensive alternative proposal contained in the association's submissions to the
Local Bills Committee."
The recommendation is not without national significance. As I said in my introductory
speech, a local authority like the Rodney County Council could have installed a sewerage
system with minimal opposition a few years ago, but today it has to contend with the sort of
strong environmental opposition that has affected us all to a greater or lesser degree.
Whenever a local authority wants to install oxidation ponds it faces opposition from
someone who objects to the smell, the midges, the appearance, or the disruption of the
natural ecology. If the local authority wants to discharge the effluent from the ponds into the
sea, it runs up against another crop of objections. Wherever the outfall goes, someone will
object that the effluent could affect local shellfish beds, that it will wash up on the beach
when the tide is going in a certain direction, or that the value of the properties in the vicinity
will be undermined.
This reaction will be experienced in closely settled coastal areas, and to an increasing
extent it is being encountered in other coastal areas, especially in the semi-landlocked areas
of the North Auckland peninsula where more and more people are competing for the use of
waterways. People want to use them for swimming, water ski-ing, boating, boat mooring,
shellfish farming, scientific research, and so on, and the discharge of sewage effluent is
compatible with none of these uses. So we have already reached the stage where public
opinion regards the use of oxidation ponds with effluent outfall into the sea as undesirable,
yet we continue to install them because we have yet to find a workable alternative. When we
install them we do so at enormous cost.
Local authorities and their ratepayers find themselves burdened with six or seven-figure
schemes, commitments which, even with the aid of the Government subsidy, will take years
to pay off. The six and seven-figure sum buys a structure for treating sewage that is unsightly
at the best of times, and unwanted wherever it goes. At the discharge end it is equally
offensive, and there are also expensive outfall pipes.
From my own experience of sewage disposal problems in my electorate, I agree that we
need to find more environmentally acceptable and economic sewage disposal methods. The
time has come to do a thorough in-depth study of overseas methods for the disposal of
sewage. I know officials have done some work in this area, but the time has come for a really
full, comprehensive, and systematic study. If we can find suitable alternatives, the environ-
mental gains will be great, and large sums of money could be saved. Those are a few
comments of a general nåture which I wanted to make at this stage.
Now I want briefly to refer to the Bill itself. It is in every respect a standard empowering
Bill of its kind, providing the usual clauses for vesting the land reclaimed in the local
authority, giving the authority to reclaim, safeguarding the private rights of people who
could be adversely affected, giving the local authority the power to carry out under contract
or licence the actual sewage work, and providing for nuisance, compensation, and bylaw
powers.
Bill read a second, and a third time.

mean that women will see the law as being too restrictive and that it will prevent them from
receiving a just hearing, so they will not go to their doctors. They will not seek the
counselling and advice that they have received in the past from their doctors, because the law
prevents their doctors from adopting a humane approach. Women will go to back-street
abortionists, or fly to Australian clinics. There is no doubt in my mind, as there must be no
doubt in the minds of any but the most naive, that abortions will continue. There may be
slightly fewer, but abortions will take place away from the family doctor, and in poor
unhygienic conditions, possibly at great cost, and maybe at risk of the woman's life.
A practical acceptable law would be humane. A practicable acceptable law would
encourage women to deal with their own doctors, and seek advice and counselling. A
practical and acceptable law will keep women away from back-street abortionists. A
practical and acceptable law would not stop abortions, but would reduce them to a
minimum. This law we are about to pass will not do that. It does none of those things. It is
ham-fisted. It is restrictive. It is extreme in the utmost. Parliament has tried to satisfy its own
conscience. Despite ample knowledge of back-street abortionists and ample knowledge of
trips to Australian clinics, members of this House, like Pontius Pilate, have tried to satisfy
their own consciences. [Interruption.]
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order!
Mr FRIEDLANDER: I want to see laws to protect the unborn child in this country, but I
want them to be humane, sensible, and workable. Therefore, I have no option but to vote
against the third reading.

out for the protection or preservation of the life or mental or physical health of the mother.
Those criteria will now be continued under the provisions of section 187A, contained in the
Bill as an amendment to the Crimes Act. In addition, we have specific provisions to deal with
extremes of age, and that rape, if it is believed to have occurred, should particularly be taken
into account in considering whether the mental or physical health of the mother could be
affected.
It has been suggested that foetal abnormality as a ground for abortion has been removed
from the Bill and that this in some way makes the law restrictive, yet this really records
nothing more than what has been the law for many years in New Zealand, since about 1908 I
believe, and certainly as far back as the Bourne case in 1939. Foetal abnormality had been
included in the Bill as a specific ground for abortion in its own right, and by removing it from
the Bill Parliament has returned it to its present status—namely, as one of the factors to be
considered by the doctors who have to ascertain whether the mental health of a woman is
likely to suffer as a consequence of foetal abnormality. It is my understanding that, under the
present law as it is interpreted in cases of serious foetal abnormality, it is accepted almost as
a matter of course that mental illness is likely to occur in the mother. If that is so now, then it
will continue to be so following the passage of this Bill, and therefore there is no amendment
on that ground.
The procedures in the Bill that have been described as the Birch amendment do no
more than seek to ensure that the law as laid down by the House is enforced and adopted. It
has been said that the Aotea clinic is only operating within the law. I am not in a position to
say whether that is so-I can only accept that a prosecution taken to the Supreme Court was
unsuccessful and assume that the abortions performed at the clinic are within the law.
However, if that is so there should be no change in the numbers that are being performed
because of the Birch amendments, which merely set out to enforce the law. If unlawful
abortions are being carried out, then the Birch amendments should prevent that happening
in the future. Why then should that hospital now say that, because of the amended Bill, it
will have to close its doors?
Miss Dewe: Tell us all about the Wall amendment.

The changed definition of the word "abortion" has been the subject of some comment

womb. My amendment related to the destruction of the foetus within the womb, and was not
covered by the definition relating to premature expulsion. I reject the suggestion that the
new definition of abortion has extended it to contraceptive measures.

"(b) Any taxpayer who is assessable for income tax under any of sections 199 to 203 of this Act
except to the extent to which, in the opinion of the Commissioner, any proportion of
sales of trading stock give rise to taxable income:
"(c) Any company to which section 42 of this Act applies:
"(d) Any company which carries on in New Zealand on behalf of a company to which section 42
of this Act applies the processing to the stage of primary metal or primary metal alloy of
any mineral as defined in that section.

amount equal to 5 percent of the value at the commencement of that income year of that trading
stock as taken into account for the purpose of calculating that assessable income.

INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be
now read a third time.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): In the Committee stage the
Opposition voted against clause 43, because it provides for greater tax relief to be given to
companies than the Bill provides for individuals. As the debate proceeded it became obvious
that the Government has a theoretical approach, which leads it to believe that if tax relief is
given to companies it may flow back and enhance the employment situation for individuals. I
remind Government members that that was precisely the attitude that cost the Australian
Labour Party the election in Australia. Labour Party members there made the mistake of
thinking that payroll tax relief was the alternative to an income tax concession.
The New Zealand public has been forced by the National Government-and the Bill
before the House includes some such measures to accept a position where it cannot buy the
goods produced in the country. The Government has said, "If you give the companies a
concession-but for heaven's sake don't call it inflation accounting-they will employ more
people, and everything will be magnificent." The member for Auckland Central put the
position succinctly and firmly. He said, "If you go on giving companies taxation relief, they
will increase their production and no one will be able to buy what they produce." That is
precisely the position, and Government members are talking a lot of nonsense. The
manufacturers will not produce if they cannot sell, and if they cannot sell they will not
employ labour.
The situation was explained as far back as the days of Mickey Savage. If the consumer
has money he will spend it on the goods of his choice; but Government members appear to
think that, by carefully choosing their friends for company tax relief, they can achieve the


## p. 5401 (#837) ###########################################

15 December
5401
Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2)
same result. We put that to the test, and the result is recorded in Hansard. Forty-four
Government members voted for the proposal, and 22 Opposition members voted against; so
Government members are doubly wrong.
During the debate we had another interesting dispute. The Prime Minister said, “Quote
me the time when I said I was going to get inflation down below 10 percent." That has a great
deal of relevance to clause 43, because the Minister who introduced the Bill said, "This is not
inflation accounting"; he was determined that no indirect references should be made to
inflation accounting. He emphasised, "This is unrelated to the general problem of inflation
accounting." Opposition members had something to say about inflation, and the Prime
Minister jumped up and said, “Quote me where I said I was going to get inflation down to 10
percent." Of course, he went even better than that, and said that he would get it down below
10 percent. In the New Zealand Herald of 22 September 1975 he is reported, first, as saying,
"There will be an opportunity next year"—and that was 1976, not 1977-"to reduce the
present level of 15 percent inflation to less than 10 percent by controlling the domestic
content of inflation." We all know how he did that-by putting up every Government
charge. He reduced subsidies and put up the rate of inflation. But, just in case anyone should
think that that is the only quote we have from him, here is another on 14 February 1976, in
which he is much more explicit. He says when he is going to do it. At that time he was Prime
Minister and running the economy. He said, "I think we have a chance in the second half of
the year of getting inflation down to under 5 percent. Our total inflation rate for the year
could then be less than 13 percent, and what I am looking to do is to get an annual rate of less
than 10 percent in the second half of the year."
Hon. M. Rata: Who said that?
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: None other than our champion economist, the self-declared
genius, R. D. Muldoon, Prime Minister-the one lone voice.
Mr Couch: And it was a good year.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: Hello, there is "Little Sir Echo" from the Wairarapa—I think from
the base of the scrum. I suggest that the Government has repeated the mistake of thinking
that politicians know better than people. It has said that company taxation is the way back to
jobs and prosperity. The people in Australia said, quite clearly, that cash in the pocket of the
consumer was the way back, and we are putting it on the line in this debate. We voted
against clause 43, because the Bill offers the possibility of a $75 million concession to
companies through tax relief, but other clauses gave no more than $59 million, at the very
best assessment, to individual taxpayers.
We are saying tonight that we are not going to vote against the Bill as it stands because
there is a concession to individual taxpayers, but we did vote against the clause that gave a
greater concession to companies. Only the company that makes a profit will get the
concession, not the one that needs relief. Priority will not be given to the company dealing in
foodstuffs or any other essential line. The company making a profit is selected. In a siege
situation, that company has rather more chance of trading its way out of its problems when
the consumer has money, but the company not making a profit gets nothing, and the
consumer who needs money to spend on essentials gets no more by clause 43, as amended in
the Supplementary Order Paper. That is what the Labour Party has done tonight.
Mr Birch: It has done nothing.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: It has served notice on the Government that, until it does
something for the ordinary citizen, it is doing nothing for anybody.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): This is the third reading of the whole
Bill and I suppose one should speak a little on what happened in the Committee, while at the
same time replying to one or two of the comments made by the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition, who thinks he has found the reason why the Labour Party crashed to such a
defeat in Australia. It was not just for that reason. It was really the Labour Party's failure in
Government, and on looking at the polls earlier this week one finds much the same thing
happening in New Zealand.
Mr Malcolm: He was not too far up in the poll.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not think he was sighted. The newest member on the
other side is the one who made the most progress, and that must be terribly galling for some
of the old has-beens.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! The right honourable gentleman would do us a favour
by coming back to the Bill. The question before the House is that the Bill be read a third
time. There is nothing in the Bill about the newest member in the House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: While you were out we were on that subject in the

15 December
Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Committee stage. We might have been out of order, but we were on the subject.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! It might have been in order in Committee. I am not a
judge of what is relevant in the Committee stage-that comes within the sole jurisdiction of
the Chairman-but I am responsible for relevancy when we are debating in the House.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It was not a question of relevancy. It was a question of
reporting what happened in the Committee, a little of which is traditionally done. If the
Chairman deemed it relevant in the Committee then by and large we report it on the third
reading so that it is recorded for posterity. I think posterity would be very much interested in
the argument during the Committee stage. However, I do not propose to go on with that. I
was just dealing with it in passing. I am sure the Deputy Leader of the Opposition wants us
to pass very rapidly over the debacle in Australia, and even more rapidly over the NRB poll
earlier this week in this country.
During the Committee stage, Opposition members failed totally to understand what this
new clause is all about. It is an attempt to preserve the jobs of large numbers of New
Zealanders, because in this Bill we have a clause which will give further purchasing power to
people next February by the personal income tax cut. The clause we are putting in tonight
will also enable producing companies, manufacturers and the like, to continue to produce so
that they can keep people on the payroll. Between the two we will next year give a little lift
to the economy. That is what it is all about. It is very obvious that no one on the other side
had the slightest inkling of what it was all about, which, although true to form, is
nevertheless somewhat distressing because they represent the second largest political party
in this country-not, I think, in membership, but certainly in numbers in the House.
Mr Malcolm: The third largest. "Don't know" is the second largest.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, from the point of view of the poll that is quite right.
The second largest is "don't know".
Hon. R. L. Bailey: A point of order, Mr Speaker. A little time ago you asked the Prime
Minister to speak to the third reading of the Bill, and you mentioned that there was nothing
in it about polls or popularity voting. The Prime Minister is persisting in following that line.
If he continues the Opposition will feel that it has the right to comment likewise. I do not
think that will help you one little bit in dealing with the business of the House. I do not think
it will help the Government very much either. The Government is here to get the legislation
through, and the Opposition is here to see that it is the right kind of legislation for the
country. My point of order is that the Prime Minister should be required to speak to the third
reading, as you requested earlier.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The requirement is that members speak to the motion before
the House, which is, at the moment, that the Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2) be read a
third time. There may be some confusion in the minds of some members about what may be
discussed during the third reading debate. Because a matter was raised in the Committee of
the Whole it may not necessarily be raised again during the third reading simply to record it
unless it happens to be related to one of the clauses of the Bill. If it is related to a clause in
the Bill it may be referred to during the third reading to place it on record. Members must
confine themselves to the general principles of the Bill as it emerged from the Committee of
the Whole. That is the point at issue, and we do not need to have any further mention of
polls.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Yes, Mr Speaker, I am sure you are right.
The Bill will give the economy a boost, which is needed at present. The Labour Government
lost the election in 1975 because it was not seen to be governing, and, in contrast to that
performance, the National Government is doing something. The Bill is a move to lift the
economy at a time when it needs a lift. The National Government can be seen to be
governing, which is why it did so well at the polls.
Bill read a third time.

electorate shall be charged to the candidates proportionately, provided that national or regional
election expenses not related to the election of specific candidate or incurred by or on behalf of a
specific candidate shall not be included in a candidate's election expenses.
(7) Section 2(1) of the principal Act is hereby amended by repealing the definition of the term
"election expenses".
(8) Every candidate shall include in his returns a list of all donations and donors of all donations
of $100 or more and in the event of the donation being from a committee or political party then the
original source of that donation.
(9) No candidate shall accept a donation of over $500 from any source apart from his own
political party and no candidate shall accept a donation of over $100 from any person who is not a
permanent resident of New Zealand or from a Company that is not registered in New Zealand or
from a company registered in New Zealand which is more than fifty percent foreign owned.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I thought we would again take urgency
for the passing of various matters still on the Order Paper, and perhaps get through it some
time later today. That would mean we would have only the valedictory on Tuesday of next
week. I am told that technically we could finish today's sitting and then meet again later in
the day for the valedictory. However, the idea does not commend itself to me. I think we
should do it properly and see how we go with the business today, and come back on Tuesday.
We deliberately left a few things last night that could have been debated. We did not think it
appropriate, despite the actions of the Opposition, to take the whole of the Order Paper as
we could have done. We can talk about a number of things this morning, and maybe this
afternoon, and then have the valedictory on Tuesday.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): The Prime Minister said that it had been suggested
to him-apparently by some of his advisers-that after completing the business of the House
we could take the valedictory later today. I suggest that he give consideration to this action,
if good progress is made during the morning and early afternoon, rather than inconvenience
all members and staff for what would be a very brief formal meeting of Parliament next
week.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I said I would consider the matter, but I
am bound to say that last night we got stuck on things, and, frankly, at a certain stage
members were just talking. I have to make provision for the same thing happening today. If
we go through the Committee stage of Bills in the way we can do, and members know we can
do, then I would be only too happy to finish today. Frankly, there was a time yesterday when
we were debating out clauses. As a result, we did not finish at the time we had
hoped-indeed, we did not finish at all. I am quite easy about it. If we go through the
remaining items on the Order Paper in a reasonable way, without debating out Bills, which
will pass anyway, then I would be very happy to come back this afternoon for the
valedictory, and get the whole thing over today.
However, I said a long time ago that I would not keep the House sitting long hours just
to save a day. We will take the number of days necessary to complete the business of the
House. I am told that the procedure I have mentioned is possible, if we can get through
smoothly. It would mean that the last of the Bills could go away for assent, and we could
then sit for those Bills and the valedictory. I should be only too happy to do that.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Smoking
1. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: Has he read the article
entitled "Illogical, Unethical To Promote Smoking-Society" in the Evening Post of 13
December, in which it is stated that "It is important that anti-smoking organisations
emphasise to Governments that tobacco is causing one of the greatest epidemics in modern
times and that it is illogical, unethical, and unintelligent to permit the advertising of such
products", and can he indicate how many anti-smoking organisations have made this view
known to the Government and what course of action the Department of Health is pursuing?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I am aware of the contents of the article, and this
view has been expressed by four anti-smoking organisations and many individuals over the
past year to both myself and the department. Their views have been brought to the attention
of the recently established Advisory Committee on Smoking and Health. A partial ban on
advertising is set out in a voluntary agreement. This precludes television, radio, cinema, and
road-hoarding advertisements, limits the size and content of newspaper advertising, and
requires a warning notice to be printed on cigarette packets. The committee on smoking and
health is at present considering the whole question of tobacco promotion by direct and
indirect advertising and is in the process of making recommendations to this end.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Does the Minister honestly believe that the actions now being
contemplated are adequate to meet the health needs of our people?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It is really not a question of what the Minister believes or does not
believe. In the final analysis, people will make up their own minds whether or not they want
to smoke. I should like to see less advertising but I think that working through the smoking
committee--which is a good committee and I hope will be influential, because it is outside
the House, with no appearance of the Government or Parliament dictating to people on
what their smoking habits should be-is likely to achieve the best long-term success.

Potatoes with Hollow Heart
3. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Has he read the
article entitled "Heart-Sinking Hollow Bite" contained in the Evening Post of 13 December,
in which the condition of hollow heart in potatoes is outlined, and can he indicate how
prevalent this condition is and whether there is any indication that the problem is increasing,
and can he confirm whether the recently passed Potato Industry Act contains provisions to
deal with this problem?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): The reply of the Minister of
Agriculture is as follows: "Yes, I have read the article referred to by the member for
Hamilton East. It is not possible to stipulate how widespread the hollow-heart condition is,
or whether the problem is increasing. A check made with the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries, the New Zealand Potato Board, and the New Zealand Vegetable and Produce
Growers Federation, indicates that no other complaints have been received. Although there
is provision for minimum quality standards in the Potato Industry Act, it is envisaged that if
the hollow-heart problem becomes widespread the growers concerned will be advised of
husbandry practices necessary to prevent future recurrences, without imposing regulations
under the Act."
Social Welfare Beneficiaries-Taxation Relief
4. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Finance: In view of
the fact that, in terms of Government policies, people on high incomes and business
enterprises have received considerable tax relief, income supplements, and/or other
benefits, does he propose to make some additional assistance available to people with little
or no other income but social welfare payments?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The Government's policy in respect
of social welfare payments is that they are adjusted every 6 months in January and July. The
full percentage rise in the consumer price index is applied to benefit rates. National
superannuation is similarly adjusted 6-monthly by passing on the full percentage increase in
the average ordinary-time wage revealed by 6-monthly survey. In addition, the rate of
superannuation for a married couple will be increased in August of next year from 70 percent
to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time wage. These regular adjustments ensure that
social welfare beneficiaries maintain relativity with other members of the community.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Does the Prime Minister not appreciate that some people have
received considerably more than those on lower incomes who have merely had cost of living
adjustments; and does he not appreciate that unless he treats all sections of the community
even-handedly he will be seen to be pursuing a policy of ignoring the needy in order to
reward those less in need?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not think that is the case at all, because what the
member should realise is that if we move national superannuation from 70 percent to 80
percent of the average ordinary-time wage we will be working considerably in advance of
increases in the consumer price index. That is the important aspect of national
superannuation-that we move gradually over a period of a year or two up to 80 percent of


## p. 5413 (#849) ###########################################

16 December
5413
Oral Answers to Questions
the average ordinary-time wage, and that is an extra. In addition, increases will be given in
accordance with wage rate increases. That is what the member is overlooking. That in
essence, is the equivalent of what he says are income supplements and/or other benefits. I
am not quite sure what he means by that. People on national superannuation get tax relief as
well, as it is taxable.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Pin money for many of them.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: He asks us to give them some more, and when we do he
calls it pin money. What he is saying is, obviously, that it is not worth giving, and if there was

Employment Schemes for University Students, South Auckland
5. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Recreation and Sport: What
student employment schemes for university students have been approved for implementa-
tion by local authorities in the South Auckland area since the inception of the scheme?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Recreation and Sport): Six different projects put
forward under the student community service programme by local authorities and other
community organisations in the Manukau, Papatoetoe, Papakura, and Manurewa areas have
been approved to date. These will provide employment for 43 students. The projects include
a survey of the needs of young people in Manukau City, the provision of holiday program-
mes by a mobile team of students, and the upgrading of two community buildings in
Papakura.
Mr Wellington: What applications, in addition to those mentioned, are at present under
consideration by the ministry?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I do not have that information. I do not intend to waste the time
of the House, but I could give the member a breakdown into the various city councils of the
figures I have mentioned.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is the Minister in a position to say if those 43 students have in
fact commenced work, or, if not, when they will do so?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Yes. The eight students employed by the Papakura City Council
to clean down, prime, and give an undercoat of paint to the exterior walls and roofs of two
Army surplus barrack buildings are due to start any day; the 16 students that the Department
of Labour will assist the Manukau City Council to employ, to undertake research and survey
work, should start next week; the grant of $5,300 to the Manukau City Council will cover the
cost of employing 5 students for 8 weeks, and they will start on Monday, if they have not
already started. That is all the information I have.
Mr Wellington: I assume that the schemes referred to by the Minister do not include
those approved for, say, community organisations, but only those approved for local
authorities?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I could go further and say that a grant of $1,100 has been made to
the Manurewa Community Co-operative to pay the wages of one student for 11 weeks; so
the information I gave was not confined to local authorities.

Hamilton Post Office Staff Numbers
7. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Postmaster-General: Can he indicate the
total number of persons employed by the Hamilton Post Office in October, November, and
December of 1976 and 1977?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): The numbers of persons employed in
the Hamilton Post Office district, including staff of the engineering branch, were as follows:
1 October 1976, 2622; 1 October 1977, 2627; 1 November 1976, 2610; 1 November 1977,

advance and, if it can, it transfers permanent employees away and brings in temporary staff,
who are employed on the understanding that their job will finish when the cut-over is made.
Because of the size of the Post Office, there is normally no difficulty in redeploying
permanent staff, and if all else fails we have a redundancy agreement providing for severance
pay.
Housing Corporation-Payments to Builders
8. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Housing: Is he aware
that contractors in the Christchurch area building houses for the State or financed by State
loans are said to be waiting for up to 3 months for progress and final payments, and that this
is of concern not only to themselves but also to subcontractors whom they in turn pay, and
will he examine the basis of payment to ensure speedier payments?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I am assured that the Housing
Corporation makes payments to its contractors and to solicitors on loan cases without delay,
but in isolated instances there may be unavoidable delays and the reasons may not be known
to the contractor. If the honourable member has information of cases in which payments
have been delayed, I shall certainly have them investigated if he supplies the particulars to
me. I should add that no building contractor in Christchurch has made representations to me
directly on this matter, even though I am in Christchurch regularly.
Hon. Michael Connelly: The Minister may not have discussed the position with
subcontractors, but will he not agree that today it takes longer to effect progress and final
payments than was the position formerly, and that this creates liquidity and cash-flow
problems not only for the business people concerned but also for the community, and this is
detrimental to business confidence generally?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I would agree with the last half of the question if, in fact, it
was happening. However, I can assure the honourable member that I have given instructions
to the Housing Corporation that there are to be no unnecessary delays in making payments.
Indeed, in August last year-that is, August 1976-an instruction was issued to the
corporation speeding up the process by which progress payments were to be made. I have
taken this matter up on a number of occasions, particularly when some comment has been
made to me on the subject, and I have yet to find any serious cases of delays that have not
been occasioned by fault not directly attributable to the contractor, or to the solicitor in the
case of loan applications.
Hon. Michael Connelly: As it appears that the instruction given in 1976 may now have
been overlooked by some branches of his department, will the Minister arrange for it to be
reissued?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The corporation is well aware of the instruction. I repeat that
if the honourable member is aware of a case in which the instruction is not being obeyed and
there is a delay in making payments I shall have it investigated immediately if he gives me the
particulars.

Heart Surgery Unit, Waikato Hospital
10. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-
SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the Minister of Health: Why has he decided to delay the


## p. 5416 (#852) ###########################################

5416
16 December
Oral Answers to Questions
establishment of a heart surgery unit at Waikato Hospital?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Hospitals Advisory Council, which is the
statutory body set up to advise me on such matters as the establishment of specialist units,
recommended that no action should be taken at this stage to establish a heart surgery unit at
Waikato. The council considered that a decision should be deferred pending: (1) an
assessment of the programmes at Wellington and Dunedin after 1 year from the date of
implementation of the recommendations of the Ross report; and (2) the submission by Sir
Brian Barratt-Boyes of a report on the relationship of his service at Green Lane Hospital to
the Waikato need. I accepted the council's recommendations, and have arranged to meet the
Waikato Hospital Board next week to discuss my decision with them.
Mr Wetere: Can I take it that a decision will be made in 1 year's time?

considered in the meantime, and that very serious consideration will be given to the effects
of what is happening in Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin. I remind the House that
only a year ago, at the request of Sir Brian Barratt-Boyes and his team, we increased the
capacity of the unit in Auckland from 12 to 15. It is quicker to get a patient from Hamilton to
Auckland than to get the theatre ready for the operation. While there is no pressure on the
Auckland unit-and I understand this is the case, and we have asked for a report on the
situation—the need for a unit at Hamilton is not as great as the need for units in other parts
of the country.
Dr Shearer: Can the Minister confirm that monthly board meeting reports suggest that
the theatre for such surgery would not be available until 1979?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No. I do not peruse the board reports in that detail, so I cannot
confirm that, but I can say that, if there is any surplus capacity in the theatres at Hamilton,
those theatres are not being used for the purpose for which they were built and for which
finance was provided.

production concerned with human relationships rather than visually spectacular events.

Molesworth and Glazebrook-Hunting Access
16. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Lands: Can he give figures of
hunting access provided to the Molesworth and Glazebrook properties of Crown land in the
South Island for (a) commercial venison recovery operators, and (b) recreation hunting?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): Access for hunting on both Molesworth and
Glazebrook stations in the Marlborough district has been limited as regards commercial
venison recovery operations. Five permits have been issued to one operator on Molesworth
since 1973, while on Glazebrook a total of 12 permits covering four operators has been
issued in a similar period. No recreation hunting has been permitted on Molesworth to date,
and it was introduced on Glazebrook for a limited period only this year. Results of these
shoots indicate that there are very few deer on these properties, and certainly insufficient to
justify a change in the present policy of restricting such operations in the interests of farm
management.
Mr Isbey: Can the Minister inform the House why rights have been given to commercial
venison recovery operators and not to recreation hunters?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I can only assume that these stations under the management of Mr
Bill Chisholm have been managed in such a way that commercial operations are being
allowed to a limited extent, because it means a quick operation with a helicopter trying to
reduce the deer, whereas the area is so vast that it is impossible to police it if large numbers
of recovery hunters are shooting on both the Molesworth and Glazebrook stations.
Mr Latter: Is it true that the Crown will grant recovery shooting permits where there is
something to shoot, but its policies have been so successful that no one but a fool would
apply for a permit where there is nothing to shoot?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot say whether those few commercial operators are fools, or
whether the three or four who have applied for shooting permits on Glazebrook are the
same. I know that the very important role that has been assumed by the Crown, with Mr
Chisholm managing Molesworth and Glazebrook for water and soil conservation purposes,
has been very successful, and I certainly would not want to interfere with the management of
Molesworth or Glazebrook under Mr Chisholm.

MILK AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Milk
Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a short four-clause Bill, which makes three substan-
tive changes to the Milk Act 1967. Clause 2 amends section 25 of the principal Act. That
section provides for the making of regulations to fix the price of and conditions for the sale of
milk. At present, only payments or non-payments can be spelt out; in other words, a vendor
can receive only the full amount or no amount at all. Sometimes, because of poor service,
some reduction in payment is warranted, but under the principal Act this reduction cannot
be made and the Milk Board can only stop payment altogether. The Government believes
that penalty is too severe, and the amendment in clause 2 will allow for greater flexibility.
Clause 3 deals with the levy paid to meet the operating expenses of the Milk Board. At
present the levy can be, and is, set at a maximum of 0.25c a litre. The Bill increases the
maximum that can be charged to 0.40c. It is considered desirable to increase the maximum
so the levy can be raised to a higher amount if necessary in future. However, no increase in
the levy can be made unless it has the approval of the Minister of Agriculture. Clause 4
provides for an appeal authority to hear appeals on decisions made by the committee-set up
under the provisions of section 57 of the principal Act-to inquire into any dispute or
difference. These committees comprise at least two members of the board-one of whom
must be the chairman. People outside the board may also be appointed, but this has not been
the tradition. The Government believes this amendment is logical and reasonable.
The appeal authority will comprise a chairman, who is to be a barrister or solicitor of the
Supreme Court of at least 7 years' standing, and in no way connected with the town milk
supply industry, and two other members, who are to be persons with knowledge of and
experience in the town milk supply industry. I shall move at the appropriate time that the
Bill be referred to the Lands and Agriculture Committee for recess study.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition is pleased that the Bill is to be referred
to the Lands and Agriculture Committee. I should like to know whether interested parties,
particularly those involved in the industry, have been notified of the contents of the Bill. Can
the Minister give us some idea of the complexity of the problems faced by the industry and
the need to establish an authority to get over some of the difficulties faced? The Minister will
appreciate those difficulties, as representations have been made to us over the past 2 years.
Will the authority be able to cater for the wider interests of the industry? I think particularly
of the consumer.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): The people involved in the
industry are aware of the contents of the Bill, and the establishment of an appeal authority
was suggested by the Public and Administrative Law Reform Committee. As the member
for Western Maori will know, difficulties have been experienced on this point over the last 2
or 3 years

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): During the Committee stage members explained

## p. 5421 (#857) ###########################################

5421
Electoral Amendment Bill
argument against it.
I want to refer briefly to the principles in the Bill. It attempts to restrict the franchise,
and to make it more difficult to vote and to stand for Parliament. Clause 2 makes it more
difficult for school teachers to stand for Parliament. Why they should be singled out has not
been explained. Clause 4 makes the residential qualification for voting 3 months instead of 1
month. That will make it more difficult for people who change jobs-people living in a
mobile society. No argument was put forward by the Government in favour of that clause,
even though it is of such constitutional importance. Opposition members drew the Govern-
ment's attention to the mobility of New Zealanders, and the fact that in Australia the
residential qualification for voting has been 1 month since 1908. Returning to a 3-month
residential qualification will disfranchise thousands of New Zealanders.
Objection was raised to clause 6, which states that there is no longer any obligation to
advertise who is standing for Parliament. It will be more difficult for people to know for
whom to vote. A person can put a classified ad in the newspaper but there is no obligation to
notify each voter in writing of the candidates standing in his electorate.
The Opposition registered its greatest protest to clause 7. An amendment is moved to
make registration possible right up to and including the election day. That system has been
introduced in the United States this year by President Carter in the Universal Registration
Act. It is law in South Dakota, Minnesota, and Maine, and has worked extremely well. I
proposed that we should adopt that principle, and moved an amendment that anybody who
is qualified to vote and who takes the trouble to go to vote on election day should be able to
register his vote if he finds he is not on the roll, and that his vote should be accepted by the
returning officer if he has the proper identification. The measure is working overseas, and
we are at least as honest as, if not more honest than, Americans.
The Opposition registered its opposition to clause 8, which allows the maximum
electoral expenses of individual candidates to be increased from $2,000 to $4,000. Members
raised the same objections that were raised by Sir John Marshall in 1975—and we miss his
wisdom. He pointed out that the clause as it stands at present is meaningless, because even
though it restricts spending to $4,000 it does not say what expenses should be listed.
Candidates do not know whether their travelling expenses during an election campaign, their
own personal expenses, or payment for their personal expenses from the campaign commit-
tee should be entered on the return.
I moved the proposal put forward by Sir John Marshall, but after reading it again I
thought it did not go far enough. I understood that the National Opposition had given an
undertaking that it would support such a proposal. I did not think Sir John Marshall's
proposal went far enough, because there is another aspect of expenses that should be
covered if we are to have tight and fair elections, making sure there is not undue outside
influence when the candidate makes his return.

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am sure the honourable member knows that a litany—as he

Speaker's ruling 40/2 which states that on the third reading of a Bill a member cannot discuss
various matters, and that, "(6) Nor may he go through the Bill clause by clause; he must
confine himself to the general principles of the Bill." There are various Speakers' rulings. I
have given one myself, after consultation with my advisers, in reply to a request from the
Leader of the Opposition earlier this session.
The ruling stated: "Members must confine themselves to the general principles of the
Bill as it emerged from the Committee of the Whole. The debate on the third reading is
narrower than that on the second reading so that matters which can reasonably be related to
the Bill, which may be discussed during the seond reading, must therefore be excluded from
the third reading. Amendments"-if there are any-"which have been agreed to in the
Committee of the Whole may be referred to and their principles discussed because they are
now included in the Bill. Amendments considered in the Committee of the Whole, but not
agreed to, may be referred to for the purpose of recording, but their merits must not be
argued and they cannot be discussed at length." That ruling was based on many previous
Speakers' rulings. Amendments ruled out of order must not be discussed.

raised by another speaker were not relevant to the debate but were in response to other

servants but that they too make the same sacrifices that most people who enter this
Parliament will recall, sometimes with a great deal of gall. A great many of us will echo that

to do so. If that were not so it would create something unconstitutional, in my view. It would
mean we would be legislating otherwise for a form of discrimination that the Labour
Opposition constantly claims it would oppose.
So we are talking about either discrimination or equality, and if we are talking about
equality we are talking about equality of opportunity and, in that sense, we must be talking
about something more egalitarian than Opposition members are prepared to
acknowledge-that is, that anybody who is prepared to undergo considerable sacrifice
through being a candidate in a political campaign must be aware that their sacrifices are
shared more or less equally. That is my philosophy and it is the philosophy expressed in the
Bill; it is what the Bill is all about.

WILD ANIMAL CONTROL BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a third time.
Dr WALL (Porirua): Parts of the Bill are good, and will allow for more effective control
of the activities of commercial hunters in the back country. However, insufficient provision
has been made for the traditional rights of New Zealanders to move freely through the back
country of New Zealand as long as they do not do any harm. The provisions of this Bill,
together with the provisions of the Trespass Act, are abhorrent to our tradition.
Crown-owned land, paid for by a token and almost peppercorn rent, will be turned into
private game parks, and the occupiers of such land, much of which is inadequately used, will
have as tight and close trespass rights as do the owners of town sections. The landowner will
be able to call on Forest Service officers to enforce those rights—a provision very close to the
provisions covering the game parks of Europe. The public, which owns the land, is being
asked to finance gamekeepers to enforce the rights given to back-country station owners.
Under the provisions, a man who leases land not able to be farmed—and there are many
thousands of acres of that type of land-can use it as his private game farm. That could not
have been done before a Government came into office that is committed to preserving the
sacred rights of individual landowners against the public rights of New Zealanders. The
member for Gisborne is interjecting. Many thousands of acres of land of the type I am
talking about are within his electorate. A landowner may accuse a person of trespassing on
his land. No one knows where the boundaries are in the back country. The landowner can
accuse an innocent tramper, walking across his land and carrying game, of being a
trespasser. The landowner can call in the Government-paid gamekeeper and have the game,
the man's pack, his car, and other articles that game can be carried in, taken from him and


## p. 5433 (#869) ###########################################

16 December
5433
Wild Animal Control Bill
tied up for 12 months without reference to any court, and without any hearing or right of
appeal. Last night Opposition members saw a gross overriding of the privileges of the
minority in the House, and are now observing this type of approach being enshrined in law.
Provided that New Zealanders behave themselves they have traditionally been allowed
to shoot game almost anywhere. Now they cannot do so on leasehold land in the back
country unless the landowner lets them. That is a far cry from the freedom of pursuit of game
that New Zealanders have traditionally enjoyed. Another freedom has been taken away by
the Government. Quietly, freedoms are being eroded one by one, by a Government that
states that Opposition members do not know what freedom is. We know what democracy is
and what it should be. Overseas visitors have commented favourably on the freedom that
New Zealanders have to hunt vast areas of the back country without paying dues, without
restrictions, and with only the obligation to behave like decent people. That freedom has
been taken away because of the combined provisions of this Bill and the Trespass Act.
I agree that the Government had to take action to control commercial hunting and the
dangerous abuses that were occurring. To do that without concern for the many law-abiding
hunters who go into the hills is totally to disregard individuals, the minority, and those with
no political clout. If the Government was concerned about the freedom of New Zealanders it
would have written the legislation in a way that would distinguish between commercial
hunters and game hunters. No one disputes the need for tight controls, but the Bill could
have defined a commercial hunter in a way that would not include a hunter who brought part
of his game home after a hunting trip. The definition is so wide that it includes everyone.
Under the pretence of controlling the abuses that are undoubtedly taking place the
Government has taken away unjustifiably the traditional rights of New Zealanders.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): It is interesting that the member for Porirua
has become a great defender of the individual's rights at 12.25 on Friday afternoon when he
had the chance to do so last night, but did not take it. He went on strike with the rest of the
Opposition and forgot all about the individual's rights. He walked out. The Bill is important,
and will protect the landowner, the Crown, and the decent recreational hunter by giving him
an opportunity to hunt. It will regulate the commercial hunting of deer, and protect the deer
farmer against people who disregard other people's rights. It will regulate against those who
poach deer from a young couple who are deer farming. Several such people came to me

member for Porirua will not. They will remember the difficulties experienced in Wanganui
because of deer poaching. As a result of making submissions to the select committee, Mr
Kirk's farm has been ravaged by vandals—the type of person that the member for Porirua
wants to protect. People went to his farm and shot 20 sheep, chopped down his father's
garden, and cut his fences. Only 2 or 3 days ago the Wanganui Federated Farmers helped Mr
Kirk put his fences up again.
The Bill is not aimed at the decent New Zealand citizen who wants to pursue his
recreation. It is directed against the people who create wilful damage and who disregard the
rights of the landowner and the relationship between town and country people. The Bill is
supported by almost everybody who is concerned that people with firearms and other means
are completely disregarding the rights of landowners in the back country and elsewhere. It is
obvious to the Labour Opposition, which itself established a caucus committee to look into
noxious animal control, that there had to be legislation. I am satisfied that the select
committee adopted a bipartisan approach to the Bill and that many of the difficulties we
have had in the past will be corrected through the passage of this Bill. For the ordinary
decent New Zealander who wants to go out and enjoy the open spaces I am sure there is
adequate protection, but for those who want to disregard the law there are penalties in the
Bill.

MARINE RESERVES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Marine Reserves Amendment Bill is a short Bill of four clauses that is of some
considerable importance. As the House will recall, the Bill was referred to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee for the hearing of evidence, and one or two amendments were made
to it, plus a recommendation to me that I should introduce a Supplementary Order Paper at
the Committee stage to alter the size of the management committees that can be set up to
manage a marine reserve. I intend to follow that procedure.
Clause 2 will allow fishing within a reserve by persons who do not hold a permit issued
under the Fisheries Act 1908, Part I—that is, persons who are not commercial fishermen can
be authorised by notice in the Gazette given by the Minister after consultation with the
management committee of a reserve. That is the significant change. The Marine Reserves
Act as at present constituted provides for a total embargo on fishing in any reserve
established under it. I believe-and the select committee agreed-that recreational fishing
should be permitted when it does not interfere with the prime purpose or reason for which
the reserve was established. The Bill makes provision for that on the recommendation of a
management committee set up to manage the reserve.
Clause 3 makes it possible for the Director-General of Agriculture and Fisheries to
initiate an application for the establishment of a marine reserve. At present he does not have
that power. Therefore, we have in all instances to wait for some organisation outside of the
Government to take the necessary procedures to initiate the establishment of a marine
reserve. I am sure the House can contemplate many instances when it might be desirable that
the Director-General should have power to initiate the procedures for the establishment of a
reserve. The applications would still go through the normal procedures, with reporting on
any objections, and would be screened in the appropriate manner. I believe this measure will
be welcomed by all those interested in marine conservation.
Clause 4 is a simple amendment that allows inspectors of sea fishing appointed under
the Fisheries Act 1908 to be rangers for the purposes of the Marine Reserves Act. This will
enable the ministry's inspectorate staff to be available for policing marine reserves. This is a
logical extension of the powers of the Fisheries Act 1908. On the recommendation of the
select committee, I intend to introduce a further amendment by way of Supplementary
Order Paper-an amendment that will extend from five to seven the number of persons who
may be appointed members of a management committee and further provide that one shall
be qualified in marine research and one shall represent the interests of the public. It is
necessary to make a further consequential amendment to the number of members who will
constitute a quorum in an expanded management committee.

McMillan, the Commissioner of Crown Lands, Auckland, who said: "The Bill under

MAORI PURPOSES BILL
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill was referred to the Maori Affairs Committee, which has reported it
back with one amendment-this being to clause 5 dealing with Maori incorporations. The
committee received detailed submissions on clause 5 from counsel acting for the committee
of management of the Taharoa C Incorporation and counsel acting for some of the
shareholders in the same incorporation. On consideration, the committee felt that the Bill
was not the appropriate vehicle by which to bring about what would amount to a substantial
change in the general objects of Maori incorporations. As it now stands, clause 5 will allow
an incorporation to go to the Maori Land Court for an order redefining the objects of a
venture within the existing framework of section 27 of the Maori Affairs Amendment Act
1967. I intend reviewing the law about incorporations next year to see whether improve-
ments can be made to the running of these successful operations.
The Bill contains eight clauses, plus the short title and clause 2, by which Part I of the
Bill is read as part of the Maori Affairs Act 1953. Clause 3 clarifies a matter about which
some doubt had been expressed, and makes it clear that the Maori Land Board has authority
to participate in various incentive schemes-for example, the livestock incentive scheme-in
respect of land that it is farming on behalf of the owners. Clause 4 is of a machinery nature
and will speed up the administration of the estates of deceased Maori who owned shares in a
Maori incorporation. Clause 5 I have already commented on. Clause 6 redefines moneys
held by an incorporation as unclaimed dividends, and allows the incorporation the use of
these funds earlier than is at present possible. The proposed amendment does not prejudice
the rights of any shareholder to claim subsequently a full refund of any money affected.


## p. 5436 (#872) ###########################################

5436
16 December
Maori Purposes Bill
Part II of the Bill contains clauses 7 to 10, which are miscellaneous amendments to
legislation affecting Maoris and Maori land. Clause 7 is self-explanatory, and is a housekeep-
ing measure to align the policy for Maori housing advances to Polynesian Islanders with that
of the Housing Corporation. Clause 8 gives effect to an earlier decision to increase by 50
percent the annual grant payable to the four Maori trust boards listed. The decision to grant
the increase followed representations extending over a long period from the boards
concerned. The increases are intended to offset to some extent the growth in the needs of the
Maori beneficiaries of the boards and the impact of inflation. I looked at the possibility of
making it mandatory that these increases be invested and not dispersed, but have left it to
the wisdom of the trustees, with a strong appeal that they should give consideration to
investing this money.
Clause 9 redefines the waters comprising Lake Rotoaira. This redefinition is the result
of lengthy negotiations between the trustees of Lake Rotoaira and the Crown, and is
necessary because of the effects on the lake and surrounding waters of the Tongariro hydro
scheme. The redefinition proposed will not prejudice in any way any unsettled claim for
compensation for land lost or otherwise affected by the scheme. Clause 10 is again the result
of negotiations between the Crown and the Lake Rotoaira trustees, and is a further
housekeeping measure to cover the situation whereby additional adjoining land may,
through a rise in the level of the lake, be covered in water.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): The Opposition has no objection to the second
reading of the Bill, but I want to take issue with the Minister about clause 5. The House
should be aware that the principles contained in the provisions of clause 5 were sought by the
Taharoa C Incorporation, which was established in 1972 for the express purpose of utilising
the ironsands of Taharoa. Because it has a diminishing asset, the management committee
has been giving consideration to the investment of its income, or part of it, to ensure the
continuity of both its income and its asset in the future. There is no guarantee that the
amount now payable to the incorporation will continue. The Government may make
changes that will alter the course of events.
Section 27 of the Maori Affairs Act 1967 sets out the objectives in an application lodged
with the Maori Land Court in the establishment of a Maori land incorporation; and the
provision that hinders the request of the incorporation is in section 27(e), which decrees that
notwithstanding a need to change or vary or redefine the purpose for which a Maori land
incorporation was so established, it must be so defined in relation to the land for which the
incorporation was set up. In this instance, the Taharoa C Incorporation is unique. It is a
mining incorporation for the express purpose of mining the ironsands. The wish of the
management committee of the incorporation is to ensure that its income, or part of it, may
be set aside, and it is not allowed by law to redefine the objectives to give it the right to do
so. The request makes sense, and it is a sensible arrangement. The committee was impressed
with that view, but not impressed about other questions, which are irrelevant for the purpose
of this section, such as the determination by a minority of owners about the dividends of the
incorporation.
Other matters are subject to court appeals, and naturally the committee struck out those
provisions of Part IV that were first sent to the Maori Affairs Committee. I am providing
members with the background to give some idea of the complexity of the question that the
committee was asked to consider. The point on which I want to take issue with the Minister
is that the committee agreed that the request of the incorporation should be met, with one
exception: that provision should not be made so that any incorporation has a general power
to invest in other than the incorporation or other interest related to the land.
Members will be aware that there are more than 170 Maori land incorporations. I
believe it is important that they should be consulted before major changes are made to any
legislation likely to affect them. When the committee considered the matter, I
understood and I was under the impression that other members of the committee did

Minister, who said that the committee thought that the amendment would meet the request
of the incorporation. The members of the Maori Affairs Committee might have been
inadvertently misled.
Apart from the changes to the principal Act contemplated by the Minister, it will be
necessary for the Government to assure the incorporation concerned that the Government
will adhere to its request. Because of the lack of time in which a suitable amendment can be
moved, the Minister has varied what he thought was the decision reached. If that had been
