CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As members are aware, the Bill was referred to the Social Services Committee,
and before I comment on the various clauses I should like to express my appreciation of the
work of the committee. Despite the short period of time available to the select committee, it
was able to give careful consideration to the issues involved and to the submissions received
from interested organisations and individuals. Those submissions were very helpful to the
committee, and indicated that the voluntary organisations and individuals concerned have a
genuine concern for the welfare of children and young persons in New Zealand. I should like
to place on record my thanks for their valuable comments and suggestions.
As I explained when I introduced the Bill, over the 22 years the Children and Young
Persons Act has been in operation it has become evident that certain sections of the Act need
amendment to clarify the original intention and to facilitate more effective operation of the
legislation. The Bill has 18 clauses, most of which effect changes of a relatively minor nature.
The change that has stimulated the most discussion is contained in clause 5, but before
commenting on that clause it may be useful if I remind members of the present legal
distinction between a child and a young person made in the Children and Young Persons
Act. A child is defined as a person under 14 years, and a young person is defined as a person
aged 14 or over but under 17 years. Under present provisions a child cannot be prosecuted
for an offence. Clause 5 amends these provisions to provide for a child of or over the age of
10 to be charged with murder or manslaughter as if the charge were being brought against a
young person.


## p. 5440 (#876) ###########################################

5440
16 December
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
It may be helpful if I explain just what the effect of this amendment will be. If a child
over 10 is alleged to have committed murder or manslaughter the preliminary hearing of the
charge will, in accordance with section 25(4) of the Children and Young Persons Act, take
place before a Children and Young Persons Court. Publication of the proceedings will be
prohibited except by leave of the court. If that court finds that there is sufficient evidence to
warrant the child being brought to trial, the case will then be referred to the Supreme Court
for hearing. That is what happens at present if a young person—that is, a person aged 14 or
over but under 17-is charged with murder or manslaughter. The Government is aware that,
if a child is convicted of murder or manslaughter, it will not be appropriate for him to serve a
term of imprisonment in a penal institution. It would quite clearly be undesirable for a child
to be incarcerated with adult prisoners. For this reason, clause 18 of the Bill inserts a new
section 103A in the Children and Young Persons Act that will enable a child or young person
who is serving a sentence of imprisonment to be detained in a social welfare institution
approved for the purpose by the Minister of Social Welfare in consultation with the Minister
of Justice.
Although social welfare institutions have limited secure facilities for short-term "cooling
off" purposes, they are inappropriate for long-term treatment. For that reason, an inter-
departmental committee is examining the feasibility of establishing a new and separate
institution for the long-term care and treatment of the quite small number of children and
young people who require to be held in secure facilities. Such an institution could be used to
detain a child convicted of murder or manslaughter. The interdepartmental committee is
aware of the need to complete its inquiry as expeditiously as possible.
Charging a child with murder or manslaughter is a departure from the present
provisions of the Children and Young Persons Act, under which a person under the age of 14
cannot be convicted of a criminal offence. However, the Government and the select
committee believe that the existing procedure of taking complaint proceedings against the
child's parents or guardians under section 27 of the Act on the ground that the child is in
need of care, protection, and control is inappropriate where crimes of murder and man-
slaughter are alleged, and that a child should not be able to be detained in a Social Welfare
institution for a number of years solely as a result of complaint proceedings. The departure
applies only to the two most serious offences known in our law, and I have no doubt that it
will be necessary to use the new provisions only very rarely. Despite the amendment,
therefore, the basic approach that a child cannot be held criminally responsible for his
actions remains intact for all but the very rare case where the child's actions have resulted in
loss of life.
Another clause that has provoked some discussion is clause 13, which inserts a new
section 42A in the Children and Young Persons Act. This will give a Children and Young
Persons Court the power, in appropriate cases, to call for a psychiatric examination of a child
or young person before the court. The new section 42A will also enable the court, where
there is medical evidence to support such a course, to order, under subsection (3), that a
child or young person be detained in a psychiatric hospital so that a psychiatric assessment
can be carried out. In the introductory copy of the Bill this period of detention in a
psychiatric hospital was limited to 1 week.
However, submissions to the select committee argued that this period would not be long
enough to carry out a proper psychiatric assessment, and the select committee agreed that
the period should be extended to 2 weeks. I am sure members will agree that, if there is
information available to the court that a child or young person may be psychiatrically
disturbed, it should, before deciding what action to take, have the benefit of a full psychiatric
report on the child's or young persons's mental health. This is consistent with section 4 of the
Children and Young Persons Act, which charges the court to treat the interests of the child
or young person as the first and paramount consideration.
The need for the new section 42A was highlighted in the report earlier this year of Mr
W. J. Mitchell, stipendiary magistrate, on the circumstances surrounding the treatment
given to a 13-year-old Niuean boy in Lake Alice Psychiatric Hospital. In Mr Mitchell's view,
the case he investigated illustrated the need for consideration of the statutory position of the
Children and Young Persons Court when it requires a psychiatric report before disposing of
a complaint that a child is in need of care, protection, or control. Mr Mitchell considered that
the court should have powers "something like those of a court dealing under section 47a of
the Criminal Justice Act 1954, with a person charged with an offence". Clause 13 imple-
ments Mr Mitchell's findings in this regard, and the new section 42A is based on section 47A
of the Criminal Justice Act, suitably adapted.


## p. 5441 (#877) ###########################################

16 December
5441
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
Members will note that the new section gives the court the authority to call for a
psychiatric examination, not only in respect of complaint proceedings as recommended by
Mr Mitchell, but also in respect of information proceedings-that is, where a young person
has been charged with an offence. In fact, there is already authority in the Criminal Justice
Act to call for a psychiatric examination when a young person is charged with an offence.
However, it is considered appropriate to have the relevant provisions, as they relate to
children and young persons, brought together in the one statute, the Children and Young
Persons Act.
Subsection (5) of the new section 42A provides that a child or young person may be
treated in a psychiatric hospital if he is there for psychiatric assessment as a result of an order
made by the court under subsection (3). I want to make it clear, however, that it will be
possible to administer treatment only if consent to that treatment is given by the young
person himself, if he is over 16, or by his parents or guardians in other cases. The exception
to this will be when the whereabouts of the parents or guardians of a child or young person
under 16 are unknown, in which case provision is made for consent to be given by a
magistrate or the Director-General of Social Welfare. The select committee agreed to a
minor amendment to the introductory copy of the Bill to make this intention clear.
Clause 15, which inserts a new section 49A, also relates to psychiatric treatment of
children and young persons. The clause makes it clear that the Director-General of Social
Welfare can arrange for a State ward—that is, a child or young person under the director-
general's guardianship-to be admitted to a psychiatric hospital as an informal patient in
accordance with the normal conditions set out in the Mental Health Act.
There has been some confusion as to whether the director-general has the authority to
arrange for a State ward to be informally admitted to a psychiatric hospital. The cause of this
confusion has been the definition of social welfare residences contained in section 2 of the
Children and Young Persons Act, which specifically excludes a psychiatric hospital from the
definition. This definition was not intended to prevent the director-general arranging for a
psychiatrically disturbed State ward to be admitted to a psychiatric hospital. Quite clearly, a
psychiatrically disturbed State ward should have the same access to a psychiatric hospital as
any other youngster or, indeed, any adult.
As with the new section 42A, if a State ward is admitted to a psychiatric hospital under
the new section 49A, he will be able to be treated only if consent to the treatment is given by
the young person himself, if he is over 16, or by his parents or guardians in other cases.
These provisions are set out in subsection (2) of the new section 49A. As with the new section
42A, the select committee agreed to a minor amendment to these provisions to make clear
the intention regarding the need to obtain parental consent to treatment.

Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori): Clause 5 represents
a departure from the principle inherent in the Children and Young Person's Act 1974,
inasmuch as under that Act a child cannot be convicted of a criminal offence. However,
under this Bill a child is to be charged and convicted for murder or manslaughter, and
therefore the Crimes Act 1961 will also have to be amended since that Act, consistent with
the parent Act, excuses everyone below the age of 10 years from criminal responsibility. The
parties opposing clause 5 as it stands-and there were a considerable number of them-did
so on five grounds. First, it contravenes the philosophy behind the principal Act, with which
I was associated at the time as Associate Minister of Social Welfare-the philosophy that a
child cannot be held criminally responsible for his actions. Secondly, it offers negative
possibilities by way of imitative crimes. Thirdly, the public interest is already protected,
since the child is removed from society to a social welfare institution. Fourthly, and
particularly, this amendment will have no deterrent effect on children. Fifthly, it is totally
illogical to isolate the crimes of murder and manslaughter. The vast majority-certainly
about 95 percent-of those who made submissions opposed the amendment on those five
grounds. They included the New Zealand Society of Social Workers, the New Zealand
Psychological Society, and the Maori Women's Welfare League. I oppose the amendment,
and will take the opportunity to vote against it at the appropriate stage.
It is clear to me that we should be considering three different types of child offenders.
The first is the child who is a psychopath and who will always be a psychopath, since that is in
the nature of the particular condition-the child who exhibits a personality type that
generally lacks ethical character, morality, emotional stability, and a sense of responsibility
to persons and social norms. There is absolutely no doubt in my mind that such a child


## p. 5443 (#879) ###########################################

5443
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
committing the offence of murder or manslaughter, or what is thought to be so, can and must
be removed from society indefinitely-regretfully, because the very nature of his condition
renders him totally intractable, incorrigible, and unable to be rehabilitated. He does not
appear to be obviously mentally deranged. He may even appear to be intelligent and normal
at first glance, but if he is a psychopath he cannot be rehabilitated and there is only one
reasonable thing to do to prevent him from committing further depredations on society.
There is no question about that.
There are two other categories of child that I want the House to consider-and I
commend the suggestion that members should vote against clause 5. There is the child who is
able to be rehabilitated; the child who might be described in clinical terms as a sociopathic
child, displaying the characteristic of being chronically antisocial and unable or unwilling to
live within the established social and moral framework, and who cannot form stable and
intimate interpersonal relations-who, in fact, has as his primary concern the immediate
gratification of his own needs and desires. Such a child would show no interest in the effect of
his behaviour on others.
Such a child is often destructive and by his actions is seen to be irresponsible. He may
experience no guilt in the face of repeated recriminations. In many cases the sociopathic
child is the product of a chaotic family background, where he was unwanted as an infant and
neglected as a child. He has a basic flaw in his personality structure, and the likelihood of
significant improvement under therapy is, I concede, minimal, but it is likely that he may
respond. Therefore, every effort to rehabilitate that child would be the most humane,
sensitive, and compassionate action that can be taken. Clause 5 as it stands will not provide
the most humane action.
The third group includes the child who acts totally out of character, and therefore can in
his formative years be rehabilitated to a certain degree, provided that he receives sufficient
qualified counselling. Considering that most of these children to be charged under clause 5
would be the innocent casualties of delinquent parents, I cannot support the clause. We
should be looking at the delinquent and neglectful parents, who are inadequate, immature,
and parents prematurely. They are the reluctant and neglectful parents of children they did
not want to bring into the world. We should consider their children, because rehabilitation
can reach those children. What is required is not legislation, but the provision by the
Government, and on the Government's direction, of adequate counselling and psychological
services where analysis is the most important initial concern. Our efforts should be directed
to providing rehabilitative and supportive counselling, not legislation that charges the child
who at present cannot be charged under the parent Act. If we cannot introduce humane
legislation, skilled and qualified counsellors must be provided.
The country is short of these services. As the New Zealand Association of Social
Workers pointed out to the committee, the staffing of our educational child psychiatry units
is inadequate. How many psychiatrists are there?—far too few for the need. We do not have
adequate places to keep these children. I am familiar with the two institutions
available-Kohitere in Levin and the Weymouth establishment for girls in Auckland. We
need more imaginative and alternative resources and treatment. Inadequate emphasis is
placed on rehabilitation at present, because the Government does not budget to provide
more staff for counselling and service. Children should not be imprisoned when they can be
rehabilitated to become worth-while citizens, especially when they are casualties of the
neglectful irresponsibility of parents and the innocent victims of a clause that will make them
criminals.
Despite the temptation to implement a punitive measure, the House should direct its
efforts towards providing an environment that alleviates the pressure on a child that might
predispose him uncharacteristically to murder or manslaughter, or, even better, to provide
rehabilitative counselling that will enable the child to return to the community. Bearing in
mind what I have said about the psychopathic child, I regret that there is no alternative but
to set that child aside from society. My experience as a child welfare officer and a social
worker makes me feel concerned about several clauses. I expressed that concern during the
committee's hearings. I believe that a mature, experienced, and maternally or paternally
inclined person should be appointed as a child advocate. I would prefer that to the provision
in the Bill that the services of a barrister or solicitor be provided.
When a complaint against a child is being heard the adversary system should not be
used. That concern was one of the reasons I introduced an amendment to the Human Rights
Commission Bill. I expressed my concern also about clause 13, which I believe does not
adequately provide for a more comprehensive and less one-sided understanding of a child's

Dr WALL (Porirua): The Bill is a panic measure in response to public concern about
one or two tragic incidents. Because of that, what should have been a considered review of
the experimental children and young persons' legislation introduced 2 years ago is hurried
and somewhat panicky. Enough experience of the workings of the present Act has been
acquired to show up some of its weaknesses and some of its strengths. It is appropriate that
this matter should be brought under review, because the legislation will be changing from
year to year for some time as Parliament and the country experiment with better and more
efficient approaches to deal with the behavioural problems of these children.
The treatment given to disordered children whose actions have resulted in a tragedy of
one kind or another is, by definition, essentially punitive. It may be that, by chance,
corrective and educational benefits will result from it. But we have left alone, and have not
attempted to touch, the matters that the member for Henderson drew attention to in the
wider group of minor offences where punishment may well have and probably does have an
effective and proper place in the treatment of childhood disorders. But, where someone has
died as a result of disordered behaviour, we intend to move. What concerns me is that a child
can place a block of wood or a piece of concrete on a railway line, the train can knock it out
of the way, and the child has committed no offence-everything is fine, but it was grossly
irresponsible behaviour. The engine may be damaged, but no one is killed, and again the
child is not subject to anything but the proceedings of the young persons board. But if
someone is killed in the accident-an event that may be totally and completely unrelated to
anything the child did—the full power of the law must come into play with all the emphasis
on detention and punitive aspects in the hope of producing better behaviour.
It concerns me that we have not thought this through sufficiently. It is also unfortunate
that we have handed the children over to the Supreme Court, but given no guidance. All
members agree that the spirit of the legislation is to produce well adjusted citizens, and we
do that reluctantly with certain measures that none of us like to see imposed on children. In
doing that we recognise that we have a different problem from the problem of adult
offending, particularly when it comes to the imposition of sentences. A criminal sentenced to
life imprisonment serves 7 years before he becomes eligible for consideration for parole. For
a 50-year-old man that means that one-seventh of his life experience has been in jail, but the
same sentence imposed on a 13-year-old would mean that the child had served one-third of
his life experience in detention.
The simple procedure of handing these offenders over to the court should also
incorporate some indication that the House intends the court to consider the time scale, as
well as any other matters that the court takes into account in the discretion it has under the
law at present. We are particularly concerned for the rehabilitation and proper education of
these children, and a cautionary note should be given to the court to use its judgment with
children between 10 and 14 years of age. The possibility of the effect of rehabilitation of a
child, one-third of whose life has been in detention, appears to me to be remote. These are
matters that concern me.
It is most unfortunate that this matter was dealt with in haste. I hope that the
Government will review the legislation in an attempt to tidy up some matters, to provide for
more effective punishment in minor cases, and to ensure that proper consideration is given
to the assessment of the serious offender and the likelihood of his rehabilitation in relation to
his age rather than to the severity of his offence.
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Government regrets that
legislation such as this is necessary. The Act has been in operation for about 2½ years,
during which time certain weaknesses have been disclosed, and the amendments are
designed to correct these. It is not hasty legislation, as suggested by the member for Porirua;
it is not panic legislation, as claimed by Opposition members; it is legislation that has been
carefully designed to provide for the welfare of unfortunate children. Thank goodness only a
few children find themselves in this position. These amendments have been designed, not
with one eye on the next election, but to deal with the welfare of children today and in the
future.
The member for Southern Maori mentioned the imprisonment of children. That was an
emotional comment, which I believe was made with an eye on the next election. I wish that


## p. 5445 (#881) ###########################################

16 December
5445
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
the member for Southern Maori and other members had listened to my comments when I
moved the second reading. I said that it would be clearly undesirable for a child to be
incarcerated with adult prisoners. For this reason, clause 18 inserts a new section 103A in the
Children and Young Persons Act that will enable a child or a young person who is serving a
sentence of imprisonment to be detained in a social welfare institution. The child will be
detained in a social welfare institution approved for the purpose by the Minister of Social
Welfare in consultation with the Minister of Justice. That provision is designed for the
welfare of children.
The member for Henderson spoke about the publicity that could result from a child
being taken to the Supreme Court on a charge of murder. Section 46(1) of the Criminal
Justice Act 1954 states: "Except as otherwise expressly provided in any enactment, the court
in its discretion may make an order prohibiting the publication, in any report relating to any
proceedings in respect of any offence, of the name of the person accused or convicted of the
offence, or the name of any other person connected with the proceedings." I have
confidence that the courts will not use that discretion to place unfortunate children in an
even worse position. I repeat that the purposes of the amendments before the House are to
correct weaknesses that have become apparent in the legislation during the 2½ years it has
been in operation.

Road User Charges Bill
Bill read a third time.
ROAD USER CHARGES BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a third time.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): For several reasons the passage of this Bill
through the House has taken longer than it should have done. Also, because of various
matters that arose during the several stages of the Bill, it is imperative at this time to place
certain facts on record. To avoid any misunderstanding as a result of any misleading
information that may have been given, I say at the outset that there has been no opposition
from members on this side of the House to the objectives of the Bill-namely, to establish
the principle of imposing a road user tax that will reflect fairly the costs caused through road
wear and ensure that those who cause the most road wear in the course of their work or
enterprise pay an appropriate share of the tax required to meet the cost of repairing it.
However, extreme differences of opinion have been expressed on the formula that
should be adopted. The Labour Opposition moved that the Bill be referred to a select
committee. The motion was not agreed to, but the facts revealed since have indicated that
the Bill should have been referred to a committee many months ago. An examination by a
committee would have revealed who was right—the Minister and the officials committee, or
the Road Transport Association. We have complained continually about the lack of real
consultation between the officials committee and the Road Transport Association. In
rebuttal, the Minister has stated that 94 meetings took place between these groups. I find it
incredible that, despite all these meetings and discussions, the two parties did not realise that
they were working from different basic figures and assumptions. Opposition members
brought these facts to light during the various stages of the Bill. In my view, the Minister of
Transport and the Minister of Works and Development should rectify the situation
immediately and demand an explanation from the officials concerned. If all parties had been
prepared to put all known facts and figures on the table, much time and argument could have
been saved.
The Road Transport Association has stated publicly, and has reiterated on many
occasions, that its members accept the fact that they must pay road tax related to the extent
of road wear their vehicles cause in relation to other road users. That is fair, and is accepted
in principle by everyone concerned. The Labour Opposition is worried about the competi-
tive situation of the railways in the total internal transport system. Thousands of tonnes of
rail freight have been lost to road transport since the 45-mile limit was abolished. At the
same time, steep rail charge increases have coincided with very extensive undercutting
among road transport operators. The publicly owned railways system cannot maintain a
viable and economic total operation while these circumstances remain.
During the Committee stage the Opposition moved an amendment to clause 9 relating
to road wear and fuel usage, and also raised an objection to clause 23. We made a further
appeal to the Government to reconsider its adamant stance on prepaid distance tax when a
quarterly reconciliation system would have been much more appropriate. After all, every
vehicle is to be fitted with a hubodometer, so that would not be difficult to do. We fail to
understand the dogmatic attitude adopted by the Government in its insistence on taxation on
a prepaid basis. The Bill is a classic example of a controversial matter being inflamed
through interested parties not having had in-depth consultations, even though different
calculations and formulas were obviously being used. This is a most regrettable situation.
I believe the passage of the Bill took longer than necessary. The Road Transport
Association, the Railways, and Government officials should have got together and put all
the facts on the table. There would then have been no misunderstanding and we would all
have known who was right and who was wrong. Basically, this was why the Opposition asked
that the Bill should go to a select committee. We felt something was wrong, because the
calculations coming from one side were so far removed from those coming from the other
side. This could not have happened if the two parties had operated on the same formulas.
How can the Minister explain 94 meetings without interested parties realising this much? He
has a job to do. He must bring out the facts, and, if he does, he will have my good wishes. I
again say that I regret the long time taken over this Bill, much of it unnecessary. Officials
from the Minister's department and the Ministry of Works and Development have much to
answer for over this delay.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): We have seen the old adage that

VALEDICTORY
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That this House do now adjourn.
My immediate thoughts are with Mr Speaker, who, because of an operation and consequent
after-effects, has not been with us since the end of August. I think that when a member of
the House is laid aside by serious indisposition our sympathy goes out to him, not because of
any position he may hold or his length of service, but because he is one of us.
Sir Roy had already notified his intention to retire at the end of this Parliament. I am
sure all members share my wish that he will make a sufficient recovery to enjoy the


## p. 5452 (#888) ###########################################

5452
16 December
Valedictory
retirement he has so well earned. That is what most of us would wish for ourselves, and we
can wish him no less. The Acting Speaker has carried out his duties with firmness,
impartiality, and dignity. Those attributes are essential to the high office he holds during the
Speaker's absence.
This third session of the thirty-eighth Parliament has lasted nearly 7 months. As
members know, we had a very short session late in February during the visit of Her Majesty
the Queen and Prince Phillip. Those 7 months are not, however, any measure of the time
members have given to their duties in Wellington-their constituency work apart. The first
select committee, the Statutes Revision Committee, sat on 10 February, and altogether
select committees of the House held 77 meetings before the session began. During the
session, select committees met in the mornings, and up until this week the number of select
committee meetings this year totalled nearly 400. Ministers apart, these meetings involved
almost all members.
This is not news to the House, but it may be useful to remind the public who put us here
that we earn our salaries. It is no half-the-year, 4-days-a-week occupation. Select committee
work also places an extra burden on a depleted Opposition, as National members knew in
the previous Parliament when the parties' strengths were exactly the opposite of what they
are now. The Government ends this session having put most of its election policy into law.
Indeed, the greater part of that was done in the 1976 session. The result could be that during
the next session more time could be available for debates on the principles actuating the
Government and Opposition parties-and this, of course, is extremely important during
election year.
The present 7-month session-118 days, to be exact-should have been enough to cope
with even the most arduous legislative programme. As it happened, two major pieces of
legislation, which did not have their origin in policy, resulted in protracted debates. These
two items were the Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill and the Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion Bill. The latter was debated almost to the point of exhaustion, in
spite of the fact that members had the report of a royal commission to inform them, plus a
wealth of submissions from interested parties. The issues were, of course, moral ones, and
now that the decisions have been made on a free vote it is my earnest hope that the same
issues will not have to be discussed during the 1978 session, when the House may have
serious economic matters to debate. To reopen the abortion question before it is shown
whether the provisions made in the present legislation are workable would be, in my view,
utterly irresponsible.
As usual, a great deal of this session's legislation has been of an amending nature.
Because we live in a changing society, legislation must be amended to meet new circumst-
ances, to correct faults, and, in general, to bring the law into keeping with the times.
Because of the unavoidable volume of amending legislation, the impression does get abroad
that Governments are continually overlegislating.
Among the new legislation this session were several major policy matters in fulfilment
of the Government's election manifesto. Among them was legislation providing for the 200-
miles fishing zone, the setting up of the Ministry of Energy Resources, the New Zealand
Planning Council, and the Commission for the Future. There was also the Human Rights
Act, the Town and Country Planning Act, a transport Act amendment providing for the 150-
km road transport limit, legislation covering industrial law reform, and several measures in
the interests of local government.
The legislative programme placed the parliamentary counsel office under severe strain.
It is proper here to acknowledge the worth of those there engaged. From time to time we
read academic criticism of the drafting of legislation, but I suggest to those ivory-tower
people that they offer themselves, even if only for a year, and show us how the job should be
done. The fact is that lawyers suitable by training and, in particular, disposition to this type
of work are hard to come by. It is a most demanding branch of the legal profession. Mr
Graham Hamilton, a parliamentary counsel who has been with our Parliament since 1947,
retires this year. In fact, he retired 7 years ago, but came back to help us out—as did Mr Jack
McVeagh who, happily for Parliament, is carrying on. Before retiring Mr Hamilton was the
Law Draftsman, as the office of Chief Parliamentary Counsel was then called, for 4 years.
Mr Hamilton brought to his job not only exceptional skills, but also a most agreeable
disposition, and he will be greatly missed.
The House sat for 118 days this year compared with 96 days last year, and 118 days in
1974. It sat 17 times after midnight this year, compared with 18 times last year. Sittings after
midnight this session occupied 41 hours 28 minutes compared with 51 hours last year. This


## p. 5453 (#889) ###########################################

16 December
5453
Valedictory
year the House passed 210 public Bills, 17 local Bills, and 2 private Bills. Fifty-three of the
public Bills were in the Statutes Amendment Bill, the measure which incorporates one- and
two-clause non-controversial matters to correct small items in existing legislation. This year
43 Bills were referred to select committees compared with 52 last year, and 21 will be studied
by select committees during the coming recess.
Some of the pressure on the House during the final stage of the session could have been
avoided if some members had not employed time-wasting techniques earlier. It has become a
habit to turn discussion on the introduction of Bills into a full-scale debate. In other than
exceptional cases, brief explanations in reply to pertinent questions should be adequate. I
am also concerned at the number of private members' notices of motion on the Order
Paper-31 in all. I do not wish to appear to be questioning members' rights, but it is my
understanding that notices of motion should be related to matters suitable for debate.
Instead, we have all too many, which, while they may amuse members on one side or the
other, or both, are neither substantial nor of a quality ever likely to merit serious debate. In
addition, such notices of motion take up time both here and in the Government Printing
Office, and waste costly paper.
It is the custom-and a good one-to place on record at the closing of the session our
appreciation of the services of many people in a variety of professions and occupations who
make possible the smooth and efficient working of Parliament. I have already mentioned
parliamentary counsel. The Clerk of the House has a wealth of experience behind him. We
have his assistance and that of his clerks-two of them women-and other staff. The Clerk's
staff had a trying time during the debate on the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion
Bill with the mass of papers produced by amendments.
The Hansard staff-now largely women-are a tradition in themselves for efficiency. I
have never heard it said that this section of the parliamentary staff was other than highly
efficient. The General Assembly Library staff continue their prompt and expert service to all
members. The committee clerks do a good job, not only for the members of the committees,
but for witnesses and others with dealings with the committees. The messengers are a
cheerful, friendly lot, and those whose duties bring them into contact with the public have a
responsible role in conveying to visitors that this is a friendly place—their Parliament. We
see many of these messengers, session after session. Perhaps some of us may now, or later
next year, have cause to envy them their apparent security of tenure.
The Post Office staff handles a great volume of business efficiently. The telephone
operators show great initiative in dealing with difficult calls as well as handling the routine
ones smoothly and quickly. Both parties have their research units, whose staff are not only
efficient but have a feel for politics. Our private secretaries and other secretaries do a great
job, and some of us, deep in our tasks, overlook their value. Likewise, the typists, many of
whom are often called upon to stay beyond the normal working time—and they do so
uncomplainingly.
The staff of Bellamy's are not the least of Parliament's staff although I mention them
last. Members have experienced courteous service from the waiters, waitresses, and bar
staff, but we seldom see the kitchen staff. I assure them that their work is appreciated; and I
mention in particular the chef, Mr Joe Pereira, almost the forgotten man in Bellamy's,
whose skills are equal to any occasion.
The Press Gallery are not parliamentary staff, but they are part of Parliament and the
democratic process. That process is far better served in this country than most by the
accessibility of Ministers and members to the news media. I read only recently where, in a
country not so far away, the Prime Minister sees the news media only two or three times a
year. What a howl there would be if that were the position here! I believe in reasonable and
even ready access to the news media, but at the same time I strongly believe that both parties
should treat the relationship with respect.
We all know that the coming year will be difficult, as indeed it will continue to be in
many countries. People whose allegiance is, to say the least, unacceptable in this House may
attempt to exploit difficulties, as indeed they are already wantonly creating them.
I appeal to all members to do their best in 1978 to counsel respect for the proper courses
of industrial action. To offer this counsel will neither stifle the free expression of their own
political philosophies nor impede industrial action by lawfully recognised channels. New
Zealand cannot afford a continuance of the industrial anarchy that is becoming a feature of
the labour scene. It will not be in the interests of the nation as a whole, or of any party in the
House, or any member of it, if this unrest continues.

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): We have now reached the end

just the length of time spent debating that has placed a strain on members. As one who has
always been concerned for his own physical fitness, I want to extend my personal good will
and sympathy to those whose health has suffered-not necessarily as a result of the strain of
the session, but clearly as a result of the total demands that work in this institution places
upon us.
At the head of the list I place our Speaker, Sir Roy Jack. I have never been a personal
friend, and I have not hesitated to criticise him, but in his time of physical suffering I want to
assure him of the understanding and sympathy of this side of the House, and-as the Prime
Minister said of his side-of our earnest desire that he should make a complete recovery to
normal health.
Both sides of the House have seen their members under pressure. The member for
Christchurch Central, we hope, is on the way to full recovery, the member for West Coast is
also obliged to be absent, but we hope that he too, will recover during the recess; we have
not seen the member for Taupo more than momentarily back in the House, and the Minister
of Education, as recently as last night, was forced at considerable physical discomfort to
attend a division. Other members have been in hospital, and I sincerely trust they have been
able to make as complete a recovery as appears to be the case.
There is a long list of people to whom we pay tribute at this stage. Many of them offer
services to members that are accepted almost without thought. I refer to the Whips initially,
because they have to carry the burden of what is often quite a personal thing in the House.
They have to be the buffers between contending sides; they get little or no credit for success
and more than their share of abuse for any lack of success.
The Clerk and his assistants are expected to be part of our debates, not to show
annoyance, not to show tiredness, although they have to put in longer hours than anyone. I
thank them for the unfailing courtesy with which they have always met members. Our
Hansard staff too, have the obligation to sit in the House for the full length of time that
members do. We take a lot for granted with them.
Others have had a more difficult year than usual, and I refer specifically to Bellamy's
staff because of the shift, because of the new premises, and because of the difficulties
associated with fitting in. The Prime Minister has mentioned the messengers. I should like to
mention also the Police, because this year there have been more occasions on which the
regular staff and those temporarily called in have been required to serve in the House.
With our own secretarial staff and typists—and I am sure those on the Government side
too-there is a realisation of the absolutely essential nature of their services. I include the
staff of the telephone exchange and members of the research unit. We accept the work that
those people do, and make extra demands on them as we become used to accepting their
services. There is also the library staff and our outside staff, the gardeners, and, in the
background, the staff of the Government Printing Office. More brickbats have been hurled
around this session about difficulties in that office than I can recall hearing before. Some
may have been brought upon them by their own action, but the pressure they are under is
clearly evident. Then, of course, I could refer to the friendly enemy who looks-not down on
us, but looks on us from above. I think most of us get our deserts at their hands. Some
perhaps get more than their deserts, a few may get a little less, but I think broadly it works
out in just proportions.
Now, Mr Acting Speaker, I should like to say a few words of thanks to you. You have
handled a difficult job: to step in, at no notice, to another man's way of doing things, and
handle the affairs of the House. Not everyone always agreed with you, but we appreciated
your good humour and tact. I most sincerely thank you for your contribution. I pay my
thanks to the deputies who have stood in on the Government side from time to time. I realise

intervention of the Prime Minister, which has not made their job particularly easy. The

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
The following written answers to questions were circulated.
Milk Price
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Finance: In view of the
Associate Minister of Finance's statement in the Evening Post of 19 October that "milk may
go up to 15c per bottle", will he advise: (1) when this will be done; (2) why the Government
wishes to take such a step; and (3) how does he reconcile this with the Associate Minister's
statement on TV during the 1975 election campaign that a National Government would
retain food subsidies?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The Associate Minister of
Finance did not say "milk may go up to 15c per bottle". This was a headline set by the
Evening Post itself. What the Associate Minister said was in fact that, without the Govern-
ment subsidy, the consumer price of milk in standard areas would be about 15c per bottle,
instead of 9c per bottle. At this stage the Government does not intend to increase the price
of milk from 9c per bottle, set in February this year.
Accident Compensation-Lump Sum Entitlement
2. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) asked the Minister of Labour: Could he explain how
the Accident Compensation Commission is able to justify the retention of more than 25
percent of the true lump sum entitlement in three accident cases each of which resulted in the
loss of one eye and all of which occurred within a 9-month span?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: If the honourable member considers
the Accident Compensation Commission has acted incorrectly in regard to certain cases he
should identify those cases to the commission, which will no doubt provide the necessary
explanation. But with over 130 000 cases presented to it each year, the commission cannot
be expected to offer any comment on the question without being able to identify the cases
referred to. The commission has the sole statutory power of deciding what amount of, and
when, lump-sum compensation is to be paid. A claimant dissatisfied with its decisions can
avail himself of the appeal processes provided for in the Act. It would, therefore, not be
proper for me to intervene in the commission's decisions any more than it would be for any
member of this House to attempt to influence the decisions of any other tribunal or court.
However, if the honourable member thinks there is a justifiable complaint, I have always
found the commission to be most willing to readily respond to inquiries from members of this
House.
Women's Rights Select Committee
3. Marilyn Waring (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has been
made by the Department of Education in implementing recommendation 6 in chapter 4 of
the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Since June 1975 an additional 90
positions have been established for guidance counsellors, making a total of about 185 school-
based counsellors in schools by February 1978. As they have been appointed these guidance
counsellors have attended post-graduate university-based counselling and guidance courses
for training. These courses also constitute a part of the training of vocational guidance
officers who are public servants, being specialist officers of the Department of Education.
Vocational guidance officers visit small or geographically isolated schools as often as existing


## p. 5457 (#893) ###########################################

16 December
5457
Written Answers to Questions
staffing and travel allocations permit. At present this is usually two or three times a year.
This number of visits should be increased following the transfer of the Vocational Guidance
Service to the Department of Labour. The expansion of vocational guidance centres and the
development of the new "Employment and Vocational Guidance Service" will bring more
schools into daily travel distance of a centre. All vocational guidance officers and school-
based guidance personnel actively encourage girls to consider the full range of careers and
occupations that are available to young people in New Zealand. The Vocational Guidance
Service has deleted all references, indicating sex bias or discrimination, from its careers
information leaflets. Although school-based guidance personnel and facilities are usually not
available during school holiday periods, vocational guidance officers, being public servants,
are available to provide vocational information and advice to persons of all ages who request
it. Centres are open daily from 8.30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and later if a client requires it, closing
only for statutory holidays. Subcentres, which are often established in rural centres such as
Timaru, New Plymouth, and Gisborne, commonly keep different hours—say, 10.30 a.m. to
7 p.m., to be more accessible to the public. The development of vocational guidance services
after the transfer of the Vocational Guidance Service to the Department of Labour will
make the service more geographically accessible to more people. Vocational guidance
officers come from a very wide cross-section of occupational backgrounds. For example,
present officers' previous occupations include: nursing, teaching-secondary and
primary-social work, accountancy, and fine arts.

Mortgagee Sales
5. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Justice: (a) How many
applications for mortgagee sales have been made to the Supreme Court since the beginning
of the 1977 calendar year, and how many of these applications have so far resulted in sales;
and (b) how does the number of sales for the first 10 months of 1977 compare with the sales
in each of the calendar years 1973 to 1976?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Up to 25 November there has been
a total of 439 applications made by mortgagees for sale under the provisions of the Property
Law Act 1952. Of these 133 have so far concluded with a sale. In the years 1973-76, for the
period 1 January to 31 October, there were 44, 19, 48, and 74 sales respectively.
National Research Advisory Council-Social Services Committee
6. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the Minister of
Science and Technology: When will the report of the special social services committee
etablished by the National Research Advisory Council be made available, and will all the
recommendations of the committee be made public?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology) replied: The report of the
National Research Advisory Council's social sciences committee was prepared after consul-
tation with representatives of social science research agencies at a workshop/conference. The
draft report was discussed at a second workshop/conference. It is a working document which
I have referred to my colleagues and their departments for comment. When I have received
these comments I shall consider the next steps to be taken. Although NRAC reports are not
usually published, because of the involvement of the non-Government sector in this report
and in its implications I shall consider wider publication of the report and the recommenda-
tions.

Power Planning-Capital Expenditure Schedules
8. Mr. MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Electricity: What are the schedules
for capital expenditure for the 1976 and 1977 plans corresponding to those formerly shown in
reports of the planning committee on electric power development?


## p. 5459 (#895) ###########################################

16 December
5459
Written Answers to Questions
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity) replied: Schedules for capital expenditure
corresponding to those formerly shown in the reports of the planning committee on electric
power development excluded the effect on costs of inflation and interest during construction.
Because of recent drastic effects of worldwide inflation and the present difficulties of
forecasting future load requirements, with the consequential effect on the commissioning
dates of future power stations, the information in these schedules is rapidly outdated and
becomes misleading. For this reason these long-range schedules for capital expenditure are
no longer published.

and takeovers have been approved and which have been declined by the Examiner of Trade

Broadcasting-Hearing of Complaints
10. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Why does
the Broadcasting Tribunal hear complaints about programme content in secret, and is he
satisfied that this results in justice being seen to be done?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: As laid down in the
Broadcasting Act 1976 the tribunal may, if it thinks fit, consider and determine any
complaint without a formal hearing, but in that case shall have regard to all relevant
submissions made to it in writing in relation to the complaint. In addition the tribunal will
determine its procedures in those areas not specifically covered by the regulations. The
tribunal has indicated that it intends to keep the complaints procedure informal and flexible
so unnecessary formality will not prevent any person with a reasonable complaint from
bringing it forward for consideration. Irrespective of the procedure followed by the tribunal
in considering the complaint, each decision is notified to the complainant and is also
published in the Gazette. Furthermore, copies (including the reason therefor) are available
from the registrar of the tribunal. I am sure that in establishing its procedures the tribunal
will be aware of its responsibilities to ensure that each complaint is considered on a fair and
equitable basis.
Detinning Plant Proposal
11. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What
progress is being made with the establishment of a detinning plant in Auckland to recycle tin
cans into scrap steel, as announced by the resources conservation officer of his department in
June 1976?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: The state-
ment made by my department in June 1976 referred to the possible establishment of a
detinning plant to recycle tin cans into scrap steel. At that time the project was very much at
a conceptual stage. Since then good progress has been made in assessing competing
technologies and operating economies. The Government has been anxious to ensure that the
project should recover tin ingot in addition to scrap steel, since such an activity would assist
New Zealand to become partly self-sufficient in tin. This has required an assessment to be
made of costs and benefits from the establishment of tin-winning facilities which could
operate in conjunction with the detinning plant. Further development work will need to be
done on the recovery of tin cans from municipal refuse. However, Pacific Steel Ltd. has been
accumulating a large stockpile of can manufacturers' tin plate offcuts in preparation for the
future commissioning of a detinning-tin winning plant. The question of proceeding with the
plant is now largely a matter of a commercial decision on the part of Pacific Steel Ltd. The
company's decision is expected shortly.
Prisoners-Maintenance Costs
12. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Justice: How much on average over


## p. 5460 (#896) ###########################################

5460
16 December
Written Answers to Questions
the whole country does it cost to keep a man in jail for a month, and how much specifically in
the Kaitaia jail?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The cost of maintaining a prison
inmate is $423 a month. For a borstal inmate it is $397 a month. These costs are calculated
after taking into account any profits or losses from industries. The former Kaitaia police jail
was closed on 1 June 1976 at the request of the police, who were having great difficulty in
servicing it. All costs were met by the Police Department, and I understand that figures
showing the cost of maintaining an individual prisoner are not readily available. The police
jail was used for arrest cases as well as for those committed to prison for 1 month or less.
Hikurangi Mines-Estimated Coal Resource
13. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Mines: What is the estimated coal
resource in the flooded mines at Hikurangi, and has the Government any intention of
exploiting this resource?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied: The coal remaining in the flooded mines at
Hikurangi is estimated to be 1 500 000 tonnes. The Mines Department has no plans at
present to extract this coal. Not all the coal is extractable. It may be possible to split pillars
and recover up to another 20 percent of the coal, but this would be an expensive operation
because the mines inspectorate would require each area to be worked to have all roadways to
it fitted with dams and bulkhead doors to contain water inflows, thereby allowing men and
equipment to be evacuated in the event of a flooding. Most of the large mines in the district
were closed by flooding, frequently as soon as pillar extraction was commenced. The coal is
overlain by cavernous limestone, which acts as a large reservoir for ground water. Some of
the coal may be recoverable by opencast means, and this has been done to a limited extent in
the past. In the long term, any Government decision on the winning of the coal remaining at
Hikurangi must be based on technological as well as financial considerations.
Women's Rights Select Committee
14. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in implementing recommendation 4 in chapter 6
of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: My department supports the idea
of school facilities being used by voluntary organisations for the development of recreational
activities for children after school and during holidays. While schools are controlled by
autonomous boards, many are responding positively to my department's request that they
provide for such activities. Some newer schools are designed in a way that will facilitate
after-school activities. A number of local bodies and sports clubs contribute to the cost of
providing additional facilities to enable after-school recreation to be effective. Outdoor
education centres are being extended, and are being used more frequently for weekend and
holiday camps.
Women's Rights Select Committee
15. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Education: What progress has
been made by the Department of Education in implementing recommendation 8 in chapter 4
of the report of the Select Committee on Women's Rights?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Eighty-five schools have official
work-experience classes, which is an increase from the 61 schools which had such classes in
1974. These cater for 1141 pupils. Experience classes are designed to assist the entry of less
able pubils into the work force and to provide work experience appropriate to the ablities of
the pupils. In addition, many secondary schools offer work exploration programmes, usually
for senior pupils. These programmes, which involve close co-operation between schools and
employers, cover the range of occupations generally available in the district. A circular
setting guidelines for such courses and machinery to implement them is being prepared in
consultation with interested bodies.
Tuna Processing
16. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Is he aware that Wattie's


## p. 5461 (#897) ###########################################

16 December
5461
Written Answers to Questions
canning factory in Gisborne is capable of processing the entire tuna catch of the American-
New Zealand purse seiners, and, if so, why are these fish not processed in New Zealand?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: If it is possible technically to have the
whole of the New Zealand tuna catch of the vessels employed by the New Zealand Pelagic
Fisheries Development Company Limited processed by J. Wattie Canneries Limited, it is
very doubtful whether it would be a viable economic proposition. The quantity of fish taken
by these vessels is far in excess of what could be sold on the domestic market, and it would
probably be difficult for Watties to market such large quantities of tuna overseas at
satisfactory prices. Further, Watties are unlikely to be able to pay the prices for the fish that
are offered by Star-Kist Foods Inc. at Pago Pago. New Zealand Pelagic Fisheries Develop-
ment Company Limited, associated in a fishing venture with Star-Kist Foods Inc. of
America, has been authorised to test the New Zealand tuna resource with a view to the
development of a large-scale New Zealand skipjack tuna industry. One of the main
advantages of having Star-Kist involvement has been that it has facilitated the availability of
large American tuna vessels with proven crews, and satisfactory outlets for the large
quantities of skipjack taken. There is also an understanding with Star-Kist that the
Government would like to see the resource processed and exported from New Zealand as
soon as this is feasible.

French Pacific Territories-United Nations Aid
20. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Has he seen
the letter in the New Zealand Herald of 18 November 1977 signed "Philip Soljak", which
states that France qualifies for United Nations aid for its Pacific territories, yet the French
claim French territories are part of France and will not allow United Nations missions to visit
them; and as the New Zealand Government contributes to the United Nations development
programme can he confirm whether this statement is correct; and, if so, will the Government
register its disapproval?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: I have seen the letter to
which the member refers. I can confirm that the French Pacific territories have, on
occasions, received assistance in one form or another through the specialised agencies of the
United Nations, as has almost every country which is either a member of the organisation or
of its affiliated bodies, or which enjoys a constitutional relationship with a member country.
The expertise of the United Nations is rightly available to all its members. Those recipient
countries which are able do so must meet certain obligations for counterpart contributions. I
understand that in the case of the French territories France has accepted a counterpart level
of two to one. With specific reference to the United Nations development programme, had
the correspondent to the New Zealand Herald checked the references given to him by the
United Nations information centre in Sydney he would have seen that the French Pacific
territories do not feature in the UNDP lists of country indicative planning figures either for
the period 1972-76 or for the forward period 1977-81. In other words, the territories are not
regular recipients of UNDP aid. Having checked the facts, I find no cause for an expression
of disapproval.

Methadone-Treatment of Heroin Dependency
29. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Health: In view of the reply given on 16
November 1977 to a previous question, in which it was advised that certain medical
practitioners "specifically authorised by the Minister of Health, may prescribe methadone
for the treatment of heroin dependency", by what processes and what criteria are such
medical practitioners selected?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: No medical practitioner in private practice
has been authorised to prescribe methadone for the treatment of heroin dependency, but, as
I stated in my reply given on 16 November 1977, as the concept of such treatment is based on
the need for proper counselling and rehabilitation procedures, only in special
circumstances-e.g., the inability of a patient to attend a clinic-would a medical prac-
titioner in private practice be considered. Such a practitioner would need to be acceptable to
the drug clinic involved. No processes or criteria have been laid down.

39. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Health: Will he outline the
manner in which the funds received from the beer and alcohol tax have been allocated in the
Auckland Hospital Board's area for community health purposes?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: A total of $878,348 of the additional
revenue obtained for 1977-78 has been allocated to the Auckland Hospital Board. The
projects for which this finance has been approved include: the decentralisation and develop-
ment of the extramural hospital services in the board's area; the establishment of an

infants and pre-school children in the South Auckland area. Other schemes include a team to
investigate specific industrial health problems and industrial noise assessment and associated
matters.

Unemployed Students-Parental Support
42. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Will he
give the guidelines for determining whether the parents of unemployed students are
financially able to support their student children?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Full-time students cannot
qualify under the legislation for the statutory unemployment benefit, and applicants must be
considered under the discretionary provisions of section 61 of the Social Security Act under
which an emergency benefit may be granted on the grounds of hardship. In exercising its
discretion the department must have regard to the particular circumstances of each indi-
vidual applicant, and these circumstances can vary markedly. Because of this no set
guidelines can be adhered to. It should not be overlooked that a parent's circumstances are
taken into account only when the applicant is an unmarried student living at home. The same
policy was confirmed and used by the last Labour Government.

Mortage Repayments
6244
44. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Housing: What are the
amounts of monthly and quarterly principal repayments involved in a Housing Corporation
mortgage of $16,000 for a term of 25 years; and how do these compare with an Auckland
Saving Bank mortgage of $16,000?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied: The Housing Corporation prime
interest rate is 8.5 percent reviewable 3-yearly, and is calculated according to an amortisa-
tion table at half-yearly rests. The half-yearly instalment is static throughout the term of the
loan. For a loan of $16,000 for 25 years at 8.5 percent the instalment is $776.96 a half year,
though a mortgagor may pay $388.47 a quarter or $129.48 a month. The initial instalment
has interest at $680.00 and principal at $96.96. Subsequent interest is charged on the
reducing balance of principal, while the principal portion increases each half year. The final
half-yearly instalment has interest at $31.67 and principal at $745.29. I understand that the
Auckland Savings Bank current interest rate is 9 percent, with quarterly rests. The initial
quarterly instalment on a loan of $16,000 is $530, being $360 interest and $170 principal. The
subsequent interest is somewhat less, but the principal repayment remains static at $170. The
instalment table is slightly less than 25 years—a little over 23½ years. Loans are not repaid
monthly, but a quarterly debit is charged to the customer's bank account and credited to the
mortgage account.
Automatic Telephone Exchanges
45. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: When will the Helensville,
Kaukapakapa, and Waimauku automatic telephone exchanges be operational, and can he
indicate whether Helensville subscribers will be included within the Auckland free-calling
area?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: On my instructions the Post Office
has almost completed a comprehensive review of the manual to automatic conversion
programme, which will include the Helensville, Kaukapakapa, and Waimauku exchanges.
When the decisions based on the review have been made I will announce target conversion
dates for the exchanges in question. There are no plans to include Helensville in the
Auckland free-calling area.
Accident Compensation-Definition of Personal Injury
46. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the fact that the
definition of "personal injury by accident" as promulgated to doctors by the Accident
Compensation Commission in its medical handbook predated the definition in the Accident
Compensation Amendment Act 1974, can he advise whether the more recent, more limited,
and statutory definition in the 1974 amendment has been promulgated to doctors by the
commission, and whether it encourages the use of the earlier, broader handbook definition,
or the later, more limited statutory definition?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The medical handbook, which was
distributed by the Accident Compensation Commission to medical practitioners, outlined
the guidelines or principles the commission would adopt in construing the phrase "personal
injury by accident" pending the possible incorporation in the Accident Compensation Act of
a definition of that phrase. The Accident Compensation Amendment Act 1974 incorporated
into the principal Act a partial definition of the expression "personal injury by accident".


## p. 5471 (#907) ###########################################

16 December
5471
Written Answers to Questions
This statutory definition is not exhaustive, nor does it attempt to define personal injury by
accident generally-for example, by a list of all essential ingredients or circumstances. What
the definition does do is indicate a number of conditions that are acceptable as personal
injury by accident; and conditions which, unless satisfied, would not normally be considered
as falling within the scope of the phrase. This partial definition enacted by the 1974
amendment to the principal Act is considered to be consistent with the commission's earlier
formulation of guidelines or principles set out in the medical handbook. It is probably better
described as being "more precise" or "more specific" rather than "more limited" than the
principles contained in the handbook. In August of this year, in a newsletter to the medical
profession, the commission took the opportunity of acquainting the profession with the
statutory definition of the expression "personal injury by accident". The commission
acknowledged that the partial definition had never been formally promulgated to the
profession by the commission. However, the commission expressed the view that the
definition was largely a declaratory definition and that it expected medical practitioners,
when interpreting the expression "personal injury by accident", to continue to be guided by
the medical handbook. I understand that work on a revised and updated medical handbook
is nearing completion and will be made available by the commission to the medical
profession in the coming year.
National Party Election Manifesto-Science Policy
47. Dr. SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Science and Technology: Can he
indicate how much of the science policy contained in the 1975 National Party election
manifesto has been implemented in the last 2 years of the present Government?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology) replied: One of the main
objectives of the Government in implementing the science policy contained in the 1975
National Party election manifesto has been to develop and use New Zealand's scientific and
technological capacity to the full. The role of the Minister of Science has been expanded, as
indicated by the change of designation to Minister of Science and Technology; a Cabinet
committee on science and a caucus committee on science have been established; the
National Research Advisory Council (NRAC) membership has been expanded, its commit-
tee structure has been revised and expanded, and greater use is being made of ad hoc
working parties to study important issues in depth. Many of these special studies, in fields
such as the social sciences, transport, wildlife, and hill country farming, have a bearing on
the organisation of science in Government. The NRAC is also currently reviewing its
advisory role to the Government, the mechanisms for establishing priorities and forward
planning, general administrative matters, and research contracts with the universities.
Scientists and technologists from all organisations have co-operated very well with the
Commission for the Future, which was established in August 1976. In addition, the Director-
General of the DSIR has been appointed a member of the commission and chairman of the
technological working party. Social scientists have been appointed to the NRAC, and a
special social sciences committee has been established. Over the last year, this committee
carried out a very comprehensive investigation of social science, and I am currently seeking
the views of appropriate Ministers on its recommendations. Research effort and facilities
have been considerably expanded in areas, such as energy and the increased processing of
our natural resources, which are important for the future development of New Zealand. The
very large expansion in the energy field was announced in the recent Budget and a new
DSIR division-the industrial processing division-will be established on 1 April 1978. Co-
operation between organisations involved in scientific research has been expanded and the
principle of joint funding and joint use of major items of equipment has been continued. The
funds provided for research contracts with the universities in fields of national importance
have been increased considerably during the last 2 years; the subsidy limits for research
associations have been increased to compensate for inflation and several have been regraded
into a higher category; and a new section of the Development Finance Corporation has been
formed to provide incentives and support for research and development in New Zealand
industry. Progress leading to the possible formation of research associations for the heavy
engineering industry and the transport industry is well advanced. In addition, the interna-
tional science and aid to developing countries policy is being fully implemented.

Adoption Act-Access to Birth Records
48. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Justice: Is it intended to
amend the Adoption Act 1955 to allow adopted persons greater access to information
relating to their natural parents?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I do not expect to have an
amending Bill on the legislation programme next session. Nevertheless, the question of
allowing adopted persons to have access to their original birth records will be carefully
examined in the course of the next review of the Act.
Education-Year-3 Teachers
49. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: How many year-3
teachers are still unable to secure positions for 1978?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Indications are that 1977 year-3
primary teachers who are mobile will have no difficulty in obtaining teaching positions in
1978. My department has instituted a monitoring system to ensure that up-to-date figures of
all young beginning teachers requiring appointments are available. The latest figures show
that there are 687 year-3 teachers still seeking positions for 1978, and, of these, 293 are
mobile. There are approximately 900 vacant positions in the primary service for next year
and all beginning teachers who are also mobile will be able to obtain employment in 1978.
Paua-shell Jewellery-Hawaiian Market
50. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: On how many occasions
since his Government took office has the trade correspondent in Honolulu or the trade
commissioner, Los Angeles, reported to the Department of Trade and Industry that markets
exist in Hawaii for paua-shell jewellery?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: The department has
received very few reports from the trade commissioner in Los Angeles or the trade
correspondent in Honolulu on the market for paua-shell jewellery in Hawaii. Although there
has been a very small trade in paua-shell jewellery over the last 2 years, the market for this
product has been limited. In a recent trade survey visit to Honolulu, the trade commissioner
aroused the interest of a large importer in paua-shell jewellery. This inquiry has been
circulated to known New Zealand manufacturers, and my department will be following up
with the exporters shortly to establish what has resulted.
Capital Equipment Credit-Public Sector
51. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Finance: What is the value of
capital equipment credit obtained by the public sector in the year ended March 1977 and in
the first 6 months of this financial year, and for what purposes was it raised?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: In the year ended 31 March
1977, drawings totalling $81.3 million were made under capital equipment credit arrange-
ments, while in the first 6 months of the 1977-78 financial year drawings under such
arrangements totalled $16.9 million. The credits under which these drawings have been
made cover a variety of equipment, including computers, rail locomotives and rolling stock,
ship conversions, and electric supply equipment.

South Africa-Statement by Acting Prime Minister
59. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of the
comment by the then Acting Prime Minister in the Christchurch Press of 24 October
indicating that an official complaint would be made by the Prime Minister on the action of
the South African Government in banning newspapers in black organisations and detaining
key leaders in the Black Consciousness Movement, could he indicate when such a statement
was made and the nature of its contents?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: At the press conference
reported in the newspaper item to which the honourable member refers, the Acting Prime
Minister did not state definitely that an official complaint would be made. He expressed the
opinion that representations from the Prime Minister might carry more weight than any
immediate reaction by the Government. By the time of the Prime Minister's return it was
evident that, with the limited channels of communication open to the Government (the
South African consul-general not being regarded as having any status in the field of political
relations), no more effective action could be taken to make New Zealand's views known
than the wide publicity already accorded to the Acting Prime Minister's original statements
and subsequent references to it.
Sixth-year Medical Students-Service in Rhodesia
60. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: How many sixth-year
medical students served in Rhodesia this year, and how are the arrangements made?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: In 1977, one sixth-year medical
student from the University of Auckland and one from the University of Otago have served
part of their elective programme in Rhodesia. Since 1971 there has been an arrangement,
made through the faculty of medicine of the University of Rhodesia, by which the New
Zealand medical schools have been invited to send two students on fellowships to work for
short periods in Rhodesian hospitals. The question of whether medical students should
continue to be allowed to serve in Rhodesia was specifically referred by the medical schools
to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs earlier this year.
