Car Assembly Plant, Stoke
63. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he received
any indications at all of (i) impending staff layoffs at the car assembly plant in Stoke, Nelson,
or (ii) the company's plans regarding cuts in levels of production?

Foreign Fishing Vessel Entry Tax
64. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Customs: How much revenue has
been taken since the inception of the foreign fishing vessel entry tax, and to how many
vessels has this tax been applied?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: Foreign fishing vessel entry tax
was introduced on 1 September 1976. During the period 1 September 1976 to 30 September
1977 there were 729 foreign fishing vessel arrivals in New Zealand ports, 53 of which were
exempted from the tax because the arrivals were due solely to reasons of emergency. The
total amount of tax collected during this period was $884,000. I would emphasise that the
figure 729 quoted above represents the number of visits to New Zealand made by foreign
fishing vessels, and not the number of vessels; if a particular foreign fishing vessel makes,
say, three visits to New Zealand the tax will be levied three times.

Telephone Connections-Te Rapa
68. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Has he seen the Waikato
Times article of 16 November in which it is claimed that a Mr Paul Butler, who was originally
told there would be a 2-week wait for a telephone when he moved in to a new house and was
later told it would not be until 1980 that he could have a telephone installed, despite the fact
the he is on a "high priority list", and could he confirm that the substance of the claims in the
article are correct; and, if they are correct, how does he reconcile this situation with the
National Party's election manifesto promise to "speed up the cabling programme and reduce
waiting lists for automatic telephone connections"?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: I have read the article. When Mr
Butler applied for a residential telephone service on 21 June this year there were no spare
numbers on the Te Rapa exchange, but it was expected that sufficient numbers would
become available through existing subscribers giving up service to provide a connection for
him in a reasonably short time. It is not possible to predict the rate at which numbers will
become available in this way. In the event the numbers released have not been adequate to
satisfy applications for business purposes and other requirements of a higher priority than
Mr Butler's. As regards this point, in September the priority allocated to Mr Butler's
application was raised in recognition of his need for a telephone at home outside business
hours. It has not been possible to confirm that Mr Butler was told that he could not have a
telephone before 1980. The position is that additional numbers will not become available
until the Te Rapa exchange is replaced by one of larger capacity in late 1979 or early 1980,
but the Post Office expects to be able to provide service for Mr Butler before then through a
relinquishment. A cable circuit is available.

GATT Multilateral Trade Negotiations-Agriculture
77. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade: How
much support has the United States given New Zealand in the MTN discussions on
agriculture?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: Until recently, progress
in the GATT multilateral trade negotiations was inhibited by the unstable world economic
and monetary conditions which have prevailed since 1974. During this period a considerable
amount of preparatory work has been carried out, however, and in this the United States has
been a major advocate of the view that the negotiations must result in an expansion and
liberalisation of international trade in agricultural products. This is still the United States'
attitude. Its general position has, therefore, supported New Zealand's major trade objec-
tives in the MTN. The negotiations are now moving forward with the adoption of a request
and-offer procedure for agriculture. Under this procedure New Zealand has lodged requests
for concessions with all its major trading partners, including the United States. These
requests and the responses to them will be the subject of bilateral negotiation during 1978.
At the same time New Zealand and the EEC have tabled essentially similar proposals for
stabilising world dairy trade in the dairy subgroup. Australia and the EEC (with New
Zealand support) have taken parallel action in the meat subgroup. These subgroups are
currently examining these proposals in detail with the aim of producing a single basis for
negotiation for each product group, and the United States has been actively supporting this
work.

Driving Offences-Alcohol
84. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Justice: How many persons have been
convicted this year of driving offences involving death where alcohol was acknowledged as a
factor; how many of these received prison sentences; and can he indicate how many received
sentences up to 6 months, more than 6 months and up to 1 year, over 1 year and up to 18
months, over 18 months and up to 2 years, and over 2 years?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: Information relating to convictions
for alcohol-related driving offences is not yet available for this year. However, in 1976, 12
persons were convicted of drunken driving causing death of whom 8 (66.6 percent) were
imprisoned. A further 16 persons were convicted of drunken driving causing injury of whom
9 (56.3 percent) were imprisoned. Details relating to the lengths of imprisonment imposed
are not available. However, a recent study by my department of a sample of drunken drivers
found that the average length of imprisonment imposed for offences of this kind was 6
months (maximum 5 years) and in practice the effective range of sentences of imprisonment
does not normally extend beyond 2 years. In addition to the above convictions there were
9381 persons convicted in 1976 of alcohol-related driving offences (e.g., excess blood
alcohol) of whom 1443 (15.4 percent) were imprisoned. Convictions for these offences are
increasing at a rate of 12 percent per annum.
Intellectually Handicapped Children-Foster Grandparents
85. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Has he read the
report contained in the Evening Post, dated 7 December, that a foster grandparent
programme for intellectually handicapped children which has been successful in New York
could work in New Zealand for all children in special care, and, if so, what action does he
propose to take?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Yes, I have seen the
newspaper article referred to. The report of the recent inquiry into church child-care services
outlines New York's foster grandparent programme and suggests that the use of part-time
staff by church agencies could be expanded along similar lines to that programme. The
responsibility for implementing such a scheme would, of course, rest with the churches
themselves, and it is hoped that the report will encourage them to do so.

Heart Disease
89. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Health: What percentage
contribution does smoking, alcohol, and obesity make to the incidence of ischaemic heart
disease in (a) European males, (b) European females, (c) Maori males, and (d) Maori
females?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The percentage contribution made by
smoking and obesity in the causation of ischaemic heart disease in any ethnic group is not
known. Other risk factors, including high blood pressure and cholesterol levels, are also
relevant. Studies do not incriminate alcohol as a risk factor, although an excess over long
periods can cause another form of heart disease.
New Zealand surveys into Maori health indicate that Maori women have the highest rate
of ischaemic heart disease in the world; and it is rising in men. Studies show that high blood
pressure and obesity are the most important factors identified in the Maori. Amongst
Europeans high blood pressure and smoking were found to be the most important factors
contributing to ischaemic heart disease, with cholesterol being more a feature in women.
Further research on obesity in the Maori is desirable, but sufficient is known to advise
against smoking and being overweight on this and other health grounds.

Teachers-Employment
91. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Education: Is he prepared to guarantee
employment in 1978 for teachers who have taught for the whole of 1977?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I assume that the member is
referring to the primary service. This being so, I am not in a position to guarantee
employment in 1978 for all teachers who have taught for the whole of 1977. However, I am
prepared to guarantee positions for all those teachers who are prepared to go to areas where
vacancies exist.
Lyttelton Health Centre
92. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Health: Has any progress been made or
agreement reached with the users group regarding the planning and/or construction of the
Lyttelton health centre?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: There has been good progress with the
planning of the Lyttelton health centre. Plans have been revised, and the doctors are in
agreement with the new plans. Other prospective users are at present considering the revised
plans. Approval has been given to proceed with tender documents, and it is hoped that
preliminary site works will be undertaken this financial year.
Primary Schools-Staff-pupil Ratios
93. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Education: Will he consider altering
staff-pupil ratios to employ more teachers in primary schools next year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I am awaiting the full report and
recommendations of a working party on the staffing of primary schools which I set up earlier
this year. Until this report is received I am in no position to consider altering staff-pupil
ratios in primary schools.
Turoa Ski Field
94. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Lands: What environmental
impact reporting procedures will be followed before any development of the Turoa ski field
in the Tongariro National Park will be authorised?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied: The Turoa ski field will be developed in
accordance with the provisions of the environmental enhancement procedures, and no major
work will proceed before these environmental requirements are met.
Maori Electoral Rolls
95. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the Minister
of Justice: Will he request the postmasters who are the electorate officers for Maori
parliamentary electorates to forward to the principal officers of territorial authorities at
periodic intervals the particulars of electors who are enrolled on Maori rolls, or who have
enrolled for Maori electorates since the last publication of rolls, in order to facilitate the
inclusion of those electors on rolls for local elections and polls?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: There is at present no way by
which an electorate officer can identify an address within a particular territorial local
authority. However, by the time the rolls for the next local body elections are prepared
facilities will exist to provide the appropriate authority with this information.

overseas exchange transactions show that transfers by emigrants and temporary residents in
the year ended 31 October 1977 amounted to $63.7 million.

Citizens Band Radio Channels
103. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Postmaster-General: Does the Government intend
to make available an adequate number of channels for citizens band radio?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: The question of additional chan-
nels for use by the citizen band radio service is presently under consideration. However,
because of demands on the limited radio frequency spectrum resources this can be achieved
only by rechannelling the present band with narrower spacing between frequencies. This
may necessitate equipment changes, which must first be discussed with radio equipment
manufacturers.
Radio Shortwave Programmes
104. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Broadcasting: Has the Government any
intention of providing more special items on shortwave instead of only New Zealand
domestic programmes?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: The Government does not
determine the programme content of the shortwave service, but I am advised by the
Broadcasting Corporation that Radio New Zealand's national programme, which is rebroad-
cast on shortwave, included a considerably increased Maori and Pacific Island vernacular
coverage since 24 October this year partly for the benefit of Island listeners. News and
magazine broadcasts are now carried in Maori, Samoan, Tongan, Cook Island Maori,
Niuean, and Tokelauan. Moreover, Radio New Zealand and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
are considering possible further developments which may take place during 1978.

Unemployment
106. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Finance: Has he seen
the report in the Christchurch Star of 24 November 1977 that "the number of registered
unemployed could climb to over 10,000" by December, with a further substantial number on
relief work, and will he pursue economic policies designed to restore business confidence
and investment and full employment?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: No, I have not seen the report
in the Christchurch Star of 24 November 1977 referred to by the honourable member.
However, as announced by the Acting Minister of Labour on 9 December, 13 053 people
were registered for work with the Department of Labour as at 2 December 1977, while 8332
were employed on special work schemes. The Government has been aware for some time of
the likelihood of significant lay-offs by firms and unacceptably high levels of unemployment
if the economy turned down too quickly. This awareness was one of the principal concerns
behind the measures announced in my statement of 28 October-in particular the special
supplementary family benefit of $25 per child paid on 29 November, the 5 percent across-
the-board cut in personal income tax to be applied from 1 February 1978, and the various
employment measures contained in the package. More recently the Government has
introduced company tax relief related to firms' stock levels as a means of maintaining
business confidence and, inter alia, of encouraging employers to retain staff.
In the longer term it is clear that the key to improving the nation's general economic
viability is to achieve a shifting of resources into exports and more efficient sectors of
production. Only by succeeding in this can a sound basis be provided for economic growth
and full employment in the future. The importance of this objective was also emphasised in
my statement of 28 October.
Pureora State Forest-Totara Stand
107. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Forests: What action does
he intend taking on the Native Forests Action Council's submission on the Pureora State
Forest, and will such action be taken in time to save the rare stand of 1000-year-old totara
contained in the Pikiariki Road area?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The scientific co-ordinating committee,
an inter-disciplinary group that advises me on ecological reserves in State forests, endorsed
the Forest Service's proposal for a 475 ha reserve in the Pikiariki Road area of Pureora State
Forest. I see no reason to ignore the advice of this expert body in favour of the submission of
the Native Forests Action Council. Logging of the remainder of the adjacent production
zone is being carried out on a selective basis, and the old totara trees contained in this forest
type are being retained as part of the residual forest structure.


## p. 5490 (#926) ###########################################

5490
16 December
Written Answers to Questions
Pureora State Forest
108. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to ask the Minister of Forests: Did the wildlife
division in 1971 recommend that two areas of the Pureora State Forest be given reserve
status, and what has happened about these two areas since the recommendation was made?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: At the request of the Forest Service in
1972 the wildlife service delineated two areas in Pureora State Forest with a recommenda-
tion that they be set aside for the preservation of habitat for the kokako. At that time the
wildlife service stated that the more important of these was the Ranginui Road area. This
area was reserved and increased in size, now being called the Waipapa Ecological Area. The
area recommended for reservation in the vicinity of Pikiariki Road had already been set
aside for logging to meet long-term sale commitments, but an important part of it, as well as
adjacent forest of a very similar type, had been established as the Pikiariki Ecological Area.
Potatoes
109. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Why
is the Government still permitting processed frozen potatoes to come into New Zealand
from Australia duty-free, while New Zealand potato growers still have thousands of tonnes
of last season's crop in store, or left to rot in the ground?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: Frozen
potatoes are included in a tariff item which covers all frozen vegetables except peas and
beans. The duty-free treatment accorded to Australia and other preferential sources with 10
percent for the normal duty rate and the exemption from import control are a reflection of
the Government's policy of placing the minimum of restrictions on imports of farm products
in order to strengthen the approaches we make as an efficient agricultural producer to other
countries for increased access to their markets. The oversupply of fresh potatoes has been
caused by overproduction in New Zealand and not by imports of frozen potatoes.
